compulsory school attendance
. If any entity other than the state allowed itself to threaten to forcibly remove children from parents who decide to educate them differently than that entity orders, we would consider it completely unacceptable. Why then?
it feels right to the vast majority of people

title: Are we celebrating!?
text:
You don't know what? Czech flag day! I consider statism to be the greatest and most dangerous world religion of the present and past; like most religions it has different churches (in the form of individual states); they have their sacred symbols (flags, insignia), places (palaces, monuments), texts (constitutional documents, founding declarations) and songs (marchs, hymns), holidays (celebrations of victory, formation), celebrations (parades, military parades), relics (standards, crown jewels), officials (politicians, officials), symbolic gestures (salutes, laying of wreaths), saints (honored by statesmen, national heroes) and ceremonies (elections, coronations). Many states celebrate their flags on various important days for them (coronations, deaths, battles, enactment of flags, etc.); in the Czech Republic it could be March 30, which is the day of approval of the 106-year-old Act 252/1920.
In 2020, it was proposed by the Czech Vexillological Society, which at the time interested few people; six years later, Babiš probably needed to act as a patriot, so he proposed it in the amendment to Act 245/2000. So do we have it? Czech flag day in the law? Nope. Not even a week before the big day, the senate returned it. That they wouldn't want to weed out the legislation with such nonsense? But somewhere! It is said that this would make the other six national symbols (large and small coat of arms, tricolor, standard, seal and anthem - from their
performance ended at the police station
I remember them off the top of my head); they prefer to rename the St. Wenceslas Day to the Day of Czech Statehood and State Symbols. The proposal will be taken up again by parliament... Hundreds of (well-paid) man-hours (of taxpayers' money) are spent telling us what day to fly the flag. How can anyone take this seriously?

title: Murray Newton Rothbard's One Hundredth Birthday
text:
Today, the "Father of Anarcho-Capitalism" Murray Newton Rothbard would have celebrated his hundredth birthday if he were alive; I see the greatest contribution of his work in the consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends - which were seemingly not very related - anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Early anarchists typically did not understand economics very well, while proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (otherwise correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.
In honor of his 100th birthday, Free Harbor is hosting a Saturday
freedom conference
; it will feature eight speakers with quite different views - from democratic to anarchist (however from three quite different directions) to self-development and spiritual. I would like us to listen to their performances and treat them as the late Murray probably would have done; please, let's try to be open to them, not to judge them and to take from them what makes sense to us - perhaps this very conference will lay the foundations in one of us for something that no one has yet invented and that is still waiting for its discoverer, which could be you. We will try to ensure that all lectures are published in
Freeport Channel
; however, nothing can replace the atmosphere at the place. I look forward to seeing you!

title: Murder is murder
text:
What would you say to a person who would murder someone he doesn't even know and excuse it by saying he's not responsible because his boss told him to do it? That's probably a pretty absurd defense. But why do we accept it for soldiers in the army? I understand that in case they have to enlist, desertion is punishable by death, so they were compelled to do the same by force; but why remove the responsibility from the soldiers who signed up for it voluntarily? After all, it is only their risk to murder someone who has done nothing to anyone in the course of their profession; even a professional driver probably has a higher chance of killing someone than the average person, but we don't tolerate it either. Why should murder in war not be murder? Just because it
the state pressures the people with its propaganda
? Will you say that "there is no other way"? Then imagine how much better the world would be if people weren't taught that sometimes murder isn't murder when it suits the powers that be.

title: Subsidy for domestics
Corruption and gambling
text:
I recently listened to a (years old) recording of a kind of discussion with Petr Gazdík; in it he explained, based on his past and "life story and background", why he would never take a bribe. Let us suppose for a moment that he was telling the truth, and that he is seriously a proud incorruptible man; immediately afterwards, with considerable pride in his voice, he declared that the gambling lobby would never break him and that he would fight against gambling for the rest of his life, otherwise he would not be able to look in the mirror. That person is very likely not even aware that they are pushing
violent persecution of some group of people and trampling on their property rights
; and you know what's worse than a politician initiating aggression towards you? Well, much worse is a politician initiating aggression towards you who cannot even be bribed to stop it. Even if all those who "mean it well" sit in the parliament (and we are far from that), the state will not start working in our favor; on the contrary, sometimes it can be even worse.

title: Owning a reputation
text:
To answer the question of whether I am infringing by damaging my reputation
property rights
(and thus I am attacking and the victim can defend himself with force), one must first determine whether the reputation can be owned. My reputation is actually people's opinions of me; reputation is what others think. And can I own the thoughts and opinions of others? Certainly not. So how could I own my reputation? It is not possible; it is not my property or decision what others will think of me. Therefore, when someone slanders me, it is appropriate to respond to it, refute the slander or ignore everything (it depends on the decision of each of us); however, it is not adequate to use physical violence and limit the freedom of speech and property rights of the slanderer, since he did not attack my property, since I do not own my reputation (that is, other people's opinions). He may have harmed me, but that in itself does not constitute a violation of property rights; if my partner leaves with him, it can also harm me, but it is not appropriate to solve the situation with violence.

title: Anti-capitalism
text: On my beautiful journey through life, I meet many opponents of anarchism or capitalism, most often both. Anti-capitalists typically dislike greed, selfishness, that some have little and others have much, inequality... These phenomena are seriously present in capitalism; but its regulations do not disappear. Greedy selfish people go into the service of the state, where they continue to dig (depending on the regime, they may focus on power, acquaintances, etc. instead of money), only the selfishness is not used to satisfy the needs of customers; and although inequality can be reduced by state interventions, it is only in such a way that the well-being of society is significantly reduced, because inequalities arise from the growth of well-being - the market is not a zero-sum game (voluntary exchange increases the benefit of both parties); inequalities typically arise when someone improves the lives of a lot of people a little, while improving himself by leaps and bounds. Anti-capitalists criticize the things they don't like, but they miss the fact that these are not the consequences of capitalism, but features of the world that socialism declaratively changes, but in reality only transforms them into something much worse.

title: Anti-anarchism
text: On my beautiful journey through life, I meet many opponents of anarchism or capitalism, most often both. Anti-anarchists typically resent the idea of a society without a central authority usurping a monopoly on violence. "Society cannot function without rules," they say; and they are right! But even the anarcho-capitalists do not care about the functioning of a society without any rules, they do not want to have those rules dictated from above by a central authority, but support their market emergence on a decentralized basis. Let everyone determine their own rules on their property, in their business; simply where he bears responsibility at the same time. And if several people collaborate on something, let them freely agree on the terms of collaboration; and if they don't suit them, they don't have to cooperate. If it becomes too complicated for people, there is nothing against it if they voluntarily start following uniform standards; but let those who do not wish such a thing be forced to do so, even if they were in the minority. Anarchy is not the absence of order; just the absence of a central authority.

title: Freedom? Democracy?
text:
We often hear the phrase "freedom and democracy"; in reality, "freedom or democracy" is more valid.
Democracy tends to be the nemesis of freedom
. What is democracy? High-flown talk aside, this is the tyrannical rule of the majority; yes, violent, because against people who do not obey the laws dictated by the majority,
the state routinely uses violence
. Will the majority decide to disarm the minority? It will happen. Will the majority decide to raise taxes on the minority? It will happen. Will the majority decide to limit free speech? It will happen. Will the majority decide that we must solve the Jewish question? It will happen. That current non-democratic regimes are typically far less free? Sure; however, this does not change the above - just as the existence of an extremely toxic green toadstool does not make a poisonous red toadstool an edible mushroom.

title: Thirty-one years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard
text:
Today marks thirty-one years since the "Father of Anarcho-Capitalism" Murray Newton Rothbard left this world at the premature age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends - which were seemingly not very related - anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Early anarchists typically did not understand economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (otherwise correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.
Murray Newton Rothbard was born on March 2, 1926; that means he would be 100 years old this year. In honor of this, the Freeport is hosting
the seventh conference
on the subject of freedom; and the first Saturday after his hundredth birthday.

title: What do you wish for at the turn of 2025 and 2026?
text:
I don't have any New Year's resolutions; if I want to change, I see no reason to wait for the turn of the year. Yet I have a wish; I would like to finish and publish the book, continue with #ne_obedience (and didn't sit down), Harbor, Hedgehog and relationships and connect a little more with my body, rest and live healthier - I'm working on everything, some things are getting better, some things are worse (with the body). It's All My Way to Freedom (and Love); I want to live in a freer society, but it is clear to me that I can only change it by changing myself.
What about you? What are your wishes? What do you want from yourself? What about others?

title: A weak state?
text:
I recently heard a wonderful argument in a discussion: "The state is too weak to defend itself against oligarchies and corporate influence." Erm... that's a rather idiosyncratic interpretation. So what about that? How to "strengthen the state"? More officials, more money, more control, more laws? Why it doesn't make sense and it won't lead to anything,
I have already explained many times
; here, however, it is even internally contradictory to the person's faith. If they believe that the state is controlled by oligarchs and large corporations (which is certainly true to a large extent), then how can the "strengthening" of that state (controlled by oligarchs and corporations) take place so that it is no longer controlled? After all, those subjects will also intervene in the entire process; and there is no reason to suppose why they should have less influence here than anything else. Do we want to get rid of them? Then let's get rid of the state! It makes no sense to claim that they control the state, but at the same time call for its strengthening; it's like upgrading the enemy's weapons.

title: State versus family
text:
Before, families were pretty solid units; parents took care of their children, who they then relied on in their old age, which of course still happens today, but to a lesser extent. Why? Modern socialist states came up with theirs
social policy and pensions
; thereby reducing the motivation of families to maintain good relations. Does that sound cynical? Is it much more complicated? Relationships aren't just about money, are they? Love can't be bought? Yes, sure! That's all true. I am not saying that if parents and children were more economically dependent on each other, there would be a paradise on earth, I am far from it; it's just that the motivation of the parent to maintain good relations with the offspring is higher if the parent knows that he will be dependent on the offspring one day, and on the contrary, the motivation of the offspring to take care of his parent is lower when he knows that the state does it anyway - and especially when he knows that this is a fundamental role of the state, which is constantly emphasized to us (
since childhood
), in addition, the state in question still pays from taxes (which means it has less resources).

title: Decade Stok
text:
Today is exactly ten years to the day
opening of Stok Free Port
; in 2015 it was a website with several authors and traffic from a few thousand devices per month (today it has hundreds of authors, traffic from thousands of unique IP addresses every day and tens of thousands per month). I created this place for libertarians to throw their thoughts (shorter than, say, a pro
Mises.cz
) and discuss them; it was the first project
Free port
, which didn't even exist at the time (and later got its name according to Stok). I liked and often said then that life has more imagination than we carry in our dreams; and really – if someone told me o
Studio
, the whole
Channel
, lectures and
Conferences
,
Hedgehog
and other projects with the reach of hundreds of thousands of people, I wouldn't believe it. Nevertheless, it not only happens, but above all it constantly motivates me to create more; I'm working on another book, a documentary about victimless crimes and preparing a big anarcho-agorist show.
For all this, I am grateful to my loved ones, colleagues, hedgehogs, but also to all of you who are still here, consuming and sharing content, helping, commenting, reacting, giving feedback and last but not least
you finance
the cost of salaries (although we also have an amazing team of volunteers), rent, gas, equipment and other expenses, for which I thank you from the bottom of my heart; without you, all of this would only be a fraction. One of the most active libertarian communities lives in the Czech Republic; awareness of us (and of anarchy) is spreading and our numbers are growing (although we are still a minority - but damned more numerous in the last ten years). Let's continue to discover, create, have a peaceful dialogue together and strive for the best versions of ourselves; and let's not forget that freedom is not given, freedom is taken - so let's enjoy it to the fullest.

Because I consider free education to be the key to a free society, I started working in

title: Revenge and justice
text: Today I will venture a little beyond the boundaries of libertarian ideas (with which this text is only very loosely related); I would like to deal with the concept of revenge, which is often perceived by people as an act of justice. I do not share this view (although I probably thought so at some point in the past, but I no longer remember exactly); revenge makes no sense at all to me, except as an effort to deter the perpetrator - or others - from harming a person. However, it is not entirely clear to me where the wishes come from, for example, that a dead murderer (perhaps a terrorist) end up "in hell" or "may his soul be damned" (let's leave aside who believes in what; although atheism is common in the Czech Republic, in the USA, for example, everyone believes in an afterlife); I wish salvation to Stalin and Hitler, may their souls rest in peace. Because why not? It will not harm and benefit anyone; why not wish bad people good things in cases where it does not harm anyone and has no (un)educational effect?

title: No toilet, yes education?
text:
We all know from experience with socialism that the state is not able to provide even such banalities as toilet paper or menstrual pads - in short, things whose need can be easily estimated and calculated; the reasons are explained by the Austrian school of economics, but let's leave the theory aside for a moment. Almost no one disputes that when the state tries to provide consumer goods, it fails; unlike the market. But why do so many people, despite the state's inability to provide absolutely trivial needs, believe in its ability to provide things that are much more complicated (education, health, justice, security...)? Especially when they witness the state failing in this day and day; above all, we must not give the market a chance, because "it certainly wouldn't work" (although there is no indication of this). So why do people still believe it? Well, one thing the state doesn't do so badly -
propaganda indoctrination always worked for him; and it is not surprising that the target is small children
.

title: Old times
text: Sometimes I hear complaints about "modern consumerist over-technological society" and its separation from "nature" (as if we are not even part of it); they say it's bad that people live in cities, use technology and don't have contact with the wild. I don't quite understand this rant; I don't understand why anyone lives a self-critical life. Why does he complain about "society" instead of giving up technology himself and spending time in the countryside instead of the city? Well, there are not many achievements of modern times, such possibility of social enjoyment, so many job opportunities and the like; yes, that's all true - welcome to the "idyllic" life of our ancestors (or rather, a "taste" of it; in reality, it was worse)! I don't see the "disease" of today in the cities or the "separation of man from nature"; I think the "disease" of today is rather how often we want something, but we are not willing to pay the price, but we complain that others who don't need it live badly.

title: Taxation of gambling
text: What will happen to slot machine or roulette addicts if the state (even more) taxes gambling? Let's start with what will definitely not happen - these people definitely do not calculate that with a higher tax burden it is not really worth playing it anymore, and they will not stop doing it. How do I know? Well, if they were capable of it, they would have calculated it and stopped playing, because it didn't pay off for them even before; they'll lose enough of the games they put in the boxes anyway - and because they're addicted, they'll play enough of those games. The amount of tax that the state imposes on gambling only determines in what proportion the money of the addicts is divided between the gambling operators and the goons from the government; it does nothing to help addicts. Taxing cigarettes or alcohol can really reduce consumption, because it makes a difference whether a smoker pays three or five thousand a month for his bad habit; however, a gambling addict will pay whatever he can for his habit (that's the point of the addiction), so the tax won't help.

title: Hope from the post office
text: For a very long time, postal services were something that various states claimed to have monopolies; and people universally believed that it was actually necessary - everyone necessarily "knew" that the free market "wouldn't work" (just as everyone "knows" today in many other fields). Today it is clear how things are; a state monopoly for the delivery of parcels is completely out of the question in the vast majority of countries. Abolishing the state post office is not something that has broad public support, but here and there someone can be found, and above all, counter-arguments have already shifted from the position "only the state has to do it" to "in most cases, the private sector is more efficient". It's great to see an industry where public opinion has shifted from "the state must have a monopoly" to "OK, let it have competition" to "somehow we could do without the state (although we don't want to yet)". So when do you think the cancellation (or rather complete privatization) of the Czech Post will take place? Will we live to see it? And when will Czech Television start ringing the bell?

title: Do the laws of the market apply?
Christian Darwin
text: Ridicule of Christians - and creationists in particular - is quite common in the atheist Czech Republic (and as a Christian - albeit one who believes in evolution - I sometimes laugh heartily at such jokes); such insinuations are sometimes thoughtful, sometimes less so, however how about the following comment: "Christians (Creationists) are completely out of their minds because they believe in Darwin whose theories don't make sense." Isn't that absurd? It is indeed; and maybe that's why I've never heard this phrase. But I heard another - no less absurd: "Austrian economics is completely out of the question, because it assumes perfect competition, perfect information and perfect people pursuing their economic interests." This is no less nonsense than the Darwin thing; the Austrian economic school not only does not use any "homo economicus under ideal conditions" models, it even criticizes them very harshly, which does not prevent many from pushing these things into the Austrian economy anyway.

title: State subsidy of science
text:
What would people do without state subsidies for science and research? So, above all, they would have more of their own resources (money), which they could decide for themselves; then basically two cases can occur: Either the person who has the money left in his pocket and the state did not collect it, decides to use it to finance some research (either directly or indirectly through the purchase of the product of the company that conducts the research - for profit or for another reason), the state is not needed for this; or would the person in question decide to spend this money (or part of it) in any other way - but what does this mean? That according to his own standards, what he spent his money on (whatever it was) brings more benefit to the person in question than the research that the state wants to force him to finance would bring him more benefit. It can be argued that the person in question will not correctly foresee all the consequences, but no one can do that at all; and if someone feels that someone else is doing it wrong, let them teach him, but
do not force him
!

title: Lists of allergens
text:
I participated in a debate about whether the state should force restaurant owners to provide diners with a list of allergens; defense
violent coercion
she relied on two arguments: The first was that "after all, no one will miss out if she writes down the allergens"; the second concerned saving the lives of severe allergy sufferers. If "no one is missing" was a valid argument for violating property rights, then for example thieves who robbed many people of only a few crowns (rounding "errors") did not actually do anything because "no one was left". And the rescue of allergy sufferers? Don't be laughed at! Those who have such a severe allergy that they are at risk of death from anaphylactic shock have to take much more care (find out about the food, ask the staff, eat in "proven" places); relying on listings that sellers paid off just because someone pushed them is nothing more than another fruit of the government's efforts to make us irresponsible ignoramuses, which can't end well.

title: The paradox of the social contract
text: If children are not capable of legal action, so parents or the state must decide for them up to a certain age, how can they be bound by a so-called "social contract" from the moment of their birth, which cannot be terminated and binds them to unconditional obedience to the state until death?

title: Thirty years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard
text:
Today marks thirty years since the "Father of Anarcho-Capitalism" Murray Newton Rothbard left this world at the premature age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends - which were seemingly not very related - anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Early anarchists typically did not understand economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (otherwise correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.
Murray Newton Rothbard was born on March 2, 1926; that means he would be 100 years old next. I should like to project it to the next Freeport Conference; so far I am considering fairly general topics - freedom or anarcho-capitalism. Do you have any tips to inspire me? Please write in the comments; Thanks!

title: Murray Christmas 2024!
text:
Would you believe that Stoky is celebrating its tenth Christmas? I find it a little unbelievable that it's been ten years since I started them; a lot has happened and changed in that time, but my approach to Christmas is still the same - I love it because in my eyes it symbolizes Christian spirituality, capitalist materialism, anarchist enjoyment of life and the divine music that I share every year. As always, we'll start
Freddie
! There will be other versions of your favorite carols this year as well
Carol of the Bells
(quite epic, but different than that
last year's
), dnb
Deck the Halls
or
Ding Dong Merrily on High
. Unfortunately, my beloved Glitch Mob don't do carols; but
this track
it suits me for Christmas this year. While
From the Ashes
since Illenia, she accompanied me for a whole year; as well as Skrux's
Blue Rose
. And what to conclude? I really don't know this year; probably
a song I don't even know
and now she started playing me on shuffle (and I like it).
I wish you - not only for Christmas, but especially for
everyday life
– above all, love and freedom; they are not only the (most important) values for me, but probably also two basic principles, according to which I try to live and respect them. However, this does not happen alone; I need to get to know them all the time. And since this knowledge has countless possible levels, it is probably a lifelong learning (and much more). In the past, I put logic and reason above emotions and feelings; over the years I realized that neither is more important - on the contrary, I find more and more their harmony and harmony. I think it's similar with love and freedom; the search for their intersections has become my new passion in life, which I like to share with you on an ongoing basis - and I intend to continue doing so. Today (and every other day) enjoy (not only) Christmas, have a good time, be happy; and finally without typos this year:
MURRAY CHRISTMAS!!

title: Twenty-nine years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard
text: Today it is exactly twenty-nine years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism" left this world at the age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

title: Murray Christmas 2023!
text:
Here we have another Christmas Day; it - and all of Christmas - in my eyes symbolizes Christian spirituality, capitalist materialism, anarchist enjoyment of life and the divine music that I share every year. As always, we'll start
Freddie
! Carol of the Bells is one of my two favorite carols, plus it has a lot of versions, so I put a different one here every year -
this year such an epic one from Samuel Kim
; a version of the latter was also recently created by my platonic love
Lindsey Stirling
. Unfortunately, they don't do my favorite Glitch Mob carols; so at least
Warrior Concerto
. I've been listening a lot this year too
Illenium
or
Seven Lions
; and I want to share about
this atypical one (and my favorite) from Emperor
. And just like last year I will close Pink Floyd;
album The Dark Side of the Moon
I was accompanied by something special this year.
I wish all people - and not only for Christmas, but above all for
everyday life
of our lives - above all, love and freedom; two values – two principles – that I consider perhaps the most important of all. That is why I am constantly getting to know them, looking for them, researching them and trying to live in maximum harmony with them; though it's more of a process - a lifetime of amazing work. In addition, lately I have been finding that they are much more related than I thought even two years ago; I'm just beginning to gradually formulate their connection, so I expect you'll hear more about it from me in the coming year - much like this year about inner freedom, which I'm also constantly progressing in knowing, as you can see from the insights I share. So enjoy your Christmas, have a good time, have a good time; and finally without typos this year:
MURRAY CHRISTMAS!!

title: The right to water
text: Sometimes we can hear from some that we have the "right to water" as a "basic human right"; such a belief is most likely based on the fact that we biologically need water to survive. However, this does not entitle anyone to force another to provide something. While the negatively defined right to water means that no one may take water from another, the positively defined "right to water" says that everyone must be provided with water; however, the dark side of positive "rights" is that someone must be forced to provide water by force, which is not ethically acceptable. In connection with this, one can encounter the fear that someone will have a monopoly on water and control everyone; however, that doesn't make sense because (ground) water is everywhere - it just depends on how deep you dig. So if the price of water rises above a certain limit, it will pay for people to dig wells; far from each having their own, they can join forces, share the water, and the monopolist is out of luck.

title: Let's focus on freedom.
text:
He came out on Friday
minarchist-tuned text
; and I respect him (which is why I released him). However, I would also like to offer an anarchist point of view. I've been hearing for over ten years not to be so radical and say this or that that I'll put people off; not to use the word anarcho-capitalism. All along I recognized the disadvantages of such an approach; but still he did what I am good at. Over time, I also found indisputable advantages: People remember it better this way, they are more likely to notice it, react to it, notice it (even if it often annoys them). I don't want to judge which approach is better; however, I am convinced that you will go the furthest if you remain yourself. Are you comfortable with subtle inconspicuousness? Write down the idea and sand the edges. Do you feel better in a vigorous dialogue? Feel free to subscribe to anarchy. Both have their pros and cons; however, nothing can replace authenticity. Not to mention that the more different ways we present our ideas, the more people we will reach.

title: Medicinal grass
text:
Someone recently asked me if I was in favor of legalizing cannabis for its medicinal effects; and guess what? I am not in favor of legalizing cannabis for its medicinal effects; I'm a supporter
full legalization (or decriminalization - it depends on the terminology, everyone means something different) of all drugs
(including marijuana) regardless of effects. It is not relevant to me whether weed heals. I know it is made into salves; I also know some shavers - they don't use it as medicine, although they sometimes tell themselves that shaving is not harmful, but that's their business. I understand the health argument, but it actually bothers me at the same time; it kind of suggests that if weed wasn't healthy, it's actually okay to ban it. But a free man shouldn't beg anyone for permission to put anything he sees fit into his body, even if it's cyanide. People like to talk about freedom, but when it comes down to it, "we need some regulation."

title: A crisis of values
text:
We hear around us about a crisis of values, a crisis of elites, a crisis in politics, a crisis of civilization and a crisis of everything. I am convinced that we would have heard such talk at any time (historical records indicate this), sometimes there were also crises in the supply of goods, food, construction, industry - depending on what the state was in charge of. Where socialism thrives, there is crisis; in the Czech Republic before 1989, for example, practically everywhere, since 1989 in education, the social system, healthcare (i.e. state sectors) and logically also in values, elites, politics... Not that our "civilization" (as a whole) is in a "crisis of values" (although some like to claim that); ordinary people are still the same and there is no problem with them. Politicians are in a "crisis of values"; and rather than a "crisis" it is a long-term condition; and that
the condition is inherent, it is not a failure of individual politicians; and as long as we have a state, the problem will not go away
.

title: Contributions to collective defense
text:
It is generally believed that
in a free market society people would pay little for collective defense (army) against an external enemy
; but how much is "little"? The only way to know "little" is to lose the war (and even that doesn't mean it was "little" for sure, she may not have had a chance to reverse the outcome at all); conversely, keeping an army at a time when there is no threat may be "too much". All this can be ascertained ex post; ex ante we know nothing. So if people in a free market society pay less for collective defense (army) than in a state, that doesn't necessarily mean it's "wrong"; for it is not clear how much is "correct". The budget of the army of the Czech Republic is (even relative to the state budget) many times lower than the army of the USA; is it wrong The answers will certainly vary and there will be different opinions with different rationales; then why is it "clear to everyone" that it would be a disaster in a stateless society (even if people paid handsomely less)?

title: Antimonopoly Office
text:
explanation,
how the free market deals with monopolies
, I have already devoted enough time, text and words; but even if someone came to the conclusion that he needs "protection" from monopolies, the interesting question is what he is actually calling for. After the antimonopoly office? After all, he himself is a monopoly on solving problems with monopolies; Do you feel the paradox? How should the state help the person in question? A state that itself usurps a monopoly on violence in a given area; is this goat turned gardener supposed to protect the garden? What is the internal logic of establishing the most brutal monopoly to protect us from supposed monopolies? Probably none at all; the state indoctrinates us all with its propaganda from childhood in school where we are told (without any justification, discussion, data or examples) that monopolies are bad because they are bad, while the state is right because it is right, and without the state there would be monopolies, which is bad. Has anyone found a deeper logic behind this?

title: Sweatshops
text: Sweatshop is a (derogatory) term for factories where people work in miserable conditions for low wages; they tend to be in developing countries where poor people do not have a better livelihood. In the rich part of the world (ours), some people find it terrible (even though our ancestors had to work like that to be well off today) and protest by not buying products from sweatshops; it is of course their business where they shop, I just feel that they are missing something: If someone wants to help the poor, they should buy goods from companies where the poor are employed in better conditions; if this is not possible (or if the desire to help is not so strong that the helper overcomes the obstacles), buying goods from a sweatshop is at least something. Buying from a competitor (perhaps local) is even worse for those poor people from the third world; so when a person who actually helps criticizes those who buy sweatshops, it makes sense, but it's absurd when he criticizes someone who doesn't do either.

title: Supermarkets versus small shops
text: Supermarkets compete with small shops, which sometimes go out of business because of it; does it harm society? This in itself is clearly not; competition is desirable. Another thing is state interference, which affects small businesses worse than large ones, which can more easily dissolve it in costs (formerly EET, control reports, various standards and clouds of unnecessary administration; the mandatory closing of large stores on holidays is rather an exception that harms the large ones). However, market forces cause customers to get what they want: a supermarket may offer many types of goods and lower prices, a small shop may offer a more personal approach or high quality of some product segments; it is impossible to objectively say which of these is better, as human preferences are purely subjective. So everyone buys where it will bring them more benefit; some stores can handle it, others not, which is not bad, quite the opposite – the consumer expressed that something else would bring him more benefit.

title: Problem: Multitasking
text:
Public administration is notorious for "problems" with someone winning a (typically construction) contract because it's the cheapest, but then screwing up on multiple jobs; an absolute classic is winning a tender with a price that doesn't even cover the costs. And for many years (I remember it since I was little) it has been "solved" what to do with it; I can't help but ask: How about selling those orders as fixed time – fixed price? The responsibility will be borne by the supplier; of course, the official is more likely to make mistakes, the space for corruption will decrease, but why isn't anyone else calling for such a solution? I wouldn't worry about finding a supplier; especially if the conditions for tendering change so that it is not a constant game of the five big firms. Most people will answer that it would be nice, but "there is a lack of political will"; and they are right - they are missing and always will be. As long as the state is the contracting authority, there will probably be no (well-intentioned) modifications
they will not have the desired effect
.

title: Drugs and weapons
text: Drugs and guns have a lot in common; however, I will focus on one not-often-mentioned aspect: There is a lot of good statistical data on both that shows quite clearly that the current regulations are doing enormous damage; even from a purely utilitarian point of view, it would be best to deregulate both drugs and guns (leaving freedom and the moral aspect of the matter aside for now). The existence of many people who simply ignore the data does not surprise me; however, it amazes me how many of them are able to completely ignore the practically identical arguments on one of those topics that they use to defend their positions on the other. Indeed, the doctrine of Republicans (right-wing conservatives) says that drugs are bad and guns are not, while the doctrine of Democrats (left-wing liberals) says the exact opposite; it's sad how many people value doctrine more than truth and use data only as a tool to beat opponents over the head, not for critical thinking.

title: East and West Germany
text:
Post-war devastated (and rebuilding) Germany was divided into two states in 1949: NSR (West Germany) and GDR (East Germany); in the first mentioned, a kind of socialism was implemented (quite a light version), in the second, rigid socialism. Although this situation was unhappy for the East Germans, from our point of view there is only one positive: The division of Germany was almost a laboratory experiment on the subject of socialism; the initial position of both countries was the same – property conditions, culture, history, mentality of the population, all of this was comparable on both sides of the artificial line. Then followed a social experiment lasting four decades; and the result was completely unambiguous and overwhelming, confirming the theory of the Austrian economic school to the letter -
socialism just doesn't work
. But the chilling question is: "How many more such experiments will have to take place before socialists learn their lesson?"

title: Pricing
text:
In discussions with various greens, I come across bizarre examples of "market failure": A house made of wood is more expensive today than a house made of some "complex industrial shit"; land with natural wealth of "incalculable value" is worth buying for an office building. For them, such things are "market failure" that must be addressed by the state; it has to do with misunderstanding
pricing process
. The fact that something is commercially worthwhile to build somewhere indicates that people want it more than the thing that is not worth building there; when it pays to build with a material, it is obviously more efficient than building with a more expensive one. Self-centeredness and humility prevent some people from accepting that when others wish for something different, such a wish is not "inferior" to theirs; instead, they call for their wish to be enforced by force, which they back up with phrases of "incalculable value" (but this is demonstrably not true from their point of view either; if something really was of incalculable value to them, they would sell everything they have to help it).

title: Twenty-eight years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard
text: Today it is exactly twenty-eight years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism" left this world at the age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

Some people don't like Christmas consumerism; no one has to participate in that either. We are masters and creators of our lives - all of us, each of us; although some unfortunately don't realize it because that's how they were brought up (

title: Holy War (against the Russians)
text: After the Russian invasion of Ukraine, many people feel the need to define themselves against the Russians; this may make sense in a certain context, less so in another. The water pipes burst in the basement of the apartment building that my close friend partially manages; so the person in question called the company where she wanted to arrange a repair. Everything was going smoothly until she mentioned that the owner of the house was of Russian nationality; to which the repairman replied that he would not do the work. He did not care that the owner did not live in Russia or the house. Of course, I support everyone's right to choose customers according to any criteria; yet I do not find this need to define myself against people by nationality happy. I find it paradoxical about the whole situation that two Ukrainian families who fled the war currently live in that house (one of them we support financially); and they are the ones to whom the water did not flow, not the owner.

title: Does the idea of gay sex cloud logic for libertarians?
text:
Text
Marriage for all
caused stormy reactions in Stoká, on social networks and in my email. I was probably most interested in the argument that marriage should not be a state (then consent), so its extension to more groups of people is said to
increases
state power. But by the same logic, we could say that if we change the building code so that more people can build,
will increase
with the power of the state, which makes absolutely no sense; or we could argue that the state has no business issuing trade cards to people (and everyone should be able to run a trade without a permit), but as long as it issues them, the fewer people who get them, the better - which doesn't make any more sense. If the state regulates, for example, the possession of arms, business, the production of alcohol, or anything else, it is certainly not the case that the more permits it issues, the less freedom; it's the exact opposite. And I almost don't want to believe that it isn't obvious to someone; rather, I think the idea of gays having sex clouds some people's logic a bit.

title: Seat belts
text: In discussions of regulation, opponents often cite seat belts to me as an example of good regulation; if they don't happen to know I'm an anarcho-capitalist, they often seize on the argument by trying to pass off the belt argument as something we can agree on. Why is mandatory seat belts such a mantra? After all, it is up to each person whether the risk is worth a little discomfort; and it cannot be decided universally, because the risk is not flat-rate and the discomfort is purely individual. So how to defend the violent repression against the unaffiliated? Some argue that the entire society pays for his eventual treatment; that's a great argument against socialist healthcare, not for mandatory belts. Others argue that someone could fly out of the car and injure others; even leaving aside the improbability of that scenario, it would be an argument for strapping everything in a car, not just people. So why belts? I believe the status quo is an iron shirt.

title: Customs, so customs
text: When a country imposes a tariff on our products, so must we; that's similar logic to proclaiming that if someone jumps out of a window, we must too. By imposing a tariff on some goods, we limit competition to domestic producers, thus harming domestic consumers (when the tariff prevents them from buying a foreign product that they would otherwise buy, we take away their best option and force them to choose a worse one); this will happen completely regardless of whether the other side also imposes tariffs. Why tariffs do not make sense is explained in some detail by Austrian economics, and even by its predecessor Claude Frédéric Bastiat in the book "What is and what is not seen"; I don't have space for a comprehensive explanation here, but I would like to give the reader a thought: What if the family imposes duties on everyone around? What if the street does it? Urban district? The whole city? Can they help each other? No? So why should a state help itself, especially when some states have less population than some cities?

title: Is the Fed private?
text:
Is the US central banking system (FED) private or public? De jure it's complicated - it's a non-profit, it's supposed to be politically independent (haha) and the Reserve Bank owns its shares, which theoretically makes it a private company; de facto (although it is formally written to the banks) its leadership is determined by the state (so much for political independence). It is something like the "private" enterprises of the Third Reich, which were formally owned by white horses, but the state determined what and when they were to do and how much to sell for and how much to pay employees. And that is precisely why a distinction must be made between "private" and "free market"; when something is private on paper but state in reality, it can do more harm than the state itself. So when you hear socialists claim that the Fed is evil because it is a private company, ask how much it is really controlled by those private "owners" and how much by state legislation; the only meaningful solution is to abolish the FED and most importantly
separation of money from the state
.

title: Twenty-seven years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard
text: Today is exactly twenty-seven years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism" left this world at the age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

title: Equal opportunities
text: Very often I hear from someone (especially various "right-wingers") that the person in question is not proposing state intervention for equality of outcomes, but "only" for equality of opportunity; but what does that mean? How to "match the odds"? Considering how different people are, nothing like "equality of opportunity" can in principle even exist; also how to "compare" the opportunities of a genius and a fool? How to arrange that beautiful and ugly people have the same opportunities? And how to compensate abused and psychologically damaged children for their suffering, so that they have the same "starting line" as others? It is well talked about, but simply not feasible; and all efforts to get closer to it are absurd, because only a few aspects of the entire colorful spectrum of life can be equalized. And it's definitely not free either; on the contrary, we have to pay dearly for such efforts, which, among other things, is also borne by the severely disadvantaged. Do you want to give people "equal opportunities"? For me, for me... but from myself!

title: The problem is people
text:
"The problem is not democracy; the problem is the people!" Unfortunately, I have already heard this sentence - seriously meant - more than once in my life; can anyone even be serious? Defending democracy - as a system of government by the people - that it's fine but doesn't work because the people are the problem is like saying that the drink from the broken roll is great, but the problem is the people who die from it. It is often used derisively in connection with communism (it is a good system, but not for the people), sometimes such criticism can be found with anarchy; so how can it be used as a defense in the case of democracy (especially from the same person who so criticized anarchy)? Well, it's simple -
democracy is our idol, cult, religion, forced idol...
We are brought up to believe that democracy cannot be bad, that criticism of it is not socially acceptable, and that if it shows lousy results, the fault must surely lie in something else - perhaps in the people.

title: The word anarcho-capitalism
text:
I feel the need to respond to one of our writers who came up with
a better name for ankap
. A lot of people have been convincing me for years that I should call anarcho-capitalism something else. About half of them think anarchism is cool, but capitalism turns people off; on the other hand, the other half perceives the words exactly the opposite - it depends on the social bubble. The fact is that at least one of those words will be against the grain of almost everyone. In addition, there is already a fairly used and at the same time peaceful word that can be used to describe anarcho-capitalism - it is "voluntarism" (which is immediately more accurate than the "multiarchy" proposed by the foreword). So why do I still call this school of thought anarcho-capitalism?
On the one hand, because it is natural for me to name things with the most accurate names possible (I don't like to play with anything, authenticity is very pleasant to me), moreover, I don't want to retreat from unpopular terms (I prefer to clean them up); but especially with the word "anarcho-capitalism" I distinguish myself and interest the listeners (albeit sometimes negatively). Countless times I have heard anarcho-capitalists talk about freedom in such a way that the listeners didn't really mind, but they didn't understand at all that the speaker was not talking about the state and "reformed" democracy with some slight modifications. I have nothing against such an approach; on the contrary, I appreciate that some have taken this path - it is good if we address several targets at the same time. However, it wouldn't suit me; it is more natural for me to call anarcho-capitalism anarcho-capitalism (which the listener will remember better anyway) and then look for words that will best explain what it is.

title: The nonsense of protectionism
text:
On the one hand, there is a broad consensus (among economists and, in fact, throughout society and perhaps also among politicians) that
voluntary exchange and division of labor leads to prosperity and benefit
; everyone understands that cooperation is the way to prosperity. It follows logically that anything which in any way restricts the exchange and division of labor causes the exact opposite, i.e. poverty and decay; the rate will of course vary according to the magnitude of such restrictions. Therefore, whenever someone proclaims protectionism, that is, the restriction of foreign trade in the name of "protection" of domestic entrepreneurs, logically
it goes against the welfare of society
; and why actually? For what reason do I need to "protect" some businessman just because he shares the same side of some artificial state border with me? If someone argues by exclaiming, "Nothing but a nation," I find it silly, but not necessarily inconsistent; but don't let anyone tell me that protectionism "helps the economy".

title: Imperfect information
text:
State interventions tend to be justified by imperfect information on the free market; however, perfect information does not exist not only in the market, but also in the state. But the state needs a huge amount of information to plan its interventions; not only more than individuals need (they try to manage "only" their lives), but as much even as much (because the state tries to manage the lives of a huge number of individuals),
that it is realistically impossible for him to get them all
. And here comes an interesting moment: The better the decision the state has to make, the more information it needs, which is not free, the subjects have to give it at their own expense, which increases with the better the state has to be informed; paradoxically, the better the state can be in terms of decision-making, the worse it must be in terms of depriving people of their resources. And what is the optimal rate? In principle, this cannot be determined, because that information is needed; therefore, changes to the researched subject change the research methodology.

title: Spreading a bad mood
text: "In the Czechoslovak Republic, the old charity, which was always considered a grace that always humiliated the poor recipient and dulled his human consciousness, will no longer have a place. Today, we are putting social duty in the place of humiliating grace." (Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk) The gifted poor man was then grateful to his donor; and perhaps he experienced humiliation that motivated him to do things better. Then came social duty; then the person in question does not feel gifted, it is no longer the case that someone gave him something, now it is his "right". And if you explain to someone that they have a "right" to other people's money and they believe it, they have nothing to be grateful for; on the contrary, it is perfectly logical if he still complains, it is not good enough for him and he asks for more. Why should he act otherwise? We cannot grant someone a "right" to something and at the same time ask them to be grateful for it; if you are "entitled" to something, gratitude excludes it, because it only makes sense when you get something you didn't have to get.

title: Politicians and politics
Practical politics
text: Politicians like and often brag that they are not theorists, but practical men who are absolutely uninterested in any theory because they need results; the voter demands it. On this basis, they often reject libertarian theories, saying that they have more important things to do; but what kind? What is their "practice" based on? A politician is not someone who stands somewhere with a shovel, screwdriver, wooden spoon or mason's trowel (although he would like to present himself that way) - in principle he is not a practitioner, because whenever he regulates, prohibits, taxes or subsidizes something, he does so on the basis of some theory; the theory that something will increase "social utility", that something will help someone, protect someone, and so on. None of this is practice with which he has experience, those decisions always flow from some theory, whether the politician wants it or not; so let's not be silenced by populist rants about the needlessness of theories, because politics is based on them - not to mention that they are flawed theories.

title: Internet anarchy
text: "Anarchy is a beautiful theory, but it can never work in practice!" This is the frequent objection of statists against anarchy. But is it really so? Of course, it cannot yet be proven whether it will work across society (until it is tried); and the opposite can certainly not be proven either. But what we can evaluate are individual areas; and a non-negligible part of our society is the Internet, in which free market anarchy reigns in practice (it is true that states sometimes enter here as well, but not in such a way that they ensure its operation, only sometimes they take someone down). People can - and to some extent do - harm themselves on the Internet; however, as a result, the Internet works (the pests globally are not able to "destroy" the efforts of those who create something valuable) and is perfectly usable even without regulations; I consider it one of the biggest "miracles" that cash-on-delivery e-shops work on an anonymous network, although competitors can spam them with fake orders. How is that? I don't know; but it's amazing.

title: Parasites everywhere
text:
We hear complaints about parasites everywhere from time to time; workers complain about the "nemakačenka", some people don't like people on benefits, others generalize it to "gypsies", in extreme cases you can even hear that the parasites are self-employed (I'm not just talking about the famous saying of the parasite Mládek, sometimes other parasitizing civil servants are heard with similar nonsense). What about that? Unfortunately, nothing within the company's current setup; as long as there is violent redistribution and
protection money called taxes
, there will naturally also be parasites, because that is the basic principle of redistribution - solidarity differs from parasitism only by the consent of the donor (or victim), so involuntary on the one hand implies parasitism on the other. It is sometimes said that non-voters should not complain about the results (which I don't think); but now I say that those who want to stand should not complain about parasites.

title: Reforms
text:
We often hear that we need absolutely fundamental reform of education, healthcare, judiciary, police and many other things; what do they have in common? All these fields are managed by the state. Have you ever heard about the urgent need for fundamental reform of the hotel industry, food industry, construction industry or even IT? So I don't. Where the free market works at least to some extent, there is no need for major reforms, as these industries reform themselves little by little as customers need; those who do it right make money, while those who reform wrong go bankrupt. On the contrary, almost everything the state does requires reform because it works poorly; and no wonder
it can't even work properly in principle
. And fully aware of these connections, I do not see how anyone can even stand up for the state; whatever the state manages doesn't work well, whatever was left to the market started to work better - so why not sell other sectors to the market as well?

title: Rational action
text: Everyone knows that people do not always act rationally; Ludwig von Mises assumes the opposite in one of the basic books of Austrian economics (Human Action). Does this mean that the entire Austrian economy is standing on water? No; it just defines rationality differently. While Mises assumes that people act rationally, he explicitly defines such action as an effort to constantly maximize one's utility (taking into account the fickle and emotional state of man, incomplete information, "non-economic" desires, changing preferences, and so on); according to his definition, even a drug addict risking his life for the next dose acts rationally. And since Mises strictly adheres to this definition, it is correct; however, it creates a confusing impression on the uninformed reader (in my opinion, this is an unfortunately chosen definition). So if you encounter the assumption of Austrian economics that people act rationally, don't be alarmed; it means something other than what you probably mean.

title: Where can the economy grow?
text: Many economists, philosophers and thinkers warn us that the capitalist economy is growing too fast, which cannot last forever; her days are said to be slowly numbered, so nothing but downfall and misery await us. But why should such doomsaying come true? Yes, we are doing great, we live in wonderful times, we are surrounded by wealth; but is there really nothing to improve? Of course it is! We can constantly invent more and more things that we wish to have; but we don't have them at the moment because it would cost us a lot of resources. But it is the hard work of people all over the world that keeps lowering these prices; the same goods can be produced more and more cheaply (and now I don't just mean financially, but in terms of the total volume of resources - including human labor). What could stop such progress? Lack of mineral resources? Hardly; substitutes are still being found for scarce resources. Great wars of states? Yes, you might... but that's not a problem with a capitalist economy.

title: Twenty-six years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard
text: Today it is exactly twenty-six years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism" left this world at the age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

title: A dynamic market
text:
In discussions about the impossibility of economic calculation in central planning, we often come across that the discussants imagine the pricing process as something that will one day end and the prices will be "set right"; with these assumptions, he then tries to figure out how such a thing could be possible in socialism (although Ludwig von Mises has already shown that it is not). However, the reality is far more complex, as the free market is not an "achievement of a state", but a "process"; therefore, the central planner's task is not only to find the "right" prices or allocation mechanism without money (and he already fails in this task), but above all to be able to adapt to constantly changing conditions and to receive, evaluate and react to information from the whole world in real time, which is simply and simply a superhuman task, ergo
central planning can never work well
(and of course this also applies to education, healthcare, the social system and the like).

title: From my taxes...
text: "And I still have to pay for it with my taxes," the right-wing conservative faces; I ask why he thinks it's unfair, to which I get an indignant answer that he doesn't want this, it's his money, so he should have the right to decide. Well, that makes sense... and if I don't want to pay for state education, health, courts, police and military, it's my money, will they support me? Oh, won't support? Come on, is that "something else"? Um; and how is it different? There are ad hominem arguments, or some very illogical appeal to the social contract and similar nonsense. And no wonder, the difference is only in individual preferences; he wants to pay the military, police, judges and teachers, but he doesn't like paying the non-profit Auto*Mat. I don't like paying either (which is wrong), the cycling activists want both (also wrong); after all, only what the person in question wants is correct... and when the wishes of similar ones are added up, a solid drink comes out.
