title: Fighting addictions
text: Addictions are crap; I also know people who are comfortable with such a state, or at least they say so (and no one but themselves can know how it really is). Whether it's addiction to drugs, gambling, porn, or any other person, I don't think there's anything to stand for (and addiction to air, water, and food isn't honey either, it's actually just as stupid as any other addiction, only we can't do anything about it); and because addictions are a problem, people usually call for state repression, which is wrong. For one thing, it has been consistently and repeatedly made clear for decades that repression is simply not the answer; above all, there is no moral justification for violence (taxation) perpetrated on entire societies in order to perpetrate further violence (war on addictions) on certain groups (especially providers of "pleasure"). Regardless of the "social benefit" (which is dubious anyway), such a thing is not excusable; what could it be?

title: The rich and the poor
text: When we talk about poor and rich people in society, we often treat them as fixed groups; therefore, whoever warns against the "opening of the scissors between the rich and the poor" (regardless of the fact that he often mistakenly focuses only on relative wealth and ignores the absolute), typically talks about it in such a way as if it were two more or less fixed groups of people, which is usually understood by the listeners as well (judging by the reactions). But the fact is that probably in the entire history of mankind it has never been so easy for the poor to become rich (or the rich to become poor); we don't have a strictly class or caste society, we don't have insurmountable family ties that would determine whether a person will be a lord or a commoner all his life. The information on how many poor people become rich (or at least middle class) varies (from country to country and statistics from statistics), but even according to pessimistic "leftist" estimates, it is tens of percent.

title: Murray Christmas 2020!
text:
As an adult, I look forward to Christmas like a little boy; far more than when I was a little boy. I love the versatility of these holidays: They are Christian-spiritual; capitalistically material; and for me personally, anarchistically non-violent, because we arrange them with our loved ones in our own way and in such a way that we only do what we really want to do. Besides, Christmas shows us (libertarians) a PR masterpiece that we (Christians) succeeded thousands of years ago: The original pagan established holiday of Saturnalia was transformed into Christmas. What do you think, will we (anarchists) ever manage to make the Day of Czech Statehood, for example, the Day of Decentralization? xD
More than Christmas I love... like music! So carols cannot be missing:
Freddie will never die...
! I also linked Carol of the Bells to you in previous years, but then I didn't know it
my favorite Lindsey Stirling also played
. I certainly won't forgive myself this year either
Deck the Halls (a rock version with a nice picture won't offend)
. Well, finally
Pentatonix singing carol in church
I see it as a celebration of the way our society has come since the church murdered homosexuals; someone can see in it the destruction of traditional values, I personally see in it God's love for each (!) of us.
I am (not only) extremely grateful to God that I can be here; that I live this life that has more imagination than I carry in my dreams. Thank you for the rare opportunity to be in the world, for the ability to learn and learn, work with yourself and be useful. And although my time in this world is limited and everything is fleeting, I cannot yet imagine a greater gift than this happy life among the best people. I believe that my happiness stems primarily from being the master of my own life; and that state begins with the realization that I create my life with my thoughts and actions. I believe in freedom; I believe in God and the power of prayer; I believe in myself and the power of meditation; I believe in both logic and the scientific method; I trust the people I love. Where will this faith take me? Hard to say; but I can't wait to find out.
I am convinced that (not only) we need freedom to grow; and I also wish (not only) Christmas to each of us. However, I cannot give it to anyone; freedom is not given - freedom is taken. So take your freedom and let others have theirs. Sometimes it takes courage; they can set an example for us
for example, soldiers who managed it in far worse conditions (and coincidentally also at Christmas)
– defied orders and were at least free for a while. Let us follow them - peacefully, lovingly, non-violently, but steadfastly.
And finally, without typos this year:
MURRAY CHRISTMAS!!

title: Move to Somalia!
text:
Statists often objected to anarchists that
the state initiates aggression against its citizens
, when he collects taxes under threat of violence, counter that if someone doesn't like it, they can move away (and Somalia is the most frequently recommended destination); I find this argument absolutely illogical to the point of desperation, but unfortunately it makes sense to many, so it's not out of the question to deal with it. So where is the flaw in the logic? Actually everywhere; if I criticize someone attacking someone else or threatening him with violence, it is of course true that the victim can run away, defend himself, dodge, deceive the attacker and so on, but none of this changes anything about my criticism of the behavior of the attacker, because it is absolutely unrelated to what defense strategy the victim chooses or does not choose. It's like using the argument in defense of the rapist that the victim should have been careful, besides, she didn't even have to be there and could even move to Somalia; if she didn't, she has nothing to complain about.

title: Interest-free loan
text:
Interest free loans are something that people sometimes expect from the government for example for students and such; many assume that it doesn't really cost anything because the borrowed money will be paid back anyway. Bridge error; interest is a natural fee for a service (loan), which is neither risk-free nor cost-free (it is associated with an opportunity cost). So asking for a loan without interest is like asking for any other service for nothing; it is a common thing between friends, which is understandable, because friends help each other (not only by lending money). In another context, however, it should be remembered that an interest-free loan is not "free" for the lender; even if the money were to just lie there and he had nothing planned with it, he can never know when he will need to dispose of it unexpectedly, just as the risk that the debtor will not return it (even if he wanted to) cannot be excluded -
and of course this risk is not "free"
(because it is always better not to undergo it than to undergo it).

title: Social contract
text:
The social contract is an artificial construct whereby everyone implicitly agrees that the state takes our resources under threat of violence and provides us with services in return; the catch is that some of us explicitly disagree—and are unlucky because the state is stronger. Let's imagine an analogous situation with the mafia, which starts collecting protection money in some territory and declares it a social contract; everyone implicitly agrees—and whoever doesn't is supposed to move away, because staying means agreeing. What makes it different? That the mafia does not provide as many services to the people as the state? For one thing, she doesn't take that much money from them, but above all - if she was providing services, is it all right? It is not! And just as I can't go sweep someone's snow (without asking) and demand money for it, neither should they do it; he's doing it from a position of strength and the social contract is just lofty bullshit to defend that
whoever has the bigger stick beats the others with it
.

title: Anarcho-capitalist extremists
text:
Anarcho-capitalists are often accused of extremism by their opponents; what does such an accusation mean? We are blamed that
we completely reject offensive violence
and not only partially; it is not unlike if the object of criticism was that we are extremist opponents of murder and rape. We should not be so militant and immeasurable, but on the contrary willing to compromise; and how? For example... rape and murder are bad, but when Pepa does it, it's nothing against anything; and we can have a reasonable dialogue about whether or not Franta could also do it sometimes. Above all, no extremism, let's approach compromises, let's not rush and not be controversial; yes, and certainly let's not say it in full, so as not to discourage more conservative-minded individuals, after all, we must not scare people who would label anyone who radically condemns rape and murder as an extremist. And the calls to not be "extremists" sound about as absurd to many of us.

title: About the disappearing theater
text:
If arts funding were left to the free market, it probably would
there have been big changes
; no one can predict what the changes would actually be, new forms of art would emerge, old ones would disappear, some cultural stands would not survive, others would. I am convinced that not all theaters would perish, on the other hand, I do not suppose that they would all support themselves; this is a frequent argument of the opponents of the free market in this area - so let's take a closer look at such a disappearing theater. The fact that the theater is not able to earn money for its operation (and I do not mean only from admission fees, but also from voluntary donations and the like) means that people value the resources it consumes more than what the theater brings to them (and this includes all emotional and cultural values, not only economic ones); that is, it should not exist in this form - it is simply not worth it to the people, so it should be reformed or disappear.

title: Minimum wage
text:
Proponents of the minimum wage most often argue about helping the poor or weak and "social justice"; at first glance it also looks quite logical - after a possible increase in the minimum wage, the poorest workers will have more money. This may indeed be true to some extent for some, which is great to see; but then there is another thing that is not so easily seen: By setting the minimum wage to a certain limit, it is not worthwhile for employers to employ workers whose work will bring them less value than the limit set by the state; and this will affect precisely the least qualified, i.e. potentially the poorest. After all, unemployment is a phenomenon caused in principle by only two factors: Either someone does not want to work for the kind of money that other participants in the labor market value their work for, or they would agree on some contractual price, but their state outlaws the agreement, which
damages both (!) parties
.

title: Civilian casualties
text:
I believe the generally held belief that civilians should not be murdered in wars is correct; however, I don't take it dogmatically in the sense of "it is so because simply because", but because someone who doesn't do anything to anyone shouldn't suffer just because he was born on the "wrong" side of the border. Sometimes people tend to condone the killing of civilians depending on what atrocities their fellow citizens have committed, which is something I strongly disagree with; everyone should be responsible for themselves, not for the actions of others just because they belong to the same nation. So I refuse, for example, to excuse Bombardier Harris for the massacres of German civilians by saying that the Germans started the war (for they were different Germans than those whom Harris burned); I do not excuse Hiroshima and Nagasaki with the attack on Pearl Harbor (other Japanese were attacked there than those who then died of radiation).
So we could continue
; a person is responsible for his actions, not for any state or nation.

title: Class conflict
Exploitation of poor countries
text: People and companies from richer countries often buy labor or minerals from people in poorer parts of the world; sometimes we hear that we are "exploiting" the poor countries. Such a thing can apply on the assumption that we would force their inhabitants to do something (or if the state or some other criminal organization forced them to do something by force); but if there is no aggression in the sense of coercion, I dare say that - regardless of the desperate conditions of the poor - their exploitation is not taking place. How is that? Trade with us improves their situation compared to the situation where we would not trade with them (and the same applies to us, there is no such thing); if someone, as a result of his poverty, gives up, for example, mineral wealth, in order not to die of thirst or hunger, his situation is indeed bad, but it is definitely better than he would be if he did not receive a similar offer (if this were not the case, he would simply refuse it and thus remain in the state he was in before).

title: Representative democracy
text:
Sometimes I indulge in
principled general criticism of democracy
(no specific type of it, but democracy in general); however, now I would like to focus specifically on representative democracy. Who becomes a representative in such a system? What are the best predispositions for getting the voters' votes? Well, being likable, popular, well-known, able to entertain people... and other similar positives. And what does a "good leader" need? Most likely, wisdom, decisiveness, morality, perspective... "surprisingly" completely different qualities. Therefore, in order for it to work at least as theoretically as it should according to the supporters of representative democracy (another thing is that in principle it cannot for far more serious reasons), it must happen that the darling of the crowds is also a capable leader (let's leave aside the fact that people follow a capable leader voluntarily); how can anyone want to rely on something like that?

title: Parasitism
text:
Modern liberals (and I don't mean classical liberals, but those "leftists" in the sense of American Democrats) like to label as parasites those who work illegally, or operate in some gross violation of the labor code; conservatives (classic "right-wingers" in the sense of American Republicans) on the other hand typically call those who receive social benefits, subsidies and the like as parasites. I think both of these groups are wrong. "Leftists" more, because the one who works for black money is definitely not a parasite on anyone, he just doesn't allow himself to be robbed by the state; "Right-wingers" are a little less wrong, however, those who take benefits or subsidies only take what someone (the state) offers them. The real parasite is the entity that robs us of those funds
it prepares with the threat of violence - that is, the state
. Inciting hatred towards one or the other is just the cover maneuvers of politicians and the creation of illusory goals; the one who steals is not an actor in the gray economy or a "sock" - it is the state.

title: Transportation of goods
text: "We live in a crazy time when some things that we can make locally, we prefer to import from the other side of the world," warn some. Is it really wrong? The answer is not so simple in today's distorted (regulated, subsidized and taxed) market, where it can vary; however, in the free market, the unequivocal answer is "No, it's not wrong!" The reason for importing goods that we can produce locally is typically that it is cheaper (even with imports). No, it's not a market failure; on the contrary, it is a question of finding the best way on the market, which in the given case consists in that import. People obviously value resources consumed by production elsewhere and imports less than resources consumed by production locally (if this were not the case, it would have to be cheaper to produce it locally); this can happen, for example, as a result of the fact that people value their time (and work) differently in different places, or that there are better conditions for the production of certain goods.

title: Wars without states?
text:
When the word "anarchy" is spoken, most people think of apocalypse, conflict, chaos and warfare; how far are these ideas from reality? V
historical anarchies
was certainly no more at war than in territories usurped by states; many will argue that this does not mean much, as the situation may be different today than before. So be it, it may be so; nevertheless, I believe that a society without a state will be more peaceful. Why? Because wars are expensive; and when states go to war, those who decide on wars do not pay for it, they finance it with foreign money, while if a private individual wants to go to war, he pays for it from his own money. I'm not saying that there will never be any conflicts in anarchy, there certainly will be, because sometimes it pays off anyway (either economically or out of hatred); however, I am convinced that there will be fewer of them, but above all, their scope will be significantly reduced, as society will be decentralized, which makes a world war, for example, a rather unlikely scenario.

title: The free market is only for the rich
text: Statists often argue that a free market would only serve the rich because there is no incentive to provide services to the poor because they can pay less; it may look like that at first and very superficial glance, but let's think about it more deeply. Suppose the statement is indeed true; we live in a society where all companies are competing to offer better and more luxurious services to the rich, while no one does anything for the poor. How do you best earn in such a company? Well, of course, not by stuffing yourself into the harsh competition of the luxury market, but by starting to provide goods (obviously not so luxurious) to the poor; instead of making a million from one customer, you'd rather make a hundred of them ten thousand each. After all, if the aforementioned thesis were true, car companies would only produce the most expensive cars, no one would build cheap apartments, only villas and so on...

title: Supporters of the free market
text: In conversations with die-hard anti-capitalists, I am often struck by how wrong these people are about what I—as an anarcho-capitalist—actually think; they push me all sorts of ideas that I don't agree with at all; for example, they make me a defender of the current banking system, big corporations and the like. But such things are ultimately understandable, because no one can properly understand everything; however, an absurd situation occurs at the moment when I explain why I do not think this or that and do not want to, to which the discussion opponent will not react by revising his views, but by forcefully asserting that I simply think so! What follows from this? Personally, I think that these people simply put the label "capitalism" on any economic or social phenomenon that they don't like; that they are anti-capitalists then follows from the fact that for them "capitalism" is synonymous with "the bad that I don't like". what is it Another win for newspeak?

title: Corporations and States
text: Many people (especially those who call themselves "leftists") dislike big corporations and argue that we need states to protect us from them; they don't even realize how much they help those corporations with this attitude (especially when they show it in the elections). It is precisely the states that favor giant corporations over smaller companies on practically all fronts; as? First, the really big players can interfere in legislative processes and eliminate their competition; yes, officially they shouldn't, but it happens (and calling for help from the state through which it happens is absurdly naive). Second, corporations will once again adapt better to the legislative and administrative burden that states distort the market. Third, large firms receive subsidies more easily; they have whole departments that can deal with it. And fourthly, we have the old familiar investment incentives; they also do not apply to small players. Does it really make sense to call for a big state "against" corporations?

title: Who does nothing wrong...
text: All kinds of totalitarian practices - especially, but not limited to, wiretapping - are often defended in the way: "Whoever does nothing wrong has nothing to fear." (And so it doesn't need encryption, secure lines... and especially privacy.) This thesis is nonsensical, on the one hand, because the state also considers tax evasion, for example, "bad", which is nothing more than trying not to get robbed; even if we ignore this aspect, the statement shows the incredible naivety of the speaker, because he perceives the state as some perfect entity free of human error or ill will (which is far from unusual). But the state is made up of people; therefore, it is not true that those who do nothing wrong have nothing to fear, because they can certainly be afraid of the misuse of information that the state collects about them (and it can be a legislative misuse even in violation of the law). It kind of reminds me of another statement, "People are evil, so we need a state." Um... and who will run the state? Aliens?

title: The complexity of society
text:
Sometimes one can come across the claim that in "primitive societies" the state may not have been absolutely necessary, because they were very simple communities, but today, as a result of the complex and complex "modern society", it is needed and "could not do without it"; few statements could be so far from the truth. How is that? Well, small communities are the only ones where socialism can work in some way, because people there know each other and can perform economic calculation "off the top of their heads" (they can simply estimate each other's preferences), for example the family; the larger and more complex society we live in,
the more difficult it is to perform economic calculation in it without a free market
. The reality is therefore exactly the opposite of what the above statement might seem: The more complex and complicated a society we have, the more difficult it is to plan centrally and the more urgently it needs a free market for the proper allocation of resources.

title: Balanced budget
text: Many - often "right-wing" minded - people are calling for a balanced state budget; however, I - surprisingly for many - do not. Why not? Because there are two ways to achieve such a state: The first consists in reducing expenses, but the second in increasing income; a balanced budget can therefore be kept within the framework of a minimal state, but also of a huge socialist juggernaut (for example, before 1989 the Czech Republic was not nearly as indebted as it is now, but it was no paradise). I personally see it as paramount that the state should have the lowest possible income; of course, a state with low income and expenditure is by far the best, but I consider low income and high expenditure to be better than a classic large state (albeit with a balanced budget). I'm not saying you have to share my opinion, but I think we should definitely think about how important the "fight for a balanced budget" is compared to efforts to shrink the state.

title: Burden of proof
How can he not be an anarcho-capitalist…
text: ...pacifist, vegan, Jainist, arbitrary anarchist? Pacifists reject violence entirely; if they are consistent, they must also reject states, and at the same time they would hardly be able to prevent anyone from trading (even if they themselves do not have to participate, but anarcho-capitalism does not require such a thing). Vegans are against the enslavement and killing of animals, often even using the formulation that they do not want to "take away the fruits of their labor"; theoretically they could be consistent statists, but only if they preferred foreign species to their own. Jains are great ascetics, they should not lie, kill, but above all their first vow is "not to take what is not given"; however, states are founded on the taking of what was not given. And finally, all anarchists - many of whom define themselves against anarcho-capitalism - reject the state, but often with it a voluntary hierarchy; but how can they prevent people from forming voluntary hierarchies without becoming a state?

title: A state-run and stateless society
text:
How is a state-run society different from a stateless one? In technology? In the management of some sectors of the economy? In centralization and decentralization? Maybe as a result too; however, they differ primarily in the absence of a coercive monopoly. Instead of an entity forcing people to do what they don't want to do and pay for things that aren't worth their money, as there is today, in a stateless society it would be left up to them to decide what they want to participate in and what they don't; that would be the most fundamental change - all others would
resulted
only from this and at the end of the day no one can predict what exactly and how it would actually happen. People often fear that no one would have "it" firmly in their hands; yes, he really shouldn't, but anyone who would like to have someone to transfer some of their rights, freedoms, powers or responsibilities to can hire him... does that sound absurd? Yes; just as absurd as when it comes to the state.

title: Job creation
text:
"Job creation" is seen as something desirable and positive; and indeed it often happens that way - if an entrepreneur employs someone, a job has been created, which typically enriches the company. However, we must not confuse the creation of a job with the creation of some useful value; if we create a job just so that someone has a job, values are not created that way - on the contrary. For example, if the government employs people to dig holes and bury them, clearly no value to society is created; however, the less obvious cases are more interesting. Whenever the state employs someone whom the people would not willingly pay, but must force them to do so,
there is waste
– people apparently value that money more than the products of the person's work; the same applies to jobs that do not fall directly under the state, but also to jobs in private companies that can fill them only because of subsidies. They are all variations on digging and burying holes...

title: Let's do business taxes!
text: Many (especially left-leaning) people rejoice when some politician raises their rich boss's taxes; the right question, in my opinion, is whether they even realize that if something like this happens, it will be them, among other things, who will have to earn from these high taxes. How is that? Heavily taxed firms have fewer funds; and since we live in a world of limited resources, taxed money will be missing somewhere. For example, in employee salaries; and even if not, the motivation of taxed entrepreneurs to increase those salaries in the future will decrease. Another place where scarcity can show is in the prices of a given firm's products; in the end, the customer pays those taxes as well (which is potentially also the rejoicing myopic leftists). And last but not least, the company may go bankrupt or be forced to cut costs by laying off some employees; So before you rejoice, ask who the bell is actually tolling...

title: We are canceling today's anarcho evening
text: Since there were COVID-positive people at Terezka's work, we are canceling today's anarcho evening; maybe there is nothing wrong with us, but we certainly cannot know, so we don't want to risk the suffocation of the Czech anarchist scene. title: What is a state?
text: Quite often in discussions about a free society I get that someone wants me to describe what I actually call a state; what else do I call a state and what no longer? A state is an entity that (negligibly successfully) usurps a monopoly on violence over some (negligibly large) territory it does not own; it is typically funded by involuntary contributions (it has the power to collect them, so why wouldn't it). Therefore, if one entrusts certain functions of today's state to a private company, it will not become a state just because of that, even if it will do "almost the same" as long as no one is forced to finance it and obey it. From this, in my opinion, it is quite clear why the state is such an evil: Relationships (business, personal, work... whatever) that are worth something are based on voluntariness; if something doesn't work on a voluntary basis, it's obviously not worth much, ergo it doesn't make sense to force it, because someone loses from it (if he didn't lose, he does it voluntarily).

title: Comparative advantage
text: Comparative advantage is one of David Ricardo's greatest discoveries; and what does it actually mean? Let's imagine a successful lawyer who is also a very good cyclist; yet it may be profitable for him to hire a messenger (on a bicycle) to deliver his package, though a lawyer could do it better and more quickly himself, yet, by attending to his work, he earns so much more that it pays him to send someone else with the package. This example is not exactly earth-shattering, and no one probably has a problem imagining it; But what does it mean? That mutual trade can pay off even when one party is no more efficient than the other; this is also true in international trade - even for states, one of which is "backward" in all respects, it can be mutually beneficial to trade. The concept of comparative advantage replaces the concept of absolute advantage (according to which a trade pays off when each party does something better than the other), which was introduced by Adam Smith.

title: We know what was wrong
text:
Ex post we often know very easily what went wrong in the past; we condemn slavery, torture, witch trials, serfdom, racism, Nazi and Communist regimes (at least mostly). Yet all those things were socially accepted and even desirable in "their" time; no one then thought of what horrors it was, although some pointed it out. How is that possible? Were people evil back then? I don't think so; I would say they are still more or less the same. So how could they do such a thing? Well, it was just normal back then and "everyone knew" it "was reality" and "there was no point in going head against the wall" and no practitioner cared about "castles in the air and naive theories" because everyone "lived in the here and now"; the only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing. And so I ask: Will we allow our descendants in the distant future to see how blind we are now to evil just because "everyone knows that
we need the state
"?

title: Public media
text: Let's imagine a medium owned by a private person, but it does not have to make money from itself; everyone has to pay it, regardless of whether it brings anything of value... and this is actually a public media (its owner is the biggest and most dangerous monopoly - i.e. the state - which, of course, promotes its interests through it like any other owner). The justification for such (mostly absurdly expensive) media is that they are supposed to be carriers of content that does not make money; but what does that mean? That people are simply not interested in that content, or rather they are more interested in the resources that the medium consumes; so we will "logically" force them to pay. They say we also need the public media to inform us about "crisis situations"; erm... when something critical happens (natural disasters, terrorist attacks...), does the private media keep quiet about it? No! On the contrary, they push back another agenda just so she can talk about what the people want.

title: Deceiving the consumer
text:
Deceiving consumers is prohibited by law: No one may deceive consumers, in particular by providing false, unsubstantiated, incomplete, inaccurate, unclear, ambiguous or exaggerated information, or withhold information about the real characteristics of products or services or the level of purchase conditions; all this under a fine of up to fifty million crowns. But how does the state treat its citizens, i.e. the consumers of its services? What does he tell them?
in schools
? For example, open lies about the fact that the free market cannot provide certain services (healthcare, social system, judiciary, money, etc.), therefore the state must (!) provide them; and it is not an "opinion", it is a demonstrable lie, because the market already provided those services in the past, until the governments took them over. And how would the state behave towards a businessman who would lie to his consumers in a similar way? Quite possibly similar to the mobsters who collect the booty; although the state itself does the same in a larger way and calls it taxes.

title: Bad banks
text:
People often call for state protection from bad capitalist banks; such a call would be laughable if it were not for crying. Why? Today's banks are not "bad capitalist" but "bad state". A free market bank has a business policy, provides people with its services, or issues money at its own discretion, and it is up to people to accept this money; if she misbehaves from their point of view, they can just get rid of her money.
Today's banks have a huge advantage from the state
, who gave them the ability to issue money, which he then forces people to accept, keep accounts in, and pay taxes in; it basically gives them the power of a cartel that they forcefully impose on us all. It is therefore paradoxical to call on the state to "protect" us against "bad banks"; it would be enough for the state to stop giving them the disgusting force-enforced privileges (control over the money they all have to receive) and let the free market solve the problem.

title: Anarchy and Capitalism
text:
"
Capitalism is the ultimate expression of anarchy and anarchy is the ultimate expression of capitalism.
" In my opinion, this quote best describes the essence of the life work of its author - Murray Newton Rothbard. Unfortunately, many (especially anarchists of other directions) do not understand it; so I would like to give them an explanation. Pure capitalism – i.e. a completely unregulated market – can only exist without state power, as any – even the smallest – tax distorts the market environment; the condition of pure capitalism is therefore a stateless environment, i.e. anarchy. And vice versa? In anarchy there is no central power to regulate anyone; people can freely exchange their goods and own the means of production, which is capitalism - even if they decide to live in communes and own the means of production communally (as long as no one is prevented from doing their own thing, which is the essence of anarchy, it will always be capitalism).

title: Interest
Prison
text:
Imagine someone doing something to you;
then what about that?
If it wasn't all that bad, you might welcome compensation; if it was something unforgivable that ruined your life, you might want to hurt that person as well (I personally find revenge unfortunate, but let's leave that aside for now). But who would use their money to build some kind of bizarre zoo on their property,
in which he would lock the offender
, guarded him there, fed him at his own expense and released him after a while? Apparently almost no one. So why in this way
we deal with those who break the law
? It is enough to obscure the circumstances of the payment a little, to hide from the people the fact that they are the ones who pay, to spread the costs among those who are not affected... and then it stops being absurd and we have a prison; a massive waste of resources, gathering criminals in one place where they learn the "craft" from each other and then releasing them into society - that's the state.

title: Price, cost, supply and demand
text: Most libertarians quite rightly understand the subjective theory of value and reject the cost theory; and indeed, the value of a property is purely subjective, changing with time and place, there is no such thing as "objective value". The price then depends on supply and demand; libertarians understand this too and take it into account in their reasoning. But sometimes they automate these thoughts so much that they fall into a logical trap and tend to claim that the price does not depend on the cost. However, this is nonsense; although price is determined not only by cost (and nothing else), but also by (among other things) cost! This does not contradict the law of supply and demand, price really depends on supply and demand, but supply is affected by (among other things) costs; of course, this is not contradicted by the fact that the found gem, for which I did not have to do anything, is worth the same as the hard-to-excave one, however, if it were possible to find clouds like this, it would already be reflected in the price.

title: Peace with drugs in the Cherubín teahouse
text:
Today at 7 p.m. we can meet live for the first time after the corona crisis - come and talk about drug issues and the war against drugs
to the Cherubín teahouse
. We like to return to the tea room for its unusually pleasant atmosphere; come try it too!

title: Abortion from the point of view of the NAP
text:
Sometimes during discussions about
non-aggression principle (NAPu)
the topic of abortion will come up; the child is the owner of his body, so it might seem that the mother has no right to end his life. But beware! There is a difference between killing someone (that is, that he would live without me, but as a result of my actions he will die - this is a clear violation of property rights to his body) and not helping him to survive (that is, that he could survive with my help, but as a result of my inaction, he will die - this is not a violation of property rights); I'm not saying it's virtuous to let someone die, but it's not aggression in my opinion. To step over a wounded man in the street I consider abominable, but to do violence to an unhelpful one inexcusable; I have similar criteria for not giving a transfusion to a dying person... and also for a mother who refuses to give her body for the child's survival. I personally don't like it, I don't agree with it, but in my opinion it is not a violation of the NAP and no one should force her to continue her pregnancy.

title: Good bankruptcy
text: When a company goes bankrupt, we perceive it as something bad or unfortunate; and indeed it is bad for its owners and employees. But from other people's point of view it is a necessary and healthy cleansing process; to understand this idea, we need to ask ourselves the situation in which businesses fail. This happens when the company's costs exceed its expenses in the long term, causing it to find itself at a loss; but what does that mean? That people value the resources a business consumes more than the goods it creates; that is, it wastes (consumes something valuable and produces something less valuable). The merciless market condemns such companies to extinction (or to a change in functioning); this is indeed unpleasant for the owner and employees, but good for everyone else, because someone more efficient will fill the vacancy on the market (otherwise he will suffer the same fate). Failure is a process that allows us to be surrounded by the best; others are doomed to go do something they are better at.

title: Social engineering
text: Anarcho-capitalists are sometimes accused of being social engineers because they "plan their utopia" which they then want to force on people; on the one hand, I can understand why some think this (anarcho-capitalism in their eyes can resemble some utopias planned by social engineers), on the other hand, nothing could be further from the truth. Anarcho-capitalists often talk about what a free market society might look like; however, they do it not because they wish to force it on someone in that form, but because they are constantly bombarded with questions like: "And how would this or that work without the state?" They then embark on various predictions that may at first glance resemble the utopian world of a social engineer; but the anarcho-capitalists only take it as an example, they wouldn't force it on anyone, because it contradicts the whole philosophy. We want to let people be free and not control anyone; this is the opposite of social engineering.

title: Property and human rights
text:
Anarcho-capitalists are often accused of dealing only with
property rights (or non-aggression principle)
, but they cough up human rights and "man" as such; here, I fear, is a pure misunderstanding of what anarcho-capitalism, the principle of non-aggression, and property rights actually mean. It is not only about the ownership of inanimate objects, but also (actually above all) about the fact that a person owns himself, his body; various "human rights" follow from this (for example, not to be killed, restricted in movement, harmed, etc.). True, these human rights are not defined in the same way as those in the Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms; mainly because, unlike LZPS, they are consistent (
The LZPS is not consistent, as it promises us rights that cannot be fulfilled without limiting some of the rights of other people
). Anarcho-capitalists are not indifferent to "human rights"; on the contrary – they are anarcho-capitalists because they really care.

title: Interest in politics
Lamenting the poverty of time
text: Socialists have always complained about the "poverty of the common man", typically advocating redistribution and robbery from the rich; however, I find it very interesting to see what they meant by "poverty" in which times. At first it meant when people didn't even have food; then it changed, the person who did not have enough comfortable housing was also called poor; over time, other conveniences were added; and today even the one who has something to eat, a place to live, a lot of free time and can even go on a more modest domestic vacation from time to time is already "poor". The state is supposed to help these "poor people". If the criteria of poverty will change like this, there will always be a reason to legalize robbery in the interest of the "poor" (they already live better today than the rich in the past). But what is it that keeps the poor doing better and better? By capitalism of course; the latter is not based on equality like socialism, but it creates so much wealth that "today's" poor have more than "yesterday's" rich.

title: Own housing for young people
text: We have a new "problem" in society: Young people do not have enough resources to buy their own housing, so they "have to" take out mortgages. All sorts of socialists lament where the world is going, what a horror it is and what we should do about it (ie how the state should solve it); and where is the world going? Well, to prosperity; this "problem" is completely illusory, because never in history have young people had enough resources to buy their own housing, this is nothing new. On the contrary, never in the past were the young (or even the old) so rich and so well provided for; we even live so well that we have forgotten that the initial state is poverty and wild inhospitable nature. Wealth, houses and technology are things that come with time; and the world is moving towards more and more young people owning their own homes... so that the socialists can whine that young people don't have their own jets.

title: Jobs
text: The doctrine of "job protection" is more or less based on the misconception of a limited number of jobs in the world (or in a country); however, this is a similar illusion to the thesis that the total wealth of the world is constant. However, neither of these is true; as wealth keeps increasing (just compare how we are now and how it was a few hundred years ago), people keep having more and more needs. Whereas before they were happy to have something to eat, today they want entertainment, travel, beautiful houses, cars... and when the time comes when they have all this, they will start wanting even more (other forms of entertainment, space travel, living on the seas or under the surface, hovercraft...). In connection with this, new jobs will be created all the time (and if one day machines do all the work, so much the better; people will not have to work, their needs will be met even without work, so they will have a lot of free time).

title: Let's regulate X!
text:
X can mean offensive violence, violation of property rights (murders, robberies, rape, destruction of other people's property...); let's leave that aside for now and talk about cases where X is anything else (i.e. non-violent, property-rights-respecting activity). So what does the call to regulate X mean? In reality, it is a call for the use of offensive violence against someone who is looking out for his own and does nothing to anyone. It means: "That man over there is doing something to himself and for himself that I don't like; let's make him stop doing it and submit to my will." If we say this sentence to an ignorant person, he will most likely condemn it unequivocally; yet the vast majority of them will support some such regulation.
At the same time, it is the same thing
, it differs only in wording. It is fascinating how powerful state propaganda is; because of her, it is enough just to reformulate the same thesis into the words presented to us by the state as "desirable"... and lo and behold, a clear rejection turns into consent.

title: Capitalist insatiable
text:
Many people dismiss crooked capitalists as "just after the money"; but what does it mean when someone in the free market (that is, without violating property rights) "goes after the money" and makes money? Such a person buys something (and consumes), sells something (not necessarily creates, but can); either it is an entrepreneur who buys resources (material, labor...) and transforms them into a product, or a speculator (or intermediary) who buys what he sells later (or elsewhere). In both cases, the value he consumed is less than the value he provided to others (even in the case of the speculator - let's not forget that value is subjective and changes over time, the cost theory of value has been disproved); his profit then expresses how much he has enriched society. Of course, a capitalist whose highest value is money may not be exactly the best life partner; to those who trade with him, however
it clearly benefits
.

title: Who "rules" in capitalism?
text: The first superficial answer might be that they are huge multinational corporations; however, for a deeper understanding, it is necessary to ask what makes the huge corporations so huge, where they actually get their influence. The truth is that they are given this size, power and money by their own customers, the "common people"; they are the ones from whom the power comes in the free market, they are the ones who rule in the free market society! If the economy were a ship, corporations are the helmsmen or the officers commanding the crew, but the customer is the captain who determines the course of the voyage; if a corporation does not serve those who voluntarily buy from it, it will not have access to their money and will lose its power. Someone may argue that a sufficiently large and powerful corporation does not need voluntary customers, because it can ignore their will and force them to pay; of course that risk exists... and such a corporation is then called in one word: the state.

title: Hated capitalism
World injustice
text: I often hear people on below-average pay talking hatefully about the "top 10 percent" and the like; they perceive it as a huge injustice that they are not among them. I find it utterly absurd; why? Because they typically belong! Even poor people in the Czech Republic are among the richest people in the world. We live in one of the richest parts of the world and here we are like pigs in the rye; all of us (even those factory workers and supermarket saleswomen) belong to the "top ten percent" (and many quite possibly even to the top five percent). Even those who live "from hand to mouth" here do not suffer from hunger (unlike masses of people around the world); unlike the majority, these people often have free weekends, work approximately eight hours a day and somehow make ends meet... but they complain that they don't have more free time, more money for better vacations, a car and the like. And when society gets even richer, they will complain that they don't have yachts, because some do.

title: Government of the people
text:
Imagine a decentralized society where people express their will through market exchanges; what they like and what they want
voluntarily finance
, while they will simply not pay for goods they are not interested in, thus clearly expressing their preferences. Projects, the outputs of which people value less than the resources they consume, will simply not arise, because in this society there will be a lack of means to implement them, since no one will distribute them by force. In contrast, let's imagine another company that functions more or less like the last one... except, sort of
democratically elected government
it subsidizes some loss-making projects (against the wishes of those with whose money it does so) and taxes and regulates some profitable ones; as a result of these interventions, some things are created against the will of the payers and others are not created, although people would like them (they are prohibited or disadvantaged). The rather fundamental question then is: Which of the two variants is more "government of the people"?

title: Homo economicus
text: Economic man is a theoretical construct used in some economic models; this is a hypothetical person who only tries to maximize his (financial) profits, buy as cheaply as possible, sell as expensive as possible and, moreover, always behaves completely logically. This model was sharply criticized by Austrian economists (especially Ludwig von Mises) for its apparent discrepancy with reality; any conclusions drawn from similar assumptions cannot then be used for the real world, because in it people simply behave differently (although they always try to maximize their benefit, not only the financial one, but also the complex one, i.e. also the emotional one). The Austrian school of economics, on which, for example, anarcho-capitalism is based, counts on real people; in connection with this, I find it absolutely absurd how often homo economicus is presented to Austrians or anarcho-capitalists as a mistake in their thinking, although they themselves point to it.

title: State employee taxes
text:
Why do civil servants pay taxes? Well... first of all, it must be said that they are paid formally, but not in reality. The state takes money under threat of violence from anyone who earns it in the private sector; those who are already paid by the state also theoretically pay taxes, but this is just an accounting trick: the state gives them X and takes Y; in fact, he could just give them X minus Y, take nothing, and it would come out the same. Why isn't that the case? Firstly, in order to make the civil servants themselves feel that they are not supporting themselves on other taxpayers (and they are succeeding, see the famous statement of the unnamed official: "If we, the civil servants, were not there, who would pay taxes on all those self-employed people?"); and secondly, to put these people in as much of a "normal light" as possible. But it should be normal to provide services based on voluntary payments; certainly not to be paid with money that belonged to someone
taken away under threat of violence
. Stop the state!

title: How much is a human life worth?
text:
In connection with the coronavirus, many are beginning to address the cost of human life in the sense of how much money it makes sense to pay to keep someone from dying; and two currents of opinion are most common:
1/ Some calculation of GDP per capita, or the market price of the values produced by a person after deducting the costs of his education and the like.
2/ The value of human life is incalculable; and anyone who attempts such a thing is disgusting, inhumane and reprehensible.
I don't agree with either approach. The first does not take into account the non-monetary benefit; the other reality (its logical consequence would be to spend all existing resources only on saving lives; no one should devote their time or money to anything else). So what is my answer? The price of each of us is different; and to save each individual it makes sense to spend just as many resources as people (including him) are willing to voluntarily pay, but not more than he himself would wish. The universal price of human life is about as much nonsense as the statement that all men are the same.

title: Failure of the individual
text:
Until
Freeport Forums
someone shared a strange text about police buzzing. Since it was only about the length of Stok, I asked the author if I could publish it here (under her name). She declined, saying she did not want to bring the police into disrepute because of an individual's failure. I respect her wishes; for those interested
I'm just posting a link
. However, I ask how obvious systemic defects of the state are people willing to excuse the failure of individuals? Yes, an individual has sinned; but what to expect if we give power to a handful of individuals selected from among those who want to be policemen under the present conditions? Or politicians - if people get power who first climb through internal party struggles to the top and then do the best PR in the election campaign, how will they govern? When a private firm cheats a customer, no one blames the particular employee at the counter where he signed the contract; so why does everyone in the state blame the employees, but almost no one blames the entire institution?

title: Dan Steigerwald in deCentral: The lecture will be, we have an exception from the government
text:
Dan Steigerwald will be speaking at deCentral today; since Babiš is a big fan of anarcho-capitalism, we negotiated a government exemption for this event.
However, in case anyone doesn't believe it, the identical lecture will be repeated on the first Wednesday of the next month, i.e. May 6th.

title: I choose you, Prymula!
text:
Because Vojtěch is a handsome man, but also a singer and a lawyer, Babiš pulled another ace up his sleeve: "I'm choosing you, Prymulo." An epidemiologist could be the winning horse in solving the epidemic! And wisdom is already falling from him; on the one hand, masks until there are zero infected, which I understand. But then we have a proposal to first ban discount events. Like seriously? Isn't it enough that government measures (some of which I think are reasonable) will hurt the economy and people won't have enough money? Will we still take away the opportunity to buy at a discount? In addition, I would be worried about the temporary nature of such a measure.
However, I consider the declaration of closing the borders for months to years to be much more fundamental. Yes, there were times when such a measure made sense; those were exactly the times when Babiš and Vojtěch told us that everything was under control and there was nothing to fear. Closing the borders in the past could have prevented the infection from reaching the Czech Republic. Now it's here; and it spreads. If its spread could be stopped and the infected isolated, of course closing the borders would make sense; but this will be done within the next few weeks (which is the question), or never (the infection will get out of control). If the infection will spread worldwide (which it probably will) and the prevalence of infected people in the Czech Republic will not differ significantly from the prevalence abroad, why keep the borders closed?

title: Profiting from someone else's misfortune is...
text: All my life - and especially in recent days - I hear that "profiting from the misfortune of others" is morally reprehensible, pathetic, scumbag and the like. Can someone (logically) explain why it is wrong when someone helps people in need and gets paid (perhaps a lot) for it? When I imagine myself in need, I would rather be the person who offers to help me for a lot of money than the person who offers nothing and just condemns the first one. An offer of help for big money can be rejected. So how can it be worse than no offer at all? Why is the one who helps dearly so often perceived worse than the one who doesn't help at all? At worst, I won't use expensive help, which makes it at least as useful as no help at all. And finally, it is not clear to me why people who so condemn "making money from other people's misfortune" usually respect firefighters and doctors, who live directly from other people's misfortune?

title: National self-sufficiency
text:
The doctrine of "national self-sufficiency" has long been quite popular; and like many popular things it doesn't make much sense on closer inspection. First, let's ask why self-sufficiency should only be at the level of a nation; wouldn't it be even better to be self-sufficient at the city level? Street? Or even families? Or to make everyone self-sufficient? Such ideas obviously do not make sense, as they would plunge us into poverty through absence
division of labor
. But how does protectionism differ on a smaller and larger scale? Only in that it is more visible in the smaller; economic laws also apply internationally: Production (for example, food) within the state suffers from the same ailments as production (for example, food) within the household; it is more efficient for everyone to specialize in what they are good at (and then exchange the resulting product with others on the free market) than for everyone to do everything. For the division of labor means wealth; isolationism and protectionism poverty.

title: Usury
text:
Most people condemn usury; however, I maintain that this is a clearly positive phenomenon. Why? If someone offers someone a loan with a dizzyingly high interest rate, there are two possibilities: Either the recipient rejects the offer, then nothing happened and the situation is the same as if the offer had not occurred; or they agree, which means that the borrower himself considers the situation when he takes the loan to be better than the situation when he refuses it (otherwise he would not borrow). What does this mean? That the creditor offered him a better alternative, whereby
improved his situation
(according to the borrower's own standards); this applies regardless of the borrower's desperate situation or the amount of interest. Whoever does not like it, let him compete with the lender and offer the poor man a loan on better terms; if he does not, the criticism of usury is then utter insolence from his mouth. Why? Especially because he didn't do as much for the borrower as the usurer, who at least offered him an alternative to a desperate situation (albeit a desperate one)!

title: Who would solve... the coronavirus without the state?
text: People have been asking me lately how pandemics would be handled in a stateless society; who would keep people in quarantine? Well, security forces, people with guns - just like today. Only they would not be subject to governments, but to private security agencies operating in the area. They would act in the interests of clients; and in the interest of health insurance companies, which should have a direct financial incentive to participate. So what would be the difference? First, in the responsibility of all actors – while a politician can screw up anything and bears no personal responsibility, market entities pay for mistakes (an unnecessarily extensive quarantine can bring a whirlwind of lawsuits and the recovery of compensation for restricting personal freedom; lax actions lead to loss of customers, reputation or money); and secondly, without the state, no one would come up with such stupid ideas as banning disease testing by private laboratories or regulating the price of respirators (which reduces the incentive to quickly produce more).

title: EU versus battery
text:
The EU is not only trying to
unification of chargers
; is trying to force cell phone manufacturers to produce only devices with replaceable batteries. It might seem that such a thing would help us; but is it really so? First of all, there isn't much consumer interest in it; if it was, manufacturers would offer such phones as a competitive advantage. However, most people like to switch phones and buy new, faster, better-featured ones; on the other hand, those who put off buying a new phone for years (like me) can buy a power bank for a few hundred. And secondly, integrated batteries also offer technological advantages: their shape adapts better to the phone, which saves space or increases capacity; in addition, they are better insulated against moisture and dirt. Although I am one of those consumers who would appreciate replaceable batteries, I don't want to impose my preferences on others; let the market decide, not the EU.

title: EU versus chargers
text: For several years, the EU has been trying to force manufacturers to unify chargers for all mobile phones and some other devices. On the face of it, this is good customer service; but what about the second and third look? First, gradual unification occurs in the market even without legislation; USB-C is a fairly widely accepted standard, so anyone interested in it has a pretty decent choice. And secondly – let's imagine that the EU had managed to push through such legislation ten or fifteen years ago; what would happen As a universal adapter, something that was used to charge at the time would probably be promoted then; and over which it typically could not transfer data. If we had preserved the development with such legislation, we would probably not have reached what we have today, i.e. a single cable for both charging and data transmission. The question is: What will we lose in the next ten years if we maintain development at the current standard?

title: Totality yesterday, today and tomorrow
text:
Totality does need some ideology to function, but not a specific one - almost any one can serve, even if some are more suitable. Of course, a totalitarian regime can be based on the divinity of the ruler, the purity of the race, the class struggle, but also on anything else from the practically endless number of possibilities that the human imagination offers. The way the state functions and its practices matter far more than a specific ideology. Totality does not lie in divinity, racial purity, or working class; it consists in controlling (almost) all aspects of people's lives, and it doesn't matter what ideology the state uses to justify these practices. In practice, this means, among other things, that every further regulation, every further extension of legislation, every further mandatory register and data collection, every further control of our lives – these are all steps towards totalitarianism; completely regardless of what we justify and excuse them with.
This is something that most people are unfortunately not aware of, so the individual ideologies of the past are demonized that we are wary of, but at the same time we are blind to the real totalitarian threats that we face every day. What are they like?
That's what I lectured about
on
Freeport Conference 2020: Totality yesterday, today and tomorrow
.
I am too
published an article on the Mises.cz server
, who inspired us to organize the conference.

title: How would the free market solve...?
text: If I had to say which question I answer most often in life, it would certainly be variations on the theme of how the free market would solve this or that; the paradox is that I can never answer with certainty. I only give people - for better or worse - guesses; not that I can't imagine various free market solutions, quite the opposite in my imagination, but firstly, I can never know which of the possibilities would arise, and secondly, I consider it very likely that the millions of entrepreneurs in the free market trying to get rich solving any problem will come up with something far better than I can ever think of. After all... if the free market could be predicted, it could also be centrally planned. So you can see my answers as a worst-case-scenario; imagine yourself (or others who have actually done so) how you would have estimated the form of capitalism today a hundred years ago. Life has more imagination than we carry in our dreams; and the free market likesmet!

title: Tax havens
text:
Tax havens are (as a result of massive state propaganda) widely hated; the people who pay taxes there, the state (and, as a result, many citizens) try to portray them as pariahs. So are tax havens harming us? No! Quite the opposite. Firstly, it is necessary to realize that untaxed money is not "stolen" (on the contrary -
taxes are robbery
and not taking them away is a defense against it); secondly, this money will not disappear anywhere, only politicians will not decide how to spend it, but those who earned it (which is only good); thirdly, even a company that would pay no taxes at all is definitely a positive force in the economy as long as it sustains itself (it provides customers with values that they value, otherwise they would not willingly pay for them); and finally, fourthly, tax havens mean competition for tax hells (states with high taxes risk companies moving to states with low taxes). I am happy for every tax haven and entrepreneur who pays taxes there instead of here.

title: Are we living in capitalism?
text:
Capitalists and socialists mostly agree on one thing; and Mises already agreed with Marx: Capitalism means that the means of production have private owners; in socialism, the state owns the means of production. So far we are clear. However, many sometimes forget that it is quite clear from this definition that "pure" capitalism or socialism will be rather exceptional states; we mostly live in a society that is to some extent capitalist and to some extent socialist (so capitalism and socialism is not binary). Because everyone tends to notice primarily things that don't work the way they wish, socialists like to say we live in capitalism, while capitalists say the opposite; how to find out who is closer to the truth? Even if we leave aside that, especially nowadays, it is not entirely clear what a "means of production" is, we come across the fact that there is a difference between who owns something de jure and who owns it de facto.
Let's imagine a hypothetical situation where the state completely decides on the means of production, but de jure the owners of the enterprises are "white horses" (they do not decide on anything); this state is undoubtedly de facto pure socialism (Hitler's National Socialism came close). In today's over-regulated world, the state does not have exclusive decision-making power, but with its regulations it de facto deprives the owner of the means of production of part of their ownership (not de jure); legislation enforces how they can deal with property, affects prices, salaries and working conditions, and in addition, we pay most of what we create to the state in taxes. To what extent the means of production are owned by the state and to what extent by the formal owner, it is impossible to say, as the degree of individual legislative restrictions is often subjective; we therefore live in partial capitalism and partial socialism (except for the sectors where the state is the de facto and formal owner; these are purely socialist).

title: Who is talking about market failure?
text: Have you noticed what examples people typically cite as so-called "market failures"? Well, the ones where their preferences differ from what others want, so the market will decide differently than they would like. A classic "market failure" is, for example, the demolition of a beautiful building in the name of allowing a supermarket to stand on the site; but what does that mean? Only so much that people's utility from that supermarket is higher than from that building; if this were not the case, those who want to maintain the status quo could buy the land for as much money as the buyers are not willing to spend (otherwise, they obviously get more use out of the land). The so-called "market failure" is then called by the statists who want the building and are not satisfied with the result of peaceful voluntary exchanges, while the supposed "correction" of the situation is to force free people to do what the statists force them to do instead of what they want.

title: GDP
text: Many people take this economic indicator very seriously; for some she is almost an idol. I am not claiming that this figure is completely useless, in reality it can be used to compare the wealth of different states very roughly (seriously very roughly) (at least by order of magnitude; if the GDP of one state is one percent higher than the GDP of another, it does not mean anything, the difference in large tens or small hundreds of percent does); however, its growth does not necessarily mean something good. There are a number of problems with this indicator; however, I consider the biggest to be mixing pears with apples (sometimes rotten) - the state adds its expenses to the value of the goods that are traded on the free market. Even if the state paid thousands of people to dig holes and bury them, GDP would increase despite the obvious futility of this activity (the same goes for all other state waste); on the other hand, the gray economy, which undoubtedly helps people, is not included in GDP... so watch out for that.

title: VAT on beer?
text: Alcoholic beer has a VAT of 21%; tapped on site has a VAT of 10%. Non-alcoholic beer has a VAT of 15%; VAT is 10% on the spot. On-site means beer at a store with facilities and not in a pitcher. Period, that's all. Although I welcome any criticism of Babiš, the government, or even the state, has this really become the most fundamental problem of the last few days? We live in a total legislative jungle of absolutely confusing and incredibly complex laws; running the smallest business means a lot of bureaucracy. And nobody really minds; not enough to make it a hot topic. Is VAT on beer really our biggest problem? Yes, let's criticize VAT on beer. But isn't the more substantial criticism of the existence of multiple VAT rates? And an even more substantial criticism of the existence of VAT itself? And the far more important criticism of the existence of taxation? And are taxes really what the state oppresses us the most?

title: Unemployment policy
text: The state has created a labor code that purportedly seeks to "protect employees"; realistically, it may in some ways "protect" the existing ones, but it definitely discourages employers from hiring others. How is that? The state does not protect those employees at its own expense, but at the expense of the employers; of course, they would employ new people more willingly if it did not entail these additional costs. And not only that! The state burdens all potential entrepreneurs with huge bureaucracy (and taxes); although a fired saleswoman could open her own business (a sales stand, for example), which would not be as complicated as it is today without legislative restrictions (accounting, taxes, hygiene standards, EET...). However, regulations reduce the number of employers and increase the number of unemployed, which, due to the law of supply and demand, fundamentally worsens the position of employees and the unemployed on the labor market. And politicians have things to deal with; the circle closes.

title: Unreasonable profit
text:
Recently, for the fourth time in my life, a communist (each time a different one) with whom I had a discussion claimed to me that due to the profits made by every entrepreneur in the chain of production (i.e. mining - ore processing - manufacturing of components - assembly of products), all products are five times overpriced, so that if production were nationalized, without those profits they would be available for only twenty percent of today's price (and since everyone said the same number, I assume that somewhere read but I couldn't find where); I'm not going to explain why this is nonsense, which I've already done anyway
elsewhere
, but I ask: If this is really the case, why instead of nationalization, why don't socialists simply create free market enterprises without profits that will produce goods five times cheaper and thereby crush capitalist competition to dust, if they can deliver goods to the people so much better than the greedy capitalists?

title: Gray economy
text:
Politicians (and not only them) like to convince us of the harmfulness of the gray economy; it is said to harm society, which becomes poorer because of it, because people pay less taxes to the state. First of all, I would like to point out that the state and society are two different things; while society is all of us, the state is a parasitic entity that drains the productive ones of us. Above all, as a result of the gray economy, no money "disappears" anywhere; although the state cannot deal with them, they remain in people's wallets. So when the finance minister talks about how much money we are "losing" due to the gray economy, what he really means is that it is not he (the parasite) who is spending those resources, but us (the hosts); it's definitely not bad, on the contrary -
we know much better how to spend our money
, than some fool. Not to mention that even if we didn't know, it was our property and it was up to us what we would do with it; each the engineer, train driver and train driver of his own luck.

title: State and ownership
text:
Is the state the guarantor of private property? He definitely claims to be one; and indeed it is to some extent. Specifically, to the extent that he tries to force himself
a monopoly on infringing the property rights of others
, in which he rebuffs other entities when they try to do the same; so yes, the state protects people's private property - but only against robbers other than the state itself. As a result of the state usurping this function, many even believe that without it private property would not exist at all; however, this is a deep mistake, because people probably started appropriating things long before the emergence of states (primitive man already used primitive tools), not to mention that even in times and places where the power of the state did not reach (for example, the USA during the time of colonization or Iceland in the early Middle Ages), the institution of private property did not disappear. So let's not be mistaken - property rights do not have to be enforced by state power.

title: Technological standards
text: Some people still believe today that we need the state to enforce technological standards; one socialist even told me in our recent discussion that without the state we wouldn't even screw in a screw because the thread would have a different width, pitch and tooth profile. Why the example with the screw is absurd, probably everyone understands at first glance: It does not make economic (or logical) sense to make a screw if I know nothing about the thread (I'd rather make both). But let's take the statement as a metaphor; what about standards for more complex technologies? If a standard is good, it pays free people in a free market to follow it; the manufacturer wants to sell his creations, which he will not do well if the buyers are unable to use them (for example, because he does not screw the screw xD). Many Internet protocols, barcodes, payment cards, USB and countless others - these are all standards that arose without state coercion...

title: Lack of humility or its excess?
text: Libertarians are sometimes accused of being self-proclaimed "everything experts" who suffer from a lack of humility when they claim that the free market can provide everything that the state now provides better and to the greater satisfaction of the people; but is there really a lack of humility behind these claims? Personally, I think it's just the opposite: Libertarians don't believe that there can be any central planner (politician, official, or more) who can make better decisions about people's affairs than they do; libertarians—unlike statists—are humble enough not to think they know what's best for others, so they don't feel called to force others to act according to their idea of a "right world." And so I am asking everyone - let's be humble, let people act, because everyone is the best expert on how to lead their life; let's calmly advise people, let's help them... but without offensive violence.
