title: Why did the state buy an e-shop for 400 megabytes?
text:
Yesterday I wrote about
state e-shop for 400 mega
. Today I would like to answer the question, how can the state afford such a thing? Well, it's quite simple. The state is not a free market firm; not serving customers. It is a monopoly on violence; and as an organization it does not have to answer to the citizens for anything. In case of major misconduct, he can punish and replace someone from his ranks, if it helps PR; but he doesn't have to change anything about the principles of his operation, because of which those errors occur, because he has power, so it's easier for him to ban competition than to do things for people. The main problem with the 400 meg e-shop is not the price; it is the involuntariness of the whole transaction that allows it to take place under such conditions at all. And complaining about the prize is, as the anarcho-capitalist Dan Steigerwald said, "...like a woman who was raped in a park complaining about not getting a flower and then being left lying in the mud."

title: E-shop for 400 mega from erar
text:
The state transport infrastructure fund bought the e-shop for highway signs for 400 mega without a tender; and everyone is on edge. Why? Well, because it's expensive. And because no sane person will buy an e-shop with five and a half items for 400 million crowns. Clearly an overpriced order! And how do we know? Simply; we know how much e-shops cost on the market. And we assume that government purchases should move in similar relationships as market ones. Well, when they differ by an order of magnitude, the hype in the media space begins. Just as Americans didn't like it when the U.S. Army
she bought a toilet seat for 45 thousand crowns or a hammer for 30 thousand.
.
We all know how much an e-shop (or a toilet seat or a hammer) should cost; but we know this only and only because there are also market prices in the corresponding industry; if they didn't exist, we have no idea. Well... and exactly this situation actually occurs in sectors where the state has a monopoly position; no one knows how much not only Pandora, but also services such as courts, police and education are supposed to cost. In those sectors, market mechanisms are almost absent, prices are more or less determined by states; and no one has anything to judge by how much they correspond to reality and how much someone would be willing to pay realistically for services of the given quality. We just trust the state that this will definitely not be overpriced; for when such excesses occur where they are easily discovered, certainly no civil servant or politician will allow himself to do such a thing where, in principle, it cannot even be discovered.

title: Surplus value
text: Surplus value is the cornerstone of the communist justification of revolutionary violence of the "proletarian working class" against the "exploiters"; and unfortunately, such an explanation makes sense not only to communists: Workers produce goods that have some value, the capitalist sells them, pays part of the money taken to the employees, spends part on other expenses related to production and keeps part (which is precisely the surplus value). However, this thinking completely ignores the subjectivity of value; nothing has an objective value in itself, that is attributed to goods by people. What does this mean? That there is no such thing as surplus value; the capitalist buys people's labor at the market price (for the worker, obviously, this price is higher than the value of that labor, otherwise they would not work for him; for the employer, it is the opposite, otherwise he would not employ them) and then sells the produced goods at the market price to customers (because for them their value is higher than this price).

title: There is no evil as evil
text:
Totalitarianism is a state in which a state seeks to control almost all aspects of its subjects' lives on a vast scale.
Dictatorship is the rule of a narrow group (or individual).
Democracy is the rule of the majority.
Fascism is a totalitarian dictatorship with significant elements of egalitarianism (collectivism), nationalism, militarism and certain forms of progressivism.
Nazism is a combination of fascism with racism (the theory of a superior race) and anti-Semitism.
If we proceed from these (generally accepted) definitions, we reach the following (generally neglected) conclusions: Totality does not have to be a dictatorship; dictatorship does not have to be totalitarian (although it typically is). A democracy cannot be a dictatorship, but it can be a totalitarianism (and sometimes it is; the rule of the majority may want to control almost every aspect of its subjects' lives). Nazism and fascism are not the same thing; fascism need not be racist or anti-Semitic (Nazism is). Not every dictatorship or totalitarianism is fascism. A police state is totalitarian, but it doesn't have to have a dictator; even the rule of law can be totalitarian (if there are sufficiently repressive laws). Democracy means the rule of the majority, not freedom and certainly not "goodness" or "protection of minorities".

title: Competitive struggle on a long-term scale
text:
Years ago I wrote about why
dumping
,
cartel agreements
a
monopolies
they do not represent a serious problem for the free unregulated market; readers accept my explanations as long as they are fields that do not have very high natural entry costs into the industry, but they often write to me that where these costs are high, my arguments become invalid. The truth is that the mechanisms I described work the same in such industries, only more slowly; on this basis, many believe that these "lags in response" by competition will increase the incentive for entrepreneurs to "commit unfair practices". However, they forget that the very high entry costs of the industry reduce this motivation: If you spend decades and many resources to gain a dominant position in a "slow and expensive" industry, it does not make sense to risk a position there for a temporary increase in profits; this is more likely to be done by those who do not have much to lose (and the competition reacts quickly to them).

title: A quarter of a century since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard
text: Today is exactly twenty-five years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism" left this world at the age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

title: What if there was no X without the state?
text: You can put absolutely anything behind X... roads, schools, charity, research... just anything. After you do that, two possibilities arise: Either we need X so much that we are willing to voluntarily pay more than what the cost of that X is; or we don't need, which means the resources we're willing to sacrifice on X won't cover the cost. In the first case, anyone who starts providing X can make money (people will pay him more than what it costs to produce X if the condition above is met); there is no point in doubting whether X would be available, because without the state it might be difficult to provide it - what can be made, someone will take care of it. In the event that we are not willing to pay the above costs for X, then X will most likely not occur at all; and that's only a good thing, because under the circumstances providing it would be wasteful (people value X less than the resources expended on it).

title: Aggression or non-aggression? That's what's going on here!
text:
Although most people support regulations and laws implemented through the threat of violence against the innocent, virtually everyone condemns the threat of violence against the innocent; do you feel the contradiction? When against the regulations
I argue with this very violence
, the reactions tend to be like through a photocopier: The person in question will first say that it is absurd; when I explain to him that violence by the state against the innocent is serious, he goes off topic and starts arguing that "it wouldn't be possible without it" (even if he were right, it doesn't disprove my claim that violence does happen; on the contrary, it confirms it); when I point it out, it's followed by another unjustified rejection, or other reasons why it doesn't work, at best a very reluctant acknowledgment. However, for most people it is a problem to even say such a thing (even though it is obvious); they prefer to pretend it just isn't happening. That is why I think most people do not accept state violence; rather they turn a blind eye to him. Let's show them the truth!

title: Information protection
text: People increasingly care about who stores what information about them; many are sensitive to it, some even so that someone does not make money based on it (targeted advertising, offering related goods and the like - I personally mostly welcome these practices, but I fully understand that someone does not). The question is why the same people who are so bothered by private entities collecting (quite superficial) information about them do not mind having (very crucial and sensitive) information collected by the state; and if it's just them themselves... they very often don't understand and downplay when it bothers someone else (for example, arguments against EET based precisely on the collection of sensitive information have been widely ridiculed). But the state is not an embodied good; the people handling that information in it are no better than those in the private sector (and for various reasons I'd say that on average it will even be the opposite).

title: Wars and progress
Free market regulation
text:
Most people imagine the free market as an absolute jungle where no regulations apply and everyone does whatever they want; to some extent this is true, but not completely. Of course, the free market is not bound by violent state regulations, but this does not mean that we cannot regulate the behavior of others without the state in any way. We have a chance
to reward those who behave as we wish
, and deny reward to those who do something we do not like; it's up to us who we do business with. Does anyone dislike animal testing? Fine, don't buy them; and the more people you convince to do the same, the more animals you save. If you are successful enough in such an endeavor, over time those who do not test on animals will dominate the market. In a free market, regulations arise naturally; one that people are really interested in, so they are able to demonstrate it with actions, not just words.

title: Murray Christmas 2019!
text:
And here they are again; my beloved Christmas! Christian clergy; capitalistically material; and for me personally, anarchistically non-violent, because we arrange them with our loved ones in our own way and in such a way that we only do what we really want to do. So my inner Christian, capitalist and anarchist rejoices. At the same time, Christmas shows us (libertarians) a PR masterpiece that we (Christians) succeeded thousands of years ago: The original pagan established holiday of Saturnalia was transformed into Christmas. This is something like if we turned Czech Statehood Day into a celebration of anarchy; I think we still have a lot of work to do in this regard. So go for it!
Carols are an inherent part of Christmas, so I'll start as always
the best
, because Freddie will never die...
Pentatonix singing carol in church
for me, they are a symbol of the transformation of a society in which the church murdered homosexuals into a tolerant society; and although some may see in it the destruction of traditional values, I personally see in it God's love for each (!) of us. And since, in my opinion, God's love is closely related to music, I already decided last year not to limit myself to carols; this year I would like to remember the deceased
Tom Petty
and I certainly don't want to miss out
Glitch Mob
. If I didn't meet your taste, hopefully it will be better next time.
Please don't be mean to each other, respect the property rights of others, love your neighbor, don't initiate offensive violence, don't hurt, don't regulate the free market, be willingly in solidarity and don't force those who don't want to - and don't exalt yourself over people who don't share our values; all these things are very closely related. Let's try to find a common language with others, spread the ideas of freedom, think critically about them and get rid of dogmas; violence begets violence, malice begets malice, hate begets hate, but banning it and restricting its expression will always bring more evil. Whenever we release our anger, the world becomes a slightly worse place; whenever kindness emanates from us, we make the world a little better. So let us not harm our enemies either, unless it is absolutely necessary; if they are hurt and frustrated, so much the worse for them, but also for us and our loved ones. Life is not a zero-sum game; and not relationships at all.
In conclusion, let me
remind this
and to quote one of the wisest men: “
Enjoy yourself.
"
MURRAY CHRISTMAS!!
(Who will write to me again this year that it's a typo? xD)

title: NAP and veganism
text:
O
I have already written a lot about the principle of non-aggression
; maybe that's why vegans ask me more and more often why I don't apply it to animals. The answer is that the principle of non-aggression is based on property rights that animals not only do not observe and understand, but are not (and it seems likely never will be) capable of understanding; then it makes no sense to me to recognize these rights towards them (if there were animals that understood property rights, I would reconsider my position). I completely understand and fully respect even those who do not want to use animals to increase their utility and I will not talk them out of it (I even consider it a certain virtue); however, I believe that choosing otherwise is not worse (nor better) in principle. And just as vegans question why I apply the NAP to humans but not to animals in general, one might ask why we don't just extend the NAP to all living things (which would mean starving to death). Does anyone know the answer?

title: "Our" resources
text: "Our" raw material wealth; "our" jobs; "our" country; and sometimes even "our" doctors (who, for example, brazenly dare to leave the Czech Republic, which was a huge issue a few years ago). We can often come across these - and many other similar - expressions in the sense that "our" means Czech; ideas and theses that arise from similar assumptions tend to be completely misguided. Why? Well, raw materials have an owner, ergo they are his; to declare them "our Czechs" denies this ownership; lands on the territory of the Czech Republic also belong to their owners, not to "us" all; and "our" doctors, that's total nonsense. What is especially mean about this argument is that it operates with a kind of quasi-property, which, however, contradicts property rights; therefore, whoever says: "My country, my rules," means the Czech Republic and indicates that "he has the right" to (jointly) decide here, thereby denying the very statement from which (my country, my rules) is based, with regard to the owners of specific plots of land in the given territory.

title: Anarchist at heart, capitalist at heart
text:
Some time ago I spoke with an anarcho-communist; among other things, we discussed his idea that everyone should "have the right" to an apartment or a house, because housing and a sense of security are among the basic human needs. I countered that although most people probably feel that way, someone may prefer other things to housing. He looked at me sheepishly and came up with the analogy that it's like if he bought everyone chocolate and I'd blame him for spoiling them because someone would prefer a donut to chocolate; he apparently missed that the state and the socialists are buying these people with their money. But that's beside the point now; as I reflected on our conversation on the way home, one thing dawned on me: We both want the same thing. Seriously. And what is it? We want people to be happy. The only difference between us is that while he is some kind of intuitive supporter of an objective theory of value, I understand that value is subjective.
Sometimes you ask me why I feel closer to anarcho-communists than to the conservative right; and this is the reason: While I am separated from the anarcho-communist and his idea of "housing for everyone" by a different perception of the theory of value, from the conservative rightist and his "defense of the traditional family" (as a result of which, for example, homosexuals suffer, which he knows and doesn't care) I am separated by... I don't know... humanity? When an anarcho-communist tells me "a flat for everyone", I understand that my aim is to explain to him that we live in a world of limited resources and to show Bastiat's "what is not seen"; however, when a staunch conservative tells me that he rejects gay marriage because "it's unnatural" (which probably won't be his real reason, because he's also not in favor of throwing away antibiotics and dying of infections, because it's natural) and "marriage between a man and a woman is among traditional millennial values" (but he doesn't want slavery with an even longer tradition), what am I supposed to think?

title: Death to speculators!
text: Nobody likes speculators; we still forgive the unsuccessful ones, because they have already eaten it, but the successful ones are condemned by the majority society. What do I say to that? These reactions are not only illogical and absurd, but above all completely inverted; for the successful speculator helped others, while the unsuccessful one harmed others. The market is not a zero-sum game! Property prices are subjective and change over time. If there is an excess of something, the price will fall; in case of shortage it will rise. A clever speculator will buy in times of surplus (helping bankrupt producers by raising the price) to sell in times of need (helping consumers by lowering the price); the person in question essentially "smooths out" price fluctuations over time. When he gets it wrong, he can do the opposite, harming others and paying dearly for it himself (as much as he harms them); paradoxically, only criticisms of unsuccessful speculators can be considered justified, but they harmed themselves in the first place.

title: Economic cycles
text:
People often think of business cycles (periods of rapid growth alternating with crises) as something that has always been there, sometimes even a feature of capitalism; however, both are mistakes. Business cycles occur as a result of (government-controlled) artificial interest rate reductions. The market has this fascinating property: If there are enough saved resources in society, due to the law of supply and demand, interest rates fall, which motivates people to invest and produce goods that they then sell easily (there are enough resources in society); the artificial reduction of interest rates motivates entrepreneurs to make the same investments, but then they will not find a market for the produced goods (society is poorer than it appeared from the false price signals).
I explained this phenomenon in more detail in my lecture on money.
However, those who are practitioners with no interest in theories can convince themselves empirically: As long as states did not artificially lower interest rates, economic cycles did not take place.

title: A zero sum game?
text:
Many argue that envy is behind the hatred of the rich; and maybe they are right (certainly in part). However, I think that, in addition to envy, a role is also played by the generally widespread belief that the market is a zero-sum game, so that when someone gets rich, it must happen at the expense of another who gets poorer. However, this is clearly not true; if it happens between two people
voluntary exchange
, everyone subjectively values the good they gain more than the good they give up (if they didn't, they wouldn't voluntarily enter into such a trade). Even thanks to this, the wealth of the company is constantly increasing; let's see what conditions people lived in a few hundred years ago and compare it to how we are now. Society as a whole grows richer; even the poor get rich. In a free market, the person who improves the situation of others the most earns the most. Therefore, when a company makes a lot of money, it is not "at the expense" of customers; both sides will improve.

title: Che Guevara as a symbol
text: If there is interest in something, in our capitalist society it will typically be available sooner or later; and various objects with images of the revolutionary Che Guevara are no exception. Many even see it as a symbol of freedom; and I can't help but wonder. The murderer of hundreds of people, who, together with Castro, helped establish a harsh dictatorship in Cuba, in which he himself held important government positions (he was a minister), ran a bank (!) and intensively centralized all power in society, he apparently found a taste in murder (not only in combat), because he personally participated in mass executions, although he undoubtedly did not have to. When the powerful (el Che and Fidel) fell apart, he moved from Cuba to Zaire, then to Bolivia; in both places, as a professional revolutionary, he continued to harm people and spread suffering; however, he did not achieve his goals, failed, was captured and finally shot from head to toe. From the photos, I think he was a really handsome guy; is this the reason why someone puts it on a t-shirt?

title: Intellectual property
text:
Many (by no means all) anarcho-capitalists (myself included)
they do not recognize intellectual property
; this certainly does not mean that I have anything against people contractually committing themselves to anything they deem appropriate - i.e. not to distribute a purchased book or even software (under the threat of an arbitrary fine for breach of contract). So what do I find unacceptable? For anyone to extend the validity of this contract to other individuals who have nothing to do with it at all. If person A creates a work, which he sells to person B, who contractually agrees not to distribute the content, but does so anyway, it makes no sense to prosecute person C for its further distribution, if he did not enter into any contract (and did not take possession of the work by infringing someone's ownership). Do you object that in practice it is difficult to prove something to person B? It certainly does; but if there is a crime that is difficult to prove, will we prosecute the innocent just because we can't find the perpetrator?
Some wonder why some of the anarcho-capitalists do not recognize intellectual property, although property rights are sacred to them; well, even if it sounds paradoxical, this is exactly the reason. Let us imagine a man who owns land, a pencil and paper; he sits down on his property and starts writing something there with his pencil on his paper. And this is the property that is sacred to us; he can do with his resources as he sees fit! To say that someone "owns" the text of a book, for example, is to ascribe to him partial ownership of all the pencils, paper, and other means of writing books in the entire universe; similar to when the state forbids people to take drugs, for example, it partially usurps property rights to their bodies, which we consider unacceptable (even if it is also only a limitation of one of the many activities we can do with our bodies; and it is no different in the case of those pencils and papers).

title: Subsidy four times differently
text:
First: Subsidies cause corruption; beneficiaries bribe officials.
Second: Redistribution wastes resources; those who run them do not work for free.
Third: Subsidies harm small entrepreneurs; everyone pays taxes, but larger entities can more easily manage the administration and meet the conditions.
Fourth: Loss-making companies waste, ergo they should go bankrupt and make way for prosperous ones; redistribution saves them, thereby distorting the market, destroying the good and helping the bad.
The order in which I have listed the disadvantages of subsidies corresponds to how serious, in my opinion, the public perceives them (while everyone sees the former as a big problem, the latter are most likely not even realized by most people); however, their real harmfulness is probably almost exactly the opposite - while some corruption basically only causes money to be spent according to the needs of another, instead of being spent according to the will of one official, supporting the wasteful and incompetent pushes the more capable out of the market, thus harming customers who have to pay more money for lower quality services. And I'm not talking about that at all
the moral side of the whole thing, because the money that the state gives out has to be stolen from someone first
.

title: Marriage is everyone's private matter...
text:
Yesterday
a text was published in Stoká
, whose author calls for the separation of marriage from the state (which is something we definitely agree with), but at the same time he is against the marriage of same-sex couples on the grounds that it would be a violation of the NAP, because he says the state forces him to consider homosexuals as spouses, while he wants to consider them deviant. However, I maintain that declaring two people married is not in itself against the NAP; something like this would happen even in a free society, where the two would not be declared husband and wife by the state, but by other free market institutions. The author could then continue to consider such a couple as deviant, which he can do even now. Of course, it would be best for the state not to interfere with the marriage at all; I agree with the separation (not only) of marriage from the state. But until that happens, I am a supporter of the greatest possible freedom and the least regulation in this area. Let same-sex couples get married, too; and not just couples.

title: Regulation of damages from regulations
text:
Many state interventions cause so many problems that they "must" be solved by... the state; as? Naive readers, who might have already thought that by interfering with what causes them, I have to mislead them - they are "solved" by exactly what caused them, i.e. additional regulations. A typical example is the socialist healthcare system and the health tax (called health insurance), as a result of which there are further regulations in the name of the health of the population and the reduction of spending on their treatment. In order to maintain the second (linked) regulation, the existence of the first is usually argued; I am not surprised by the statists, but sometimes even libertarians fall into such a logical paradoxical trap, since they would be in favor of abolishing both, but as long as the first exists, they support the second. Examples: "The state is taking free market funds from us to solve the migration crisis, so entry into the country needs to be regulated." "Vaccination must be compulsory until health insurance is voluntary."
However, this reasoning is the road to hell for a libertarian; regulation that can be repealed without causing problems for anyone that would not have happened without the existence of other government interventions to look at. Example: Opening borders is a problem because of social benefits; the abolition of social benefits is a problem because of the labor code (people will have trouble finding work); repeal of the Labor Code is a problem due to obstacles in business (employees have worse conditions for starting a business when their employer does not suit them); removing barriers to doing business is a problem due to tax evasion; tax evasion is a problem because of pensions and so on. If we recognize any of those problems as serious enough not to disturb the regulation, taking into account the interpersonal incomparability of utility, then we cannot argue against anyone who declares any other to be serious; the only way, in my opinion, is always to deregulate.

title: Immature people
Choosing a partner
text: I remember a scene from a movie (I don't know which one) where Simona Stašová says: "I'm not going to marry someone who voted for Bush." The line, at least I think, was meant to be humorous and exaggerated, which I'd guess wouldn't be reason enough for most people; and since I think it is somehow different in my head, I would like to ask how you, dear readers, feel about it? For me personally, having my partner be an anarchist is pretty essential to the relationship; even minarchism (in the sense of limiting the state to the army, police, courts and maybe some infrastructure) I will still bite, but anything else would be completely unacceptable to me - I can't imagine living with a woman who wants a big state with all that violence (or doesn't even realize the extent to which it occurs). I will be glad if you write to me in the comments how you see it; regardless of whether you are libertarian or not, how important is it to you that your partner shares these values with you?

title: Protection money
text:
Let me quote something written by OC a long time ago - an anarcho-capitalist whom I respect very much, because he has inspired me in what I do for more than ten years; this is a (fictitious) letter you get after you move into a new house:
Dear Neighbor,
I welcome you to our quiet and pleasant neighborhood. Of course, I take care of her peace of mind, and it costs me a lot; therefore, it is only fair that these costs be spread over the other neighbors as well. Today is Monday; if you do not send CZK 50,000 to my account by Friday, I am afraid that my representative will personally come to you at the beginning of next week for CZK 100,000. If you throw him out of the door, he will come again and with him a group of armed men who will kill you if you are not spared and if you do not pay. If, against all odds, you should kill them or drive them away, the next day a group twice as large and better armed will arrive.
Everyone else on your street is happy to pay their annual fee, on time and properly; I hope that you will not become the disturber of our peaceful and friendly coexistence.
Your M.V., v.r.
Pretty crap huh? And if I told you that M.V. is the Minister of the Interior and that protection money is called taxes... would that change anything? If so, why? Feel free to write in the discussion xD

title: Free slavery
text:
May I voluntarily sell or donate myself into slavery? There is no consensus on this issue among libertarians (neither famous authors nor in our community); and I with my answer: "Definitely yes!" I am adding to the side of those who are currently in the minority. However, I cannot answer otherwise; why? It would not be consistent with the non-aggression principle and basic libertarian principles. What does it mean that I am someone's slave? That I am his property, he owns me, he can give me orders and if I resist, he can even kill me. However, if we grant that people have the right to sell their organs (even if it costs them their lives), and also that they have the right to borrow things (both of which libertarians allow), then I can sell all my organs to anyone, and he can lend them to me for use as long as I obey his every command, or as long as he pleases; then I am his slave, he owns me and decides about me.
And whoever opposes this must question my right to sell my organs or the buyer's right to lend them to me; however, perhaps no libertarian will do that, so if he wants to be consistent, he must recognize the legitimacy of voluntary slavery. Despite this, some object, for example, that even if someone owns my body, he cannot directly control it, but this is not a condition of ownership; even animals can be owned and we cannot directly control their bodies either. The objection that the fact that I give up the possibility to act freely invalidates the contract at the moment of its conclusion also does not stand; if I sell or donate a heart to someone, I die, thus certainly giving up the ability to act freely in a much more definitive way, yet I would be hard-pressed to find a libertarian who would want to take away the ability to sell or donate a heart. So why couldn't I voluntarily become someone's slave? Whether we like it or not, this is a consistent consequence of the principle of non-aggression.

title: The Evolutionary Argument
text: People often ask me why, if anarcho-capitalism is so good, it hasn't won the "evolutionary battle" with states; I realize that his answer, "What is not, may be," seems rather silly at first glance, so please take a second look. Human society is still developing, that development will probably never end, and we can see from history that people believed a lot of nonsense and atrocities often took place in society, which seemed justifiable to everyone, but it only took a few (tens or hundreds) of years for everything to change; for example, slavery was here for many thousands of years and clearly won the "evolutionary battle" with societies without slaves, but then everything broke - the paradigm that had been valid since the beginning of the age collapsed and turned to dust in an instant. In order for this to happen, people fighting for the right cause must not have assumed that if slavery had been around for so long, it couldn't be that bad. But it was. It is. And always will be. Just like the states.

title: What a Wonderful World
text: Some time ago I received an interesting question in a discussion - someone asked me if, as a libertarian who sees taxes as theft and laws as aggression, the world seems terribly evil and bad to me; I would like to share my answer here. For I told him that certainly not, for I find the world an absolutely delightful and fascinating place; yes, of course we don't have as much freedom as I would like and we see bloodthirsty robber states around us, but that's not all! We must not forget all those cooperating people who are already working together and creating values; we must not forget the enormous progress (ethical and technological) that drives humanity forward. And things (except for the occasional ups and downs) are looking up; slavery has practically disappeared, there are fewer wars, the standard of living (of the poor and the rich) is rising, for the first time in history more people are suffering from obesity than hunger... and while not everything is perfectly fine, the world is a wonderful place to live.

title: Medicines, drugs and double standards
text:
I find the topic of "drugs" interesting, as it is surrounded by many myths that are released into the world, especially by states, to defend their "war on drugs"; I dealt with their destruction
in a word
i
in writing
and added i
something more subjective
. Although some drugs are undoubtedly a reliable tool for slow (and sometimes quite fast) suicide, the state (since school years through various anti-drug programs) gives us every illegal drug in this way (it portrays the legal ones in a completely different light); then many don't trust the government (which is fine) so much that they automatically believe the opposite of everything the state says to be true (that's already dangerous). Some people - coincidentally often those "natural" and suspicious of pharmaceutical companies - then underestimate the drugs; although they are skeptical, for example, of vaccinations and often of antibiotics, they are not afraid to experiment with completely untested drugs or methods of their use; please don't let the state manipulate us to either side!

title: Parallel with slavery
text: As some have astutely observed, I relatively often compare the institution of slavery to the state on many different occasions; I would like to write a few lines about that analogy. It is not directly about us being slaves to the state (I probably wouldn't even call it that), but rather about the majority of people's attitude towards those two institutions: Today, although almost everyone considers slavery to be bad, it wasn't like that a few hundred years ago; and it is very interesting to see how people then looked at those who began to come up with ideas for its abolition. It was downright impossible. It would spell economic disaster. Slaves would not be able to take care of themselves. It was a beautiful theory, but unusable in practice. These were extremist and radical ideas. The idea that a slave could disobey a master was about as absurd as the idea that a citizen could disobey a policeman on duty. But the change came extremely quickly...

title: Security above all...
text:
How long does it take for a person who has never been interested in the issue to think about whether a society could function without the state? It's a lot of topics, questions, unknowns and thinking about alternatives; in my opinion, such a complex and complex issue will require hundreds of hours of reading and thinking, but let's say that you don't have to think about everything that much, so we can assume tens or at least units of hours. I can't imagine anyone who could think it through in a matter of minutes; yet the vast majority of people respond within seconds without ever having heard of it. How is that possible? Those concerned are simply indoctrinated by state propaganda; it was explained to them that we need the state and that's just the way it is. Therefore, when we try to convince someone that the state is immoral, we do not start from scratch, but from the conviction of the person concerned that we are definitely wrong; what about that
Separation of education from the state is the solution.

title: Who writes history?
text:
Although I am not a historian and do not know anything about the academic sphere in this field, I would like to convey to you, dear readers, the assumptions of two historians that I found very interesting in my conversations with them; both argued that research grants are handed out by people who already have some idea of what happened in the past, while they don't want to fund research that is about something vastly different from their version. In my opinion, this may not be a conspiracy at all (I don't really like you, by the way, as a big fan of Hanlon's razor), it makes sense anyway - those people simply consider funding something they don't believe in to be a waste of money; however, the consequence of this – quite logical – approach is the severe complication of the possibility of correcting major errors in the current perception of history. If this happens, the reason is not malicious intent, but socialist subsidization of historical research; the solution would then be – similarly to many other places –
free market financing
.

title: Without the state, it would disappear!
text: When I talk about a stateless society, I often encounter objections that something (anything) would disappear without a state, so we need a state; interestingly, the counterargument is quite universal regardless of what it is specifically about. The absolutely fundamental question is: Does the given thing bring more benefit to people than how much benefit would be brought to them by the resources that the thing consumes? If the answer is in the affirmative, then the objection falls; people would buy it even without the state (either independently, or they would agree to it, but they would definitely give up the necessary resources, because the resulting product is more valuable to them). If the answer is no, then the thing should not exist and the state should not artificially keep it alive; why? Simply because people can use the necessary resources in a different way to bring them even more benefit; and since we live in a world of limited resources, we should not waste them.

title: Two interviews
text: If I wait somewhere, I read; that's why I don't even mind waiting. However, a few days ago I found myself in a situation where I had to wait and had nothing to read, so I just sat and thought; however, I was distracted from this by two conversations I witnessed. The actors of the first of them could be the owner or director of a company and probably his salesman; they were frantically figuring out what to do to make customers feel good and want to come back. The second interview was probably conducted by two nurses; they collectively cursed at how someone could afford to come without an appointment and shared tricks on how to "punish" the person in question (make him wait longer than necessary so that he doesn't allow himself to do this anymore). Can you see the difference? While some fight for customers, others harass; why? Well, the clients bring resources to one, while they drain them from the other; do the nurses think about it like this? Most likely not; and they probably don't even realize it.

title: Hatred of capitalism
text: Capitalism is hated by a lot of people (as is anarchy, but let's ignore that for now); why actually? But I think we should not ask "why" but "what"; what do these people really hate? Typically one of the following two things: Either the "wild capitalism" of the nineteenth century (compared to today) or contemporary (state-linked) corporations; hating nineteenth-century capitalism because people lived in worse conditions than today (though better than before) makes about as much sense as reviling the invention of the steam engine because today we have more powerful machines, while calling state-linked and over-regulated corporations (which sometimes make laws through lobbies and limit competition) capitalist shows a severe misunderstanding of the term. Capitalism means free markets and voluntary exchanges, not lobbying and bribing MPs; and it's up to us to explain it to people.

title: Respect for authority
text: Many often complain that "today's youth" (of course worse than the former - like everyone) has no respect for authority, which they would often like to solve with war, or at least strict discipline in school; but what will the youth learn by these means? To grovel before an authority that these people did not choose for themselves; how can such a thing even be considered a virtue by anyone? Respect and healthy humility are of course very desirable, however, they must come from within the person concerned - he himself chooses who deserves his respect, who is worth following; but if we impose on him whom he must obey, we only make him a puppet, dull his will, and teach him to "shut up and walk." Do you notice how often this can be encountered in, for example, schools? And no wonder; it is of course useful for the state to educate obedient citizens - the teacher can then easily be replaced by a policeman, official or politician. Do you really want this for your children?

title: Dead horses and their poo
text:
Over a hundred years ago, someone in New York realized that there were too many horses; he found out how fast these horses were multiplying and approximated further developments: Sometime in the second half of the twentieth century, people in New York will be wading through a meter-long layer of horse excrement, not to mention a flood of dead horse bodies. Does this seem absurd to you? Well, yes to me; on the one hand, the author somehow forgot about cars (not that they existed in his time), but above all, that even without cars, people would have solved the given problem far before they had to wade through feces on the streets. How is it that when it comes to horses, everyone sees how absurd it is to think like this, but when someone comes up with sustainable development based on equally absurd assumptions, they take it seriously? At the same time, all models of sustainable development are based on just such predictions and the assumption that people will not react to emerging problems...
________
Edit: According to some it was London, not NY.

title: Key Libertarian Moments
text: I have spoken to many hundreds of libertarians in my lifetime; when it came to what led them to this way of thinking, there are usually some specific turning points that those concerned are typically very clearly aware of and remember - in my life, the biggest libertarian "aha-moments" were two (one related to the fire department, the other to the law) and a few other fairly fundamental ones. A beautiful moment was described to me by Dominik Stroukal, who was convinced by Murray Newton Rothbard and his commentary on the selling and buying of children; In short: The transaction is good for the seller, the buyer, but most importantly for the child! And what convinced you, dear readers? Please confide in the comments; I'm not just asking this, I'm trying to find the best arguments. I would like to find a strong common denominator in as many stories as possible; I then want to apply it to my rhetoric.

title: Let's blame Nemakachenka!
text: A lazy person who doesn't want to work and just depends on the social system is a favorite target of hatred, especially of right-wing conservatives; why is that? At first glance, a quite understandable idea: "He who does not work, should not eat." (In connection with this text, I recommend especially right-wingers to google who notoriously used this phrase.) But why should everyone work? If someone is satisfied with poverty or beggary in exchange for a certain freedom and a huge amount of free time, that is after all his business and only his business; and if he begs for a living, it is nothing against anything at all. The moment the state comes to ask for alms, a problem arises; but who is its originator? A beggar who is just taking advantage of what he (the state) has been told is his "right" or one who is handing out money from someone else? Blaming the former makes about as much sense as blaming instead of the thief for stealing the one whom the thief gifted.

title: Ankap in Heaven xD
text:
What is the sentence that makes an anarcho-capitalist angry with a left-wing socialist and a right-wing conservative?
"I support the right of married gay couples to defend with fully automatic weapons their shops with over-the-counter drugs of all kinds, which are also sold there by underage employees unregulated by any labor code."
Although this is a somewhat peculiar way of presenting the libertarian worldview, it is not for nothing that it is said that an anarcho-capitalist is one who does not add the word "but" after the sentence: "I am a supporter of freedom."
Drug and gun regulation are, at first glance, relatively unrelated topics; and upon a little more detailed research, we find that typically the proponents of deregulation of one would like to regulate the other with all the more vigor. But why? Logically speaking, the argument for deregulation of both is almost identical in principle. Do you disagree? So come and talk to Terezka and me; then you'll probably disagree even more. However, you will definitely get the opportunity to passionately debate the given topics and try to convince others of your opinion; or maybe learn something new.
We look forward to seeing you in the evening
Bar Nebe
!

title: Heaven on Earth
text: People often complain about how the "common man" is doing badly and his situation is getting worse and worse, so the government needs to intervene; frankly, I can't think of any popular myth at the moment that would be further from the truth (at least in Europe or America). First, the "common man" has never been better off in history than he is now; we have enough (often surplus) drinking water, food, we live in houses where there is heat and light, we enjoy a huge number of achievements of the modern age. Second, the situation of the "common man" has probably never improved so rapidly; virtually every conceivable metric shows that we are getting better. Thirdly, never has so little labor been required of the average man to support himself; so we have clouds of free time (compared to perhaps all conceivable periods in the past). And finally, fourthly, this is happening precisely despite government interventions; they can only make our great situation worse.

title: Inability to reconsider opinions
text: Anarcho-capitalists are sometimes called fanatics, and very often statists suggest that they are unwilling to change their views and admit mistakes; I find such a statement interesting and somewhat paradoxical. After all, almost all of us were brought up to be statist; almost everyone originally believed in the state. Anarchists for some reason had to go through at least one fairly fundamental change of mind and admit a mistake during their lives; the statists could also, but did not necessarily have to. How then can statists accuse anarchists of the inability to reassess opinions and think critically, when they have already demonstrated this ability at least once in their lives? Of course, it is possible that anarchists can be wrong in their views on the world and statists can be right, but the chance that someone has been fanatically manipulated is higher precisely with statists, because they believe what was instilled in all of us in elementary school.

title: Private is more expensive than state!
text: There is a very popular belief across society that is largely undisputed – the private sector is more expensive than the public sector; yes, it is recognized as having a higher quality, but in terms of price, in the eyes of almost everyone, the state is cheaper. But why should it be so? In fact, there is no reason for this, the state is not able to create goods more cheaply than a private person; on the contrary, it is more expensive because, in addition to the goods themselves, you also have to pay for bureaucracy, officials, central management and the like. The difference is that the payments are hidden, and while we see the full amount of the money we pay to a private company, with state services the taxes are separate (and moreover divided into many components, so that the state takes about two-thirds of what we earn); but above all, we are manipulated by similar myths from an early age through the state education system, whose goal is to spread propaganda. That's why we don't believe in dogmas and always ask for reasons.

title: Belief in socialism
text: Again, it was not so long ago that many people generally believed that the economy had to be centrally controlled or we would starve, because something as important as food production and distribution could not be left to the free market, so both were arranged by the state - and it seemed that way; after the revolution, what many feared happened... and lo and behold, suddenly things started to work better. And to the "big surprise" the other sectors that were privatized did the same; however, many remained in state hands to allow their notorious problems to continue. In connection with this, two questions come to mind: How is it possible that even if everything that the state no longer cares about prospers better, so many people still object that it would be different for exactly what is still state-owned? And how can anyone believe that the state, which cannot provide even such a primitive thing as toilet paper on the counters, will take good care of, for example, education or healthcare?

title: Anarchists and other anarchists
text: There is a rivalry between anarcho-capitalists and anarcho-communists (and not only between these two schools of thought, but also many others related to them; I take those two as an example for others); the anarcho-capitalists accuse the anarcho-communists of inconsistency, while the anarcho-communists in turn accuse them of not being real anarchists. I have nothing against it in principle, but it strikes me how little both camps know about their opponents, towards whom they define themselves; in fact, most anarcho-capitalists draw their knowledge of anarcho-communists from other anarcho-capitalists who mock and caricature them (the exact same thing goes the other way around). It is always sad to see criticism of capitalism like: "Capitalism is when the state gives privileges to banks." On the other hand, it (the anarcho-capitalist critique of anarcho-communism) is no better; therefore, I recommend to all who want to criticize the anarcho-communists to go and talk to them directly first.

title: Fluid gender and sexual identity
text: Recently, we can hear more and more about people who are not sure of their "gender" identity. Now I don't mean "pure" transsexuals, they are already clear about their gender, it's just that this "clarity" doesn't match their physical bodies, which can be solved with surgery; I'm talking about people who simply don't know, they feel they are alternately female and male, or even beings of completely different genders. I respect their identity (although sometimes I get a little confused about what gender to call them - and I only know a few), I don't think it's any of my business; that is why I am surprised by the increasingly frequent cries of defenders of family values, where the world is going and that this threatens the traditional family. What? How about? I cannot imagine the state a family must be in, threatened by the existence of someone somewhere who is not clear whether they are a woman or a man; I think that pro-family warriors should mainly take care of their families and leave others alone.

title: Tax against work
text:
Interestingly, excise taxes are often defended as reducing consumption; a tobacco tax reduces smoking, an alcohol tax reduces drinking, a fuel tax motivates people to save fuel (and nature) and so on. This logic makes sense, taxes can indeed influence people's behavior; not that it would be good, that's it
it always ends up hurting someone
, but it works. The question then is, what effect does the income tax have in this sense? By taxing work, we actually demotivate the payers of this tax to work; because they will receive a lower reward for their work. Combined with various unemployment benefits and support, this is actually quite an effective tool to discourage people from working. More or less the same can be said about the VAT; although it has a different name, it has more or less the same effect, only not on employees, but on entrepreneurs. And how much different do you think it is in the case of such levies for social and health "insurance"?

title: Muh... the road?
text:
Many people consider it a serious problem of a free society that even the road network would be owned by private owners; why it would not be such a problem, I explain for example
in his series on anarcho-capitalism
. However, it is noteworthy that although questions like: "What if someone doesn't want to rent me their road in the city?" we often hear, almost no one asks: "What if someone doesn't want to rent me their apartment in the city?" How is that? Well, apartment rentals work more or less on a free market basis and there is no problem with them in principle; and yet there is no reason why road owners should behave any significantly differently from apartment owners - everyone just wants to make money, and very few people are interested in owning land and doing nothing with it (in which case they can always sell it). Yes, sometimes there is an uncooperative owner of the road, just as today we sometimes encounter an uncooperative apartment owner; however, most of them behave normally.

title: Ankap versus an ideal world?
text: Often in discussions about anarcho-capitalism, one gets into a situation where the statist comes up with an example of what bad could happen to someone, and asks how the market would solve the given situation; it can be non-payment of health insurance and dying of an illness, or a child being abused by parents, and so on. Most free market advocates then begin to respond to such objections in various ways (charity and so on); nothing against that, but I think the very first thing that should be said is that even the existence of the state will not prevent such cases - many people die as a result of bad medical care in the socialist healthcare system, many parents abuse their children despite the laws. No one claims that anarcho-capitalism means an ideal world where evil never occurs; into the defense of anarcho-capitalism not against the state, but against the ideal world, but we allow ourselves to be manipulated by every acceptance of the objection: "What if <unlikely situation>?"

title: Get used to the teacher, accept the politician
text:
About the direct indoctrination of children in state schools, which they are forced to attend as part of compulsory schooling, otherwise the state will kidnap them from their parents and expose them to propaganda anyway
he wrote
i
he said
enough; however, I would like to mention another aspect of this monstrosity: Since children are forced from an early age to accept violently imposed authorities in the form of teachers, they grow into people for whom this model of behavior becomes completely natural, so that they then automatically accept other authorities that they did not choose - the state, government and politicians. The danger of schools is therefore not only in direct indoctrination, but also in the fact that everyone accepts involuntary authorities as the norm and "necessary evil"; of course, this does not mean that authorities (in general) are bad - I consider only those that are forcibly imposed on a person to be harmful. I do not believe that part of "preparation for life" should be involuntary submission; voluntary acceptance of authority yes, but it cannot be forced.

title: Compulsory school attendance
text:
Most people perceive compulsory schooling as something beneficial, without any deeper societal discussion about it; because it is one of those things that "everyone knows" and "it's obvious"... so "obvious" that the vast majority of people don't even realize (and are surprised when confronted with this fact, they often tap their foreheads and find it absurd) that in reality compulsory schooling (regardless of its possible benefits) means threatening parents from the state that they will either send their child to school, or they will simply be kidnapped by a social worker and
forced to complete that indoctrination by the school anyway
. And what do I mean by indoctrination? Well, for example, just how one-sidedly compulsory school attendance is presented in schools, its benefits are talked about, but the disgusting violence it represents is completely hushed up; the state through schools teaches children how to be "good citizens".
Such a thing is not a coincidence, it is not even a conspiracy, it is quite a public matter; you only have to look at the White Paper, the National Education Program, it is quite openly discussed there - teachers of all subjects are supposed to make good citizens out of their students. Imagine if there was any other organization besides the state that would do something like this - forcing your children to get their education under the threat of taking it away by force; what if some church made your children religious? What if McDonald's turned your kids into "good customers" and you couldn't say no? Would this situation be corrected by the fact that the children would also learn other things there? And if not, why tolerate something similar to the state? Sure, the state has the power to enforce it; having power and using it however
doesn't mean it's ethical or excusable
.

title: An anarchist revolution?
text:
Anarchy is (mainly due to the attitudes of many left-wing anarchists, i.e. anarcho-communists or anarcho-syndicalists) in the eyes of most people associated with (violent) revolution; I personally believe, however, that at least anarcho-capitalism cannot be achieved simply and simply through revolutions. Why not? Well, even if a revolution were successful and an anarcho-capitalist took power over the state, he basically has two options for what he can do: He will give people real freedom; but people today want a state, so the first thing they will do with that freedom is to establish a state. The second possibility is that he forbids them to form a state, thereby becoming the state himself. People can be forced by force to build a better tomorrow of socialism, to gas Jews in the name of Nazism, or to vote in a democracy,
however, they cannot be forced to freedom
; they have to want it themselves first, but if the overwhelming majority of people already want it, there is no reason to make a revolution.
Which brings me to another seemingly unrelated favorite question, such a dilemma; sometimes someone asks me in a discussion if I had a button that I could use to cancel the state overnight, would I press it (mostly they allude to the fact that if the state disappeared out of nowhere, chaos and violence would probably ensue). But such a choice is, in my opinion, pointless; either people want the state, but when I cancel it with a button, they immediately start it again, or they don't want to, but then there's no need for buttons. It makes no sense to decide whether to "uninstall" the state immediately or not, because the state can only be removed as quickly as the people themselves want; so if we want to abolish it, let us convince and show the advantages of freedom! I don't even think that the people would then democratically "vouch" for freedom, but rather that if the majority does not recognize the state, it will disappear regardless of any elections (but of course, as society changes, it will be reflected in those elections as well).

title: Dull masses?
text:
Quite a few people (and I was one of them years ago) feel that "average people" aren't smart or capable enough, can't take care of themselves, and are generally the "dumb herd"; each of the elitists who proclaim this, of course, considers himself above average (how else; after all, most people consider themselves above average). But where does the belief that "almost everyone is a self-righteous idiot" come from? In my opinion, this is due to the fact that we all have things in our lives that do not interest us, we do not orient ourselves in them, and we do not even have a great interest in them, because our priorities are elsewhere, from which it follows that we all appear to be idiots in at least something; however, with ourselves we understand the reasons, we understand and we apologize for it, while with others we do not, because we see their shortcomings in what we ourselves consider essential.
Perhaps every person is a complex individual who has his own weaknesses and strengths; he develops what he considers important and stagnates in what he is not very good at. And just because we constantly see many people around us behaving unwisely from our point of view, the "average person" does not have to be demented; on the one hand, in many other things, we will behave unwisely from their point of view, but above all, we typically do not know the entire context of their actions, so what may seem stupid to us may simply be the result of the people in question having different set priorities and something different to us being important to them (which, by the way, complicates our assessment of their qualities). I recommend to anyone who sees idiots around him to think about whether he himself can often appear exactly the same to those around him; I am not saying that people are "equal" and "equally good", but rather so much that it is not much to judge.

title: The path of peace
text:
I can't count how many times in my many years of being a libertarian I've witnessed anarcho-capitalists calling minarchists scumbags, minarchists calling anarcho-capitalists fanatics, and anarchists of all stripes waging their never-ending war over who is a real anarchist and who is just playing; these are simply disputes in which the ad hominem argument does not go far. I personally always regret it, especially when I know from experience how easily such unnecessary conflicts can be avoided in the vast majority of cases simply by not wanting to argue and behaving in a friendly manner; the opposing party almost always agrees to such negotiations after a while (it is true, recently one ankom told me to take a conciliatory approach and to go to hell with the understanding game; however, this happens only rarely), seriously try it sometime: Look for common ground, try to understand the discussion opponent.
I'm not saying you have to agree, just don't treat the person you're debating with as an idiot just because they have a different opinion; rather, try to look for common points of contact, it happens much more often than it might seem. Then you might be surprised to discover all sorts of interesting things; for example that
anarcho-communism is not necessarily inconsistent
. Let's ask ourselves the basic question, what are we trying to do: Convince people, or let off steam and send someone to hell? In the second case, everyone can handle it on their own, but I would like to remind you that by provoking an argument, you will drive your opponent into an emotional state in which he will not be willing to accept the opinions of others, which is counterproductive; not to mention that even from the point of view of those watching the debate, a civilized discussion looks better than demented bickering. I understand it's hard sometimes; however, I highly recommend it from my own experience.

title: Detection of indoctrination
text:
On your own
the first lecture in Polis
I expressed an idea that many later returned to in conversations with me, as they considered it essential; that's why I'm going to write about her today. Being exposed to propaganda tends to result in indoctrination that partially blocks our critical thinking; we then approach things in such a way that we "know" everything in advance, we do not look for arguments and information with the aim of finding out the truth, but only to confirm our opinion. The bad news is that it's not just about statists and state propaganda, but even after seeing through, one can fall into the same trap on the opposite (or any other) side; I personally found myself operating this way a few years ago when thinking about anarcho-capitalism: I "knew" in advance where the truth was, and stopped approaching the arguments of opponents as something that could convince me. The good news is that in order to correct the situation, it is enough to realize and fully admit it, and the attitude itself will change.
How to detect such a state of mind? I'm afraid that everyone has such darkened corners; it has always fascinated me, I am actively working to uncover them and I believe it is a never-ending process. I consider the simplest method of detection to be our reaction to a thought which we encounter for the first time; if it is complex and we have never thought about it, we cannot quickly decide whether it is nonsense. If we know immediately that something "is completely absurd" and look for arguments in retrospect, we can be sure that we have been indoctrinated in this direction; as an example I like to use the analogy of a soldier who kills on the orders of a superior and an employee who kills on the orders of a boss... almost everyone immediately "knows" that this is an absurd comparison; only then are they looking for reasons why actually. It's not about whether the simile fits at all, but about the process: "I know what it's like right away; only then do I go looking for an argument." Maybe I will write about other detection methods sometime next time.

title: Child labor
text: Child labor is now considered a bad thing in our latitudes and civilization; and it's no wonder, because in such a rich society it doesn't make sense for children to work - firstly, they can get a much better job later thanks to their studies, and secondly, there is a huge difference between the value of skilled and unskilled work. In other times or parts of the world (in a poorer society), however, this unfortunately does not apply; children work simply so that the family can survive at all - not only does the family not have the resources to study them, but often not even to feed them. How to change such a situation? Only in such a way that the given society becomes rich; and certainly not by imposing a ban on child labor on them. Working in insane conditions sixteen hours a day is appalling; however, other options (starvation, for example) are even worse - if they weren't, they'd use them. However, by banning, we will force them to do exactly that - to choose the worse option.

title: Individualism does not lie in isolation
text: Libertarians are individualists by nature; however, many people understand the term a little differently than they do, because they assume that it is about isolating yourself from others, and you can often come across that someone contrasts individualism with cooperation, cooperation in a community of people. I don't want to argue here about which meaning of the word individualism is "correct", because I consider it irrelevant - after all, what's in a name? What they call a rose, even if called otherwise, would smell the same. However, I would like to point out that anyone who criticizes libertarians as those who reject cooperation has not understood the following fundamental difference: Voluntary cooperation is one thing, which is one of the basic ideas of the Austrian school of economics, by the way, but coercion is something completely different; no libertarian rejects peaceful cooperation, on the contrary, they all strongly condemn its coercion from a position of strength.

title: Excuse by authority
text: If a police officer does a prank (say, harassing citizens) within the limits of the law (or even required by law), a huge number of people tend to excuse it by saying, "He had to do it, he was just doing his job." I reject such an argument; partly because the guards in the concentration camp were "just doing their job", but above all because each of us is personally responsible for our actions. It's remarkable how everyone understands this in the private sector (everyone recognizes that it's absurd to excuse a murder, for example, by saying that the killer was ordered to do it by the boss), but so many people turn a blind eye to the same when it comes to the state (almost everyone excuses the murders of soldiers by saying that they were just following orders); why is that? Well, the state simply has better PR; propaganda takes place on all fronts, the youngest are already indoctrinated as part of compulsory schooling. When you excuse someone for "just doing their job," ask yourself if you would excuse them in the private sector.

title: whine about "today's"
text: The grass was greener and the girls more beautiful; we hear complaints all the time about "these days" and it's popular to exclaim how screwed up everything is. At the same time, we live in wonderful times, we are having a good time, never have so many people lived in prosperity; in the USA and Europe we are drowning in abundance, never before have so few hours of work been enough to provide a person with the basic necessities of life, never before have people also had so much free time. Even in the rest of the world, which is worse off than we are, people are getting richer like never before; there are more obese people than starving people in the world. So why the constant whining about bad times? The reasons are clouds; however, this one caught my attention: Imagine five amazing things that could happen to you within an hour of finishing reading this text; do you have Good; now think of five bad things. Wasn't the second one easier? To me, both are the same; however, the vast majority of people come up with bad things much faster. Why actually? Answer in the comments.

title: Voluntariness
text:
When anarcho-capitalists define themselves against the state running or funding something, they very often face accusations that they are against the thing itself (for example, when they do not want the state to fund art, statists say they are against art as such); unfortunately, this is not always a targeted argumentative fallacy, as the person concerned very often does not really see the difference between "not wanting people to be forced to do something" and "not wanting that something". Still, voluntariness is one of the most important aspects of anything; there is about as much difference between a theater financed by admission and other voluntary sources and a theater paid for by the state as between two people making love, expressing their sincere love, and rape. This, of course, varies enormously morally, which is far from everything; even from a utilitarian point of view, coercion is a big problem.
Why? Because of
the impossibility of economic calculation
; anything that is voluntarily funded has the property that when it starts to consume so many resources that people would benefit more from them than from the resulting thing itself, it starts to generate a loss and something needs to be done about it (changed, canceled...), while when something is run by the state, there is no way to know if it is a god-awful waste of resources. By waste, people often refer to a situation where, for example, the state buys something expensive that can be obtained more cheaply; this is undoubtedly true, but the far more fundamental question is whether the state should buy this "something" at all! How do we find out what it brings
more benefit than the resources needed to do so
? Well, very simply; we'll let people decide whether to voluntarily purchase it or not. What are you?
will not buy voluntarily
, it obviously won't do them any more good than the resources they have to spend on it; and what will bring them more benefit, they will buy. Laissez-faire!
