title: Everything cannot be converted into money
text:
The objection that everything cannot be converted into money is a relatively logical response to the efforts of some people to ignore the non-monetary benefit of various goods and consider only their financial benefit or price/performance ratio; on the contrary, however, it is not at all a logical answer to
conclusions of the Austrian school of economics
, which also sometimes converts a lot of things into money, but never without including a non-monetary benefit, taking into account all the subjectivity of value for each individual. So how does the Austrian school of economics convert goods into money? Well, the price of anything is equal to the higher of the following two values: The first is the highest offer, how much someone is willing to pay for that property, the second is the lowest offer, for which the owner of the property is willing to sell it; it naturally follows, among other things, that there can be (and are) things whose price expressed in money is infinite, but which are only those that someone owns and does not sell.
Therefore, if someone owns something that he is simply not willing to sell under any circumstances, it is not exchangeable for money at that moment; on the other hand, all other things that someone is willing to trade with can be "recalculated" to money, and this in a very meaningful way: The price of the property is the highest offer from possible buyers, or the lowest offer for which the owner will sell (the higher of the two values). This is an open market price and absolutely everything is included - artistic value, emotional value, commemorative value, charitable value, just everything; how is that possible Well, when someone sells or buys something, he includes in the price his knowledge, emotions, humanity, intuition and everything he is capable of; and precisely for that reason, it makes no sense to argue against a free market economy by saying that "some things cannot be converted into money" - people acting on the market "convert" into money exactly what and only what can be, and that includes all non-financial aspects.

title: Human preferences
text:
Surely you know a lot of people who, on the one hand, agree with the restriction of freight traffic in the city, but at the same time they are bothered by paying more for goods (the price of which will increase as a result of such restrictions), or they sign a petition against the construction of a mall or a parking lot instead of a park, but then they shop or park there more than they ever went to the park, or they go to protest against factories that pollute the environment, but then they still buy and use their products a lot; they do so because many times they are not aware of the connections themselves, which is perfectly fine, no one can know everything. But what does that mean? That asking people their preferences (or letting them democratically vote on them) doesn't produce results that correspond to reality; their true preferences cannot be ascertained except by letting them act in a free market—
only by actions, not by words, does a person demonstrate what really benefits him
.

title: Ice creams
text: It has been a few decades since many people made a living as ice cream workers; they mined ice and sold it to people to keep their food cold. Then came the fridge; and thanks to profit-seeking capitalists, it soon became available to almost everyone in both Europe and the US, millions of refrigerators flooded households en masse. But... the icemen were losing their jobs in droves; today there is quite possibly not one in the whole world. And with elevator operators, for example, it's not much better; how many people lost their jobs because of automatic elevators? So I could go on. But would it make sense to "protect jobs" in those cases? No! It is only good that the ice-makers have been replaced, their work has lost its meaning, and people can refrigerate food better; those in question then went to do other things instead of the ice business, contributing to society. In retrospect, almost everyone understands that this is right; but why do so few people understand the same when it comes to the present?

title: Advertisement
text: Many of us see advertising as a necessary evil, some even want to limit or ban it, saying that the world would be a better place without it, and they don't like that ultimately the customer pays for advertising; so why not outlaw advertising? Even leaving aside the moral reasons, advertising has, among other things, an informational benefit for all who are exposed to it; after all, how else would we orient ourselves in the abundant supply of goods offered to us by capitalist entrepreneurs? Even just the message on the product packaging, or any information about the product anywhere, is a form of advertising. So we are only talking about measure; but how to determine the right one? Well, let companies compete in the free market; whoever advertises too much will also spend too much, thereby losing their competitiveness; the very fact that advertising costs are reflected in the final price of goods is the reason for reducing its quantity.

title: Street lighting
text:
Sometimes we can come across the claim of statists that without the state and public budgets we wouldn't even have street lights; the truth is that where people would depend on it, there would be public lighting, but not elsewhere. But is it wrong? No; just the opposite. Where people purchase public lighting voluntarily,
they obviously benefit more from it
, than if they used the resources needed to build it differently; on the contrary, where they don't opt for it, they make it clear that they have a better use for those resources (otherwise they would voluntarily build lighting), so it's better for them not to have it there (and have something else instead). This is where the popular argument about black riders often comes in - people will be less motivated to pay when they know they can "ride" on others paying for them; this is really true, it is very difficult to exclude someone from the consumption of public lighting.
But is this a reason to forcibly extract resources? If it were, one can defend the forced selection of resources for anything just because there is black passengering, or some other objective (physical and given by the nature of the world) reason why the given thing is made more expensive by some externality. Non-excludability from consumption is a property of a given good that makes it more expensive – just as a swamp on a plot of land increases the price of building in that place, black passenger traffic increases (for payers) the price of public lighting; yes, if the conditions were different (the land was dry or black passenger traffic was more solvable), the goods in question would be cheaper, but that (in no case) is not a reason to forcibly force people to pay for it if they are not voluntarily interested - that good will still bring less benefit than what the resources they paid for it would bring to people (if it wasn't the case, they will pay voluntarily).

title: Regulation to protect the weak
text: Regulations are mostly defended on the grounds that the state protects the weak; for now, let's leave aside whether the forceful enforcement of such protection is morally justifiable and look at its concrete effects on small, large and huge firms. A large company has its accounting and legal departments, which can deal with the new regulations as needed and adjust the processes in the company so that they comply with the regulations. Huge companies (in addition to the above) often have lobbyists and other means with which they can influence legislators and block seriously unpleasant, expensive or threatening regulations. However, small companies do not have any of the above options, and any regulation of their business can be potentially liquidating or very painful for them. This protection of some weak ones ultimately only endangers other weak ones, and often very fundamentally; please let's not forget that.

title: The industrial revolution
text: As such, the Industrial Revolution is rightly considered a very progressive period in human history; however, I see a remarkable contradiction in how the "wild capitalism" of that time is perceived. Workers' toil in appalling conditions, child labor, capitalism is blamed for all of this; however, this does not make sense given what we know about the Industrial Revolution. Before her, people toiled from dawn to dusk in the fields, even with their children; then, thanks to capitalism, conditions gradually began to change for the better. Of course, compared to what we have today, people were worse off, but capitalism undoubtedly improved their situation compared to what it was before; yet, for example, child labor is vehemently associated with this very period, while all the millennia before, when it was completely common, are for some reason neglected. So before we condemn capitalism, please consider the context.

title: Drivers; why?
text:
Totally
the first text in Stoké
(i.e. except
the welcoming one
) dealt with the meaning of driver's licenses (or state licenses to drive motor vehicles); I present in it several arguments why this is nothing more than useless bullshit. Yet their existence is considered self-evident, right, justified and meaningful by almost everyone; therefore, I would like to point out here again the main reason why, in my opinion, they are absolutely useless: In theory, they are supposed to prevent people who can't drive from endangering others on the roads; but if someone is so irresponsible as to get into a car and drive off into traffic without having acquired even the minimum set of skills that can be learned in a driving school, and is willing to risk property, health and human life (including his own) to do so, how could the threat of a police check, a possible fine or a driving ban (not that he is allowed to do so now) deter such a person?

title: Democrats-liberals, libertarians, Republicans-conservatives
text: Dividing the political spectrum into left and right is relatively problematic, as these concepts are already incredibly desecrated, media-twisted and unclear; in the Czech Republic, it is basically the case that wherever a political party places itself, that is where the media presents it (completely regardless of the program and possible activities in the parliament). In the USA, the situation is a bit clearer, there are traditionally two fundamental political camps: Democrats (let's say leftists) and Republicans (let's say rightists); while Democrats defend personal freedoms and suppress economic freedoms, Republicans do exactly the opposite. For some reason, most libertarians tend to identify with Republicans (given the choice); and I ask the plenary a question for discussion: "Why?" I personally find the libertarian philosophy equally close to and far from both camps (we promote personal and economic freedoms); however, why do so many libertarians see it differently? Thanks for the answers.

title: There is no "insurance" like insurance
text:
What is insurance? A voluntary contract between an insurer and an insured, which typically obligates the insured to pay relatively small fees to the insurer, who will pay the insured a relatively large amount of money in the event of a loss event defined by the contract; it is essentially a high-odds bet on an unlikely event that the insurer takes because it sets a favorable rate, while from the insured's point of view it is essentially a service fee. A tax is something completely different - by its very nature it is not voluntary, people are forced to pay it under the threat of violence (from the state), it is something like an extortion (but taxes have better PR); moreover, the amount of taxes is typically not related to what services and to what extent the payer receives them, but is determined in some other way (very often it depends, for example, on his income, or on how much he spends, etc.).
And then we have such things as health "insurance", or social "insurance"; what is remarkable about them is that they have very little in common with insurance, in fact only the name, however they are not voluntary and the amount of the "insurance premium" does not depend on the risks, the probability of a harmful event, or the amount of the insurer's payment (if it occurs). These payments have all the characteristics of a tax, while practically none of the characteristics of insurance (in particular, for example, social "insurance" is paid more by the insured and the rich, who are logically less likely to use it, and vice versa); however, because it would not sound good that we are taxed at approximately sixty to seventy percent, the state is trying to create an illusion in the citizens that this is not actually the case, if it calls rather large taxes by another name, but Shakespeare rightly noted that: "What by name? What roses are called, even called otherwise, would smell the same."

title: Rational ignorance
text:
Very often we can hear from critics of the free market economy about alleged market failures caused by information asymmetry, or by the fact that someone does not know something, for example due to a lack of education, so that he is then unable to make a qualified decision; therefore, according to those concerned, a state is needed to correct the situation. Now let's leave aside that it doesn't fix and at best just consumes a lot of resources for nothing (at worst it damages); I would like to focus here on the alleged "market failure", which in my opinion is not really a market failure at all. It is important to realize that information and education are not free goods, as it is necessary to spend a minimum of time (and typically a little more) to acquire them; when someone does not have information, we often only see the disadvantages of that state, but we forget that the person saved resources that he did not have to spend to get it.
Basically, before we get some information, we can't know for sure whether the effort we spent to get it paid off or not, because we don't know it at that moment; there is nothing left for anyone but to try to guess using their own experience, since we do not have a crystal ball for predicting the future. And because people are different and our experiences (and personalities) are different, some simply prefer information over other things (like free time), others don't; however, this is definitely not a market failure, everyone simply chooses what they think is best for themselves. And calling information asymmetry a market failure is like saying the market failed when I missed the bus while the daily jogger caught it - we both chose what we think is best for us, which gives us different advantages and disadvantages in different life situations; and if we are not satisfied with it, we can change our lives.

title: Trade balance
text:
A "positive" trade balance means that the price of goods exported from a country exceeds the price of goods imported; the opposite is called a "negative" trade balance. It is fixed in the consciousness of the people that we should strive for the first of the above states; but is it really desirable? A "positive" balance of trade means that goods are leaving the country whose market price is higher than that coming in; it is the opposite with money, however, if the country keeps a "positive" trade balance all the time, the money will only be devalued by inflation, because it will never be spent, because then the goods flowing into the country would have to have a higher value than what is leaving it. It can be compared to when you earn, you save, but you never spend the money, you just dissolve it in inflation; this analogy, by the way, explains why it makes no sense to argue that a "positive" trade balance creates jobs (yes, it does, but the goal is not work, but its products).
So is it appropriate to strive for a long-term "negative" trade balance? Well, that's a futile effort in the first place; it would be great if others were constantly giving us things with a greater market value than we are giving them, but this state of affairs is not sustainable. So what is desirable? After all, laissez-faire: The greater the interest in, for example, Czech goods in the world, the stronger the koruna will be, which will naturally increase the price of those goods, ergo the interest in them will decrease; on the contrary, little interest in Czech goods in the world will cause a weak koruna and low exchange rates, as a result of which the price of the goods will fall, which will again increase interest in them. We can keep track of the trade balance for the sake of interest (of course it is not desirable if it involves bugging businessmen by customs or the statistical office), but it is foolish to think that some official or economist can decide whether it is "correct" for it to be "positive" or "negative"; that's something that
only the market can
.

title: Guns are bad, huh?
text:
Have you ever noticed how the majority of people who have never come into contact with firearms, have no particular interest in them, and don't even have anyone around them who owns any firearms and makes no secret of it? Based on many years of personal observation, I have to state that their relationship to firearms is typically very negative, although if they become more interested in the issue, or if they have a passionate shooter around them, their opinions usually change significantly; after all, it is not surprising when we consider that firearms are in principle the same as, for example, knives or sticks, only far more effective, but in principle they are tools like any other. And when it comes to the ability to easily and quickly kill as many people as possible, explosives, which are not so much a problem to make at home, will do just as well for a similar purpose; however, the vast majority of people simply do not desire such a thing.
So how is it possible that people who are not interested in the issue are so often a priori more or less biased against guns? I see no other explanation here than
omnipresent state propaganda, which tries to impress people from childhood
present firearms as something inappropriate or hostile to be wary of, and anti-gun activism as something noble; why does the state have this interest? Well, because an unarmed citizen is easier to control even in extreme situations; we can also notice that precisely for that reason, the same weapons in the hands of the police and the army are not presented and perceived negatively. Not to mention that the fewer people who own a gun, the less resistance there will be to constant (especially European, but not only) regulations, which unfortunately affect the shooter more and more; and we have one of the best gun laws in the world in terms of freedom. Hopefully it stays that way.

title: Transparency
text:
A transparent environment around public funds is something that all politicians keep promising us, and many of them use it as a sort of fix-it-all charm; unfortunately, the voters (and especially the young and left-wing ones) very often believe them and often repeat it after them. However, transparency is not the solution to our problems for two reasons: First, we have public administration and the state in general is already so big that even with full transparency of all transactions, there will be such a large number of them that it will be impossible for anyone to control them (and if it happens, it means another sea of lost time and inefficiency); and secondly, apart from completely obvious and glaring cases, it is not clear even in a transparent environment what the state does in the interest of citizens and what it does not, because
directive (not market) controlled economy does not allow for economic calculation
. Therefore, transparency solves practically nothing in our situation; the only solution is shrinking the state.

title: Everyone subsidizes; we must too!
text:
I often hear that "we" (apparently meaning the Czechs) have to subsidize "our" (probably Czech) farmers because other countries do it too, which gives them a competitive advantage; and related to this "logic", I wonder if the goal of agriculture is to have something to eat, or simply to have agriculture. What will happen if farmers subsidize all countries except the Czech Republic? Well, people in the Czech Republic will get the opportunity to buy goods that will be subsidized by taxpayers from foreign countries; and farmers? Well, some can compete with it (then there's no problem), others can't; but what does that mean? That these people obviously consume resources that people use for their business
they value more than the product these entrepreneurs supply them with
, ergo it is better for them to go do something else, or change their business in some way; we will not starve to death (if there was a threat, then these farmers would no doubt feed themselves).

title: Title business
text:
"If the state didn't grant accreditation and didn't monitor who can issue degrees, everyone could set up a school in the free market and just sell diplomas," is a very common argument against
free market education
; and it also makes sense... that is, before you think about it for at least half a minute. Why is it possible to sell titles today? Well, simply because they have value in today's world; and who gives them here? State; precisely those accreditations, the "guarantee" of certain standards, state matriculation exams, but also the requirements for education for civil servants. If degrees are not given value by the state apparatus, the real value of a diploma will flow only from the reputation of the one who grants it; and if some entity starts selling diplomas just like that, it will devalue them, for which it will soon pay.
On the assumption that the state will not give any accreditations and each educational institution decides for itself under what conditions it will give its students which certificate, then employers will stop having requirements like "high school graduation" or "completed higher education", but will also start to be interested in which school the diploma comes from and what it actually means. It makes no sense to buy it from someone who will simply sell similar certificates, because everyone can immediately issue them to themselves, or come up with any title; in the free market, no one will prevent anyone from doing so, as a result of which the meaning of "having a degree" will be lost, but it will only matter who awarded it (and to prevent counterfeiting, each educational institution can, for example, provide a web interface where you can verify who actually graduated and how). So the argument about selling titles on the open market is absolute nonsense.

title: Nature and tradition
text:
In this text I would like to deal with two very similar and quite often used arguments, which I find both absolutely equally stupid and meaningless; we can meet them mainly in debates about freedom, the state, homosexuality, pedophilia, but also interpersonal relations. According to the first, something is right because it is natural; the other tells us that something is right because generations of our ancestors have done it, so we should stick to it. Both sound reasonable at first glance, but upon closer reflection we find that neither makes sense. Of course, I'm not saying that if something is natural, or if the clouds have been doing it for generations before us, we shouldn't even consider whether it might not be a good idea - because very often it will be; on the other hand, I consider it a road to hell to accept such things thoughtlessly and use historical experience or nature as an argument.
Why? Well, it's natural, for example, that if we get an infection that our immune system can't deal with without antibiotics, we'll die; Should we therefore resign from medicine and die? Generations of our ancestors believed that the Earth was flat; should we take it for granted? No! Of course, there are many other cases in which what is natural, or proven by generations, really makes sense, but there are also quite a few where we simply invented a better way; for that reason the arguments of tradition and nature are worthless. They are roughly on the level of saying that if something is a means of transport, then it must necessarily be a car; it may or may not be true, ergo it cannot be rationally argued, it is simply necessary to come up with another defense of such a claim... and exactly the same applies to arguments based on nature or historical experience.

title: Bastiat on democracy, I on emotions
text:
Claude Frédéric Bastiat declared almost two centuries ago: "Good God! What an effort it is to prove in political economy that two and two make four! And if you succeed, people will start shouting: "It is so obvious that it is boring." - And then they will proceed to vote as if you had not proved anything at all." Doesn't that remind us of something? Well, yes to me; but why does this keep happening over and over again? Because a huge number of people make decisions on the basis of emotions, and the rational basis for such decisions does not interest them at all, often even rather distracts them; how many times have you seen someone make a claim based on certain arguments that you later disproved and the person just went to find a new one to stand their ground? Alternatively, have you experienced someone defending their position with arguments that were mutually exclusive and conflicting?
This - perfectly normal - behavior says only one thing: None of the arguments such a person makes are the real reasons why he holds a certain point of view (if they were, their refutation would convince him); real reasons tend to be emotional. I have long lived under the belief that taking a stand based on emotion is inferior; in recent years my opinion has changed - i think it's ok (of course it's not ok to initiate violence based on it). But where am I going? Most people (and libertarians especially) dismiss and deride emotional reasons; then what is the result? Will it change anyone's thinking? No; the people in question somehow rationalize their positions and lie to everyone (especially themselves) that they have logical arguments, which does not help anything, on the contrary, it may seem meaningful to explain something logically to such a person, although it is impossible to succeed in this and another path must be chosen. Let's be careful of too quick judgments...

title: Efficient tax collection
text:
Effective tax collection is the bane of many politicians, who, when they manage to collect more money in taxes than their competitors, tend to even brag about it; it is important to realize that this bragging is not equivalent to the joy of the owner of a private company from higher profits, because these mean (if the company is not connected to the state) voluntary payments from customers, ergo also quality work on the part of the service provider, which obviously satisfied the needs of its clients well. But when a politician levies higher taxes, it is not doing something for someone for which that person would give them their money, but simply forcing people to hand over even more resources to the state against their will, under threat of violence, without any increase in wealth in the process, on the contrary; bragging about such actions is then something like a robber bragging about how many people he has hurt and robbed.
One of the popular tricks to increase tax collection and still win the sympathy of a large part of the electorate is to raise taxes on the rich and big companies; even if we completely ignore the populism of such a move and the motivations of envious socialists who applaud such looting, this approach shows quite clearly that the goal of the state is nothing more than to grab as much as possible - more taxes from those from whom it expects to be milked a little more. So the next time you hear populist talk about progressive taxation and a more friendly tax system for small businesses and entrepreneurs, don't be fooled; it's not a favor from the state, but purely the fact that the tax burden is already so high that the taxpayers wouldn't have to bear it, so they need to be relieved a little so that they don't stop pouring completely (not that I don't agree with every tax cut, I'm just trying to show things in a wider context).

title: Sustainable development
text:
Sustainable development is a doctrine that is very popular especially among young people, but not only among them, most consider it to be at least a good (though perhaps not very realistic) idea; for me personally this concept is nothing more than classic ill-conceived nonsense - these are very popular these days by the way (poses don't cost a lot of energy, thinking does). Our world is dynamic, society develops very quickly and technology even faster; sustainable development basically ignores this. Its advocates tell us that we should not use non-renewable resources because they are running out, but they ignore the technological development that, for example, a hundred years ago coal was the majority of consumption, today it is oil and no one knows what it will be in another hundred years; and development will absolutely logically reflect the shortcomings of the given time - the less oil is needed, the more its price will rise and the more the search for alternatives will pay off.
What if we mine everything, you ask? Well, those businessmen are not idiots who need a civil servant to guide them; the closer it gets to "extracting everything", the more society will lean towards renewable resources, because then it will also start to pay off financially (raw materials will be scarce and their price astronomical). Well, if that's what it's all about, why not switch to renewables now? Well, simply because it gets better the better the technology we have; therefore, it is not worth wasting resources on it now, when in tens or hundreds of years (it is hard to say when it will be necessary) the same result can be achieved with much less effort, or some completely different solution will appear that we cannot even imagine today (and in a market economy it will always be possible to make money from what is needed) - only an arrogant fool, a left-wing intellectual, a politician and the like feel that they can plan it better.

title: Worshipers of the state
text:
"Absurd. For example, a loud football fan eats a football and insults educated hipsters in the humanities, but then they pay for a theater performance. And the same hipsters, for example, insult football fans as primitives and nags, and pay for the football matches. And the only thing they agree on is that it's reasonable and it simply wouldn't work otherwise, because we'd all shoot each other here. Oh yeah."
So sounds one very true and brilliantly worded
comment in Stoké
; and since I consider it to be of very high quality, I would hate for it to fit. Marek28 thus commented on state subsidies to support sports; and I would allow myself another thought.
For what reason do the two aforementioned groups agree on state interventions, instead of each voluntarily paying their own? In my opinion, simply because for both, a "good state" means that they can force their opponents to pay, while they will not pay them - let's look at the rhetoric of everyone who defends the state as such, but does not like where the funds are going right now ("The state is needed, but it should..."); they generally don't mind forcing someone to pay for something they don't want - they only mind when they're on the victim side, but they find the enslavement of others desirable. They don't say it in those words, but the meaning of their message is clear; What does this mean? They're either true ruthless thugs or they've been so massively hammered into their heads that it's okay to obfuscate the point; personally, I think the latter is the case for most people... so let's show them the truth.

title: Communists yes, Nazis no?
text:
Have you ever wondered why the Nazis are persecuted by the fools for every nonsense, uniformed monkeys search their apartments in the early hours of the morning, destroy their belongings and hurt them in the name of fighting a dangerous ideology, while the communists, who already profess more or less the same values (the only difference is which groups of people they want to persecute more and which less), are not only not banned, but even sit in parliament? The answer is quite simple: there are simply more Communists; and buzzing such a large group of people is not easy because they might resist. It is far better to find a similar ideology, which is professed by a few desperate people, whose social danger is currently minimal, because there are really few of them, however, it is all the easier to target them, show activity and pretend that we need monkeys in uniform because they protect us from them.
And what is the name of the principle on the basis of which the Nazi demented people were banned from their hobby, while the communist ones were not? Well, it is the right of the stronger; precisely the right of the stronger that many fear would prevail in anarchy. The catch, however, is that the law of the stronger still applies today, across various social institutions, the only difference being who is the "stronger"; somewhere among the bushmen it is the one with bigger muscles and a club, in capitalism the best or richest entrepreneur, in feudalism typically the one with better origins, in democracy it is the darling of the crowds with the most votes. Always and everywhere someone will be stronger and another weaker, with the former typically having more options (which of course can be at the expense of the latter, but it doesn't have to be); the question is how do we measure that "strength" - should the "strong" be the one who best satisfies the needs of the people or the biggest populist?

title: Vacation in the Protectorate
text:
I recently watched on the Internet (albeit only sideways on the second monitor during other activities) the documentary historical reality show "Holiday in the Protectorate" (from 2014); the point of the show was that the selected family had to live for some time (weeks or months) in a simulated World War II environment (if anyone were to ask, I don't consider the series to be total shit, but I probably wouldn't recommend it to anyone more than as a soundtrack). The goal was to bring the viewer closer to how (terrible) life was back then; and although today we live in a wonderful time (in my opinion, probably the best in the entire history), I could not help but notice certain similarities, which the performers, most probably also the screenwriters, and I can imagine also the majority of the audience, completely missed, and therefore I would like to point them out.
One of the first horrors the family had to go through in their new environment was the censorship of textbooks, from which "unsuitable" authors and "dangerous" ideas had to disappear; one of the contestants even commented that it is something completely unimaginable nowadays. Really? Back then, Hitler simply banned Czech authors, today we ban Hitler. Another shock came when our family was hit with a twenty percent tax for the benefit of the Empire; people were justifiably indignant at how crazy this crap was, after filming was over, they were expected to return to normal life with a total tax burden of sixty to seventy percent. The icing on the cake was then a reminder of how Hitler seduced the poverty of the time into food speculators; this is also a big difference compared to today, where nobody accuses speculators of anything in such a populist way, right? Yes, we live a fairy tale these days; however, it still applies - beware of bullies.

title: Corruption, an eternal theme
text: Almost every political party has the fight against corruption in its agenda; why isn't it working? That the bad guys would always take over? Typically yes, but that's not the reason. Corruption is an inherent part of state power, because it stands and falls on the fact that its people have resources that are not theirs, but that the state has plundered from its subjects; such an environment creates the potential for corruption in itself by the existence of public funds. Every control body then runs into exactly the same problem, because it is itself corruptible; just by being tasked with fighting corruption, he has gained the power that gives him the incentive to allow himself to be corrupted. Is there any solution to this situation at all? Yes, sure; if the state does not have public means and resources, there is a complete lack of motivation to corrupt it. No control body, no politician with empty promises, simply no one will be able to stop corruption as long as there are public funds; when these disappear, the problem disappears with them.

title: What causes poverty?
text: Sometimes we are faced with the following question: "What causes poverty?" But the answer – to the surprise of many – is that poverty is not caused by anything; it is a natural state. Men are by nature poor, and have nothing but what is freely around them; none of what we call wealth (or at least not poverty) is available in and of itself, all of these goods had to be produced by someone - and just because we're so covered in them at the moment, we feel like it's something everyone's entitled to (and many of us like to forget that in order to get something, someone has to produce it too). I do not think there is any point in asking what causes poverty, which is a natural state and is not caused by anything; for a far better question is, "What causes prosperity?"

title: Pretended time preferences of ecologists
text:
The average Democratic politician's typical planning time horizon is about one term, so these parasites rule in a flood-after-us style; green eco-terrorists are no different from them in this, but as part of their media theme they pretend to have significantly lower time preferences when they explain to us that we should give up various goods in the present in order to help ourselves (or our descendants) in the distant future. Many people believe that the more you plan ahead, the better; but is it really so? It is not; for two main reasons. The first reason is that time preferences are a purely individual matter - some people prefer to feel better now and pay for it later, others the other way around; both of these approaches have their advantages and disadvantages, the assessment of which depends on each of us, and it is not possible to objectively decide which approach is "better".
The second reason, easily understandable for those who are not intimately familiar with the principles of the Austrian economic school, is the impossibility of predicting the future (and especially the distant future), which means that it is not excluded (in addition, it is sometimes very likely) that we will currently take some costly measures dictated to us by ecologists, so that in the end it turns out that it was completely unnecessary; for example, we will limit the production of materials that slowly decompose in nature, so that in a few (dozen) years we will find out that thanks to progress, we can not only decompose them, but also gain something from it. Of course, nothing like that may happen, but no one can know, we are all (even the most educated among us) left to the field of conjecture; therefore, everyone should make their own decisions without being forced by anyone (especially the government) to follow the ideas of eco-terrorists.

title: The fight against inequality
text:
In the last many decades and especially years, the "fight against inequality", by which we typically mean wealth inequality, has grown enormously; for a moment, let's ignore how such a fight typically takes place, i.e. that the state takes by force from one to give something from the loot to someone else, embezzles a little and simply wastes a large part of the resources, and let's focus on what the fight is actually based on - it is a generally (and quite without thinking) accepted assumption that inequality is bad and we have to get rid of it. The first question is why inequality always automatically means wealth inequality; people are not equal in terms of mental and physical attributes, talents, talents, character traits, charisma, in fact inequality prevails in absolutely everything. So why artificially try to induce a kind of post-confidential equality in the aspect of wealth? Is it okay to turn the rich fool to the intelligent pauper? Isn't the other one already at an advantage?
However, I consider the question of why inequality is bad at all to be far more serious; almost everyone takes it as fact that there is no point in discussing it, but I refuse to accept it. Take, for example, complaints that workers in certain professions are poor because they have to toil many hours a day for little money; these complaints are only because there are other professions where this is not the case, but they completely ignore the fact that a few decades or hundreds of years ago most people worked in even worse conditions, which was acceptable then because many people were just as bad, whereas today it has become unacceptable only because it is no longer the standard and there is some demand for equality. However, can someone logically explain to me why a certain level of poverty is unacceptable not depending on its absolute level, but depending on how most people are doing at the time?

title: Cheap shunt
text:
Someone recently asked me in a discussion how I, as a libertarian, would deal with the market failure of producers of all sorts of things driving their price down at the expense of quality, because customers hear low prices more than anything else; my answer was, understandably, that I would not solve it in any way, because it is not a market failure, but rather efficiency. If people prefer to buy cheap and low-quality products, it means that they prefer them to expensive, higher-quality ones; there can be many reasons: financial need, planning an upgrade (in the past, people bought washing machines or refrigerators for twenty years; today they don't, on the other hand, new products also offer new functions, designs, etc.), joy from more frequent purchases and product changes, preference for a larger number of low-quality items over a smaller number of higher-quality items, but also missing information (a customer may prefer a cheaper item because they do not know that the more expensive item will last much longer).
First, note that the market always responds to the wishes of consumers regardless of their reasons; this is only a good thing, because precisely thanks to market mechanisms, a change in consumer preference was revealed, which would be difficult for a central planner to estimate, since even people themselves often cannot formulate it (in fact, on the contrary - how many times do we hear begging for a low life span and how little praise is given to the benefits arising from it). Second - and this is very interesting - even a change in preferences due to lack of information is not a market failure, on the contrary! Even obtaining information costs something (at least time); and until we have the information, we typically can't know for sure whether it was useful to us, yet we have to decide whether or not to sacrifice time to get it. Therefore, those who buy uninformed are indeed in a worse situation from the point of view of purchase, but on the other hand, they have saved time that they could have used in other ways; is it worth it How to whom; so let's let everyone decide.

title: People are stupid, we have to protect them (from themselves)
text:
You must have heard the phrase in the title of the article countless times; not necessarily expressed precisely in these words, but essentially hidden behind the rationale behind most regulations and laws. Now, let's ignore for a moment that the realization of such protection through the state is
immoral
a
effectively unfeasible
; suppose we have a tool that can seriously provide that protection. What will happen? The price people have to pay for making bad decisions will drop; as a result, the motivation to make good decisions also decreases (making good decisions takes time, effort, and sometimes education, which again requires time and effort; and above all, often requires responsibility). Quite logically, people become comfortable and become less responsible, but also more stupid (intelligence also needs to be developed and trained, an untrained brain stunts just like an untrained muscle); good, but they will be protected so it wouldn't be worth it after all, you think?
Um, let's look at the other implications; a society with more irresponsible and stupid people will need even more protection. And what happens when they get it? Of course, he will again become comfortable, lose some responsibility and cleverness, which will again lead to another need to mitigate the consequences of bad decisions; but what's worse? There will be more children raised by irresponsible parents, thus society will begin to degenerate in such a way that each succeeding generation will require a greater degree of protection from itself; and where will it all lead? To the absolutely stupid, uneducated and irresponsible dumb masses of people who can't even wipe their own asses; and we're still talking about conditions where there's a magical way to protect these people from themselves without it costing them anything. There's no such thing in the real world, unfortunately... or for goodness sake?

title: The most dangerous religion
text:
Buddhism? Judaism? Christianity? Islam? Although people in the world have committed all kinds of atrocities in the name of many beliefs, none of the commonly known religions come even close to the most dangerous of all in the brutality and fanaticism of their believers; it is a religion that is responsible for the dead and sheep and fanatics clearly the most, theirs
indoctrination takes place all the time and in various places
, and it is extremely treacherous also because it is typically not even considered a religion, although it exhibits all its features – yes, you guessed it, it is statism. Like other religions, this too has its dogmas ("we need a state, otherwise we would kill each other"), which are practically not discussed and, above all, not critically thought about, sacred symbols (flag, anthem), priests (politicians), ceremonies (elections) and more holy wars have been and are still being fought in its name than in the name of anything else.
However, statism has one more peculiarity; it is the only religion which really has the characteristic (so often attributed to Islam of late) that it is aggressive by its very nature, and by principle requires violent propagation. How is that? Well, in all other religions, trends can arise (and do arise) that continue to recognize belief in God or some holy men, but do not demand the imposition of a given belief on others (we can argue about how significant this is a deviation from this or that holy book, but in practice it is a state that can be reached and achieved); however, in the absence of that element of coercion, statism simply ceases to be statism - whoever demands that the state have power only over those who voluntarily agree, essentially ceases to be a statist and begins to be a libertarian (in other words, actually the opposite of a statist, since he is de facto defined by imposing anything on others through the state).

title: Run the state like a business (and fuck the economic calculation)
text:
Everyone has surely heard some smart guy expound on the wonderful idea of "running the state like a business"; and many even believe that libertarians must be on the hook for it. How did this idea come about? Well, the state has problems with inefficiency, private companies are often efficient, so why not try it? This is primarily because it is not possible - companies do not have any magic of efficiency, their clouds are absolutely inefficient; the whole "magic" lies in the fact that the ones that work poorly cannot make money on themselves, so they go bankrupt, ergo only the efficient ones stay afloat in the long run (and the moment they slow down, they are replaced by others on the free market). There is no such thing as "running a business" as there are a huge number of ways to run a business; and no one knows today what methods will be competitive tomorrow, but the market will mercilessly take them over, which is out of the question in the case of the state. Why?
Since the state collects funds for its functioning by force and provides services regardless of
there is no meaningful metric of state effectiveness
; and if someone "manages it like a company", it may mean a prosperous company, but far more likely a bankrupt company (which will never go bankrupt, because the losses will be paid by the taxpayers), while which of those possibilities occurred is in the stars, because it cannot be known even ex post (although it can be estimated). The entrepreneur is clear - as long as his company prospers in the free market, he manages it effectively, as soon as it stops prospering, it means the opposite; but what state? A politician starts to "run it like a business", but how do you know if it has helped and what is it good for compared to the previous state? You can look and guess by eye, or run a bunch of different statistics and look very scientific... but how do you evaluate the benefit? He doesn't even have units...

title: Collective guilt and scumbags
text:
I have noticed that many people find it inconsistent the position of almost all anarcho-capitalists, who on the one hand vehemently reject collective guilt, but on the other hand are able to declare that the cops are pigs; why is this inconsistency only apparent? This is because collective guilt means blaming someone for what other members of the group to which the person belongs have committed; for example, to excuse Hiroshima and Nagasaki because of what happened before at Pearl Harbor is a typical example of collective guilt, because the specific people who attacked Pearl Harbor were overwhelmingly not the same people who massacred the atomic bombs a few years later, they just belonged to one nation. Of course, nation does not have to be the only criterion, it can be religious affiliation, skin color or other parameters; regardless of whether a person was born with them or acquired them during life, he is not responsible for the actions committed by someone else.
So is there an exception for uniformed monkeys? No. We also judge them only by their actions; but in order to be a policeman, a person has to do immoral things (starting with the fact that he signed up for the services of the largest criminal organization in the given territory as a rapist, ending with the fact that during his service he actually violates the principle of non-aggression every time he legitimizes someone, stops him in a car, etc.). Similarly, when I pass any judgments on murderers, robbers, thieves, or sexual predators, it is not for what other members of that group have committed, but for what each of them must have done to be included in such a group; it is actually a group defined by some action or behavior - and if we condemn this particular action, then it is not an application of collective guilt to condemn the whole group, since all its members committed exactly what we condemn. And it is precisely on this principle that the widespread condemnation of policemen as swine works.

title: Are we living in totality?
text:
The vast majority of people will answer this question no, because we have a democracy; and with regard to the propaganda that the state pushes into us already during compulsory school attendance, such a naive answer is not surprising. First of all, let's clarify the difference between totalitarianism and dictatorship: One of those terms describes the extent of state power, while the other describes its concentration. Dictatorship means the concentration of power in the hands of an individual or a small political group without an opposition or other entity limiting that power; it doesn't matter how the rulers rule (mostly cruel and totalitarian, but not a requirement). Totality then describes a state where the state significantly intervenes in practically all aspects of the lives of its subjects; however, power in totality is not necessarily held by a single person or a small group. Totality often goes hand in hand with dictatorship, but both regimes can exist independently.
Democracy is indeed incompatible with dictatorship, because either the people or the monarch (or a select group) can have unlimited power, both cannot occur at the same time; however, the existence of a democratic system does not exclude totalitarianism, because even a democratic state can recklessly intervene in all sectors of the lives of its citizens. I am also personally convinced that the trend towards socialism (and as a result also towards totality) is
an inevitable inherent feature of every democracy
, in which the right to vote is not significantly restricted in any way; and the Czech Republic is a shining example of this - just look at the Civil Code or the Labor Code (and not only that). Whether you come to the conclusion that we live in totalitarianism or not, remember that although dictatorship is mutually exclusive with democracy, the same is not true of totalitarianism.

title: Voter shopping
text:
Many people (including politicians) are very negative about "buying" votes and "bribing" voters; doing it openly and directly (paying someone to vote for me) is even against the law, so it's done through donuts and such. However, if politicians really wanted to exclude this phenomenon from society, it would be very easy; and as a side effect, only those who are really interested in the political situation and mean something to them would still vote: Let the state stop paying money to political parties for votes obtained (thereby depriving them of part of the funds for bribing voters) and use this money differently - let every citizen have a choice at the ballot box to either vote or receive cash. It would be almost impossible to bribe voters under such conditions with a donut or a sausage, because whoever would vote just for the sake of it would rather take money for not being elected (or both, after all, the elections are anonymous).
However, politicians will never push through something like this, because on the one hand they are concerned with the dregs of the elections, but above all it could also turn out that for the majority of people who still vote (and that the voter turnout is not exactly breathtaking even today), that vote is not worth even a few crowns; how far would voter turnout drop in that case? Not that I consider the whole thing a particularly good idea, it wouldn't save the misery of democracy anyway, but the problem of "buying" voters would be solved once and for all; but why doesn't anyone put such a thing into practice? Well, simply because politicians mostly don't care; they (and by no means only they) will keep talking about it, but they will never risk a drop in voter turnout from the current plus or minus half to maybe a tenth, because then someone might start questioning their legitimacy, so we will rather wait
Zeman's fines for not voting
.

title: Helping the poor?
Global warming
text:
Even if we ignore the falsified statistics and pseudoscientists, they are already reaching for public money by fabricating evidence and creating catastrophic scenarios based on uncertain
weather forecast for tens or hundreds of years
forward, I admit the objective fact that in the last one hundred or one hundred and fifty years, when we measure the temperature, it has warmed a little; however, we have no evidence that human activity has a negligible effect on it. However, even if she had, it is questionable whether this is a problem at all; and if so, it is not clear by how large. On the other hand, we know demonstrably that the Earth has a tendency to cool enormously and warm itself - regardless of the existence of heavy industry, automobiles or other modern technologies (even without them there were ice ages, or green pastures in Greenland); the crucial question is how significant are the few degrees or tenths of degrees of warming possibly caused by humans compared to the tens of degrees caused by nature.
Unfortunately, no one knows the answer, everything is just more or less substantiated estimates, but de facto, on the one hand, no one can say what effect human activity has on the global weather, but above all, it is not at all clear what the really long-term (that is, not tens or hundreds, but thousands or more years) trend of temperature development is and what the greenhouse gases and other side effects of technology actually cause; are we adding to the already ongoing warming? Or are we delaying the next ice age? I'm afraid that with the current level of knowledge, nobody just knows. So how to approach it? Simply letting everyone make up their own mind; until there is proof that global warming is actually harming anyone (or will realistically harm anyone in the future), it is not acceptable to initiate violence against anyone who does so just because one thinks it might ever cause some harm.

title: Why don't machines take people's jobs?
text:
Perhaps everyone has come across the fairly popular scare that machines and technology in general are taking people's jobs; and many believed this economically unsubstantiated claim. So let's show why this is not true; it can be explained simply like this: Human needs are practically endless (once we have food and drink, we want housing, when we have housing, we want a car, after the car, entertainment, then more free time, even more entertainment, and so on - this is of course just an example), so if some of them are provided by machines, there will not be unemployment, but a demand for more goods, which will again create jobs. Most proponents of theories about "taking away work with technology" will admit this, but the objection will immediately come that there will be work, but not for unskilled labor. But even that doesn't make sense; why?
Well, suppose the machines drive out of the market all the unskilled workers who become unemployed; what then? Even these people will have needs that need to be met (drink, food, clothing, a roof over their heads, and the like); that could be done by the rich with technology, but the unskilled workers have nothing to offer them (their work is not wanted by the machine owners), so basically two possibilities can arise: Either the rich will give them goods for free (which is not very likely, but if that happens, unemployment itself ceases to be a problem), or a group of unskilled unemployed will start asking and offering work to each other; they will be poorer, but not unemployed, because in the worst case they will essentially create a parallel economy, which will of course develop (among other things thanks to the know-how of the mechanized part of society). So you can sleep peacefully in connection with the machines.

title: A failure of capitalism?
text:
We often hear around us that capitalism is failing; the current problems (typically caused by the state and its regulations, sometimes not obvious at first glance, but often are) that our society faces are presented as evidence. Why is this argument completely incorrect? Well, mainly because we simply don't live in capitalism, but in some kind of mix of capitalism and socialism, while problems appear mainly in those fields that the state regulates more (education, healthcare, etc.), on the other hand, those in which the state does not interfere much (for example, IT) are functional.
Capitalism is a system in which private individuals own the means of production and can do with them as they please; socialism, on the other hand, means that the means of production are owned or controlled by the state. Nowadays, although most of the means of production are still owned by private owners, it is no longer so hot to manage them; the state, by its regulations, limits the owners in how they may and may not use their means of production. After all, the fact that most of the money we earn, we hand over to the state and its central planning, the minority we keep for ourselves and spend on the market can also be considered a relatively authoritative indication - that's not capitalism, is it?
Not to mention that our society - despite the state and socialism - is still thriving; yes, sure, there are problems, but just look at what relatively poor people can afford even today: a roof over their heads, enough food, hot water, entertainment, information and education, free time, affordable means of transportation, lots of clothes. Who had access to such things a hundred years ago? Only the richest; and it is only thanks to capitalism that this prosperity has spread among the broad masses who are now so often opposed to it (although there is practically no one among them who does not use the gains of capitalism).
After all, what is capitalism actually based on? On the free market and voluntary exchanges! And the magic of voluntary exchange is that it increases the utility of both parties involved; if this were not the case, and the utility of at least one of the parties would fall from the exchange, that party would never enter into it voluntarily. Despite all the ambitions of central planners and regulators, each of whom knows best how the world should work properly, the best and easiest way to achieve prosperity is simply to let people act, willingly exchange goods and make their own decisions; well, this system is called capitalism.

title: Money as something inappropriate
text:
Money
, income, debt and financial transactions in general represent a sensitive topic for many people; why is that? Well, I have observed two reasons: The first, which I completely understand, consists in the protection of private information, which can (especially in connection with the state) be easily used against each of us; however, I often see another reason, which is not just a simple lack of information – money is often perceived as something bad. I'm sure you've all heard the scornful statement that someone does something "just for the money"; but what's wrong with that if the thing itself doesn't hurt anyone? Prostitutes and prostitutes, porn actors and porn actresses, drug testers, sometimes even businessmen, they all tend to be
crossed fingers therefore
that they do their work "just for the money"; similarly, people who are "too much for money" are condemned. Not to mention the socialist fabrications that money is the root of all evil.
It is remarkable that despite this rather negative view of money, people find work mutually rewarding.
very easy to exchange
(and it happens on a massive scale day in and day out for billions of individuals around the world), for something very virtuous; while it is money that most people work for. Not to mention that their far more important function (than motivation) is to transmit information about the real world, which makes money in my opinion
one of mankind's greatest inventions
; therefore it is a shame that so often (and from early childhood, see fairy tales) we lead young children to have a negative attitude towards them. I do not say that we should raise them to be misers, but I certainly do not think it is good to fall to the opposite extreme; money is an extremely important part of human society, its usefulness should not be neglected and the desire to acquire it (in an honest way) should definitely not be condemned, rather the opposite.

title: Murray Christmas 2018!
text:
I finally got around to it; it's Christmas again! Perhaps no other holiday so amazingly combines the spiritual, the material and the possibility not to follow what "should" be done, but to arrange things in your own way and better; so the Christian, the capitalist and the anarchist in me rejoice. At the same time, Christmas shows us (libertarians) a PR masterpiece that we (Christians) succeeded thousands of years ago: The original pagan established holiday of Saturnalia was transformed into Christmas. This is something like if we turned Czech Statehood Day into a celebration of anarchy; I think we still have a lot of work to do in this regard. So go for it!
Like every year, I will give space to the music; Christmas is all about carols, so I'll start right away
the best
, because Freddie will never die... I can't help but send that too
this
and not to point out that our society has gone from a state where the church murdered homosexuals to a state where they can sing in church; feel free to write to me about the destruction of traditional values, but I don't care about those, because I believe that God really does love us all (!!) and Pentatonix singing in church pleases him (unlike the homophobic outbursts from many of my brothers and sisters in Christ). And since love, life and music are more connected than I've ever felt before (thanks to R.), I won't limit myself to carols; if you have a moment, try to play
this
, or to look back on the past year with sound
this beauty
. I'm sorry if I didn't meet your taste; hopefully it will be better next time.
Please, let's not be mean to each other, respect the property rights of others, love our neighbor, don't initiate offensive violence, don't hurt, don't regulate the free market, let's be willingly in solidarity and don't force those who don't want to - let's not be superior to them; all these things are very closely related. Let's try to find a common language with others, spread the ideas of freedom, think critically about them and get rid of dogmas; violence begets violence, malice begets malice, hate begets hate, but banning it and restricting its expression will always bring more evil. Whenever we release our anger (even towards collectivists), the world becomes a slightly worse place; whenever kindness emanates from us, we make the world a little better. So let us not harm our enemies either, unless it is absolutely necessary; if they are hurt and frustrated, so much the worse for them, but also for us and our loved ones. Life is not a zero-sum game; and not relationships at all.
In conclusion, let me
remind this
and to quote one of the wisest people: "Love yourself."
MURRAY CHRISTMAS!!

title: The limits of democracy
text:
The vast majority of people, as a result of state propaganda, adore democracy; many even take her as
good by definition
. But what are its quantitative limits? It is evidently not true that when the majority of any number of people agree, the minority should submit; or perhaps there are supporters of each group of hooligans together with the victim being able to vote on who will walk away with the money? So is a larger number of individuals needed to minimize the risk of error? So why don't the people of the whole world vote on, for example, global redistribution? How many of Europe's lovers of democracy would voluntarily invite billions of bushmen from the poorer parts of the world to a vote on the forcible redistribution of wealth? And what would be their arguments, why not? Would something be said about primitives unable to understand our situation? But how many primitive voters in the Czech Republic influence things that they do not fully understand, just because they got a sausage or a doughnut?
So the question arises, why should a system of determining the legitimacy of human action, which shows absurd results on a small and global scale, be the ideal for nation-states? Why should it be correct at this granularity when it fails at every other? Of course, one cannot throw off the table without further arguments the possibility that, although democracy will lead to misery in most groups, it works well precisely at the level of nation-states; on the other hand, I see no reason why this should be the case, when states often represent quite artificial political constructs (for example, Czechoslovakia Masaryk compared to other powerful states). Isn't it all a coincidence that democracy is inherently amoral and unjust on every scale, and in borderline cases it can be seen at first glance, while in our reality it prevents a sober assessment of all the misery of state indoctrination we are exposed to since childhood?

title: Armed company
text:
Although the Czech legislation regarding weapons is one of the less strict compared to other European states, freedom as such can only be spoken of rigidly, because one simply cannot legally go and buy a gun or ammunition just like that - you need a permit from the state (which for many weapons cannot even be obtained); not to mention that politicians and the media constantly try to stigmatize gun owners, make them into extremists, and often publicly state that owning a gun is not a right, but a privilege, while we hardly have a single politician on the political scene who welcomes and supports an armed society.
The libertarian rationale I encounter most often is that the government is afraid of an armed society because in such a society the military or police as a whole is not stronger than the civilians, so in the event of a civil war whoever controls the state's armed forces may not win. They are of course right about that, but I don't think that it would be the main reason, because I don't suppose that Czech politicians would seriously think about a civil war, because there is no such thing as a slippage (and if there is such a thing as "national nature", then the Czech one is quite at odds with it).
Personally, I think it's addiction first, responsibility second and self-confidence third; until the fourth for some other reasons (including civil war).
Dependency – unarmed citizens are dependent on the police; the armed ones are able to defend themselves and subsequently see even better how useless (and harmful) the uniformed monkeys are.
Responsibility - an armed citizen assumes a certain responsibility that he did not have until then, which can make him more responsible; and that is precisely what conflicts with the interests of most politicians.
Self-confidence – politicians want citizens to look up to them in case of problems; those who are armed can solve part of the problems (security) themselves, ergo they don't look, or look less.
An armed society means a freer society, for the people will accept some of the responsibility that the state assumed for them in an unarmed society; therefore, let's strive to make the thunder stick a completely normal part of life for as many people as possible. And let's not forget that the moment a government starts disarming its citizens, it means that they will soon need their weapons...

title: Newspeak: poverty
text: Perhaps each of us sometimes reads - or hears - something about how many people live "below the poverty line"; usually we learn about it in connection with some alarming news in the sense that such people are increasing, or at least not decreasing. So does this mean that even though our society keeps getting richer, the poor have less and less, or still the same? No! Doesn't mean! Can you guess why? Well, the so-called "poverty line" is nothing more than a bureaucratic construct that is constantly being redefined to divide the population into rich and poor in whatever proportion suits the powers that be; yes, it's that simple - if we were to define "poverty" in the same way (and no libertarian definitions are needed, just use the bureaucratic standards of the past), we would find that the number of poor people is constantly decreasing.
