title: If everyone took care of themselves...
text:
"If everyone takes care of themselves, eventually everyone will be taken care of."
This sentence, in my opinion, perfectly illustrates the essence of most of the problems in the world today; everyone has a need to control everyone else's life, social engineers know best of all what is best for whom, socialists want to centrally plan absolutely everything. The idea of someone taking care of themselves is considered by the current establishment to be blasphemy against the biggest, most widespread and most dangerous religion of our time - statism.
Just look around at newspapers, politicians, various bloggers, read their articles; they mostly deal with mass problems at large and dictate what they should and shouldn't do to others as part of their solutions. At the same time, it would be enough for everyone to look at their own and not to invent nonsense: If you invent something for yourself and find out that you made a mistake and bear the consequences, you simply reconsider the decision, because you feel its consequences firsthand; but if someone makes decisions about others in this way, then even if his mistake is revealed, the person in question often stands behind him out of pure vanity, because someone else bears the consequences and no stranger's blood flows.
Of course, the typical objection is that some people can't take care of themselves; their loved ones or family can take responsibility for such people (which is not against anything), but even then there will be a certain (small) percentage of those who are not capable themselves and have no one else. Well, all the people who don't like the principle described above can take care of you (and some others too; I personally also donate part of my income to help people who, in my opinion, need it); however, nothing entitles anyone to come to someone and forcefully deprive them of funds that the person in question does not want to give himself.
Yes, I admit, the result will be that some one here and there will end up badly; on the other hand, it is happening now and will always happen. The difference is mainly that we currently pay an absurdly high tax to the state for it; and by that I don't just mean most of our income, but also the freedom that the state deprives us of with its laws. We have come so far that the idea that everyone should take care of themselves and not interfere in the lives of others (unless both parties agree) is considered extremism; please let's not be manipulated by this - it is right for people to make up their own minds.

title: State business despite
text:
An acquaintance of mine likes South America very much, where he spends a month or two every year; sometimes he tells me about the conditions there and it's always interesting stuff. He recently told me that although official unemployment there is quite high, the eye of the authorities does not see that far; the consequence of this is that even the officially unemployed can earn a decent living - for example, he met a woman there who made a living by boiling a cauldron of food every morning, loading it on a cart and going out into the streets to sell, so that in the evening or afternoon she returned home with enough money to live comfortably.
How easy is it to make a living as an unemployed person when there is no state and no bureaucracy to bind everyone? Who couldn't cook a cauldron of stew, buy fresh bread and sell it at the stand? And when it stops bringing it out? Simply change the assortment, sell or produce anything else, start practically from scratch in a small way, without the need for larger investments; and it doesn't even have to be about cooking - anyone with a garden can buy chickens and sell eggs, everyone can learn to weave baskets, or thousands of other things. How many people would try this if it weren't for bureaucratic legal terror?
But under the current dictates of the state, which takes care of absolutely everything by law, such a person must obtain a permit, at least a trade certificate, another certificate for working with foodstuffs, familiarize himself with all standards and comply with them, register income, pay taxes, issue receipts, and now also have an EET. How many rounds of bureaucracy does he have to go through before he finds out if his idea is even profitable and feeds it? He'd better get rid of it, especially when he has a social system and benefits at his disposal, because socialist pies are also (or actually mainly) jobless.
Sure, it's best for politicians if the unemployed don't fend for themselves; they can then show activity, create the impression of their indispensability and within that
make people dependent on the state
. After all, as some cow from ANO taught us in connection with the introduction of EET, business only makes sense if the person in question pays taxes from it; if someone goes bankrupt who does not report his income, it is said to be no harm, because such a business was useless anyway. And as long as we elect representatives, they already have a similar view of business, unfortunately nothing will change in the whole matter; and when, for the worse.

title: Through the eyes of the outlaw
text:
During my life, I had the honor of discussing with many freedom-restrictors and prohibitionists, whose motivations varied greatly, some were just afraid of something, while others I would describe as notorious prohibitionists who need to have absolutely everything covered by the law; as they arrived at their conclusions in very different ways, it has long seemed to me that they were quite different considerations, coincidentally leading to the same conclusion. Quite recently, however, I found out that there is one logical error in their thinking, which is common to almost all limiters and regulators (except for the downright actively evil ones, who are fully aware of the consequences of their actions; but in my opinion, they are a negligible minority); so what kind of mistake is it?
Well, this is a fairly widespread idea - when something is banned, people very often imagine that the thing will simply disappear; the basis of all their reasoning is based on the simple idea that when the state prohibits something, it is basically the same as if the given thing disappeared from the face of the earth and ceased to exist at the moment of prohibition. What more, at most, some more enlightened prohibitionist can see is the ineffectiveness of regulations; they typically understand that the disappearance will not be complete, but only partial, because not everyone obeys the law. However, virtually every prohibitionist ignores the costs of enforcing the restrictions, the negative side effects, and certainly not the restrictions on freedom or the distortion of the market; calling for bans is then a logical consequence of such thinking.
It is certainly interesting for the prohibitors to present these objections; he typically either downplays them, ridicules them (for example, many people respond to the objection that a typical ban implies the use of aggressive violence against innocents by declaring the absurdity of such a claim), or simply ignores them. However, it is evident from most of the reactions that the person in question did not try to compare the costs of regulation with its benefits at all (not that it is possible; we are referring to the interpersonal incomparability of benefits, but in order for the prohibitor to even understand this, he would first have to try to compare); he just sees something he doesn't like, so he automatically wants to ban it (gambling, drugs, Islam, prostitution and so on).
I know that not all of them are like that, some are among the outspoken villains who understand the consequences of their actions (and forbid for personal gain); however, I strongly believe that most banners do so for the above motives (they believe that banning will solve some problem). For that reason, all those who support bans on anything need to be constantly reminded of the cost of such measures; and the price is really high, because it is not only about the fact that the enforcers of the regulations could do something productive instead of their "work" (and their time is not free), but above all about the consequences - restriction of freedom, violence against the innocent, increasing the potential for corruption, possible creation of mafias (prohibition). Please, let's constantly highlight these costs to all banners; let us repeat again and again that almost every state ban in practice means the use of offensive violence against the innocent, although people don't want to hear much about it!

title: Ancient civilization
text:
The ancient civilization is often spoken of as a model of virtue, a great society from which we could learn a lot and, for example, the famous Islam killer Bill Warner sets it up as the opposite of the barbaric Islamic world, which enslaved people since its inception; to mention slavery in this context appears to be quite absurd considering that the entire ancient civilization was based on slaves (free people were a minority in that society). Similarly distant from reality is also the romantic idea of duels between heroic Romans and the "barbarians" of the north; what was it really about? Well, the Roman legions were simply conquering more territory, whose original inhabitants were subjugated, massacred, enslaved and tortured in the process; the conquering practices of the Roman legionnaires were not matched by their cruelty even by the Nazis, who surpassed them in scale, but this was only due to population growth and technological progress.
Ancient Greece is often referred to as the cradle of democracy; and it really was in a certain limited sense, however, it was definitely not a democracy, which would mean "the government of (all) the people", because real democracy took place among a handful of privileged (free citizens), while the majority (slaves) did not participate in the decision-making process. Paradoxically, this was the reason why those first democracies exhibited
greater stability than the current ones
(not that both kinds aren't crap, though each a bit different); although it is of course true that ours gradually developed from such a civilization, it was in no way a society from which we should take an example - we have come a long way as humanity, we have learned from many mistakes, and we should not lose sight of the fact that idealizing the past can be quite dangerous in many ways.

title: Identity, identification, authorization, state and identity cards
text:
Today, it is a matter of course for almost everyone that we have documents such as an identity card with which we can identify ourselves, the state has a central database of citizens and collects an inordinate amount of personal data about them; it's interesting how many people react with extreme irritation when private entities behave similarly (and even do it just for fun, the law forbids them), but in the case of the state, it leaves the same individuals cold. The existence of such measures is presented to us as a "necessity" without which society could not reasonably function; despite this propaganda, we easily overlook the fact that even a hundred years ago, ID cards were not compulsory (this was introduced by a certain Adolf, who helped to finally solve it), two hundred years ago they did not exist at all, and if we go back another hundred or two hundred years, we will come across the absence of records in the matrix - people were simply not registered in any way, yet no doom occurred.
Of course, it can be argued that in times when people did not travel nearly as much, everyone was in an environment where everyone knew them, identification was not needed, whereas in today's globalized world the requirements are higher; and of course that is true. On the other hand, in today's world we have cryptographic means, unknown to our ancestors, by which the problem can be completely solved;
exhaustive (and in my opinion underrated) article
OC wrote about it - one of the smartest and most uneducated anarcho-capitalists I know. Wondering why it doesn't work that way when it's so good? Well, simply because the state already does it in a different (albeit worse, more expensive, more exploitable and crappy) way, so there is no interest in spending additional funds on another system when the state system will exist anyway and we have to pay for it anyway; however, if this were to cease to exist, a market solution would replace it practically immediately.

title: Market and "fair" prices
text:
The purpose of this text is not so much to convey a message, but rather to provoke a discussion on a topic that has been bothering me lately; I'd like to know what other libertarians think about this. Model situation: A person close to me gets into a critical situation in which it is necessary to perform a tracheotomy immediately in order to survive, but I cannot do this and I do not have the tools for it; there is only one doctor in the area who can perform the procedure and has the equipment for it (other help will not arrive in time); the person in question agrees to it, but demands all my property in exchange. We can all (libertarians) probably agree that he has a right to do that; however, my question is - is it a "pig house"? At first glance, I'd say yes, but...
So that the discussion does not go in a meaningless direction, I explicitly emphasize again that I am not solving here
NAP
; from the point of view of the principle of non-aggression, of course the doctor's actions are correct, he can do it, he does not violate anyone's rights, and I have no right to force him to perform the procedure by force (whether it be putting a gun to his head, or first promising him property, but then not doing anything to him and violently defending against his attempts to take what belongs to him). Of course, even NAP compliant stuff can be crap; for example, cheating on a partner, betraying someone's friendship, cheating on someone who has helped me for a long time, hurting someone's feelings for fun, and many other similar things can be done in accordance with the NAP.
At first glance, I would classify the actions of such a doctor in the same category, on the other hand, some time ago there was a discussion in Stoká in which someone said something to the effect that the doctor should charge the market price; and at that moment I thought: What is the market price in the given situation? Of course, this varies in time and place (the price of water in the desert is different than at a dam), ergo I wonder, isn't "all my property" really the market price? I'd almost say yes given the circumstances. And if the doctor has no relationship with me, why should he provide me with a service below the price? From this point of view, it seems pretty obvious to me that his actions are not "crap".
On the other hand, I would call it "crap" if a doctor in a similar situation, where it was my loved one, but not me (and no one he could hurt), let the injured person lie on the ground, stepped over him and went on (although he has the right to do so, of course); I perceive failure to provide first aid (if someone can do it and it does not pose a risk to them) as a disgusting act. But charging a market price for it (and perhaps negotiating it quickly, so that when a loved one of the injured person says that he will not give his entire property, but "only" a million, to perform the procedure) can hardly be bad, can it? The well-known example of selling "overpriced" gasoline in areas affected by a natural disaster, where the only gas station will remain untouched, can be demonstrated that such behavior is not only okay, but even desirable and "socially beneficial." Is there anything different here?

title: Taxes - mandatory or voluntary?
text:
Have you ever wondered what happens if you don't pay your taxes? Well, it comes down to it - if it is a lot of money and you lie to the state about your income, you will be legally kidnapped and put in a dungeon straight away; if you simply do nothing, the state will call, then send bailiffs, and if you defend your property from them, there will also be sadistic monkeys in uniform, who, if you resist, will either snap you like a dog or put you in a dungeon for an even longer period than in the previous case. In fact, it's no different from a mob collecting firebombs; the difference lies only in the legality of one and the illegality of the other, in other words, in what some goons voted in parliament.
However, one can sometimes come across this statist argument: "But I pay taxes voluntarily."
Of course, we can doubt whether this is really the case, and whether the person in question would pay taxes in the amount demanded by the state even without the threat of force; but even if it were so, the taxes cannot be justified by it.
Why? Well, if this justification holds up, any act of violence for which there is at least one victim who doesn't mind being a victim and basically wants it that way can be excused this way.
For example, we could say that going to the park at night to rape women is okay, because there are those who would sleep with a rapist even without a knife to their neck.
Unfortunately, state propaganda can be seen incredibly clearly on the issue of taxes; not only is an action when someone simply refuses to hand over their money to the aggressor commonly considered "theft" in connection with taxes, but on top of that, many people think to argue that he pays taxes voluntarily, so everything is fine. Just imagine how absurd it would be in a different context - for example, you tell someone how you were robbed, only to find out from the person you are telling it to that nothing actually happened, because the last time they robbed him, he didn't really mind, so why are you complaining; but different standards apply to the state, as the teacher at school taught us...

title: Wasting food
text:
You know those pictures of piles of food being thrown away while African children are starving? They are often accompanied by some deeply moral message about our selfishness and how we should be ashamed of throwing away something that is in need elsewhere; I have two major objections to these superficial messages, which I intend to refute completely:
1/ Food here and food in Africa are two different goods; the cost of transportation is astronomical compared to the cost of the discarded food, in many cases it would be cheaper to grow new food locally.
2/ Considering how much food our society consumes, it can be considered a miracle (of the free market) that there are so few surpluses; It's simply not possible to hit the mark on consumption exactly - so do you prefer surpluses or hunger?
After all, who wants to return to the previous regime of queues for meat? And even then there were surpluses.
Not to mention that there were times when even in Europe people were starving; but then came the industrial revolution and wild capitalism which solved this problem. Let us be glad for it and wish the same to Africans; however, let's not be ashamed of the fact that we have those surpluses - on the contrary, let's be grateful for them - it does no harm to anyone and is a natural consequence of the prosperity in which we live.

title: Alcohol does not belong behind the wheel?
text:
I was just listening to a discussion about the drug problem in which some drug addict "refuted" the thesis that
drugs are different
, people do too, so the effects of using narcotics vary, ergo it's not fair to ban everyone the same; the person in question used the analogy that, for example, alcohol behind the wheel affects different people differently, yet the law applies to everyone the same and no one even thinks of questioning or discussing it. So not only has it occurred to me many times, I've even had such debates before, but I haven't written about it yet; and the fool, by taking the correctness of such a law as a given, led me to believe that a short text on the subject would do no harm.
Not only does alcohol affect different people differently, but above all it does not automatically make everyone a bad driver; only to some degree (which is itself very individual) does it reduce the abilities of the drunk. And there are undoubtedly people on the roads who will be even two per thousand better drivers than youngsters who have just left driving school; not to mention the fact that some people start reeling after a few drinks, while others just get into the mood after the same amount, with their motor skills and reaction time remaining virtually intact. So alcohol not only reduces the ability to drive in different people in different ways, but above all from a different basis (some are much better drivers than others).
From this point of view, it really seems absurd to punish people according to how many parts of alcohol they have in their blood, since some completely sober driver is more dangerous on the road than a drunk professional with millions of kilometers on the road; so what is the solution? Laissez faire, I say! Only the free market can come up with the answer. Perhaps private insurance companies and road owners would completely prohibit alcohol behind the wheel, perhaps they would allow a certain limit as a flat rate, or they would determine the dependence of permitted drunkenness on kilometers driven without accidents, or address it only in the event of an accident or not at all; and I think the most likely option is that they would come up with something that I didn't even think of here.
Not to mention that it's not even clear that the optimum lies at the point where alcohol causes the fewest accidents; we must not neglect the possibility that traffic participants will voluntarily undergo an increase in the risk of an accident in exchange for the benefit of other things (convenience and so on). And a similar possibility is not at all improbable, because, for example, everyone who leaves home and goes to a pub for a beer (even on foot) demonstrates his preference for taking certain risks to satisfy some needs; it is therefore not unrealistic for people to think similarly in connection with driving. The problem, of course, is that
without a free market we will never find a solution to the problem, because it is simply impossible
.

title: Let's shop at home
text:
It's surprising how often one hears calls to buy "homemade" goods, especially food, even though it's been almost two hundred years since Frédéric Bastiat made it absolutely clear what nonsense it is; to those who happen to be unfamiliar with it, I warmly recommend the work "What is and what is not visible" (good news for those who do not like long texts, this is short and readable). However, patriotism is strong, emotional, and state-sponsored; not to mention that being visible, having influence and being able to convince others has, unfortunately, almost nothing to do with being right or preaching delusion.
Supermarkets are even being ordered by some new law to label food with flags to show what goods consumers are buying, as the belief that it is "right" to support "homemade" products enjoys a relatively non-negligible popularity; In this way, people are falsely convinced that they are actually somehow helping themselves by buying "domestic" goods, because the prosperity of "their" state means benefits for them personally. Not that it is not true to a certain (very small) extent, but these advantages are quite negligible compared to the disadvantages that market distortions bring with them.
There are many ways to refute these delusions, I will choose the one that seems easiest to me: What is the essence of the market? The best producers and suppliers of certain goods make the most money because people voluntarily pay them for those goods; the worst ones fail. And it is this principle that is the most advantageous for consumers, as it ensures that they get exactly the goods they want; if we prioritize "domestic" goods at the expense of foreign goods instead of monitoring other parameters, it can easily happen that we give a chance to a manufacturer or supplier who, although Czech, is not as good as a foreign one.
So I am definitely not saying that we should not buy Czech goods on purpose; only that if we choose only according to quality and price, while ignoring the country of origin, we will support the best manufacturers and suppliers regardless of where they are from, but if we include the country of origin in the criteria, we may get worse Czech goods or services instead of better foreign ones next time. Personally, in addition, when given the option of choosing between Czech and foreign goods with otherwise identical parameters, I take the foreign one in order to balance the various patriotic tastes of my fellow citizens xD

title: How to move to a free market?
text:
The goal is a free market, a stateless society, i.e. anarcho-capitalism... how to get there? Privatize? If so, how? Auction off state property? Give it away? To whom and how? All at once? What about opting out of government "services"? Of which? In what order? Creating parallel structures? I would be very interested in your opinions; and in as much detail as possible, as well as reasoned, including the options you considered and rejected (and why). Please share them in the discussion? For I believe that there is no "right" way; in my eyes they are just more and less bad. Although I am convinced that some are better than others, my goal now is not to influence, but rather to learn something.
If someone is not an anarchist and his goal is a small state (or at least smaller than the current one), it does not matter at all; describe the path you would like to take from your current state to your dream state.

title: People fooled by advertising
text:
"People don't know what they want, they are manipulated by advertising, we need to regulate it to help them!" So goes the common objection against the consumerist market society; and I continue to be fascinated by the thought process of those who float it: "I am educated, aware, unmanipulated and wise, I am not affected by the corporate ads, I have seen through what millions of people have not; so now I will be the savior and help them...against their will, through violent state intervention." Sometimes such a person, if he is particularly conceited, will throw in the analogy of how parents bring up children; then he drinks the idea down with a latte from his favorite hipster cafe (but marketing doesn't apply to him, he's a hipster because he wants to). He lacks humility, respect for people and their wishes, tolerance for choosing a different lifestyle and the realization that he is not better than others - the more strongly these qualities are rooted in a person, the more the person in question promotes
free market
.

title: Traffic jams
text: Traffic jams seem to be the necessity of our time; and it is quite logical that when there are too many cars, the roads simply get clogged and the traffic is not smooth. How to solve it? I have no idea; no one else knows either, so it's probably a necessity. Such necessities have already existed; so, for example, there were times when traveling around the world in eighty days seemed almost a miracle, just as it was clear that objects heavier than air do not fly, talking to someone halfway across the world is impossible, and a person moving faster than sixty kilometers per hour will die. However, resourceful individuals with the motivation to do great things have always managed to find solutions through the thorny path of trial and error; and against such problems some traffic jam looks like a strumpet. But none of those who could solve it has the motivation to risk anything, because it has a warm place and everyone has already accepted constipation as an inevitability; so why bother and risk losing the favor of voters?

title: Safe colors
text: Cars of some colors can be seen better on the road, others less so; imagine - purely hypothetically - a regulation that bans "dangerous" car colors - red and yellow can be seen well, but away with grey. For some time now I have been seeking opinions on this regulation from proponents of (other) regulations with whom I debate; and guess what? Almost everyone is against it; even advocates of mandatory seat belts. I address the question of why this is so; it is a typical regulation, which consists in the prohibition of something "unnecessary and vain" (which no one so-called "needs", it is just a "whim") in the name of safety (and we also have the popular argument of endangering not only oneself, but also the surroundings), ergo there should be similar opinions on this as on alcohol or talking on the phone while driving, but they are not. So what's the difference? Personally, I think that this is just media massage and what is currently "modern" to ban. Do you have a better explanation?

title: Children of unschoolers
text:
As many readers know, I work in
Freedom of learning
; and because its members and supporters often put their beliefs into practice (with great results, by the way), their children often do not go to school. This is not pure unschooling, the current legislation does not allow it, because children have to be tested; and that's where something fascinating happens. These children simply do not understand why they should go through the process; they ask if the examiner doesn't know what they're asking to help and explain (which would make sense), but then when they find out it's an "examination" they don't understand the point of the whole thing. Why should they prove what they can do to a stranger, from whom they want nothing? One would see such a mindset in a schoolboy; because he is trained to do things simply because he is ordered to do them - and trying is normal. At the same time, the question: "Why should anyone test me?" is an example of critical thinking; however, this (despite declarations to the contrary) is not desirable.

title: Suicides
text: One possible—albeit somewhat morbid—way to gauge population satisfaction is to track suicide rates; of course, it has its pitfalls (it only measures the number of the least satisfied and a lot of other factors affect it), but also advantages ("survey" will not affect any lying). And what does this metric say about some popular claims that we were better off "under the communists"? Well, under the previous regime, an average of 24 people per hundred thousand inhabitants were killed annually (in the five years after 1968, even 28); since the revolution we have an average of 16 suicides for the same number of people. So people committed suicide "under the communists" fifty percent more often than today! Of course, I am not saying that a person who would otherwise be happy will kill himself just because of who is in the government (I personally do not believe this explanation even with Palach); however, I believe that the political system affects people's lives enough to make some (not all) reasons for suicide.

title: Neoliberalism
text: Neoliberalism. The New Liberalism. What does that actually mean? The original meaning and many more recent ones can be found on Wikipedia; and a mention of how many times the meaning shift has occurred. Currently, the term is used almost exclusively by proud leftists, mostly as a slur. However, when you ask them for a definition, the answers tend to be non-existent or extremely vague (even the panel discussion on the topic "Diagnosis: Neoliberalism", for which I visited the Clinic, began with an explicit statement that they would not define the term, which they followed through), so when something comes out of them, it is usually a statement that it is a process of loosening state regulations, "free marketization" of society and privatization of state property; however, this contradicts the fact that by neoliberalism they often refer to the current reality, where the trends are exactly the opposite. So I ask—especially to proud leftists if they read this: Is the word “neoliberalism” more than a slur and a cliché?

title: New drugs
text:
Some people are appalled by the ingenuity of drug manufacturers, who from time to time come up with new narcotic substances, the destructive effects of which are often worse than those drugs that have been on the market up to that time; in recent years, for example, it is the crocodile substance, which got its name because it can damage its users in a similar way to a crocodile bite (pieces of their body fall off; and it is not surprising if we look at what this substance is made of). Where does such a demand for these drugs come from? Well, they are mostly created as substitutes for others that are more expensive (for example, some have started replacing cocaine with meth, and heroin with the aforementioned crocodile). And what causes such a high price when the production cost of drugs is negligible? Of course states and their regulation; she gave birth to all this crap"
the war on drugs
", without which no desperate person would want to inject the compounds of gasoline, thinner and hydrochloric acid into their veins.

title: Gay weddings
text: Perhaps all libertarians will agree that the state should not interfere at all in marriages (heterosexual or homosexual), just let everyone deal with their own affairs as they see fit. Unfortunately, the situation today is that the state is usurping decision-making in this area (as in almost everything); and the rulers ordered that only two people of different sexes can marry (two people of the same sex can register their partnership, other combinations are not allowed). And some libertarians take the position that if the state shouldn't do weddings at all, we certainly shouldn't support gay weddings either, since that's closer to a "no state wedding" state; however, this does not make sense as long as the state disadvantages unmarried couples over married ones in many ways. Marriage currently, from a purely practical point of view, allows relaxation of some state regulations; and as long as these exist, we should not be able to deny marriage to anyone - regardless of gender or number of individuals.

title: Is stealing BTC a violation of the NAP?
text:
One of my readers asked me a question: When someone steals Bitcoin, they are in violation
non-aggression principle (NAP)
? The "theft" in itself (that is, sending a signed transaction that moves BTC from one address to another) is not, in my opinion, a violation of the NAP. No one can own a private key (it is a sequence of bits, in principle it cannot be owned, it can only be known and kept secret) or prevent others from signing transactions (thereby violating the NAP), therefore dealing with "foreign" BTC is not a violation of the NAP. The question, however, is how the "thief" got the key; there, most likely, a violation of the NAP has already occurred (even if he didn't break into anywhere, but hacked some device, it is still a violation of the NAP, because it involved dealing with someone else's property - that device - against the owner's will), although in theory it might not have to (if the "thief" had seen and remembered the key, for example).
You can watch the recording of my lecture on this topic from the Bitcoin is Retro conference on the Freeport Channel.

title: Cost versus benefit
text:
They say that in a blind test, people taste wine better when they think it was expensive; cheers! In the 1980s, the U.S. Army bought a toilet seat for forty-five thousand crowns, adjusted for inflation, and a hammer for thirty; if they told the soldiers, maybe they would shit and hammer better. When it broke, the taxpayers got screwed; however, they had to do so on boards two orders of magnitude (!) cheaper. I'm here some time ago
compared the budget of the anarchist Wikipedia and the state-owned Czech Television
; how did it turn out? Everyone understands why not spend thirty grand on a hammer; because we know the market price of the hammer. However, there was a time when it cost far more resources to make a hammer even on the open market than it does today; the toilet seat didn't even exist then. In light of this, I ask: How do we know that spending on public education, health, the judiciary and the police is not another hammer in thirty liters?
How much should they "correctly" cost?

title: We are dying out!
text:
Social engineers have a problem; and as it happens in a state-run society, we have it with them. In the Czech Republic, the birth rate is low, the population is aging, the nation is dying, the apocalypse is approaching; not that there would be any problem at all, if the comrades in the government hadn't invented an infinitely stupid pension system long ago, which assumes that this won't happen (and not that anyone would have noticed the whole thing at all, if it weren't for the CZSO and the state records of every fart). However it happened, the state (again) made a mistake; and instead of correcting it by phasing out the pension system, he is trying to save the situation with more mistakes.
Child allowances, maternity allowances, tax write-offs for children, and now perhaps even a reduction in social insurance for more children, these are all measures intended to stimulate citizens to have more intensive procreation; something like when a farmer has cattle and needs more cattle for economic reasons, somehow the lords of power look at us. They devised some pension system based on the assumptions that once held; and that would play so well that now the plebs are disrupting their plans, no such thing, you will give birth nicely!
By the way, what kind of people will the state's motivational methods be effective on? Do you want to increase the birth rate by giving financial benefits to people with children, dear social engineers? Holy goodness! At best, it will simply have no effect; in the worst case, it will mean that someone will start having children because they received subsidies from the state. People overflowing with love, who are able to pass on the best to their offspring and raise them to be decent people, will certainly provide excellent protection. As a result, the next generation will be even more dependent on the state than the previous one; and worse, I highly doubt that this is some diabolical plan, just the normal cycle of things where demented state solutions are quite naturally created and supported by stupid statists.
The next question is, of course, what is the correct number of people in the Czech Republic? Ten million? Eleven? Nine? Hundred? One million? Although our society with ten times or one tenth the population would look quite different than it does now, living conditions would change, but who knows exactly how? There is no one who could convincingly justify why ten million people in the Czech Republic is a more correct state than nine million there; the only argument for trying to get the ten (and more) is the poorly set pension system. But why use social engineering to mitigate the consequences of a bad decision when the right solution is
change this decision
?

title: Collective guilt against racism?
text: From time to time, the Roma activist Ivan Veselý appears in my field of vision, who from time to time comments on various happenings in society; I remember his statement about the Germans, whom he does not trust and dislikes because of the Holocaust ("they killed our elites" - meaning Roma), and also about the Muslims, whom he would have impaled if he had to fight them. Let's say his second statement could only have been about those Muslims he would have gone to war with, however, he doesn't trust the Germans across the board (even without the war) because of what their - long dead - fellow citizens have done. Isn't that ironic? His theme in life is that people should not judge all gypsies based on bad experiences with some individuals, but he himself applies this approach publicly (albeit to another group); however, the person in question - like many others - unfortunately does not understand that the solution is not to "kick" for his group against others, but to get rid of collective guilt once and for all and set an example for others.

title: Stand for safe roads
text:

As I had scarcely slept the two previous nights, weariness fell upon me, and I did not want to drive at all; however, I was the sober one of the two of us and, according to the state, more fit to drive, although not realistically (not that I was so tired that I couldn't drive, but Terezka would have done better). Two beers (drinked during the evening) may slightly impair the driver's abilities, but less than my fatigue (not that I should fall asleep and crash, but I would react more slowly to crisis situations); not to mention that despite her age, Tereza is one of the best drivers I know (and I publicly admit that she drives better than me in my opinion). But we didn't want to risk her driver's license, so the one of us less qualified at the time (although still qualified) got behind the wheel; let him live

Let's change that!

title: Local optimism, global pessimism
text:
The leading UK market research agency Ipsos MORI in their 2013 research “The Perils of Perception” revealed a phenomenon that I found very interesting; they asked people about the intensity of various problems (crime, unemployment, drug addiction, vandalism, immigration, garbage on the streets and others), how they perceive them in their surroundings and nationwide. The results were truly remarkable: All problems (without exception) were perceived by respondents to be more serious at the national level than in their locality; in other words, "I don't have those problems much around me, but others do." You know what that reminded me of? "
I can take care of myself, but others need to stand because they are too stupid.
Just as almost no one has crime, junkies, vandals and immigrants around them, but everyone knows that "somewhere in the world" there are clouds of them, almost no one is stupidly ignorant, but of course they know that the vast majority of others are.

title: Cancellation of cash
text: Recently, we can hear here and there about the restriction and then the complete abolition of cash; what would it be for? Well, the state would have absolute control over all monetary transactions that take place; whenever you pay someone something, an electronic trail is left for the uniformed monkeys to follow if necessary. Then, in principle, even the EET would be useless, because the state would see much more. Of course, it won't happen overnight, people would chatter, but we are getting closer to it step by step (too large cash transactions are already restricted by law); and when some "Western developed country" abolishes cash, our politicians will start giving it to us as an example worth following, because "an honest person has nothing to fear." It's understandable to cry, but what about it? Fortunately, we still have cryptocurrencies; the abolition of cash could give them a huge scope.

title: EU and free trade
text: Paradoxically, a common argument for the EU is the free market; thanks to our membership in the EU, we can benefit from the benefits of open borders and a free market, for which we supposedly "have" to pay the bureaucracy that regulates the markets (which is a paradox - regulate yourself to the free market). If other countries subsidize their producers and the Czech Republic does not, Czech producers will become less competitive, but Czech customers will be able to buy cheaper (subsidized from abroad) goods; and if someone thinks even further and it happens that all Czech businessmen go bankrupt, their employees lose their jobs and have no money for anything, I recommend not to end the thinking here, but to think about one more step (his thorough thinking will explain why even that catastrophic scenario will never happen).

title: Private public transport
text: "That can never work," many argue; Public transport must be subsidized, otherwise it would not support itself from tickets. Why? Well... this argument is based purely on the fact that the way it is at the moment, the transport companies are unprofitable and perform horribly despite the subsidies; and when something is certain today, people tend to believe that it cannot be otherwise. But it doesn't make sense from the point of view, because people want to travel and there is no reason why it shouldn't be possible to make money from it (and if it really didn't work, it would mean that people are simply not worth the real costs of public transport, ergo it doesn't make sense to force them to pay). Anyway, years ago, for example, the subway in New York was private, today, for example, in Hong Kong, public transport is mostly private and works without problems; does that surprise anyone? Certainly not me; if we allowed private individuals to transport people en masse and unregulated, for example around Prague, I am sure that we would be very pleasantly surprised by the result.

title: No driving; and for what?
text: Zdeněk Neusar from the Ministry of Transport threatens drivers with a driving ban for six months to a year for crossing out the EU flag on their registration plate. And you know what's interesting? As statists always defend laws (whether during their introduction or against their abolition) by their necessity; the license plate is said to be necessary, because how else will the heroic police turn out to be a criminal villain. Then some horror will appear in our legal system, from which, formally speaking, it follows that crossing out the EU flag on the registration plate can be punished by a driving ban. Such a thing is quite obviously at absolute odds with how the law was reasoned. But this is where the popular statist argument comes in again: "The law is the law." Badly made laws are constantly being forced upon us, which are supposed to prevent some evil, but in reality affect even things quite harmless; and when someone points it out, instead of dealing with a poorly made law, there is an appeal that we must obey even a bad law. And so freedom dies to the tumultuous applause of the crowds...

title: Everyone understands Ankapu
text:
I make software for a living. I have devoted tens of thousands of hours in my life to programming, algorithmization, logic, databases, mathematics, computer networks, hardware and other related fields, during which I am still learning; it's a never-ending process where I make mistakes, learn, improve, and become more and more of an expert. People typically don't question my expertise; at most, sometimes another programmer disagrees with me, he has a different opinion on some things, which we sometimes discuss - and we don't always agree, but we both understand the topic, so it has its head and tail. Only once did someone who had spent no more than a few minutes or hours thinking about programming start to explain to me how I was doing it wrong; it was an aggressive pensioner and people tapped each other on the forehead. Even customers, if something doesn't work as it should, don't come to advise me how to program it correctly; because they know they don't have enough information and experience to make sense of it.
I spent no less time in my life studying anarcho-capitalism, political philosophy, ethics, Austrian economics, praxeology, the free market, the history of various forms of totalitarian regimes, and the like; I have also read dozens of books, thousands of articles, led countless discussions and written and created a few things myself, made mistakes, learned and am constantly improving my expertise. I encounter her questioning on a daily basis; most often by people who usually did not deal with the topic for more than a few minutes in total.
They don't take a second to study the historical polycentric legal systems before telling me they can never work. For some reason, they feel that they do not need knowledge and information here; they do not perceive that they are behaving like the pensioner mentioned above. Of course, I do not rule out the possibility that someone will study everything and still not agree; of course it happens, just as I don't agree with every programmer on professional issues. But at least the discussion makes sense.
I can be wrong and make mistakes in anything; be it anarcho-capitalism or programming. But in order for someone to be able to meaningfully point out these errors, they must first have at least a general understanding of the topic and familiarize themselves with what I am claiming and in what context. Everyone understands this about programming; however, masses of people who hear about anarcho-capitalism for the first time will react with rejection through some absolutely basic and countless times uttered argument like: "Without the state, who would build roads? Besides, justice, medical care, education and security would only be for the rich. And all this does not take into account the average person." Of course, I could have erred in refuting such arguments, but such an error cannot be detected by merely repeating the argument; you need to find out something about the given topic, study it, think about it and have a serious debate. Disproving a decades-old school of thought at first glance is about as likely as someone finding an error in complex source code because they've seen The Matrix.

title: Paradox of parliamentary immunity
text:
MPs (and senators) have immunity, on the basis of which they can only be prosecuted with the consent of their colleagues (and offenses against them are dealt with only by colleagues); imagine if you were like that too, you can only be prosecuted if your colleagues at work agree. As an anarcho-capitalist, I only see it as
the mockery of the powerful by the common subjects
; but what are the "official" reasons for fooling the public? It is said that this is so that deputies (or senators) cannot be "bullied" by unnecessary lawsuits, which could paralyze the activities of the parliament (or senate); do you feel the mockery? Legislators create a system of law, while needing an exception to it so that it cannot be misused against them (its creators)! So they create an exploitable cinder block in which we have to live (citizens also have no immunity so that their companies cannot be paralyzed through the legal system), but they themselves need an exemption to protect them from the consequences of how they screwed up their jobs!

title: Together against propaganda!
text:
The fight for freedom begins in the minds of the little ones; and we all know the establishment is winning across the board so far. Not only does it completely control education, but also the public media and pays for its own propaganda with our money. For example, look for the video "Democracy is cool" on YouTube - little kids sing about the fact that anyone who doesn't want democracy is a slob (financed by the EU and the Ministry of Education and Culture); regardless of whether you agree with that view, try to imagine the uproar and outrage over the abuse and manipulation of children if a church or political party tried such propaganda. However, the state and democracy are idols, in their name anything is allowed. Worse, however, is that similar propaganda is fed to our children by the public broadcaster CT; just try searching for the show "Bankovkovi", the episode "Taxes". Again, it is not so important whether you agree with the wording, but it is perhaps anything but "objective and balanced"; when providing information about the state, people subconsciously ignore this rule (and the law). This time, though, I'd like us to do more than just state that it's wrong. I wrote CT
open letter, which you can read here

And once people start talking about them on social networks, in discussions and on their servers enough for the media to notice (and here I can reveal that I already have some media arranged; but we need more), the topic will resonate in society. And this topic is actually ankap itself and state propaganda; this is exactly what needs to be conveyed to the people. It's often said that you can't change anything by clicking, that you need to get up your ass and go do something; however, this does not apply here. If you really want to help, you can. It won't cost money, just a few minutes of time. Go spread the letter. Do you have your website? Favorite discussion forum? A social network? Newsletter? Please flood them. Elicit discussion, reaction; and disagree. If we do it thoroughly enough, it will attract the attention of the big media.

title: Piggy in a concentration camp; not to mention the state
text:
I'm watching Seznam duel, where there is a debate about Piggy in Lety; there used to be a concentration camp, and now the state is buying the place for more than a quarter of a billion to build a memorial there. This move is advocated by the populist Daniel Herman. As? By referring to the pieta, the suffering of the victims and so on, against which not even half a word can be said, because the Nazi concentration camps were really pure evil; the question is whether this is a seriously relevant argument. There is certainly interest in having a monument stand on the site; on the other hand, there is also an interest in having a piggy bank standing in the same place. What about that? The owner of the piggery makes a profit from it corresponding to how much benefit it brings to society as a whole (that is, to the people who eat the pigs); on the other hand, there is an intangible benefit to many people from a possible memorial. How to compare these two incommensurable values? Well, quite easily: Are those interested in the monument willing to fold and pay the owners of the piggy bank enough to give it up? If not, then apparently they want that memorial less than many want a piggery.
Unfortunately, nothing like that was heard in the duel. The opponent of the folklorist Daniel Herman was the Communist Josef Skála, who was only able to relativize the problem in an attempt to objectify the non-objectivable; his entire argument was more or less that there were other places where similar and worse atrocities were committed, so we should start with those. In principle, he makes exactly the same error in reasoning as his opponent: He puts his wishes and his subjective feeling above the preferences expressed by people through their actions in the market. If they consider Lety to be more important than other places, then it is not right to force them to build monuments elsewhere first. It is sad that two totalitarians clashed in the discussion, who, although they each have a different idea of what to spend the looted money they did not earn and on which they are parasitizing, but they agree on one thing: It is necessary to take that money from the people under the threat of violence, because a bunch of elitist politicians can make better decisions about it than the robbed people. It is sad that no one represented freedom in the debate.

title: Twenty-three years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard
text: Today it is exactly twenty-three years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses left this world at the age of 69 - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism"; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

title: Murray Christmas 2017!
text:
And here they are again! Again, I was looking forward to it like a little kid (I look forward to it more and more with age) and again it's divine! We live in absolutely amazing times, the world has never been better (just look back decades or hundreds of years); and Christmas has never been as consumerist as it is now, which my capitalist self appreciates. My anarchist self comes into its own in the sense that we spend time with loved ones in such a way that no one is forced into anything and everyone does what they want to do, nothing is mandatory; of course, few years everything comes together, sometimes there is no tree, other times candy, other times less presents, but we always have heaps of love and satisfaction. My spiritual and Christian self experiences the spiritual side of things; yes, I know that if the Bethlehem comet was indeed 1P/Halley, Jesus was most likely not born in winter, however, I believe that he died for our sins, which is timeless, I am grateful to him all the time and thank him continuously, so I don't care when it is celebrated (the term Christmas is also a great marketing move of the ancient Christians; originally, at that time, another - already established - holiday was celebrated). Well, the connoisseur in me will appreciate all the great food! In short, from every conceivable point of view, I love Christmas... snow... winter... but also spring, summer and autumn... the world... life! So love with me xD
Well, and since another thing of God is music, carols cannot be missing! Let's start right away
the best (click here to listen)
; or what is dead can never die (Greyjoys about Freddie xD). And I dare to call carols from the following two groups a Stok tradition (I put carols from them here every year, although different each time): Celtic Woman and Pentatonix; both bands have great musicians (with Pentatonix, as far as pop, I draw your attention to the breathtaking instrumental vocals that you might mistake for instruments), which is my primary motivation for putting them here, but there are also secondary reasons. In the case of Celtic Woman, the
I like to look at the beautiful Chloe Agnew while listening
; and Pentatonix... I like that we live in a time where they can
obvious homosexuals stand in the church and sing a carol
, without being burned. I am convinced that God truly loves us (all of us!!) and is pleased to have Pentatonix in his tabernacle; on the contrary, I would say that he is saddened by the atrocities allegedly committed in his name by homophobes of all ages, which is my appeal to many brothers and sisters in Christ.
Please, let's not be mean to each other, respect the property rights of others, love our neighbor, don't initiate offensive violence, don't hurt, don't regulate the free market, let's be willingly in solidarity and don't force those who don't want to - let's not be superior to them; all these things are very closely related. Let's try to find a common language with others, spread the ideas of freedom, think critically about them and get rid of dogmas; violence begets violence, malice begets malice, hate begets hate, but banning it and restricting its expression will always bring more evil. Whenever we release our anger, the world becomes a slightly worse place; whenever kindness emanates from us, we make the world a little better. So let us not harm our enemies either, unless it is absolutely necessary; if they are hurt and frustrated, so much the worse for them, but also for us and our loved ones. Life is not a zero-sum game; and not relationships at all.
So have a good time, enjoy life and - after the experience of the past years, I declare that there will be no typos now -
MURRAY CHRISTMAS
!!

title: A robbery called taxes
text:
Recently I was asked to explain a statement that I very often refer to in my writings - that
taxes are robbery
; I will therefore give a short and clear justification: Whoever does not pay the tax and ignores all calls to pay it, the state will send a bailiff; and whoever refuses to talk to him and give him nothing, violence will be used against him by the police; in other words, taxes are a coerced payment, making them morally indistinguishable from ordinary robbery. The objection that the state provides citizens with some services from taxes has no chance of standing; Or does a robbery stop being a robbery when the attacker buys something from the victim (or someone else) with part of the stolen money? The argument that those who don't like it don't have to live here doesn't make sense either; it's like saying that a robbery in a dangerous park in the middle of the night isn't a robbery because the victim didn't have to be there and could have gone somewhere else.
"Money or life," that's what it's all about.
Robbery, tax... what in the name? What roses are called and called differently would smell the same.

title: Uninsurable
text:
In debates about the unnecessaryness of the state, one can relatively often encounter the question of what will happen to people who suffer from some serious and expensively treatable congenital disease, ideally one that can be detected before birth, which means that no insurance company will be interested in them; and what is my answer? Well, of course no one can predict the market, but I can imagine, for example, insurance for parents to whom the insurance company will offer a future contract for their child's insurance for an additional fee; I can also imagine insuring children even before conception and many other solutions. That similar services do not exist today? That is true, but why should they exist in a socialist health care system where everyone will be insured? Logically, there is no demand for something that the state offers for so-called "free"; if it stops happening, demand will arise - and where there is demand, there will also be an offer, because you can make money from it.
My fiancee called the principle "insurance against the uninsurable"; I consider this designation to be absolutely accurate. Insurance is similar to betting: If there is an event with a low probability of occurrence, I can bet for quite a bit of money that it will occur, and when it does, I can win far more (because the chance of winning was small); and as long as people are willing to bet, there is no reason why those bets should not be made by someone who calculates the statistical odds and designs favorable terms for himself. Why shouldn't it then be possible to bet that if a child is born to me affected by disease X, I will receive Y crowns, where Y is the price of treatment? If I am willing to bet significantly more than Y times the odds that the newborn will have disease X, someone rich will be found to make the bet because it is profitable; after all... if people come to you and offer 100 crowns for the fact that you will pay them 900 crowns with a 1:10 chance, will you refuse?

title: Compulsory war
text:
One does not have to go far for the idea that conscription should be reintroduced; however, I am not entirely sure that all those who ask for this really fully understand what they are asking for, because the state propaganda has gone so far that many people no longer even think about what is hidden behind each of the euphemisms used by the government. So what is conscription? So, above all, it is about slavery; true, typically time-limited, but the gist is that conscripts are forced (!) to submit to the whims of other people the military designates as their superiors. Whether they bully them or treat them quite "well" is irrelevant; a slave owner who does not abuse his slaves and is "good" to them as much as possible does not cease to be a slave owner. Are you, then, supporters of compulsory war, really supporters of slavery? I think mostly not, you just think it's an exaggeration to call military service that; but is it really so?
If you tell someone in an African country where female circumcision is a common practice that it is a disgusting barbaric atrocity, they will probably also find it exaggerated, because in their reality it is a quite normal thing; she will probably answer something along the lines of: "I went through it as a child too, and at least I'm not fucking myself." A chilling analogy to the notorious: "I was in the army, I was bullied, but it benefited me, at least I'm not such a slob like today's young people." What do I mean by that? That the way we perceive something emotionally is influenced to an extremely strong extent by how common that thing is in the environment where we live - if we get used to it, even absolutely horrible things no longer shock us; in such a case, let's forget about emotions and follow logic: Even if we don't have to perceive war as slavery, in reality it is (a person is forcibly forced to obey someone's orders); and how can such an atrocity be justified?

title: The War on Drugs
text:
O
the state's war on drugs
(and actually about
drugs themselves
) I have already written a lot; from a moral point of view, there is no justification for the aggressive violence of the state against the producers and sellers of illegal drugs, nor for restricting the users' choice of how to dispose of their bodies, and certainly not for forcing the taxpayers to fund this aggression, while from a practical point of view, state intervention causes the increase in the price of narcotics, the crime associated with them, countless ruined lives as a result, and above all, it simply does not work (
a picture is worth a thousand words
), which
is well known
even to those who waged the war against drugs for decades. It is therefore an activity that costs a huge amount of resources, causes crime and unfathomable suffering, and moreover has no results; the ideal of fools and politicians, who already feed the public with fairy tales and lie to them about the benefits of the whole thing.
However, recently, while reading some text about the drug trade in prisons, one more thing occurred to me: The state is not even able to ensure that its prisoners do not fet! Even in maximum security prisons, where each cell is only a few square meters, with bars everywhere and guards who have the power to search Muggles' personal belongings at any time, order them around, manage their daily schedule and constantly check them, the state is unable to "win" the war on drugs; but if it fails even in an almost laboratory and ideal environment for exercising its power, how can anyone believe that it can succeed in the real world, where it has been wasting resources for decades without tangible results? We can discuss whether at least the set goal is correct (in my opinion it is not), but the fact that the chosen means do not lead to it, perhaps could not be more obvious...

title: The hell called elections
text:
Many ask me who to vote for; I'm just saying that I don't know. I have no idea who you should vote for; I don't even know if you're supposed to vote. Although I certainly don't consider not voting to be stupid or wrong, I personally have always voted; and I will vote as long as the message I would send by not voting is perceived as disinterest, not disapproval.
I categorically reject the thesis that I would legitimize democracy or the state with my vote.
Although it is not clear to me who you should vote for, I dare to say that the most dangerous is the vote for Babiš; in my opinion, the choice of the People's Party or KSČSSD is slightly better (although still terrible); I consider voting for SPD or Úsvit, Zelené, TOPka or STAN rather stupid (but again slightly better); I don't consider the choice of the other parties to be so bad, because they are too small to cause real damage or a "lesser evil" (compared to the rest). I would just like to add to the Pirates that they are far from being as "anti-system" as they present themselves (on the other hand, still better than all the parties above); there are many socialists among them.
If you want to vote "against the Socans or Babiš" - or "so that the vote doesn't go to waste" - and you want to avoid voting for a small party, I would probably (with reservations) recommend the ODS, because it can perhaps be described as the least evil of the "big ones"; although in the past it has sharply shied away from the fight against a very large state (despite promises), thereby tripping up its voters, lately it is perhaps trying to make amends (I judge from watching their votes and speeches), but it will still take some time before they gain at least a shred of my trust. However, I consider the argument of the "loss" of the vote to be wrong, because the vote will almost certainly "lose" anyway ("it won't be lost" only if the election turned out at least a little differently without it, which is almost impossible). On the contrary, one strong argument for electing smaller parties is being forgotten: In addition to the fact that they can get money for votes, it is primarily a motivation for their members, for whom the difference between one and three percent can mean the difference between devoting their time to that party and to something else.
That is also why I will - with great self-denial - vote for Svobodné. I have a huge number of reservations about that side; unfortunately, there is no party I have less reservations about. I don't want to go into detail here about everything that bothers me about Svobodny, but considering how many libertarians there are among the readers, I would like to mention one thing: Two (unofficial) factions are fighting in Svobodny - libertarians and right-wing conservatives; and since the former are rather idealists (although many of them do the politics in practice), while the latter are "real politicians" (take that as a strong euphemism), unfortunately it is precisely the libertarians who leave the party more often simply because they have no stomach for some of the things that take place there (not that such things do not happen in every political party). What can a voter do about it? I can only think of one thing: circling. I'll throw it to the Liberals (although I don't seriously consider them "my representatives", but that's how it goes in a democracy) and I'll try to support the libertarians with preferential votes.
Some want to do the same, but they don't know the Liberal candidates, so they asked me for advice; I don't know who you should circle, but here is a list of those whom I would circle, because I consider them to be decent people or libertarians (the list is subjective and incomplete; I do not know all Svobodné): Tomáš Pajonk (not the first by chance), Jana Urzová, Zuzana Haberlová, Terézia Mlýnková Išková, Igor Bogdanov, Jakub Cyrani, Josef Káles, Jaroslav Suchánek, Pavel Mises (yes, he changed his name xD), Alois Sečkár, Jiří Kubíček, Ondřej Martínek, Michael Kopecký, David Král, Jiří Pánek, Martin Rumler, Petr Pořízek, Jan Šebelík, David Forbelský, Jan Matějka, Jiří Zapletal, Zenon Kuder, Jindřich Pilc, Miloš Bém, David Pokorný, Oldřich Peprla, Roman Bartolšic, Jan Mikula, Radim Smetka, Vítěslav Stanovský, Jaroslav Marsa. I would not choose from the Olomouc and Pilsen regions; I don't know much about the candidates from Olomouc, but unfortunately I do about the ones from Pilsen. Do with it as you wish. The choice is yours. I'm not too sure, maybe I'm wrong, so take me with a grain of salt.

title: A rational bad choice
text:
Intellectuals like to gripe about how awful it is who people vote for; their votes can be bought for a doughnut, a sausage, a beer, a nice smile from a billboard... are voters that stupid? No, quite the opposite; they are smart and know what is best for them. What are the costs of making the "right" (informed) choice? Hundreds of hours of researching party programs, the credibility of politicians, the basics of economics, predicting the effects of this or that law; assuming you don't have this as a hobby, this is an extreme expense. And what is the profit from the "correct" (conscious) choice? Well, none; unless the "right" candidate loses by one vote (which has probably never happened anywhere), the outcome of the election is exactly the same for each individual regardless of how they voted. So if you don't care about politics, "sloppy" or no choice is a perfectly rational solution, not a mistake. And where is the mistake?
In democracy itself
; it just doesn't work for real people.

title: Bad father? Three years in the cold!
text:
Some idiot encouraged his young daughter to hit a pillow with a baseball bat and imagine she was beating up gypsies or Muslims; the person in question is obviously a douchebag, so he filmed everything and published it on the Internet. And you know what? He is accused of inciting hatred and endangering the upbringing of a child, for which he can serve up to three years. I do not deny that the father is a dull brute for many reasons; but he didn't abuse his daughter, he just passed on his (albeit perverted) values to her. If we accept that the state should forcefully dictate to people how to raise children, we are heading straight for hell. And whoever thinks that he is not in danger because he is not such a limiter, I remind him of Martin Niemöller: "When the Nazis came for the communists, I was silent; I was not a communist. When they closed the social democrats, I was silent; I was not a social democrat. When they came for the trade unionists, I was silent; I was not a trade unionist. When they came for me, there was no one left to speak."
The point is certainly not that we should perhaps approve or even accept such a style of education as our own (I personally find it disgusting); but if the state will be the one who decides what is acceptable and what is not in education, it is not such a problem to change it so that next time something could be objectionable that we would not even imagine today and consider it completely absurd (parents of fat, aggressive, religious or vegan children can become persecuted, add anything). And the way to prevent this can hardly lie in trying to enforce across the board such prohibitions and regulations as suit us (because similar totalitarian practices always get out of control in the end), but in
absolute refusal to let a policeman, official or politician decide
about things for which children and their parents are ultimately responsible anyway.

title: Is our country free?
text:
It could certainly be worse (see DPRK); on the other hand, the state determines how we should educate our children, what we should lead them to, what values we must not pass on to them and which must be passed on to them through the education system; what goods we are allowed to sell, buy and under what conditions, what services we can provide and to whom, that we must register our potential company, report its earnings and pay taxes from them in the currency determined by the state, which they also force us to accept; it dictates who we may hire and whom we may not refuse, under what conditions people can work for us and for what reasons we can fire them; what we must not say publicly, what art and culture we must contribute to; how we are to pay for medical care, who may and may not treat us and what drugs they may use, and if that fails, who may not help us die; it also decides what substances we can inject into our bodies, from what age we can have sex and from what age we can watch it on the Internet; the official checks what we fuel with, what we drive; what means of transport we may own, under what conditions we may drive them and whom we transport; which weapons we may own and carry; the state determines how and where we can build our own house; what data we may send to the Internet; which pets we can keep... and that's it
very incomplete list
.

title: Two years Stok
text:
Today is exactly two years to the day
opening Stok

FREEPORT CHANNEL
