I thank each of them from the bottom of my heart; and thank you to everyone else who participates in the running of Stok, even by comments, and to all readers. Please bear with us; and if you can think of something on the topic (especially a positive one, but it doesn't have to be), don't hesitate and start writing too!

title: Roaming aftermath
text: The EU banned roaming and the Eurocrats pretended that we should all kiss their ass for it, because they are saving us (with our money) from bad operators; and at first glance it may seem so serious to someone, but as I say: "You can't outsmart the market." In Norway (it is not in the EU, but the regulation also affected it) the prices of mobile services have risen by more than half, in Denmark by an average of 60 euros per customer per year, and the British are not much different (depending on the operator); Slovak operator Orange, on the other hand, charges for "overuse" of services abroad. I was in Belgium in July, where I didn't pay for roaming, but I didn't get data (which could be solved with the operator, but always only for a few hours; then he turned me off again). So rather than helping anyone, the whole event was EU PR; and I wonder how much better or cheaper services the operators could provide us if the money that the regulation cost went directly to them.

title: Nocebo: The State Causes Cancer!
text:
Nocebo is the opposite of placebo; while the placebo effect consists of healing based on the patient's belief that he is being treated (when in fact he is not), the nocebo effect worsens his condition based on perhaps expecting negative side effects of the drug (which he is not actually receiving). Disgusting pictures and warnings about all the horrible ways cigarettes can harm our health are now required by law to appear on every cigarette pack; why shouldn't the nocebo effect show up here? Every time a smoker takes his cigarette from a pack colorfully depicting the potential negative health consequences of his action, he is convinced that he will get sick; and if he believes it, his mind can seriously cause the disease. So not only the state
inexcusably violates proprietary rights
cigarette manufacturers when it regulates the appearance of their boxes, but even more so it harms the smokers it declaratively protects.

title: First day of school 2017
text:
The school year begins; the state forcibly forces parents to send their children to school where they will be
indoctrinated by propaganda
, which of them
will create obedient citizens
. Who would defy something like that and insist on it, the children will be forcibly abducted (!) by a social worker (with the possible support of uniformed monkeys, if necessary); a euphemism for this behavior - completely unacceptable to most of us if the state did not do so (which clearly shows the power of
that propaganda
) – school attendance is compulsory.
Let's get rid of her!
And there is another thing which is our children
indoctrinated similarly to the state; this is democracy
– the idol that, if you refuse to worship, you will become the object of ridicule of the believers of the most widespread religion, that is, statism. However, there are still those who consider that propaganda to be insufficient and would like to toughen it up; I will face one of them – Bohumil Kartous – on September 18 in a debate in
Parallel Polis
. I hope to meet you there; and I wish the students the best of luck for the next school year - don't get too shaped.

title: 2017 Holiday Mode Off
text:
The holidays are over, so Stoky resumes its standard operation.
Many thanks to all the libertarians who listened
my challenges
and delivered their texts over the holidays; please keep it up.

title: The mafia called the state
text:
When I talk about the immorality of the state, I sometimes compare it to the mafia; although there are a lot of technical differences between those organizations, but from the point of view of ethics, they operate on the same principle: In some territory, they threaten people with violence to pay them. The victim then either has to move elsewhere, conceal income (with the risk of retaliation), pay, or be liquidated. The mob is typically weaker, so it unleashes terror, has less patience, and soon turns to violence; states tend to be stronger, ergo they can afford not to be so brutal, they proceed more slowly and do not intimidate so explicitly... at least that's what I'm saying; unfortunately, this is not always true.
I am posting a link to the article here
, which shows how it can also look like. This brings us to another difference: the Mafia does not have such good PR because it does not control the entire education system, so it cannot convince its victims that it is not actually evil; the state is very good at this - its victims feel that a mistake has been made, they find it "strange" (that's how a man whose life was destroyed by the tax office put it), but they don't reject the state as a whole.

title: How much does butter cost?
text:
Recently, the media has been informing us that the price of butter has risen; I didn't notice it myself, because I don't look at price tags when buying food, but judging by the comments, it caught the attention of many people. The chairman of the Agricultural Union of the Czech Republic, Martin Pýcha, said that people should get used to paying fifty crowns for a quarter of a kilogram of butter, because it is a normal price; however, many traders react by buying cheaper butter from other countries (which, by the way, shows how harmful high tariffs and protectionism in general could be). The real problem, however, is not slightly more expensive butter, but absurdly high subsidies and a huge degree of socialism in agriculture. No one has any idea how much butter is supposed to cost. Mr. Pýcha claims that fifty crowns is a "normal price", but he cannot know that, because the "normal price" is determined by supply and demand, which in our case, unfortunately, are massively distorted by taxes and subsidies. It's sad that nowadays
there is no way
, how to find the market price of butter; and almost everything else.

title: Fries are unhealthy: BAN
text: In the EU, they found out that French fries are unhealthy (wow, who would have thought) because they contain a lot of acrylamide (OK, I didn't know that), so no one should eat or sell them (and we are at home, social engineering is the main method and product of the EU). The representatives of the twenty-eight member countries of the European Union agreed that measures need to be taken to force people to submit to their next invention; this time in the name of reducing the risk of cancer: "Today we have taken an important step in protecting the health and well-being of citizens," said European Commissioner for Health and Food Safety Vytenis Andriukaitis. When smoking was banned, I argued that it would be possible to ban junk food with exactly the same arguments; what was described by my opponents as an absurd and impermissible sloping surface is now becoming a reality. How much freedom and responsibility will they take away from us? How much self-righteous idiots do they want us to be?

title: Discussion in Polis: LGBT Pride Week
text:
Today at 4 pm I will participate in a panel discussion in Paralelní Polis; the topic is quite controversial and the guest list even more so. We will debate about the march and the pride week of the LGBT community.
The aim was to invite people with a wide range of opinions to the same table - the nationalist and extreme opponent of LGBT Pavel Matějný was invited as the organizer of the protest march, the objectivist Luboš Zálom, the anarcho-capitalist Urza and the transsexual LGBT activist Marie Feryna from the radical left (Marxist), who accepted the invitation, but then withdrew her participation saying that she refused to sit at the table with Mr. Matějný, which caught many attentions other leftists (even the leftist media) who exacerbated the situation and tried to cancel the invitation to Mr. Matějný or the entire discussion through threats and intimidation, which of course they did not succeed (for the sake of fairness, I add that these threats were made by individual leftist radicals who apparently acted for themselves, not on behalf of any organization); instead of Maria Feryna, David Mařák, the president of the LGBT association Charlie, accepted the invitation despite great pressure.
The interest in the discussion is apparently considerable, the media and probably also a number of activists are expected to arrive; as some have expressed fear for their safety, professional security will oversee the smooth running of the event. The fact that the reactions to the entire event are more controversial than expected is also evidenced by the fact that I am writing here "pride week" and "pride march", but not its name, because the lawyer of that organization has already threatened me with a lawsuit for trademark infringement (and the absurdity is that the consultation with another lawyer shows that his threats may not be completely empty; what does this say about the legal system of the Czech Republic, you can guess for yourself).
I will look forward to seeing you;
come out

title: Search on the Czech Post
text:
Everyone certainly has a lot of stories with the Czech Post (me too), so I won't go into detail about them here; however, what has fascinated me for years is the search in their information system (such a program from the days of MS-DOS), which has the remarkable property that it lacks the absolutely basic function that one would expect from such a tool - namely, to enter a name into it and find all shipments for the person in question. Instead, the recipient has to know whether they are looking for a letter, parcel, cash on delivery, registered letter, letter from abroad and the like - I don't know exactly how many of those categories there are - and the postal workers search in each one separately; is it really such a problem to write a function that finds any shipment with a given name? It certainly isn't, but why bother if the customer is going to wait; bearing in mind that the entire juggernaut is paid for by the taxpayer who
he has no choice
, the quality of service doesn't matter at all, so why bother...

title: Uniformed monkeys have a harvest
text:
A guy from Opava went to walk the dogs by car; he left the window open in the car to let it air out in the meantime. And what the hell, monkeys in uniforms were walking around; so the real, unadulterated police buzz began. The person in question coughed on them and drove off; A spokeswoman for the Flies commented: "He claimed it was his business, he had done nothing wrong and was not going to deal with anything. He then got behind the wheel and rudely drove away from the scene. If he hadn't done that, the incident almost certainly would have been resolved with a reprimand." That's how they steamed his band-aid. And for what? He was not conformist enough; if he licked the Bengs' shoes and kissed their ass, he wouldn't have to pay, which they openly admit. In other words, "Subject, we'll boo you, but show us the respect we don't deserve, or we'll force you to pay." And why all this? Well, because the law states: "A driver who intends to move away from the vehicle [..] must take such measures that the vehicle [..] cannot be used [..] by another person without authorization."
Boaters were buzzed by 279 uniformed monkeys all over the Czech Republic; checked 606 boats, 93 docks and gave 520 boaters a breather (boaters' buzzer we are here
repeatedly
solved
already last year; inclusive
breath tests
). What is it good for? The worn-out excuse like with cars doesn't really work here: "After all, the driver endangers not only himself, but also those around him!" But besides its crew, who does such a canoe really threaten? Sure, very hypothetically another canoe, however, if its crew is also not under the picture and if they use their brains, they will wash out as much as possible, which simply happens from time to time on the water and everyone expects it. But this is not about any security, protection or help, just like with the open windows in the car, it is only about keeping subjects under pressure, rebuking the egos of needy existences in the service of the police, reporting their activities and robbing some of that money into the insatiable maw of the state. Or does anyone have the feeling that the police are doing this for us?

title: Germany as a company
text:
Despite German libertarians, I know conspirators who believe that Germany is not really a state but a large corporation; as it happens, the clues to that belief are basically stupid, for example that German citizens are called Personalausweis, not Personenausweis (the former means something like an employee card, the latter should logically be a citizen, although it is not). What interested me about it? Proponents of the conspiracy theory and their opponents (although they disagree on whether Germany is a company or not) agree that it would be terrible if it were true. They live in a country controlled by some entity that somehow works; as long as the entity is called a state, everything is fine, but once it turns out to be a company, it would be a disaster, even if nothing changes in its functioning at all! Can you imagine a better example
state propaganda
? If an entity does something unacceptable, it is enough for people to perceive it as a state and everything is fine.

title: "Her words killed him."
text:
Two deeply depressed teenagers in Massachusetts shared their misery for several years; as is often the case with depressed people, they alternately gave themselves strength, alternately wanted to die, both were unstable and down. He then decided to kill himself with exhaust fumes, however he hesitated and called her; she just saw the world black (although they had previously tried to find a solution to their depression) so she told him to kill himself. He did it; she let him die, she didn't call for help. In terms of
principle of non-aggression
she did nothing wrong; freedom of speech includes this. From the human point of view I dare not judge; maybe at that moment she seriously believed it was the best solution (but I don't know). And from the point of view of the Massachusetts court? Twenty years in prison! Leaving aside the principle of non-aggression, I have two questions: How is the world supposed to be better after her imprisonment at the expense of the taxpayers? On the basis of this precedent, will someone be convicted, for example, for a depressing text on the Internet, if it inspires a suicide?

title: Seattle and the minimum wage
text: In Seattle, the minimum wage was raised to fifteen dollars an hour; unsurprisingly, it had exactly the negative effects that Austrian economists have been talking about for decades. Now, however, a study has been created for this, the results of which are "shocking", because they refute the results of some earlier studies that are supposed to "prove" the opposite. The creators of the study present the conclusions (long known to Austrians) that the minimum wage harms the least qualified workers (they start losing their jobs when they do not earn for themselves); for example, according to economist David Autor from MIT, a study can influence research in a given area and completely change the perspective on a given issue. On the one hand, it would be good to change it; on the other hand... why is that study needed? We still have valid laws of praxeology, ceteris paribus; so studies can show anything depending on other influences that cannot be eliminated or measured, ergo they neither disprove nor prove anything.

title: Up to five years behind bars for six cannabis seedlings
Anarchy in practice: the city of Gurgaon
text:
Gurgaon is an Indian municipal city, but in which only less than five percent of its area is subject to municipal authority; the remaining ninety-five percent are held by private individuals, and they provide all the services in question
we have been teaching since school years
, that the market cannot provide them – economist Shruti Rajagopalan wrote of the city: "It shouldn't exist, in theory." But there is; and it is successful - its population is growing by hundreds of thousands of inhabitants per year (it has already exceeded two and a half million people). Sure, it's in India, so it's no paradise on earth, but people definitely do better there than in other cities, as evidenced by the extreme migration to Gurgaon; if people have a choice, they choose the free market over the state. It probably won't surprise anyone that the biggest horror in the city takes place in the non-privatized part where public services and "social security" are provided; the market can simply do better. Want to know more? Martin Pánek translated
interesting article on the topic
.

title: Renovate before demolition
text:
In Pardubice, a transport hub will be built in front of the station, for which a large subsidy (108 mega) can be obtained; however, its condition is that noise limits must not be exceeded in any of the surrounding houses. This might make sense at first glance, but not in the case of houses that have to be demolished as part of the construction of that transport hub; however, the grant writer did not think of that, so... Pardubice must first soundproof the house, for which there is already a demolition plan, for almost two megabytes - and then demolish it. One would like to say that poorly worded eligibility conditions are to blame, but this is only partially true – poorly worded conditions cause less obvious inefficiencies to surface so that everyone can see and laugh at them (as many do); without it, the subsidy will also not be effective,
which is its inherent property
, but it stops being so obvious.
A centrally controlled economy is doomed to failure…

title: Hamster totality
text:
Socan Stanislav Křeček on Airbnb: "The situation is no longer tolerable. Cities must take measures to regulate. They must realize that short-term renting is not a normal way of using an apartment..."
Anarcho-capitalist Urza: "The state is not tolerable! You must realize, Mr. Křeček, that the owner of the apartment should decide on the use of the apartment, not the parasitizing members of parliament who live off the stolen taxes."
Křeček: "...and it harms the state's housing policy."
Urza: "Then the state's housing policy is bad!
The state is immoral
; but if you want to at least pretend to be there for the people, you can't at the same time claim that his policies are against their wishes.''
Křeček: "Apartments must serve people, not business."
Urza: "And who runs this business? Martians? Is this targeted manipulation, or do you really see it that way? Or are you just using the word people as a synonym for your interests?"
Křeček: "They also violate tax laws, the vast majority of entrepreneurs do not report income. Such activities should be monitored."
Urza: "So we're home! No people vs. business and such chatter; it's just that someone has a profit from which they don't pay protection money to the state for your salary, Mr. Křeček, so all hell breaks loose."

title: Štěch stepped in the shit...
text:
If we step on shit, we wipe it off and move on; not so socan Štěch, who stepped properly, but instead of wiping, he decided to get a little dirty in it. Instead of
after his statement about the use of self-employed people and their contribution to GDP creation
he kept his mouth shut, he decided to "improve" it by asking us to snap at the neighbors: "For example, in Denmark, if someone is unemployed and doing his own thing, the neighbor will just say so, because he is also being robbed of his money, which he puts into the system." Dude, seriously? For one thing... what kind of alien-grazing monster is this, why is he the president of the senate, why do I have to feed this parasite... but above all, what is the logic behind this "robbing"?
The state takes someone's money by force
and he claims that a neighbor did it, which is why he is being robbed, because the neighbor's state did not succeed in turning over so much. That it is the logic of a leech fed by forcefully collected money makes sense; however, the sad thing is how many
manipulated by propaganda
it eats citizens.

title: Wikianarchy
text:
Wikipedia is not run by any government, it is funded by volunteers; anyone can write there, they don't need a license, they don't need to prove expertise, or they don't need anyone's permission. No one has a right to it, it is not guaranteed by any law; it is not copyrighted and has no regulatory authority. When it started, everyone "knew" it was going to be shit and everyone would just be trolling or writing nonsense. Yes, sure, sometimes someone really trolls and some nonsense can be found there, but it is still an amazing project with a huge benefit for clouds of people. This is how anarchy works in practice; even though everyone "knows" that "it can never work". And how much does it all cost? About sixty million dollars, i.e. a billion and a half crowns a year; by the way, this is several times less than the budget of Czech Television. How is that possible? Well,
CT does not have to - and cannot - be effective
, when it does not earn for itself and people are forced to pay it - no stranger's blood flows; unlike Wikipedia, which has to support itself somehow.

title: More controls!
text:
"The Airbnb application in Prague 1 has completely changed the conditions on the housing market. The phenomenon of shared accommodation, if not regulated, is very dangerous for every city," declared Prague 1 councilor Ivan Solil from the ČSSD; mayor Oldřich Lomecký from TOP09 (she takes notes with the ČSSD) confirms this: "We cannot allow the Prague 1 district to lose its function of housing, that is why we are calling for rules." Why can't you let it happen, you cocky paps? Do you know how people are supposed to live in Prague 1? Where do you get the smug belief that you know better than the owners of those apartments what is good for Prague? Even if everyone from Prague 1 decided to rent their apartments, what's the point? Nothing at all!
You are nothing but parasites
; you should be glad we feed you. Lomecký continues: "Tens, hundreds of apartments are flooded by someone we don't even know who he is." Well, what does anyone (except the owners) care? If you don't make a living as decent people, at least don't play savior.

title: Štěch: Entrepreneurs parasites v2
text:
Socan Milan Štěch has devised a way to drive tens of thousands of employees to companies: He wants to increase levies for self-employed people so that they can be employed; he says that no one knows what their contribution to GDP creation is (no bullshit; he actually said that), and they are not used effectively (which, according to him, no one knows). What would I say about that... I have no words. First of all, there is an audacity calling to heaven when a parasite, who has been straying in the senate for over twenty years, preaches about work
stolen money
, before the revolution he was in the Communist Party for ten years and in the meantime made a career as a professional trade unionist; how does this brute dare to evaluate the workers who feed him? Secondly, it is a typical populist social-democratic attempt to spit on the self-employed and compare them negatively with employees, but this time extremely demented; because few things will harm employees as much as tens of thousands of self-employed people who will become employees and compete with them in the labor market. Tykravol, may it happen to his constituents!

title: Tax Freedom Day
text:
Tax Freedom Day is a date that divides the calendar year into two parts: From the beginning of the year until that day, people work for the state; only from that day until the end of the year can they work on themselves. For example, if we
the state took
half of what we earn, tax freedom day would be in the middle of the year. Since each person pays taxes a little differently, the result depends on the methodology used; for example, according to the company Deloitte, the day of tax freedom will be tomorrow, while such a Liberal Institute set it for May 29 this year. I'm trying
count everything
, what the state costs us, so my tax freedom day does not come until August; to different people on different days according to how much they pay in excise and the like. Whether that date falls in May, June, July, or August, the thought is appalling; let's realize how many months since the beginning of the year we've been working on a parasitizing state... and who happens to shorten it, the politicians (and, unfortunately, many citizens) will brazenly call him a thief.

title: Cryptocurrencies and the economic crisis
text:
The state is forcing its non-market money on us, causing an economic crisis
; the question is not if it will come again, but when the next crisis will occur. And as an anarcho-capitalist and holder of several cryptocurrencies, I can't help but ask: When the crisis comes again, what will it do to the Bitcoin (and other) exchange rate? I can imagine two fundamental opposing influences: Pure speculators will start (panicked) selling because their reason for buying was a quick profit; on the contrary, those who hold cryptocurrencies out of distrust of the state or
opposition to fiat money
, in my opinion will buy. But which ones are there more? Quite obviously, people buy cryptocurrencies for both reasons; and I doubt that anyone can know how essential either is. But I think that the economic crisis will test this. What do you think, dear readers? In which direction will the courses go in the crisis? And are my reflections on the reasons for the rise or fall of the price at all meaningful? I welcome any reasoned opinions; Thank you.

title: Litecoin in Subway!
Squirrel bridge for four megs
text: There is a bridge for squirrels in Sokolov; yes, you read that right, it's just a bridge over the road, they built it there in 2012 and it cost four mega (seriously, I'm not kidding). I can't imagine who would defend this, or even agree with it, but if any die-hard environmentalists are reading here, know that five (yes, seriously five) rodents have used the bridge during its entire existence (there are cameras installed, so it's an accurate count); that makes about eight hundred thousand crowns for one pass – great, isn't it? For that money, I would easily carry those squirrels across that road by myself; after all... who doesn't? However, the zone of absurdity still does not end, because the bombers are sitting at the Sokolov town hall until the end; when confronted with the status of the project, City Hall's response was (now hold on): "We believe this animal protection project makes sense." What to add? Well, another one of those things that would be funny if they weren't crying.

title: Penalty for "like"
With a naked man behind bars!
text: A certain guy from Vizovice likes to work in his (!) garden naked; he doesn't do anything to anyone, he doesn't interfere with other people's property, he is even willing to get dressed at the request of his neighbor (that is, not forever, but if she asks him, he will get dressed for the given day as part of good neighborly relations). Nevertheless, the person in question told the television that she was afraid to invite visitors, so that they would not be disgusted by it; her worries on my head! There's a hill of fun; however, the person in question succumbed to the social climate of today's state and betrayed her neighbor to the fools... And this is where the ass ends. The uniformed monkeys informed the man that he was suspected of the crime of disorderly conduct, for which he could go to jail for up to two years. Why? Because he mowed his (!) garden naked; and because the neighborhood crack is starting. And above all, let no one defend it with the nonsense that his freedom ends where that lady's freedom begins; that border is quite clearly defined by the fence between their plots - and it was not crossed.

title: You have the word: social housing
text:
A few weeks ago, the topic of the program You Have the Word was the Social Housing Act; I only got to watch the episode now, but I was really interested. The guest of the show was, unsurprisingly, my favorite Marksová,
of
which
again
she was falling
hers
traditional
socialist
wise
; surprisingly, however, there were those who sovereignly trumped her: "I don't want housing benefits, I don't want to burden the state, and I also have my pride; give me a social apartment by law!" I couldn't believe my ears at first listen and replayed the video to make sure it was for real... and indeed. Well, apart from that it's everywhere... but there were two other people who said the same thing during the hour; Of course, Marks did not disappoint - she repeated several times that it was a matter of pride and that she understood them. What kind of propaganda did the state use to convince these people that social housing is falling from the sky? What is their pride? Totally burying your head in the sand? How do housing benefits differ from social housing?
I've always thought that renaming payroll taxes or social and health taxes to insurance won't have much of a real impact; but when I hear this and see people whose "pride won't allow" them to take housing benefit, but call for social housing, I reconsider my opinion - what those things are called has a noticeable impact in the real world. When there are people who don't get housing benefits, but do get social housing, they do it out of conviction and say that they "don't want to burden the state" (so they probably really don't know that someone has to pay for the social housing), it is probably important to solve (in my opinion, absurd) questions such as whether civil servants pay taxes; and even now I attach even greater importance to stressing that taxes are renamed protection money, that laws are enforced by the state by force, that every regulation inherently contains aggression and the like. Let's fight newspeak; let's not give it to the state for free!

title: The sharing economy
text:
Uber, Airbnb, Zonky, Doginni and many other platforms that compete with "official" entrepreneurs often move on the edge of the gray economy (or beyond); nevertheless (or rather precisely because of this) they are successful, they are winning in the market competition to the full, and the states do not know what exactly to do with them. Sometimes they prohibit them, sometimes they regulate them, but sometimes there are also judges who agree with them and support them; The "official" competition in the given fields typically hates them because they often have trouble standing up to them, which in itself says something about what customers want and don't want. Today from 16:00 I will discuss this topic in a panel discussion in Polis; among the other discussants will be, for example, the chairman of the Association of Taxi Concessionaires, Daniel Tarljovski, whom I am very much looking forward to. Come and have a look and, above all, join the discussion. I look forward to seeing you in
Parallel Polis
.

title: We don't work for the state!
text:
"Ethical hacker" crypto-anarchist Palo launches Slovak and Czech versions of the initiative
We don't work for the state
(respectively
We do not work for the state
); companies (or individuals who sell something) can apply for it, as long as they do not work for the state, do not receive subsidies and, ideally, compete with the state, or accept cryptocurrencies. Those who register determine the amount of discounts they want to provide to other registered members (three types of discounts are possible: for not receiving subsidies, for competing with the state and for accepting cryptocurrencies), then they can draw discounts from other members themselves. The minimum condition is therefore at least not to work for the state and not to receive subsidies; sign up, spread both sites and ideas of independence from the state - it makes sense! The discounts mentioned above are more of a by-product; the point is to create a platform of people who actively reject the state, compete with it, spread cryptocurrencies and cooperate on an economic basis.

title: Another flash of the power of propaganda
text: More and more often, dear readers and listeners, you write me emails discussing libertarian topics; thank you for them, they are mostly useful dialogues. Recently, in response to the lectures, an astute listener, a supporter of the so-called Zen State, wrote to me; I don't want to deal with that concept here (you can google it), I'm not a fan of it. As part of that – very interesting – discussion, the person in question declared that she identifies with the ideas of anarcho-capitalism, but does not want to call herself an anarchist, because anarchy has violent periods behind it (sic!); this very thoughtful lady (this is not irony) espouses the Zen state, but feels an aversion to anarchy for its violent history. But what about the bloody nature of states (based on violence) that killed three hundred million people in wars in the last century? Given how our debate has progressed so far, I expect the person in question will reconsider; however, that ingrained subconscious resistance to anarchy is everywhere...

title: Freaks in the streets!
text:
Today is World No Tobacco Day; and enters into force
a totalitarian law restricting the freedom of pub owners
to decide whether smoking is allowed in their establishments or not. Most of the arguments by which this amendment was defended consisted in the fact that if we already have totalitarianism anyway, we can easily tighten it up a bit more (the pub owners are already restricted by a lot of regulations; because of the socialist healthcare system, we all bear the costs of treating smokers; the state is supposed to take care of the health of the population; "state, set up a non-smoking pub in the village" and many others); and in a similar totalitarian spirit, some town halls intend to solve the problems caused by the ban (people will go to smoke in front of pubs): For example, Prague 1 has hired anti-smoking patrol officers to go around and boo smokers (how noisy they are, where they throw their cigarettes, etc.); if you meet them, please let them eat it (without violence) so that they think carefully about what they actually do for a living.

title: When the EU kills freedom of speech...
text:
Ministers of EU member states approved a plan to force Google, Facebook and Twitter to
tougher censorship
; and they should censor the advocacy of terrorism as well as hate speech. Leaving aside the ethical side of the matter, i.e. that each of the above-mentioned companies should decide for themselves what content they want to show their users, this does not solve anything in practice; just because we forbid people to talk about a problem, it will not disappear by itself, but on the contrary, the ballast of the "underground" will be added to it, and the spreaders of similar opinions will consider themselves martyrs (and their listeners too). And while the ministers were at it, they immediately approved yet another buzz for video streaming services (such as Netflix): European films and TV shows must make up thirty percent of their content; you can't even comment decently on this anymore, because the people in question probably already screwed up in the cinema. The feeble-mindedness of this regulation is more than evident.

title: Trains for 650 gigs
text:
Minister Ťok wants to play with trains (and the government approved it in the plan for the next decade); it will cost 650 billion (please note the order of the number; it is not just "a lot", it is more than half of the state budget) and we will pay for it. Of course, there will be a trade-off for this – very fast trains will run here; the problem is that it is not at all clear who actually wants it and how much, which is characteristic of state decision-making, which is inherently burdened
impossibility of economic calculation
. What does this mean? That if we let an official, a minister or some Ťok decide whether to build trains or something else, he has no chance to do it well (even if he wanted to); because it cannot determine the subjective preferences of all taxpayers. The only way to not get it wrong is to let people decide about their money; if the track will be financed only by those who want it, it can only be created if it was really worth the cost to the people.

title: How to steal mail?
text: You won't believe it! The thief called the post office, introduced himself as a police officer, and said he was going there to disinfect the money after the chemical attack, so the manager should close the post office and let him in through the back door; this clever lady actually did, she brought him all the bills, the man (wearing a chemical suit - so the cameras wouldn't catch him) sprayed them with a sprayer and asked the postmaster to go flush the metal money down the sink, which she did, leaving him there with the money and... no surprise, she didn't find him there. A few questions come to mind: Would something like this happen in a private enterprise? For example, at a gas station... would the branch manager react the same way? I probably wouldn't rule it out completely, but if I had to choose a target as a thief, I would also choose the post office. And what role does the boundless faith in the state play in the whole case, i.e. its uniformed monkeys, to which a decent person does not contradict and does what they are told? I suspect that it is not completely negligible.

title: Tax office rip-off
text:
Today we pay taxes on practically everything (there is even a death tax called inheritance tax), the purchase and sale of real estate is no exception, even on this the state fattens its pockets; why? Mainly because
can; he is stronger, has a "bigger stick" and we have no way to defend ourselves
. A few years ago, the tax office changed the rules so that the tax payer was not the seller, but the buyer; it happened, and the law also granted some exceptions (for new apartments), for which the citizen naturally had to humbly apply. The requests kept rolling in, they were approved, until one day... the tax office realized that it had actually approved some of the (already approved) exemptions stupidly; so what about that? The law is the law and the subject must pay (sometimes hundreds of thousands); and even with interest and penalties (!) for late payment!! Yes, you read that right. However, our rulers are merciful, so when a subject requests (!), they will forgive him the penalty (no interest). Can you imagine the (entirely justified) uproar if a private entity did this?

title: Gift markets
text: You can buy goods in the regular market; it goes something like this: You conclude a purchase contract with the seller (note, the contract is not a signed paper, but an agreement; the paper is only proof that it took place), you pay him the money, he hands over the goods to you... then he has to register this transaction electronically with Babiš. In the gift market, you don't buy, you give yourself a gift; it goes completely differently: You conclude two gift contracts with the marketer (not the seller) - the subject of one is your gift of money to the person in question, the subject of the second is that the good man presents you with his goods... and that's the end of it, because no one has yet implemented electronic records of donations. Donation markets have already been successfully held in Hradec Králové and Letohrad; another fifty cities are interested in organizing a similar event. Great so far! What do you think will come next? Will it turn out to be illegal dodging? Or will EED be introduced? Or does the state cough up small fish?

title: Innovation week
text:
The Innovation Week organized by the European Leadership & Academic Institute has just started; on their website, we can read that the Prime Minister of the Czech Republic, Bohuslav Sobotka, officially accepted the patronage of the Innovation Week of the Czech Republic 2017. Ha-Ha. That's what I call a guarantee that it just can't go wrong. It is an event focused on innovation, modern technologies, artificial intelligence and the concept of smart cities; overall, it might be nice if it was a privately funded activity, which it is somewhat, but far from completely. Why am I writing about this? Well, Parallel Polis decided to organize a lecture on the given topic and approached me to see if I would take it on, which I happily accepted; if you want to listen to me and have a little discussion on the subject, come tonight at half past seven. Although this lecture does not belong to the cycle Anarchocapitalism, it will nevertheless touch on the topic in some way. I look forward to seeing you in
Parallel Polis
.

title: Alza accepts BTC!
text:
Years ago, I bought a drive from Alza with parameters that were different from those advertised, which the seller solved by changing the product description and brazenly pretending that I was mistaken and it had always been like that (he did not respond to the evidence from Google cache); I stopped buying from them.
By repeatedly ignoring the ban on sales on holidays, they almost won me over a few months ago
; and yesterday I decided to become their customer again (and bought there straight away). Why? The owner of Alza and his wife visited Parallel Polis to discuss the state, they agreed with us on many points, they liked the idea of Polis, Freedom of Learning and my lectures... and last but not least, cryptocurrencies; what happened then Their Head of Internet Marketing announced yesterday that Alza is introducing Bitcoin payments! I hope more stores follow suit; cryptocurrencies are thus not only becoming popular, but people have more and more options where to pay with them. What about you? Are you buying them yet?

title: Urza in Polis: Who would build roads without the state?
text:
I am a month ago
lectured on public spaces and freedom of speech
; this lecture eventually led to a very interesting discussion (part on the record and part off the record), as a relatively large number of supporters of state protection, especially of various interesting buildings, showed up. The topic was very closely related to the impossibility of economic calculation without a free market.
However, since this is a very extensive issue, I was forced to divide it into several lectures; last time we didn't deal at all not only with ecology, but above all with any transit function of public space, which would include, for example, the statists' favorite roads, because the question: "And who would build roads without the state?" almost every libertarian has heard it many times. It is to her that I want to answer this evening; be sure to come, especially if you don't agree. And if you have someone around you who might be interested in the topic, or if you would like to show them an anarcho-capitalist point of view, bring them along.
After this lecture, I will be silent for quite a long time, as the exam and holidays will begin; the next lecture will be on October 18 (!) at 8 p.m. and its topic will be the social and pension system. However, it is possible that in the meantime some (rather probably more discussion) ankap meetup will take place in Polis anyway.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

title: Everyday micro-racism
text: Oxford University has sent out new rules to students in its regular newsletter aimed at curbing racial intolerance; is it really needed there? And if so, how do the rules help? Let's take a look at them. For example, students may not ask a student of color where they originally came from; but even "better" is that they can't even avoid eye contact! It is said to be "micro-racism". Therefore, if a man glances at a woman of another race, she must return his glances, but in the case of the same race she does not have this obligation; and this is no longer micro-racism... this is racism like a cow! Don't all those politically correct geniuses realize that these kinds of measures accentuate racial differences? Don't they understand that in this way they can make racists out of those who have never dealt with any race at all? One can only hope that other institutions will not follow the example of the University of Oxford.

title: Sobotka shares the loot
text:
Although the elections are still quite far away, they are slowly approaching; and Sobotka needs to buy votes, but why would he do so on his own, when he has the stolen money of all of us at his disposal - so he wants to increase the salaries of civil servants. It's not unlike a hood of pirates splitting it up,
what they looted
; After all, the additions should be made (apart from firefighters) primarily to policemen, customs officers and bailiffs, i.e. executive rapists, who already form the front line of state oppression and the acquisition of resources through robbery. Moreover, this act demonstrates another step in the progression of the "death cycle of democracy" I am talking about
he lectured in Polis some time ago
: Politicians promise people that they will take care of them (at someone else's expense), which if they do, the number of dependents on the state (and civil servants) will increase; an increase in dependents on the state means more votes for politicians who promise people to take care of them (at someone else's expense). The circle closes: Democracy inevitably leads to socialism.

title: The Pope on the libertarian invasion
text:
I occasionally hear a joke among foreign libertarians that I would translate roughly as follows: "Libertarians are busily plotting to take over the world and leave you alone." (You can google “libertarians diligently plotting leave you alone” in the pictures.) Guess who took this little bit seriously? Pope Franciscus. He warned the world against the invasion (sic!) of libertarian values on our culture and education system. The danger of our delusional paradigms is said to be that we are not interested in the "public good" and in our belief that "only individuals assign value to things and human relationships, ergo only individuals decide what is good and what is bad"; he said that - surprisingly - very nicely, maybe I'll use it somewhere... I understand that he doesn't like it that much, because he would prefer to have the monopoly on what is good and what is bad; and his church always got along better with the state than with the libertarians xD
I am a Christian, but not a Catholic, because I am building a personal relationship with the Lord, for which I do not need a mediator in the form of a priest and certainly not a pope; in such moments I am glad for it, because the Pope's speech does not evoke a dilemma in me, but an infinite joy. Why joy? Dear ones, the head of the church, which surely has over a billion sheep, is talking about us! That means we do what we do well! As Gandhi said, "First they will ignore you. Then they will laugh at you. Then they will fight you. Then you will win." And this Pope's speech is the first swallow of that third phase; if the late Rothbard had lived to see it, he would surely have been glad. So let us continue our efforts; let's write, talk, spread, explain, try to understand people and not be rude to them, let's do our best. For this is the way to freedom; i don't believe i'll live to see a free market society, but i'll do my best... get involved too!

title: The right to children
text: Who decides whether we deny a woman who wants a child the possibilities of modern medicine? The state, how else... and the powers that be have determined that if the person in question is not married, she is unlucky. František Adámek, a deputy from the left-wing ČSSD, tried to change this – unfortunately unsuccessfully; Jitka Chalánková from the so-called right-wing TOP09 was most strongly opposed, as she herself is married, has four children, and would like to impose her values on others, and the state gives her that power. Her reasoning: "The right to a child is not a basic human right." Well, how about? Does this mean that what is not a "fundamental human right" is prohibited by the state? She and other members of parliament agreed that it was not a medical issue, but an ethical one. Well of course! It is whether people are free to enter into voluntary transactions or the state will come in and start prohibiting them; the ethical question is: "Is it legitimate for Mrs. Chalánková, together with the other deputies, to decide from a position of power who and how is allowed to reproduce?"

title: You have the word: Become a cyber spy
text:
Almost every episode of "You Have a Word" is a massacre (except for the boring ones about diets and the like); mostly statism and the results of indoctrination by state propaganda abound there, but in the last part about cyber espionage, to those classic bon mots ("Whoever has done nothing wrong, has nothing to fear.") there was added lying manipulation of such dimensions that it surprised me (and I think similarly everyone who has at least a little idea about network security). A proponent of government wiretapping of citizens' network communications argued that foreign hackers could attack our power plants, chemical plants, water plants, and other strategic targets; someone from the audience and the presenter said that it is of course possible, because today everything is controlled via "those computers". It was simply a classic professional discussion in which all knowledge is drawn from hacker action movies; Of course, I don't blame anyone for ignorance, the problem is that in a democracy everyone has a voice.
No matter how skilled a hacker is, he can only attack "those computers" he can physically connect to over the network. So if the computer is not connected to the Internet, the person concerned is out of luck; as one of my teachers used to say: "The best firewall is a meter of air." (This statement no longer has as clear a point in the days of Wi-Fi as it did in his youth.) Of course, those who deal with the security of a nuclear power plant know this; so critical systems run offline. Unfortunately, this did not come up in the discussion for long, until after a while the tragic representative of the Pirate Party spoke uncertainly, and embarrassedly objected; however, the professional uncertainty emanated from it so much that the opponent wiped it out with the Stuxnet virus (attacking industrial systems running on Simatic), which is a completely irrelevant argument (monitoring network communication does not protect against a virus transmitted from a flash drive to an offline machine). But the Pirate was so insecure (he had been wiped out by the given opponent before) that he preferred to leave the topic alone.

title: Who doesn't crack like he doesn't live (EET edition)
text: You can't teach an old STBák new tricks; but he can teach the young. For example, a twenty-three-year-old man from Domažlice called the emergency line 158 because he could not find the fiscal identification code (confirmation that the sales were electronically recorded) on his receipt for a transaction for 12 (!) crowns. Can you imagine what goes through the mind of such a person? How does he think? What did he feel during that event? For what reason did he do it? I can think of several possibilities, I can't agree with any of them; and I would really like to know how many such people live among us... unfortunately even that one seems more than enough to me. I will not, however, class this story among those which would be laughable, if they were not, of course, to cry; Why not? Because in the end it was a joke after all: The uniformed monkeys came there, found the fiscal identification code on the receipt, the crooks showed it and he walked away in shame; this story was worth the money it cost me in taxes xD

title: Illegally opened shop
text:
In the days when Stoky was quite in its infancy,
we were discussing the law prohibiting sales on holidays
; it was still in the draft stage at the time, but passed as expected. Well, now it bears fruit! ČOIka had a head start on Easter Monday, as it checked almost three hundred shops, three of which were "illegally open" (we should start getting used to this bizarre phrase, which would be laughable, if not crying). they now face a fine of up to one million crowns (5 million for repeated violations). And you know what? All three shops had been vandalized; I wonder what kind of a whore a person has to be to do something like that, and I hope their identity gets leaked somewhere eventually. Anyway, the state introduced this law on the grounds that families should be together on holidays, because politicians know best what is good for them; yes, it is ordered to strangers... but what if the state started at home? For example, those fiddling controllers from ČOIka...

title: Urza in Polis: Public Space and Freedom of Speech
text:
A fortnight ago I
lectured on weapons
; even staunch anti-gunners turned up, which I very much welcome, and I find it very surprising that their views did not remain unchanged throughout the evening. The subsequent debate was very interesting.
The topic of today's lecture will be public space and freedom of speech in a stateless society; what do these two seemingly unrelated topics have in common? In fact, more than most people think, they are indeed closely related; and in the evening I will explain how exactly. We will talk about parks, squares, forests, so-called "public interests" and many other related things (among which the freedom of speech is primarily included); definitely come and discuss, especially if, in your opinion, we need a state to manage these spaces. And if you have friends or acquaintances who don't agree, or who might be interested in the topic, don't hesitate to bring them along!
The next lecture, to which you are all cordially invited, will exceptionally not be held in a fortnight, but in a month (May 17 at 8 p.m.); its theme will be: "Who would build roads without the state?"
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

title: I have a right to a pub
text: Unfortunately, the ban on smoking in pubs has passed and there is nothing we can do about it, because the laws in practice are constantly increasing, but with exceptions, no one cancels them, ergo, we thus solemnly join the "developed" countries of the EU, which are often argued against; however, even more common is the argument, which I call at work: "I have the right to a pub," which is often explained with the words: "There is only one pub in our village." The best answer to it came from Stok's comments from the author of TaxationISTheft: "So what? If I go to a bookstore and they don't have the book I want, should I start asking the state to make it there?" It is precisely such a senseless demand even in the case of those pubs; not to mention a pretty accurate summary of the current state of the sprawling state I read recently, I don't even know where: "I wouldn't want to own a pub. The idea of someone getting drunk in it, lighting a fire, and me kicking them out before giving them a receipt is a real nightmare."

title: The best president is a bad president
text: In my opinion, the position of the president of the Czech Republic has an amazing ratio of prestige to real power; the head of state is a media-exposed figure, but he doesn't have that much power (not that he doesn't have any at all, for example, he appoints the members of the Banking Council of the CNB) - in other words, given how much he is seen, he can't do that much damage. That's why I think it's not so bad from a libertarian point of view if the president is already a total badass; why? It provokes people, to whom it is easier to explain the absurdity of democracy and state propaganda; for example, such a Zeman represents from this point of view a president who constantly does exactly what I want him to do - namely, shame. But his election period is slowly coming to an end, and I really would not like to see any Karl (the same evil, which looks more acceptable at first glance); however, according to my information, a candidate will be presented soon, who should playfully trump Zeman in embarrassing... and whoever thinks it's not possible, let them watch the media xD

title: Discussion in Polis: State versus Labor
text:
Today at 4 pm I will participate in a panel discussion in Paralelní Polis; the topic will be the recent events at the Rohlik.cz company, where on March 10, foreign police raided on suspicion of illegal employment and took away 85 people without charge, thereby paralyzing the company's operations. Come too, you're all invited, whatever your views; in addition, you can get coffee or beer for bitcoins (and if you don't have BTC, you can buy them directly on the spot) with the certainty that the transaction will not be electronically recorded.
Go outside.

title: Urza in Polis: Weapons
text:
Two weeks ago I
lectured on drugs
; the hall was packed again, for which I thank all of you who came. I am really glad to be able to impart the ideas of a free society to other people; I am grateful for anyone who listens to me and at least thinks about what I say. And I will continue to try my best not to disappoint you xD
Tonight I'm giving a lecture on the topic of guns, which is a rather stylish follow-up to drugs; however, unlike the last lecture, we will not discuss weapons from a technical point of view, but this will be replaced by many interesting statistics and hard data. But that's not all! We will focus on the effect of weapons on the psyche of decent people and criminals; we will talk about the differences between an armed and an unarmed society, not forgetting their relationship to the government. Finally, we will open up the topic of heavy weapons (a lot of heavy ones - fighter planes, battleships, tanks and artillery) and their place in a stateless society. Be sure to come and discuss - especially if you're pro-regulation; and bring your friends with you, ideally those who have never heard of anarcho-capitalism, but might be interested in the topic.
In addition, you are all invited to a lecture that will take place in two weeks (April 19 at 8 p.m.); its theme will be public spaces and freedom of speech.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis
.

title: Consequences of the raid in Mironet
text:
It is May 2000; uniformed monkeys forcefully (against the law) break into the Mironet company, confiscate computers, accounting and accuse the owner of software piracy, only to find out after two years that... sorry like, a bug crept in, you're innocent, sir, so goodbye. However, the person in question is not a sheep and tries to defend himself against this will; he is suing the state for 626 million, which is like a fuck off, you get 23 megabytes and still be happy, keep quiet and shuffle your feet, filthy subject, says the High Court in Prague. Case continues, lawsuit, dismissal, statute of limitations, appeal, it can be found on the Internet (including hateful comments); But you know what I find most interesting about all this? Absolutely no one considers the absurdity of a situation where some entity (the state) damages someone and then the same entity (the state again) judges the case; if it was a private company that would judge its own disputes, that would be a roar!
However, state propaganda is strong...

title: Election 2017: Another crackdown on property rights
text:
For the first time this year, the pre-election campaign will be governed by the latest amendment to the electoral law; the head of the Office for Financial Control of Political Parties, Vojtěch Weiss, declared that anyone who wants to stick their own (!) poster with a political theme on their own (!) fence, shop window or window (that is, not only the promotion of a political party or movement, but also its defamation) must register in his office's tampering database - those who do not do so will be
sanctioned
a fine of ten to one hundred thousand crowns. That registration is also not a piece of cake, one either needs a transparent account, a website and other essentials for it, or one has to be registered by a political party; this will especially affect those who do not want to do a campaign, but an anti-campaign (for example, various haters of Babiš); I'm wondering if this also applies to Stoky, which is certainly not a poster or a large-scale device, but I don't know if it is a "communication medium" according to the law... what do the lawyers here think about it?
And now in Stoká we will once again visit the waters where there are things that would be laughable if they weren't crying: Deputy Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies Jan Bartošek (KDU) declared: "I find it strange to interpret the law in such a way that everyone who places a banner on the fence must register as a supporter." The head of the Constitutional and Legal Committee of the House of Representatives, Jeroným Tejc (ČSSD), responded: "It is not possible to interpret the law ad absurdum and ask people not to be able to express their opinion. [...] But it is up to the authorities how to interpret the law." And you know what? The two geniuses approved the moronic law (and in addition to their parties ANO and Úsvit - let's point to them); that's how law-making works in our country (and unfortunately not only here): A bunch of incompetent idiots approve something, somehow imagine it in practice, but when they find out that another incompetent bureaucrat puts the law into practice differently, they sigh that it's up to them, because "the law is the law" (yes... and where does it come from).

title: Internet or electricity can be, EET must be
text: Based on the fact that most people have an Internet connection, Babiš introduced a general obligation to register sales; unfortunately, this also applies to the minority who have to manage it somehow. For example, the ruins of the Cimburk castle are located in deep forests, where they have not only Internet, but not even electricity; however, the state commanded, so the subject has no choice but to submit. Connectivity itself isn't that much of a problem, electricity is; therefore, it was necessary to purchase a generator to the ruins and haul canisters of fuel there, as a result of which the entire treasury came to some sixty thousand - then the increase in the entrance fee was surely a coincidence, because the two things are obviously not related. In connection with similar cases, I always enjoy it when somewhere Babiš exclaims how the establishment of EET is a negligible amount; sure, for the vast majority of people it can be, but that is no justification for the brutal bullying of that minority, even though democracy stands for it.

title: Urza in Polis: Drugs
text:
Two weeks ago I
lectured on the topic of education
; I consider the lecture to be very successful, because probably the most people arrived so far (certainly over one hundred and fifty), so not only the chairs ran out, but also the place on the floor and the stream (which was exceptional, not normally) was watched by thousands of people. Thank you all for your attention; especially to those who came and of them especially to those who discussed.
Tonight I will lecture again; the topic is likely to cause some controversy again, as we will be talking about drugs. We will discuss drugs themselves, their effects, dangers and risks, because although we learn in public education that drugs are bad, there is basically nothing about them themselves, so there are many myths circulating in society (some of them demonize drugs, others downplay them; in my opinion, these two phenomena are very closely related and you can learn why at the lecture); but of course I will also deal with the state's attitude towards drugs, towards our freedom and the drug war, which has been raging without visible results for many years, during which it has ruined countless human lives.
I also cordially invite everyone to the next lecture, which will take place in a fortnight (April 5 at 8 p.m.); her topic will be guns in a free society.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 8 p.m
Parallel Polis

title: Terror to inclusion
text:
The state has invented that it is simply good for many disabled children to go to normal schools; however, some parents have the audacity to think they know their child better than the official, which is why they refuse to integrate them. And it is precisely these brats that the socialite will take to task; why? Well, because refusing inclusion is against the child's interest... and who judges what is the child's best interest? Yes, that's right - the state, who else. Not that I think inclusion is bad in all cases, however, it should not be decided by the government, but by children, parents and schools;
education should be voluntary
– and that comprehensively (so no one should deny anyone the opportunity to get an education, or force them to get an education; and the exact same thing should also apply to educational institutions), while the last institution that should interfere in this is a band of robbers – called the state – living off the money.
Let's prevent the indoctrination of our children
, as we can.

title: The new Freedom of Learning website
text:
In
Freedom of Learning has finally launched a new website
; and I would like to use this opportunity to recommend Stok readers to familiarize themselves with the interesting ideas that we spread in Freedom of Learning - you can start, for example
manifesto
, in the creation of which I also participated and I fully identify with him (especially with his fourth point). Why do I find the ideas of freedom of learning (now with a small s) so crucial? In my opinion, state education is one of the key – and I think even the most important – sources of state power; yes, sure, it is carried out by the police and courts, however, the reason why it is so widely accepted by people lies precisely in the propaganda that we are all exposed to since childhood, when our minds are still being formed, and as a result it is very difficult to resist it. Let's not expose our children to the same and try to prevent the state from indoctrinating them!

title: The state crushes the Czech roll
text:
The company Rohlík.cz delivers food to people that they order via the Internet; receives and processes three to four thousand orders in Prague every day (I saw an advertisement on one of their cars that said they had already delivered over a million of them). Something like this is clearly a great initiative, because the customers get food at favorable conditions (otherwise they wouldn't order it), the employees earn the best they can within their means (if not, they work elsewhere) and the business owners also get their money's worth; as long as they don't hurt anyone, that is
clearly beneficial
completely regardless of what some politicians or officials think about the conditions under which people work there, as long as they do so voluntarily (and of course regardless of whether they pay taxes or obey other laws, as long as they do not harm anyone). Why should anyone be bothered by this? For what reason should anyone object?
However, the armed fist of the state decided to crush Rohlík.cz, because it does not like that foreigners work in their warehouses under conditions that, in the opinion of officials, contradict the laws; a lot has already been written about why the Benga behave disgustingly as always (first they arrested dozens of people, thereby paralyzing the company's activities, then they legitimized them and found out who actually broke the law and who didn't - even the innocent were therefore restricted in their freedom). However, the criticism that the state is going too hard seems insufficient to me; I see the biggest problem in the fact that such things happen at all, and people who voluntarily cooperate for the benefit of everyone, without harming anyone, are persecuted for their activities by idiots, who already parasitize on their activities, which is all defended by the fact that something is in the laws. Something like this should definitely not be an argument for using violence against someone who has done nothing to anyone and, on the contrary, is beneficial.

Parallel Polis

title: We bought a lift for a disabled person
text:
Kevin Preiß is a wheelchair-bound young German libertarian; however, since his home is not barrier-free, he has been able to go out for years only if his loved ones take him there and back. The lifting platform that would solve the situation costs a quarter of a mega (that is, in crowns); and although the state presents itself as an entity that cares for the disabled, it has kicked Kevin out (well... it would have paid him the lift if it had cost half, which would have been possible, but in another house; it won't even pay him half that way). When my ex-girlfriend found out about the situation (she lives in Germany and knows a lot of libertarians there), she thought of doing a fundraiser... most of the needed amount was raised in three days, a quarter mega within a week; Kevin gets a lift, problem solved.
Although libertarians are often accused of being callous and unwilling to help others, I think the opposite is true; not only because I myself devote quite a bit of my resources to help those who need it (in my opinion), and I am far from alone among libertarians in this approach, but above all it makes sense - when you think that the weak should be taken care of by the state, you don't have that much motivation to do it personally (of course, it is individual and there are many of those motivations), while if you live in the belief that solidarity should be voluntary, you simply have a tendency to be simply voluntarily solidary (again, not without exceptions). This won't just be the case for libertarians, though; if solidarity is not enforced by the state, people will feel more responsible for the state of the world around them... when there is no possibility of calling a politician to solve problems, the tendency to solve them by oneself will increase.

title: Guess... golf?
text:
We have over a hundred golf courses in the Czech Republic and more are constantly being built; however, the number of players is decreasing, which logically puts golf resorts in financial trouble. Whoever thought that the solution would be to let the unneeded go bankrupt while the popular ones prosper is probably a little old-fashioned; current politics understandably dictates: "Let's give the successful and subsidize the unsuccessful!!" That's what motivates people; and so the EU pours hundreds of millions of crowns in subsidies to these failed golf course operators. Remember that the next time you hear from someone how the balance of money that we send to the EU and that we get back is favorable for us; yes, it comes out that way in accounting, but the money collected from taxes appears on the outgoing side
under threat of violence
, while nonsense is being financed on the income side. It's like someone taking a thousand from you to buy us something you absolutely don't want, don't need, and can't sell for two thousand; will you thank him?

title: Gore-Tex? Prohibit!
text: Most of us are probably familiar with Gore-Tex; amazing (and quite expensive) clothing material, which, although waterproof, is breathable and therefore breathable - absolutely priceless for chundras (similar materials are used not only for jackets and trousers, but also for shoes). I applied some myself; and I was lucky because in my tramping days there wasn't yet a wise almighty EU to ban it. But now the situation has changed and the ban is on the table; well, finally - what else would we do? Reasons? Toxicity (so now I'm seriously worried about what years of wearing Gore-Tex will do to me) and ecology - it takes too long to decompose. Well, even if, I really wonder what it will do to ban this; we produce an incredible amount of glass and plastic that will decompose...well...maybe never, while banning Gore-Tex and similar materials, which are produced like spitting in the sea compared to the above, will save it exactly. Logical...

title: The state destroyed, the state subsidizes
text:
Small grocery stores are dying; dozens to hundreds of them are closed every year in the Czech Republic. Why? Although there are undoubtedly more reasons, one of the indisputable ones is the regulations that increase operational costs intolerably - hygiene regulations, occupational safety, employee protection, inspection reports and many others, plus all the red tape that follows; you can't just open a shop and start selling, the law forbids that. Of course, the same laws apply to supermarkets, but they have entire accounting, legal and HR departments that deal with it; as a result, the exact same regulations affect small players much worse, because the difficulty of the duties associated with it is certainly not linear with respect to profit or turnover, so larger entities are favored by the state (small shops simply cannot afford to allocate even one person to take care of these things).
Current solution? The state subsidizes these small establishments; just like Ronald Reagan said: "If it moves, tax it. If it keeps moving, regulate it. And when it stops moving, subsidize it." A reasonable solution? Cancellation of regulations (
ideally also taxes
) and bureaucratic duties associated with it; small shops can then
to compete freely in the free market
and see what people actually want. And what about Miloslav Hlavsa, director of the cooperative network Konzum? "I don't like subsidies." Great so far; unfortunately, the person in question continues: "Operating food stores in small villages is not a business and should be included in the law as a public service." As an entrepreneur, he does not want subsidies; however, he misses the good old pre-revolutionary practices. What to say to that? The whole thing is so absurd that I don't even know; but if the state did not distort the market, who would the politicians actually save?

title: More aggressive cops...
text:
Uniformed monkeys Ondřej Bína and Přemysl Rückl stopped a van driver in Českolipska because his rear light was not on; they did so in heavy snow in a completely demented place (downhill road in serpentines), where the driver was afraid to stop, lest someone take him down. He slowed down, flashed his blinkers, making it clear he wanted to stop, but that wasn't enough for the cops; Přemysl Rückl justifies it as follows: "The car should stop immediately, not after two minutes. When the driver wanted to call 158, the uniformed bandit pulled him out of the car, sprayed him with tear gas, knocked him to the ground and kicked him; the official explanation is that they were afraid he wouldn't reach for a gun, they suspected he might be a robber and should have stopped immediately. Vermin! Compared to that, I am
recently escaped
still good enough.

title: Regulation of discounts
text: Some time ago, the regulatory authority forced operators to increase LTE coverage for high-speed Internet; God? Eeee... semi. Oddly enough, it cost something, which was reflected in the prices; the office does not agree with that. What to say about that? It would be laughable if it weren't for crying. But now the Minister of Industry and Trade, Jan Mládek, will go to hell; he will look at the discounts. He wants to prohibit operators from offering discounts to clients by law (which, by the way, most of them enjoy); wtf? Yes, just make it more expensive in the name of the law, let it be fair. Motivation? So here I am not exceptionally betting on the old well-known good-naturedness in combination with stupidity; I consider more likely the scenario that one of the big operators does not like the current market situation and wants to get rid of discounts, however, if he did it himself, customers would go to his competition, so he pulled the strings and wants to ban it across the board. After all, we have the state to protect us from those evil corporations!

title: Urza in Polis: Democracy
text:

lectures in Parallel Polis
culture, art and we also touched on the protection of monuments and works of art; since the period of exams and viruses was over, over a hundred people showed up again. title: Four day work week
text: TOP09 started a debate about when and under what conditions the Czech Republic will be ready for a four-day work week; Kalousek conditions this by improving labor productivity, while the unions above all demand that the reduction of working hours should occur across the board for everyone, and the biggest problem for them would be if it happened only in certain industrial sectors, but the furthest away is of course the favorite Stok Marks, which long ago founded a working group called Work 4.0 for this purpose and is about to visit Germany, where the debates on this topic are said to be further. For now, I'm just shaking my head and wondering why these bombers should decide this? What if we would rather abolish the entire Labor Code and leave working hours and all other requirements to the agreement between employers and employees? At least unions would regain their original meaning and stop being just a group promoting their interests through legal (but illegitimate) violence.

title: We do not cook for refugees!
text:
For the second time, ČOIka has fined the Grand Italia pizzeria from Hrušovan nad Jevišovka in South Moravia (with an amount in the tens of thousands), because the owners dared to put up a sign stating that they do not cook for immigrants. In addition, I would like to note a few things (I will start from the least important and continue to the most important): First, I consider the actions of the restaurant owners to be quite stupid and as a guest I would probably go elsewhere; secondly, many of their customers see it differently, support the restaurant and even want to pay the fine; thirdly, I would be quite interested in whether the people in question seriously broke the law, when technically they only threatened to break it with the sign, which is probably not allowed anymore; and finally, fourthly, regardless of whether the law was broken, I find it grossly immoral and unjustifiable for the state to force someone to serve and cook for someone they don't want to serve.
The real problems in the Czech Republic associated with migration (especially due to the real absence of a larger number of immigrants) are paradoxically not caused by immigrants, but by the state, which interferes with people doing what they want in their own way and for their own sake; let anyone who doesn't want to serve immigrants not to serve them, because there are plenty of people here who will gladly serve them (and we won't interfere with them, of course). Let everyone be free to decide whether they want to be a xenophobe, a racist, an Islamophobe, or an Islamophile; as long as no one initiates violence against others, it is basically only and purely their business. What will be the result of forcing people who obviously do not want migrants here and hate them to cook for them? Will they perhaps start to like them or respect them more? Not by mistake! Quite the contrary – they will be all the more angry that the state is imposing on them. Even leaving aside whether the fines are crap (which they are), they won't do any practical good either.

title: Petition for freer education
