title: Implementation and non-disruption of laws
text:
When I wrote the day before yesterday
on toll gates financed from the EU
, in addition to yesterday's thoughts on European subsidies, one more thing occurred to me: Have you noticed that once a law is adopted, the declared goal of which is to increase security at the expense of freedom, it is practically never repealed, even in the case when it becomes clear that the increase in security did not occur, while the reduction of freedom did? Basically, no one even thinks of breaking such restrictions, so we keep layering more and more of them on top of each other.
A typical example is the points system: Its enforcement was defended through media manipulation, we heard politicians preach about piles of dead on Czech roads, while the supposed solution was to introduce a points system, which they say will certainly improve this situation. There were long discussions about it, the law was approved, only to later show that the accident rate not only did not decrease, but even increased (which may not have been directly the fault of the points system, in any case it did not bring the declared benefits); what should be the next logical step in such a situation? Of course, the abolition of such a system; but, of course, no influential person seriously considered this at all, on the contrary, we can witness police whining about the need to tighten up and score more points.
Even if we were to assume for a moment the legitimacy of the state and similar measures, it would be reasonable to debate similar legislative changes, and then possibly implement them, however, when it turns out that they did not bring the expected effect that their supporters declared, the only meaningful solution is to return to the original state. However, such a thing is completely unthinkable, because once the debate on the given topic is over and the law is passed, no one will return to it, even if the arguments for its introduction prove to be invalid in retrospect. Even for politicians who were previously opposed, the problem ceases to exist; lifting restrictions is practically out of the question.
I believe that as long as the Czech (and unfortunately not only) legislative process works in this way, it can be safely stated that any victory of freedom is only temporary, while any triumph of evil seems to be permanent; look at the ban on smoking in pubs and restaurants, for example - the temporary victory of freedom a few years ago, when the ban was not passed, has been replaced by its adoption in an even harsher form, and it does not seem possible to get rid of it. This is simply not fair; but what about that?

title: European subsidies
text:
When I wrote yesterday
on toll gates financed from the EU
, I remembered that sometimes you can read how someone evaluates the financial advantages or disadvantages of our membership in the EU; it is typically the difference between the amount that travels from the Czech Republic to the EU and the amount that comes from the EU to the Czech Republic. While something like this may make sense at first glance, there are a number of reasons why such reasoning is fatally flawed.
Briefly, the absurdity of such balances can be shown as follows:
If someone takes a thousand crowns from me and then buys me things for eleven hundred, will I make money from it? Well, if it hits my preferences exactly by buying something that I would buy anyway, then yes; but the more likely option is that he buys me something I don't want, so we both end up losing out on it (I would prefer something else and he had to pay me another hundred crowns).
And what about European subsidies?
1/ This money is usually deliberately invested in something that its recipients would not choose (if so, they will pay for it themselves, ergo there is no need to subsidize it).
2/ In order to obtain subsidies, certain conditions must be met, which is typically not free either (there is another waste here, when various entities try to satisfy the EU bureaucracy rather than satisfy the needs of their clients). A completely absurd example is, for example, Prague companies moving outside of Prague, for which they receive subsidies for the creation of jobs outside of Prague (in reality, of course, no new jobs are created, it is only a matter of moving them, which also costs a lot of time and fuel due to the commuting of employees).
3/ Sometimes European money is used for something downright counterproductive or even evil (for examples, you don't have to go far, see toll gates); not to mention the psychological effect of dependence on central authority and increasing immoral redistribution (subsidies are often drawn by someone completely different from the one who had to earn them).
4/ It is necessary to pay an army of people who take care of a completely unproductive subsidy-related bureaucracy instead of doing something useful.
As a result, it is almost certain that the vast majority of people lose out on subsidies (unfortunately, not only the European ones).
Let's not be manipulated by anyone who claims that we benefit from EU membership because the Czech Republic's income from the EU nominally exceeds levies; while in one direction money flows completely unconditionally, in the opposite direction the conditions are quite strict. There is no such thing as a free lunch, despite what politicians like to tell us.

title: Devil's tool: toll gates
text:
Hundreds of millions of European subsidies will once again serve their purpose, and we will be one step further: Toll gates with cameras recording the number plates of all passing vehicles will be installed on Czech highways; it will then be possible to determine the average speed of each car that passed between the gates from the timed data on the crossings, so that those whose average speed was higher than the maximum allowed could be sent a ticket straight away. Fascinating indeed, isn't it? Especially in combination with the unconstitutional – but valid – law on the administrative offense (abbreviated SPRDEL) of the vehicle operator, which allows fines to be collected even if the driver has not been identified, we have a lot to look forward to.
The supporter of this measure, a kind of scumbag Jindřich Frič from the Center for Transport Research, is surprised by the fact that the state has not used toll gates in this way for a long time; I'm basically surprised too, because it's an absolutely ideal tool for ... kin, it's so demonic that I don't know the reason behind this measure in the first place, because I can think of at least four:
1/ Good old cashiering of drivers; the possibility of quite effortless filling of the state coffers, which will still be applauded by many citizens, does not occur every day.
2/ Good old propaganda; there are still people who really believe that similar measures will lead to safer roads - what about the fact that they have repeatedly proven to be dysfunctional (for example, such a point system; against all odds, the number of accidents increased with its introduction, on the contrary, more people started avoiding accidents).
3/ Good old Big Brother; what will happen with the data from the toll gates? Officially nothing, of course, but otherwise... knowing the detailed travel history of all highway users can be quite valuable information. Not to mention that I can imagine how in time someone will come up with the idea that the data could be used for a police investigation, so it will be officially stored... and then some Babiš will think that something else could actually be done with it...
4/ Good old tightening of the screws and strengthening of state power; with every such step, the state lets its subjects know that it can and will interfere in every aspect of their lives, simply because it has to. The longer and more intensely it happens, the less strange it seems to people; for the next generation, for example, toll gates will be a necessity that simply cannot be abolished, because "then there would be piles of corpses on the roads".
And what do you think about it, dear readers? Your opinions are welcome in the discussion.

title: Censor Babiš
text:
Babiš came up with a new law on gambling, according to which the Ministry of Finance could block illegal gambling houses; Of course, the casino owners who have a license from the state are excited - do you see how well the state protects us against monopolies? However, this is far from everyone, especially not the foreign ones; for example, the largest poker room in the world, Pokerstars, tried to negotiate such a permit with the Ministry of Finance, but somehow it didn't work out due to the completely meaningless conditions from the Czech Republic (I suspect that it was something like 40% tax plus VAT). However, quite unsurprisingly, people play where they want to play, not where Babiš would like, which probably doesn't make him completely happy, because he would prefer to decide absolutely everything.
As much nonsense as this law is in itself, I fear that it is only the vanguard of a far more extensive censorship; as soon as the ban on casinos is passed (and many debaters on Novinky are already applauding this), the logical next step will be to attack feelings through child porn. The censorship of sites with child pornography will probably come as a whirlwind, I can imagine the crowds of citizens excited to sacrifice another piece of their freedom for the illusion of a safer society; and that's not even the worst in itself. The biggest danger lies in the fact that people will start to perceive the censoring of what we don't like on the Internet as a standard. And I really would not like to live to see the moment when I have a discussion on the censored Internet with statists who will convince me that a free Internet is a utopia, it would never work, and moreover there are incredibly sophisticated technologies that simply need state management, otherwise it cannot be done, because without regulation, private individuals would not be able to operate, for example, DNS, which would cause the guaranteed end of the world; no, I seriously don't want to answer the question to young socialists in a few decades, what would happen if the state didn't regulate the Internet and someone bought the domain www.kdo-by-stavel-silnice.cz, which they would then sell for ten million crowns...

title: The (non)final solution to the immigration issue
text:
What I consider to be a good solution to the immigration crisis, I already am
described
a long time ago (and even then I started to be a xenophobe to the sun-lovers, a traitor to the Islamophobic); In short, I hold approximately the following opinion: First, liberalize society (primarily abolish laws on discrimination and protection of minorities, social benefits and unnecessary redistribution, the minimum wage and the entire labor code and, last but not least, the regulation of the sale of weapons, in addition, change the law on self-defense so that if it is serious self-defense, then it is automatically appropriate), then calmly open the borders (but definitely do not invite anyone here, do not give anything to newcomers; this will probably sort things out by itself hard-working from slackers, because slackers have no reason to flock to places where they don't get anything for free, especially if their neighbors have an overcrowded welfare system).
However, I myself have to admit that the disadvantage of this solution is its complete unenforceability in practical democracy, where it is very difficult to implement anything that has anything to do with real freedom, because it is a regime based on the dictates of the majority of voters to all people; so what about that? For a long time I didn't think of anything, not even a pleasant weekend spent in Moravia with twenty libertarians brought me closer; however, I took the chairman on the way back
LvMI
and in the discussion with him, he came up with a somewhat anarcho-agorist solution, which I consider to be almost as good as the above - but, unlike him, quite feasible, since to a certain extent it consists in maintaining the current state:
Officially let's reject immigrants, but realistically let's not catch any here and let's not guard the borders (even the police are great at doing nothing). So what? An illegal receives nothing from the state, so he cannot live on any benefits; so it will deter the homeless refugees. The rest will work illegally, pay no taxes and create demand for services independent of the establishment. And the more transactions that take place outside the reach of the state, the better. An illegal is also very unlikely to complain if he becomes a victim of discrimination.
Of course, it's not ideal, but I feel that it is (except for the occasional police intervention on the one hand and some acceptance on the other) the status quo, and so far it works (immigrants don't really flock to us, as they prefer countries with an overburdened welfare system). So I think it's strategic to try to do the following:
1/ Maintain the current (relatively strict) immigration policy.
2/ Define yourself against any attempt to close the borders (putting this power in the hands of the state is dangerous anyway).
3/ Rejecting any increase in the budget or even the powers of the police (this is even more dangerous than the closed borders), not giving them tasks beyond the existing ones.
4/ Trying to convince the Islam killers that better than banning Islam en bloc (i.e. restricting freedom) is allowing anyone to discriminate against anyone (i.e. expanding freedom).
It is a rather delicate balancing of power between the Islamophobic and the sun-loving, while the first-named should not be allowed to strengthen the state or immediately introduce totalitarianism, while the second would be advisable to prevent unlimited #acceptance for foreign money (as soon as we start feeding the refugees here, there will almost certainly be a lot of others who will demand the same). I've only had this idea in my head for about a day, so it's not that thoroughly thought out, so I'd appreciate any criticism or opinion in the comments (you can contribute even without registration).

title: Higher level of propaganda
text:
Very often, when I'm doing something at the computer, I have some audiovisual background in the form of a movie or series running on one of my monitors, but from my point of view, they're mostly bullshit, I don't pay too much attention to them and I don't return to them anymore; if something interests me, I'll play it again in peace. One of the many series I watch this way is Criminal Minds; and I have to admit that the third part of the fourth series seriously caught my attention to the extent that I would like to share my impressions with you and add one observation at the end.
Plot description:
Somewhere in the US there is a self-sufficient libertarian gated community living in a gated community cut off from the world. The FBI doesn't like that one of the libertarians is sleeping with a fifteen-year-old girl, plus he has multiple wives; it bothers some other police department that they have illegally kept weapons there. The state is understandably unable to function effectively and coordinate its activities, so the moment the FBI sends its agents to the place to map the situation, the settlement is also attacked by the intervention team, whose task is to help and protect against illegally held weapons, which they try to achieve by shooting at libertarians; however, they resist the attack, all the while stressing that they just want the police to leave them alone, even allowing them to retreat and treat a wounded fellow attacker, but keeping the FBI agents captive. Then comes a relatively long negotiation, during which the libertarians repeatedly tell the cops that they just want them to be left alone, which they refuse, saying that they can't because the law is the law, as well as mapping the situation, which in turn brings the discovery that the sex between the fifteen-year-old girl and her husband was voluntary. It all ends with the police gathering more force and attacking the libertarians, they lose and many of them - including the "abused" girl - die.
Do you think any of the screenwriters decided to promote libertarian ideas? Surprisingly no. The main positive heroes are the tails from the FBI, the series portrays libertarians as evil. That this is not possible within the above plot? Well, I wouldn't have believed it either if I hadn't seen it; but the "canvas" can handle anything, for example the following situation:
After the SWAT team storms the libertarians' home, the FBI protagonists discuss another strategy, with the line: "We have to disprove [the libertarians] the idea that [their leader] has forced upon them that we are an army that wants to destroy their home." Unfortunately, not in the sense that they now have to manipulate them and force them to believe delusions, but that they will explain reality to them, and the delusion is, on the contrary, the idea that a police intervention unit attacking a settlement because of "crimes" without victims represents to the residents an army that wants to destroy their home.
At first glance, the whole thing is actually not that interesting, because there are clouds of movies and series showing good cops and bad criminals; however, typically in them we see criminals doing bad things and policemen heroes who generally only seriously protect innocent citizens (sometimes they violate some property rights, but mostly not fatally). I understand such films and series as classic propaganda, the state is simply idealized in them. Here, however, it went to such an extreme that the action of the police was seriously portrayed as a brutal attack on innocent libertarians who repeatedly demanded only peace, only to be massacred without mercy; yet everything is served up to make the viewer identify with the sky-high crap. The screenwriter is at best a sycophant of the establishment, at worst even so manipulated that he no longer found anything strange about the whole thing and it was "absolutely clear" to him that the police acted "correctly". I wonder how many of the sixteen million Americans who watched the show's premiere got it on their heads; and I'm afraid we're certainly not moving in the tens of percent here, maybe we'll be happy for a percent. Has propaganda really advanced so far that it is not necessary to show the state as a heroic organization because people will applaud and identify with it even when it commits obvious wrongdoing?

title: Disarmament
text:
"When the government starts confiscating people's guns, know that you're going to need them before long."
Does anyone know the author of this quote? Unfortunately I don't; I will be glad if you broaden my horizons. But whoever it is, unfortunately it makes sense. And what the hell he didn't want, this problem is even becoming topical, as the government came up with an amendment to the law, according to which the validity of a firearms license is shortened from ten years to half, but above all, it authorizes the police to confiscate weapons on the basis of indications that the owner may suffer from a mental disorder; therefore, this is not a case where the person in question does not pass the psychotests, a mere report is enough to confiscate his weapons until he passes the psychotests.
That this is a great way of "resolving" neighborhood disagreements is probably obvious to everyone at first glance; Do you mind a neighbor who happens to own a firearm? Do you feel that he is a fool? Call the police! Not only can they temporarily confiscate his weapons, but on top of that, he will have to undergo a series of psychological tests.
Does anyone have the feeling that the police will certainly be reasonable in such cases? But come on, as if you didn't know those uniformed monkeys. Sure, you might just get lucky, but you might not; either because they will be in a bad mood, or they won't want to risk trouble (just imagine that they don't take away someone's gun, after which he actually commits something, that will be a mouthful for the media), or they may just need to show some activity, or you will be unsympathetic or sympathetic to them (ideally with connections).
Even the corruption potential there can be created by more resourceful individuals; for example, such a conscientious citizen who will constantly inform the gun owner, while the latter may not even know that the nice uniformed authority, who decided not to bother him for a certain fee, is in fact in agreement with the informer.
This may not be a complete terno, because the question is how much the gun owner is willing to pay in such a situation, however, it is an act where a police officer can practically arbitrarily harm someone, temporarily confiscate some of his property and force him to undergo (and pay for) a psychological evaluation, all of which can be defended by saying that someone snapped. In connection with this, it occurs to me that psychologists who make a living from these reviews can also sue, or get someone to do it.
And finally, it's a completely unprecedented form of good old-fashioned pure police buzz; the uniformed monkeys can arbitrarily harass anyone at any time, take away their weapons, and drag them down with red tape just by getting someone to testify that they complained. This is perhaps an unplowed field in the Czech Republic, the question remains, of course, with what vigor the bastards will get into it, but it could be a problem.
In particular, it depends on whether and how much it will be possible to repeatedly take those weapons from someone in this way; the thug will report the person in question, Benga will confiscate his weapons, he will go to psychotests, pass, get the weapons back... and how long can this torture be repeated? Immediately? In a week? Month? How about half a year? If anyone has a more concrete idea about it, I would definitely welcome it in the discussion.

title: You know the one about the anarchist, statist and immigrants?
text:
This is how an anarchist said years ago: "The state will not protect us against an external threat; the solution is a free society so that we can defend ourselves."
The statist yells at him: "Shut up and go read Rothbard, you detached theorist; of course the state will protect us!"
And the years go by when suddenly...
Statist: "The state did not protect us from immigrants! Politicians force us to feed them and drag them here, even if nobody wants them! The government has failed! They are traitors!"
Anarchist: "Of course, I've been saying that for years; the solution is a free society so we can defend ourselves."
Statist: "Shut up and go read Rothbard, you detached theorist; of course we need a better state and better politicians!"
After reading the lines I have just written, I think it is not very good even as a joke; the problem is that as a reality it is far worse.
This always runs through my head when I read the various Hamples, IVČRN activists and similar stuff, I often recognize among them the exact people with whom I debated years ago about the inability of the state to secure its citizens against risk; even then I was rather indiscriminately sent by them to where the sun don't shine. When, after a while, they themselves saw their mistake, instead of holding their noses, they realized that the anarchists were right, so maybe it would be worth listening to them (I'm not saying to become an anarchist, but to think about whether there might be something to their theses at least partially), they reject and ridicule the anarchists' solutions even more sharply and aggressively than ever before.
To err is human and unfortunately for many people it is also unpleasant, so they tend not to admit their mistake; as long as they don't admit it only to those around them, it's not so bad, but it's worse when they don't even admit it to themselves. Then instead of listening to the one who was right when they weren't, they kick the person even harder.
I am not saying that refugees are not a threat, but what I am trying to solve is certainly not turning to the state; at the most, with the fact that he gave us freedom in discrimination and self-defense, the possibility not to pay immigrants anything compulsorily and he did not try to invent some global solution for everyone (which in principle is not even possible), but left it up to each of us. Well, I won't repeat myself, I already wrote about this topic after all
article
.

title: The purpose of a driver's license is to...
text:
...state bullshit. And otherwise?
Officially, it is justified by some talk about road safety, playing on emotions and the like; but does it make any logical sense at all?
I'm afraid not, considering the following aspects:
1/ A driver's license is owned by many people who practically cannot drive at all; given that it is issued for ten years, quite a few people get it at eighteen, but then they don't drive (for example, they don't have anything), and after a few years, the few hours of driving in the presence of an instructor mean practically no difference compared to if the person in question had not driven at all.
2/ Many people who know how to drive absolutely perfectly do not have a driver's license; these are typically professional drivers who are scored by the state, take away their driver's license and thereby deprive them of their business. They may be able to drive completely safely, because points are not only given for dangerous driving, but also for not wearing seat belts, talking on the phone, exceeding the speed limit (even if it is not dangerous at all) or having lunch with beer before driving.
3/ In reality, even today, nothing prevents anyone from going out on the road even without a driver's license, and if he really doesn't know how to drive even as he would have learned in a driving school (and that's no bad thing either), it's quite possible that he will cause an accident even before a preventive road check stops him. Another possibility is, of course, that the policemen start chasing the person in question somewhere; and when they find that they are unable to catch him, instead of taking it as a confirmation of his driving skills, they set up live roadblocks of innocent drivers and plan some massacre like in March 2013 on the D1 highway.
4/ The vast majority of people have an instinct for self-preservation, so they don't get on the road without at least learning how to control the vehicle (this can be seen beautifully in those who take a driving school, then for some reason don't drive, after which they start again years later - although the law does not prevent them from just jumping into the car and going into traffic, they typically learn again); and if someone is already such a fool that he is not deterred even by the risk of destroying his car and himself, the hypothetical possibility of a police check will hardly stop him.
So what's left?
The police and the authorities that issue driver's licenses can thus be employed.
In addition, it can generate other so-called "crimes" without victims.
Finally, it is possible to extort drivers through the threat of confiscating driver's licenses; especially when driving for a living.
So, yes, the purpose of the existence of driver's licenses is only and only state buzz, they have no other meaning.

title: Welcome to Stoké
text:
SEWERS OF THE FREEPORT
they welcome libertarians in particular, but also anyone willing to have a reasonable discussion.
The purpose of this site is to publish ideas that are too short, simple, obscure, or unsorted to make it into the article itself; and of course discussion of such texts. The authors thus have the opportunity to clarify their ideas in cooperation with the discussants, who can thus influence their opinions.
However, observations that have no ambition to become articles have their place here; observations you write, for example, on social networks and the like. However, unlike social networks, where such posts are scattered among everything possible, Stoky will collect only what is somehow (even remotely) related to freedom (and of course anything from Stok can also be shared on social networks).
You can discuss in Stoká either completely anonymously, or you can register (with registration you get several benefits); new topics can only be added by authors who can become regular discussants or libertarians publishing on other websites (after agreement with the owner of Stok).

title: About self-directed anarchy in Bratislava
text:
One of the biggest supporters of the book Anarchoagorismus wanted me to perform in Bratislava in his reward at the Startovača; he invited me to an interesting and pleasant space, where he brought an inquisitive and (healthily) critical audience who, although they did not have a very deep knowledge of anarchism, showed an interest.
Over the years, I have been slowly learning to be more receptive, empathetic, attentive to the audience and respond to their energy - this is probably the work of a lifetime; here, however, I feel that I succeeded perhaps the most so far – I perceived the atmosphere and I think I spoke relevantly to individual interviewers and opponents.

title: Freeport Studio: Dealing with Cops for Beginners with Jíťa
text:
In the winter, D-FENS and I had a lecture about (not) talking to the cops; and in the spring he appeared in a livestream of the Free Port on the same topic. In terms of information, these were very rich and substantial events; however, more people responded that they were too complicated for them.
That's why we decided to do one more livestream with Jíťa - she is one of those who would need further explanation. Seasoned veterans probably won't learn anything new here (but they can give advice); we can help beginners not to be afraid of policemen and other representatives of the state.

– Jíťa; Freeport volunteer; an adult in Ježek without a cage; anarchist

title: Freeport Studio: Freedom, the Atomic Bomb and (Mental) Health
text:
Interesting texts are published in the Sewers of the Free Port; this week they tackle various topics from mental health and child addictions to health and safety in science to the connection of AI with self-directed education - everyone brings an interesting perspective and I also add something to them (for example, a story about a "workshop" with a plutonium core on the table).
However, I devote most of my time to the stories of several psychiatric patients in different hospitals; it wasn't always the bad experiences, but unfortunately they outweigh the good ones. One of them came into my life quite fundamentally; and showed me again how easily socialist healthcare can kill quietly.

title: Freeport Studio: How not to lose at 4:36? Do not play (play with ČT and ČRo)!
text:
Babiš's government pushed through the first reading of the law on the abolition of concessionaire fees; it happened exactly a week ago (ie Saturday 24th October) at 4:36 AM, after which the time became a symbol of resistance to this move - a lot of people mobilized to express their opinion (agreeable or critical).
What is at risk if the government succeeds in changing public media to state media? And what happens if it fails? Why is he even trying? And why in this particular way? I answer these and many other questions (from an anarchist point of view) in a three-hour video, where I also offer a solution; I also respond to a lot of content (not only from ČT and ČRo).

title: Free Port Studio: About ČKMA and crypto business with Adam Chvaja
text:
When I criticized the Czech Cryptocurrency Association for a too devout approach to the state, I also declared a willingness to conduct a dialogue; and that really interested one of its founders, who started talking to me immediately and finally accepted an invitation to the Studio.
I enjoyed the interview, as we first talked about the Czech crypto business, state regulations and the overall state of freedom in society; and perhaps even more pleased was the off-camera interview with the guest - during which I definitively believed in him everything that I previously (perhaps a little) doubted.

– Adam Chvaja; founder of ČKMA; cryptocurrency entrepreneur; anarcho-capitalist

title: Home seminar on migration, money (and other aspects of life) in anarchy
text:
More and more schoolchildren are watching Freeport; and some sometimes try to invite me to school. In the long term, it blocks leadership in about two-thirds of the cases (even more often since the #no_disobedience era - in fact, always so far); however, students don't give up and come up with other ways, such as an apartment seminar.
This time we tackled various aspects of life in anarchy - from migration to money to defense against an external enemy; it didn't just stop at anarchy, we also discussed evolution. I love how many people came in their spare time with an interest to discuss interesting issues; even the teacher.

title: Studio Freeport: Not only about the economy with Sara Polak
text:
I deeply respect Sara Polak for her open-mindedness, humility, multidisciplinary perspective and, above all, her willingness to learn with love and to share the acquired knowledge; I believe that it is precisely from such an approach to life that freedom is born - for individuals and entire communities.
This time we covered the basics of economics, which Sara was interested in; I like that she came up with the fact that she doesn't understand economics and would like to supplement her knowledge. It ended up being an interesting conversation about anything and everything.

– Sara Polak; anarchist; seeker of truth; researcher; anthropologist; techarchaeologist; popularizer of artificial intelligence (even before it was cool)

title: Dialogue between a democrat (Jan Dobrovský) and an anarchist (Urza)
text:
Jan Dobrovský was supposed to speak at the "Free Port Conference 2026: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow", which unfortunately did not happen; however, because I wanted this dialogue so much, we organized another event together with Students for Liberty at the ABC Theater for this purpose.
Despite high expectations, the discussion pleasantly surprised me in some ways; although I disagree with Jan Dobrovský on a number of things, I respect him for his openness, which helped us find understanding even where I would not have expected it before. I myself took away a lot of interesting knowledge; and I look forward to the next time.

– Jan Dobrovský; podcaster; journalist; dissident; businessman

title: Debate and screening of The People vs. Larry Flynt (Freeport & SFL)
text:
Students for Liberty came up with a great idea - to show libertarian films with an introduction before and a discussion after the screening; this could entertain not only fans of Freeport and SFL, but also attract to us unknown people curious about the film itself.
I chose People vs. Larry Flynt as the first movie; although it seemed for a long time that we wouldn't be able to find a cinema to show it, we finally did - and I believe it was worth it, because this film is about freedom on many levels, which I point out before (and after) the screening(s).

– Jonáš Kurus; national coordinator of Students for Liberty; economics student; libertarian; dialogue creator

title: Freeport Studio: Living in Truth with Tim
text:
Tim asked me to do a livestream on a topic that he himself considers current and I consider very important, namely living in truth; the latter goes hand in hand with authenticity and is a (necessary) condition for inner freedom (in an extreme case, perhaps even sufficient, which I don't know yet).
At the same time, it will be the first livestream to which a guest will join remotely, specifically Tim from Italy; I hope (although I don't really believe) that without technical problems. I am really looking forward to the interview; the connection of anarchism with self-development is more and more relevant for me.

– Tim; libertarian; maybe an anarchist; youtuber; student of political science and philosophy; LGBT activist

title: Freeport Studio: Analysis of the principle of non-aggression for animals by Tomáš Prchal
text:
This year, Tomáš Prchal came up with the extension of the principle of non-aggression to animals; the main difference between this act and its ilk is that I find it really elaborate - in fact, the most elaborate I've come across so far (and the first to "provoke" me to a reaction).
However, in my commentary on his lecture where he introduces this concept, I explain why even this concept does not seem sufficient to me; as part of this, I get very deep into the very essence of NAP - I explain various things here that I have never gotten to before.

– Tomáš Prchal; libertarian; vegan; animal rights activist; artist; athlete

title: Anarcho-Capitalism: Economic Mistakes and the "Mistakes" of Politicians
text:
The June lecture from the cycle Anarchocapitalism will again be on an economic topic; we'll discuss what politicians do wrong, but also why - not every economic "mistake" is a serious mistake - it's often a cheap way to score political points that someone else will pay for. Unfortunately, politicians are also supported by some libertarian economists when they need to be relevant to government; I'm happy when they advise the government instead of the socialists, but on the other hand, unfortunately, it also has the opposite effect. I would like to talk about the economic mistakes that occur in democracies without regard to specific policies; I want to show it with specific examples, quite possibly we will also touch on something current (depending on the state of Hormuz). I will try to provide a counterweight to the views commonly presented in the (mainly public) media; we will deal with price and margin ceilings, but also people's favorite pastime - finding the "culprits" of high prices and making uninformed judgments about "fairness".
Presentation: https://prednasky.urza.cz/ll/

title: Freeport Studio: About prison, pedophilia and sexuality with two guests
text:
In addition to external freedom, which is limited primarily by laws, the creation of the Free Port also deals with internal freedom, which is limited, among other things, by social norms or taboos; and pedophilia is unfortunately one of the most controversial.
In this video, we are dedicated to the imprisonment of a pedophile who did not harm anyone, he just downloaded (completely consensual) content from the Internet; also sexual deviations, which we try to de-taboo. Comments are welcome; ideally written with an open mind…

– Tim; pedophile; former prisoner; holder of child pornography
– Anna Honzíková; Freeport volunteer; anarchist; holder of child pornography

title: Interview for Reporter magazine
text:
For me, Reporter magazine is synonymous with quality journalism; I appreciate their work, so I was very pleased (and gladly accepted) the invitation to talk about anarchy, the book Anarchoagorism, self-directed education and other interesting topics.

– Tomáš Poláček; lifelong avid journalist; traveller

Another #disobedience event was about respect (especially towards children, so also about adultism) and also focused on inner freedom; I broke not only laws, but also social norms - including norms regarding sexuality - and tried to break various taboos in front of witnesses on the record.

title: Freeport Studio: Commentary on the Pros and Cons of Banning Children's Phones
text:
The reactions to the shows (especially from the public media) are becoming more and more interesting to me; and from your comments I think it's mutual, so I intend to continue it. In September, as usual, I would like to focus mainly on children, adultism, education and schools; this time to Babiš' blanket ban on phones for children in schools.
I also take the liberty of criticizing the public media (specifically ČRo) for, in my opinion, a rather biased attitude towards technology bans (telephones, social networks) for children; although there is not even a scientific consensus on their harmfulness, the public service media present the views of only one side, with which they scare the public.

title: He went on his own to the war in Ukraine (worse sound in the first half)
text:
I managed to realize and record an interview with a warrior and a medic who went on his own to the front line of the war in Ukraine; there he helped the Ukrainian soldiers and taught them medicine and tactics, although mostly (with some exceptions) he did not intervene directly in the fighting.
I found the reasons why he stopped doing it after a while extremely interesting; we discussed those (more interesting for me) in particular in the second part of the interview - in that one, moreover, the problem with the sound, which unfortunately occurred in the first half, does not persist.

– anonymous warrior; expert in tactics and medicine; a direct participant in the war in Ukraine

title: Freeport Studio: Commentary on the Pros and Cons of Suffrage from Sixteen
text:
The reactions to the shows (especially from the public media) are becoming more and more interesting to me; and from your comments I think it's mutual, so I intend to continue it. In September, as usual, I would like to focus mainly on children, adultism and its impact on society; this time to the right to vote for individuals over the age of sixteen.
In this piece, I was particularly interested in the opponent of this proposal; his practically only argument was the alleged excessive emotionality of young people, in which I see a paradox considering the fact that the person in question was actually just appealing purely to emotions and creating some impression on others without any justification.

title: Urza at the House of Freeport on living anarchy for the second time, July 2026
text:
The Living Anarchy Talk at the Freeport House Summer Residency was a huge success; so much so that listeners requested a sequel on the same topic - and there were a lot of them, including some who weren't at the first one.
I tried to talk about the same topic from a different point of view; we analyzed the connection between anarchy and self-development, i.e. living it in everyday life. I explained why I feel the need to define a new anarchist direction, which, in addition to external freedom, addresses the internal one; this is unfortunately neglected by many people (including most anarchists).

title: Freeport studio: Schooling (not only) in childhood with Anička Rous
text:
In September, as usual, we will focus on the topics of education, education, (dis)self-management or adultism; this time we will focus, among other things, on the pitfalls or destructiveness of positive motivation, which is considered appropriate because there is no obvious harm.
The guest in the Studio will be Anička Rous, our long-term follower and participant of the stay; he will step out of his comfort zone and talk not only about his childhood, but also about parenting - education plays a significant role in both.

– Anička Rous (https://pokecosvobode.cz/ ); self-directed anarchist; self-directed mother; self-directed seeker of truth; a self-directed follower of Freeport

title: Talks of Anarchy at Freeport House, July 2026
text:
One of the authors of Conversations about Anarchy came to the 2026 Freeport House Summer Residence, where he expressed an interest in filming an interview with me, which we did in the presence of other participants; I am happy for this connection of our projects.
Dominik wanted to talk about the path to anarchy, about the real possibility of transforming society from statist to anarchist; although I believe above all in the individual transformation of each individual, I have nothing against philosophizing on a societal level as well.

– Dominic; co-author of Talks on Anarchy; co-author of Anarchoreading; libertarian; anarchist; (Austrian) economist

title: Urza at the Freeport House on Living Anarchy, July 2026
text:
My second talk at the 2026 Freeport House Summer Residency was on living anarchy; at first it looked like there wouldn't be that much interest in it, but over time dozens of people arrived who interestingly asked a lot of questions more or less connected to anarchy.
I tried to present to the audience the idea that freedom cannot be established; if we want to have it, we have to start living it in our own lives. One must focus on the inner world, not just the outer world; too much focus on the outside world (even to achieve freedom), in my opinion, even actively harms our goal, which can be solved by self-development.

title: Urza in the House of the Freeport on the edge of self-governance, July 2026
text:
My first talk at the Summer Residence at the Freeport House 2026 was about the edge of self-management; the turnout was huge again, which makes me happy. I think that every such action brings us all at least a little closer to freedom.
We have addressed the edge of self-management; what is the difference between children to whom parents leave 100% self-control, and between their peers to whom parents give some restraints, even though they may be really close to self-control? I personally observe a really big difference; including their relationship with their parents. We also discussed how to get as close as possible to the ideal of full self-management.

title: Students For Liberty: Nonviolent Communication and Anarchism
text:
Teodor Kuběna from SFL came up with an interesting idea - the connection of anarchism (and the principle of non-aggression) with non-violent (and non-aggressive) communication; that's why he opened a dialogue with Petr Sucháček and me.
Nonviolent Communication changed my life; and so I was very happy to talk about it with someone who deals with it professionally. I think we ended up dealing with it more than anarchy; but that didn't bother me at all (we also honed in on education).

– Petr Sucháček; educationalist; theoretician, practitioner and lecturer of nonviolent communication; mediator; co-author of the Nonviolent Podcast; popularizer of science
– Teodor Kuběna; libertarian; national coordinator of Students for Liberty

title: Free Port Studio: Shaking Ankara, or how to destroy CT and the freedom of children
text:
Although I announced a holiday break in the last video, the current political situation made it impossible for me not to comment on the attacks against freedom organized by the current government; and during the filming of the video I was reminded a lot that everything bad is good for something.
Since the beginning of this government's mandate, it seems to me that the most visible political affair is typically some kind of nonsense (Turk's alleged hazing or Pavel in Ankara); the effort to concentrate power (cancellation of concessionaire fees) or money (Šebestyán as Minister of Agriculture) and especially a direct attack on freedom (banning phones in schools) thus receives less attention than it could.

title: Studio Freeport: Holidays 2026, info about the book and what's next?
text:
Another (perhaps the most productive) season of the Freeport is coming to an end; during the holidays, our traffic will be a little smaller again, as viewership and readership decrease in the summer, I would also like to finish the rest of the last months, but above all, I really need to rest, catch up and get back to normal.
I made this video to say goodbye to you for two months; but also in order to bring you closer to what we are doing now, what we are planning, where the Free Port will go. Last but not least, in the video you will learn current information about the publication of the book Anarchoagorism; also a (possible) topic of the next Conference.

title: Urza about #disobedience for Maxim (Info.cz)
text:
Pavel Vondráček invited me for an interview after the #no_disobedience event; and I was very pleased that he actually found it mild to boring - not that I want to be boring, but the more people my actions don't disturb, the more freely we can live.

– Pavel Vondráček; journalist; publicist; chief editor of Info.cz; editor-in-chief Maxim; traveller

title: Studio of the Free Port: About (the beginning of) governance with Libor Vondráček
text:
The chairman of Svobodný, Libor Vondráček, made it not only to the parliament, but also to the government on the SPD candidate; despite this, he is willing to go to the Freeport Studio and talk about the pros and cons of this government commitment to freedom.
We began with the achievements of the person in parliament and in government; we continued with the price he had to pay for it. Judge for yourself whether this makes sense from the point of view of freedom; for me personally, this is a demonstration of why the political path does not work, even if someone really tries.

– Libor Vondráček; Chairman of the Free Citizens Party; (government) MP elected for the SPD

title: Home seminar (not only) about crypto and abortions
text:
More and more schoolchildren are watching Freeport; and some sometimes try to invite me to school. In the long term, it blocks leadership in about two-thirds of the cases (even more often since the #no_disobedience era - in fact, always so far); however, students don't give up and come up with other ways, such as an apartment seminar.
This time we mainly dealt with cryptocurrencies, but we also got to abortion and other topics; I liked the inquisitiveness of everyone involved (and quite a few came), thanks to which everything took place in a very creative and friendly atmosphere. I consider the time spent in this way to be very effective for freedom.

title: Freeport Studio: Commentary on You have a word about economic fallacies
text:
At your instigation, I have commented several Pros and Cons; I found that I enjoy it, moreover, your responses are very positive, so I decided to continue in this format - this time I chose You have a word, and even two (representative) parts, both of which dealt with the economy and pricing, respectively.
I think that in this piece I clearly show how the so-called "public service" media fails - for the sake of a good "show", logic, economics, facts and the law of providing objective, verified, balanced information in its entirety are set aside for the free formation of opinions; unfortunately this leads to unfreedom...

title: Urza about peaceful (crypto)anarchy for CryptoByte
text:
The invitation to the next year of the Liberec CryptoByte conference made me very happy again; again this year, I chose a rather non-technical topic (by local standards), but one that I consider very important and relatively current for the crypto community (unfortunately, it seems to me that it has been the case for at least several years).
I was talking about love and a peaceful approach (not only) to the spread of (crypto)anarchy; I explained why (non-dogmatic) dialogue is important for freedom and why, for example, the quarrels between Bitcoin maximalists and crypto-enthusiasts are, in my opinion, harmful to freedom (especially in the long term).

title: Digital (non)dependence in Erazim in Pilsen
text:
Nowadays, a very popular topic - children and technology - resonates with Pilsen Erazim; at almost every self-governing school it comes to the table sooner or later. The Erazims decided to invite me to a meeting to share my experiences and opinions; and I'm very glad we had a good chat.
In addition to the topic itself, we also got to a more general fear behind the idea of limiting technology to children; I believe that bans on technology and anything else are related - and the talk does a great job of showing how they are connected and that it's actually the same principle applied to something else.

title: Freeport Studio: AI (and regulation) with Karolína K.
text:
Karolína reached out to me wanting to discuss potential AI regulations; or will it work without them? Is AI really a threat? Or, on the contrary, a functional helper? Or both? What about that? Will the states help this time? Or rather damage as usual?
In the Freeport Studio, we will address AI from the point of view of freedom; big topics (especially threats) tend to be used for centralization, which of course also interests Karolína, balancing on the border between statism and anarchism (ever closer to the latter).

– Karolína Kváš (https://karolinakvas.cz/); tarot rebel; authoress; traveler; anthropologist; blogger; creator; coach

title: Freeport Studio: Commentary on the Pros and Cons of Mr. Nobody vs. Putin
text:
I guess I'm getting quite amused by the reactions to the shows (especially from the public media); moreover, you talk about them and I get a lot of positive feedback about them, so I will probably make more and more of them. This time I decided to comment on the Pros and Cons part about the movie Mr. Nobody against Putin.
In the framework of this piece, I am not criticizing the Czech Republic in any way; however, from my point of view, I was fascinated by Adam Sybera's fanatically anti-Russian narrative - I find his commentary on the (in my opinion, excellent) film very hateful, so I decided to create a certain counterbalance (although his debate opponent, Petra Procházková, performed this role no less well).

title: Anarcho-Capitalism: The Different Faces of Anarchy
text:
The May lecture from the Anarchocapitalism cycle will actually be more of a dialogue between two people than a lecture. You may know Matěj Krejčiřík from the "Free Harbor Conference 2026: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow", who introduced collectivist anarchism; this happened as part of one (probably unsuccessful so far) attempt to connect the Czech individualist and collectivist anarchist scenes. I have carried this idea with me for a long time, but every time I tried to implement it, it failed; the collective from AC254 is doing significantly better, although our attempts to find a common language cost both sides a lot of energy, but we continue. We would like to conduct some of our dialogue publicly; because we are trying to find out the differences between the way of looking at the world, which we can certainly also help - both with our questions and with the effort to understand.
Presentation: https://prednasky.urza.cz/ll/

title: Studio of the Free Port: About real politics with Robin Čumpelík
text:
Robin Čumpelík invited me to his podcast Innovations of the Republic, where we talked after the recording - he told me about his experiences in state administration and real politics; and it seemed like a very good topic for conversation.

I consider this – unfortunately neglected – topic to be very essential for understanding the functioning of the world around us; practically all people communicate with each other using prices, but the vast majority of them do not understand and do not understand this system at all - which is fine until they start trying to regulate it.

title: Anarcho-capitalism: Your topics (primarily NAP and animals) or questions and my answers

However, these won't typically be quick questions and answers, rather dialogues on request; you can bring topics for contributions to the book or through the Slido app, making sure that it's not just the loudest people who speak. Whoever comes up with it will have the primary opportunity to talk to me about the chosen topic; if it is not comfortable for the person concerned, he can choose any representative, or express a wish that only I myself comment on the issue. Changes or refinements to these rules can be agreed together on the spot, or even in advance; I will be glad for any comments. Given the nature of the event, I think it's likely that it could stretch into the late hours of the night; I hope we have an enjoyable and rewarding time together for all of us. Thank you!

title: Anarcho-Capitalism: Three Economies for Rothbard
text:
The March lecture in the Anarcho-Capitalism series will take place two days after the one hundredth birthday of the late Murray Newton Rothbard; and that's why I decided to dedicate it to him. Since in February and April I want to focus more on personal freedoms and anarchist ideas, I would like to dedicate March to economics; specifically, we will look at the great contributions of the Austrian school of economics to the whole of economic science - some of these findings form the basis of mainstream knowledge today, while others (although in my opinion also true) do not enjoy such acceptance. In addition to explaining the theory, I also intend to show practical applications of the knowledge of the Austrian economists; they are long dead, sometimes unfortunately even overlooked, but economic science still draws from their knowledge. In the lecture, I will also try to show that their discoveries also affect our everyday lives; and we can improve them through their full understanding and practical application.
Presentation: https://prednasky.urza.cz/ll/

title: Karel Šindelář: Freedom without a center – mind, nature and being (KSP26: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow)
text:
The eighth speaker of the "Freeport Conference 2026: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Karel Šindelář with his lecture "Freedom without a center: mind, nature and being".

Freedom can turn into a distant ideal, that the very idea of "one day I will be free" can create distance, desire, fear and the need for security - that is, mechanisms that paradoxically move us away from freedom. The same can also be a consequence of trying to define freedom firmly: Every definition creates a center, an authority or an arbiter. On the contrary, even one's own mind can be decentralized, similar to society. It is possible to release the inner "central authority" that evaluates, controls and directs. Indeed, the greatest lack of freedom can be rooted in our internal mechanisms of fear rather than in states and institutions. However, one can walk freely even in the midst of restrictions – much like the landscape, which is not the enemy but the environment. The lecture is not meant to bring ready-made answers, but to offer a common space for questioning our certainties, ideas and need for control.

Karel has long been devoted to contemplative practice and the themes of fear, death, love, life and freedom. He has been living a nomadic lifestyle for six years with his wife, three children and a dog. Although this was not always the case, today they do not feel part of any school of thought, ideology, movement or state. More than creating new definitions, he is interested in direct experience and observation - what can actually be experienced, not just named.

title: Milan Mikulecký versus Urza: Democracy or anarchy? (KSP26: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow)
text:
The seventh speaker at the "Free Harbor Conference 2026: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Milan Mikulecký in a debate with Urza on the topic "Democracy or anarchy?".

Democracy represents the status quo – the system we live in whether we like it or not; anarchy, on the other hand, brings the possibility of change, but with the question of whether and for whom such a (non)system would be suitable. Milan Mikulecký debates with Urza about this and other topics.

Security analyst, pilot and one of the founders of the Skupina D association, Milan Mikulecký held a number of managerial positions both in business and in state administration in the Czech Republic (he acted as an advisor to several defense ministers) and abroad. Today, he serves as the Director of European Operations at the American Heritage Museum. He is also a member of the Active Reserves of the Special Forces of the Army of the Czech Republic. In his spare time, he tries to combine his love for flying and historical technology with work in the non-profit sector, and is currently fully involved in two projects: TMFC z.s. and Group D z.s.. He is the author of the Hlas na púšti podcast, which has been published regularly on the Novinky.cz server since 2023.

Urza is an anarchist author; forms the autonomous educational initiative Svobodný přístán and operates in the self-managed Ježek bez klece school. He wrote over a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media and the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism; the first Czech book about anarchoagorism from his pen is already on its way! For over fifteen years, he not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, education, the free market and the role of the state in society, but also lectures, discusses, talks and makes videos; you can find more at https://www.urza.cz/. For him, freedom is a lifelong theme, which he devotes himself to both theoretically and practically – finding ways to live it in the everyday world.

title: Linda Herrmannová: Individualism (KSP26: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow)
text:
The sixth speaker of the "2026 Freeport Conference: Freedom Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Linda with her talk "Individualism".

Individualism is - in a nutshell - the ability to respect all emotions (and the resulting needs and preferences), both your own and those of other people. This is one of the basic building blocks of a satisfied and balanced society. Unfortunately, in today's world there is desperately little room for the expression of emotions - so in this lecture I will try to bring individualism to the awareness of more people. I will break down its principles, what it implies and why it is important to us as humans.

Linda is a graduate of the self-directed Jezek without a cage school. Although she went through six schools in her life, she does not consider her education to be the most important part of her personality. During high school, she started creating content for social networks, the main content of which was ecology, philosophy, art and mental health. After graduation, she also started a business on social networks, but it did not fulfill her in the long term, so she took a different path. Now she supports herself by working in a cafe and in her spare time she devotes herself to self-development, psychology and other social sciences. She works above all to make me happy and feel at peace in myself, which she succeeds in doing for the first time in her life. In the future, she would also like to help other people.

title: Krejča: Anarcho-collectivism or Urzo, dude, be a collectivist (KSP26: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow)
text:
The fifth speaker of the "Freeport Conference 2026: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Matěj Krejčiřík with his lecture "Anarchocollectivism or Urzo, dude, be a collectivist".

The lecture will offer a historical-theoretical excursion into anarchism - from the original anarchism "without adjectives", through its main branches of thought, to agorism as a specific strategy of non-political resistance to the state. Emphasis will be placed on the comparison of anarcho-capitalism and anarcho-collectivism: their ontological starting points, the concept of freedom and the role of the market.

Matěj is an agorist with nearly ten years of continuous practice in the theory and daily functioning of anti-state structures. For eight years, he has been actively involved in building an agorist network of real estate and services, both from the perspective of operators and users. Specifically, he is involved in the Agora protocol project, agorizes farmers, participates in the running of an anarcho pub and helps create a global agorist network of land and relationships aimed at creating parallel economic and social ties with minimal impact of state regulations. He is a doctoral student in information science, where he focuses on the use of decentralized technologies for scientific communication.

title: Urza: Anarchoagorism - A Practical Path to Freedom (KSP26: Freedom Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow)
text:
The fourth speaker of the "2026 Freeport Conference: Freedom Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" was Urza with his lecture "Anarchoagorism: A Practical Path to Freedom".

Libertarians (especially anarcho-capitalists) understand that (and why) central planning doesn't work; however, this often does not prevent them from thinking of freedom as something that can be centrally planned - they desire to live more freely so much that as a result they fall into the same trap as statists, when they are too eager to believe that the answer to their needs can come "from above". However, we cannot talk our way into freedom; nor can it be imposed on anyone who is not interested in it - not only does the end justify the means, but centrally controlled decentralization doesn't even make sense, it's an oxymoron. What about that? The answer comes from anarchoagorism – by creating agoras (islands of freedom based on voluntariness and spontaneous order), disobedient individuals can locally shield the power of external authorities; the goal is not to defeat or dominate the state, but to exist in parallel independently of it.

Urza is an anarchist author; forms the autonomous educational initiative Svobodný přístán and operates in the self-managed Ježek bez klece school. He wrote over a thousand libertarian texts on the web and in print media and the first Czech book on anarcho-capitalism; the first Czech book about anarchoagorism from his pen is already on its way! For over fifteen years, he not only reads, thinks and writes about freedom, education, the free market and the role of the state in society, but also lectures, discusses, talks and makes videos; you can find more at https://www.urza.cz/. For him, freedom is a lifelong theme, which he devotes himself to both theoretically and practically – finding ways to live it in the everyday world.

title: Tomáš Roud: Why is the political path necessary even for anarchists? (KSP26: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow)
text:
The third speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2026: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Tomáš Roud with his lecture "Why is a political path necessary even for anarchists?".

The state eventually comes to everyone – no matter how hard you try to ignore it. If I don't agree with that band of robbers, I can try to lead them and make them not be like that... The political path is not pretty, but it is necessary if I want to really change things around me.

Tomáš has long been committed to a libertarian and voluntarist view of the world. He describes himself as a libertarian, voluntarist, anarchist, bitcoiner, investor and mentor. He is the founder of the Libertarian Party Voluntia and at the same time a monogamous husband and father of four children. For more than 13 years, he has been running stays in the dark near Kutná Hora, where people embark on a journey of deeper self-discovery through the experience of silence and isolation https://lecba-tmou.cz/. He says that freedom can only come about through the voluntary interaction of all involved. He himself is constantly working on deepening voluntary relationships with others.

title: Martin Čaban: Freedom and democracy need each other (KSP26: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow)
text:
The second speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2026: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Martin Čaban with his lecture "Freedom and democracy need each other".

Can there be freedom without democracy? And democracy without freedom? How is democracy related to violence? Does it minimize it? How does one who considers it the best institution see the weaknesses of democracy?

Martin Čaban is a Seznam Zpráv commentator with a focus on politics and economics. He has been following the Czech political scene for more than 20 years, especially with an emphasis on the health sector, but also on budget policy, social issues and, above all, the pension system. He does not avoid looking at party politics and behind-the-scenes political games. For twelve years, he worked in the economic daily E15, where he successively held the positions of editor, commentator and deputy editor-in-chief. For a long time he also contributed to the professional magazine Zdravotnické noviny. Since March 2020, he has been working as a commentator in the editorial office of Seznam Zpráv. He relates to freedom as its everyday, perhaps even undeservedly privileged and grateful user, who is ready to defend it if necessary.

title: Jan "Bluebird" Bumblebee: Murray Newton Rothbard (KSP26: Freedom Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow)
text:
The first speaker of the "Free Harbor Conference 2026: Freedom yesterday, today and tomorrow" was Jan "Blue Bird" Čmolík with his lecture "Murray Newton Rothbard - intellectual background and the concept of the social contract".

The fruits of the work of Murray Newton Rothbard - the "spiritual father" of anarcho-capitalism - we all know and reap to some extent in the Freeport Channel; however, let's also look at its roots and explore the intellectual background from which it originates.

Jan Čmolík works as a self-employed person in the role of interim manager, focusing on the restructuring of commercial companies. In his practice, he focuses on optimizing processes and eliminating redundant or duplicate activities that do not bring added value. He gained experience in a wide range of fields – from the textile, chemical and food industry, to engineering and metallurgy to the field of transport. In addition to his professional activity, he has long been concerned with the relationship between the ideas formulated by the classics of economics and the reality we live in today. He is the author of Economic Irregulars - an abridged history of economic thought, which he published under the pseudonym Blue Bird. He perceives the topic of freedom as key. He himself says that his relationship to freedom is irreconcilably and intolerably positive, because he lived in real socialism until he was 23 years old.

I was very pleased when he accepted my invitation to the livestream in March, where we will discuss how to (not) talk to the cops; we will follow up on the successful November lecture, in which, among other things, there was an inaccuracy, which we will correct.

title: Anarcho-Capitalism: Freedom; self-management; self development; sharing
text:
SEK3 wrote: "Agora, anarchy, action!" It came to me while writing a book on anarchoagorism: "Freedom, self-governance, self-development, sharing!" And when I say that it happened during the writing of the book, I am actually talking about a process that has been going on in me all my life; until now I have managed to describe it in a few words, behind which lies the synthesis of various knowledge and skills that I have learned all my life because they attracted and fascinated me without (on a conscious level) understanding their connections. However, something inside me guided my steps to the point where I was able to see - and subsequently describe - these connections. I would like to share this knowledge at the February lecture from the anarcho-capitalism cycle; I have said enough about the connection between self-governance and freedom, but I would also like to deal with self-development and, last but not least, why reducing the transaction costs of transferring information leads to freedom, which is another reason why it makes more sense for me to seek the truth than to convince people.

text:

title: Anarcho-Capitalism: Hayek's Monetary Economics from the Critique of Price Stabilization to the Denationalization of Money
text:
In December, Štěpán Drábek will speak as part of the Anarchocapitalism series with his lecture; will deal with the contributions of F. A. Hayek, an Austrian philosopher and economist with Moravian roots, to monetary economics. Specifically, he will focus on Hayek's early criticism of the stabilization of the price level (the work Prices and Production), which according to him initiates the economic cycle, and on Hayek's proposal to separate money from the state (the works Denationalisation of Money, Choice in Currency and others). I will also focus on the remarkable development of Hayek's attitude to the possibility of the existence of non-state money over time - from his work The Road to Serfdom, through The Constitution of Liberty to Law, Legislation, and Liberty.
Presentation: https://prednasky.urza.cz/ll/

– Štěpán Drábek; economist; analyst at the Institute of Liberal Studies; libertarian; seeker of truth

title: Freeport Studio: About Ježek, NAP and NEP with Phil from Ježek
text:

We talked a little about the Hedgehog beforehand, but we were constantly drawn to freedom (in a relatively abstract sense); finally, Fil came up with a superstructure of the NAP called the NEP (non-enslavement principle) - we discussed this using examples from the human and animal kingdoms.

– Phil (http://lucidael.com/jazyk-lasky); janitor in Ježek without a cage; anarchist; bitcoiner; libertarian; seeker of truth; lover of life

title: Urza and Teri discuss the prize of the state
text:
Teri wanted to discuss the price of the state lecture with me again; she was interested in certain aspects of it that she wished to discuss specifically (such as pensions or investments). I myself am very happy about it, because in the six months since its preparation, a lot of things have come to light in different ways.
I consider the most fundamental finding that, with the greatest probability, it costs us (although it cannot be calculated exactly) up to 90% (or maybe even more) of what we produce; not that he's taking it all from us - much of it will disappear in state-induced regulatory inefficiency.

– Teri the Idealist; anarcho-capitalist; author of the podcast "And who would build roads?"

title: Freeport Studio: About self-management at camp with Aslanexe
text:
A supporter of the Free Port, Aslanex, told me that he would like to discuss self-management in the Studio in groups that are not together for a long time (such as in Ježek without a cage), but only for a short time (for example, at a camp that lasts a few weeks at most).
We discussed the limits of voluntariness; and I liked Aslanex's openness - it made us run into the classic problems that many (potentially) self-directed collectives face in their early days. Hopefully someone will take something from our dialogue...

– Aslanex; supporter of the Free Port; leader and organizer of (over time possibly self-managed) children's camps

title: Urza in Talks of Anarchy: On (dis)obedience
text:
Lukáš Pazderník is a long-term supporter (and occasional author and commentator) of the Free Port; I like his way of thinking and I enjoy our discussions - so I happily accepted the invitation to Anarchy Talks again - this time in person.
The topic was – perhaps quite unsurprisingly – (dis)obedience; however, we didn't just talk about #disobedience actions, but in general about how to work with yourself. I think that on this topic it is becoming increasingly clear how freedom and anarchy are connected to self-development.

– Lukáš Pazderník; anarchist; volunteer; philosopher; supporter (and occasional author and commentator) of Freeport

title: Studio Freeport: About politics (and Voluntia) with Matěj Kotulán
text:
Matěj Kotulán approached me after one lecture and started talking about his (lifelong) disillusionment with politics; he is currently a member of Voluntia, but he has been trying to be politically active all his life (since elementary school) (in student governments, parliaments, etc.).
I see his disillusionment as an (empirical) confirmation of anarcho-agorist theories; even so, Matěj continues to follow his political path, which I do not fully understand, but in my own way I recognize it and definitely respect it. I like to have a dialogue about these topics and discover other corners of the political path.

– Matej Kotulán; gay politician; member of the Voluntia; libertarian

title: A talk on anarchoagorism for the Philosophical Circle at ZČU
text:
This is the second time I have come to speak at the Philosophical Circle of the University of West Bohemia in Pilsen; not only because I always like to revisit the city where I spent the first eighteen years of my life, but above all because the students were interested in anarchoagorism, which I have been intensively studying lately.
Many people came to the discussion, including the well-known Objectivist Jiří Kinkor; the topics were diverse - at first we dealt with rather practical things such as insurance for old age, over time we gradually began to focus on philosophical questions regarding freedom and, above all, what we can do for it.

title: Freeport Studio: How (not) to use artificial intelligence?
text:
Artificial intelligence is an amazing tool of recent times; I solve a number of problems myself with her help - not only did she save me hundreds of hours of time, but she probably also improved the quality of my outputs to a large extent. Having worked with AI as a programmer before "it was cool", I acknowledge its boom in recent years with gratitude.
Unfortunately, it also comes with a lot of people who don't know much about this tool, but are not reluctant to use it and rely on its results; and since I observe this phenomenon around me more and more often, I decided to make a video in which I analyze some unfortunate (but actually also happy) uses of AI.

title: Tim and Urza celebrate November 17
text:
On November 17, Czech citizens celebrate the holiday of democracy; so Tim and I joined, even though we're not exactly Democrats. I took on a couple of signs and we threw ourselves into the maelstrom of the big city; the goal was to conduct a dialogue about freedom, democracy, the state, anarchy and other topics.
Despite our differences of opinion, we did not encounter expressions of hatred or intolerance; on the contrary, we managed to strike up a lot of peaceful conversations with passers-by, whether they agreed with us or not. I hope you enjoy them as much as we do!

– Timofey Kozhuchov; libertarian; maybe a little anarcho-capitalist; youtuber; student of political science and philosophy; LGBT activist

title: Freeport Studio: Christmas Talk 2025
text:
I was alone at this year's Christmas talk; and I decided to treat it differently than usual - I left out Czech and world (political) events, about which I already said a lot in the moments when they were happening, but I don't want to draw attention to them again. Do you miss it? If so, write in the comments, they can be in a year.
Throughout the video I talked about the Freeport, its projects - both past and future, successful and less successful; I also outlined what awaits us (not only) in the next year. Of course, there were also Christmas wishes for you and thanks for everything you do for the Port (and there's not a lot).

We started the conversation with the benefits and threats of artificial intelligence; and we moved pretty quickly to funding science. Although Tomáš Mikolov understands the harmfulness of subsidies (especially in agriculture), he finds them beneficial (or perhaps necessary) in certain fields.
