Indeed, it is remarkable that although practically everyone is willing to agree with more or less all the statements found in this text, almost no one is able to see the consequences resulting from them; we will deal with them in the next chapter, within which we will refer to this one.

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: Perhaps everyone knows by now that socialist central planning is failing; you don't have to look far for examples from history. Now, dear readers, please stop for a moment, think, and answer in your mind the question why this is so. How would you describe it in one sentence? If your answer is that everything was owned by the state, so no one had an incentive to look after it as their own, plus everyone stole everything, this chapter will probably give you a new perspective.

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: This - probably the most common - answer is true, but it does not describe the biggest problem of central planning. Motivating managers of state-owned enterprises to make the same effort as managers of private enterprises is not an insurmountable problem. The theft of property cannot be completely eliminated, but it can be limited by various measures. Because the problems of motivation and theft are often seen as practically the only ones, many people still advocate partial central planning. However, central planners encounter another – much more serious – snag, which, although not so notorious, is practically (and theoretically) unsolvable.

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: In the last chapter, we described how the invisible hand of the market guides people to properly allocate scarce resources: When something is expensive, the market, through price information, will limit the use of that resource; and vice versa. Indeed, market prices express the relative scarcity of resources, thereby effectively coordinating human activity. In socialism, market prices do not exist, there they are replaced by prices set by the government, which have nothing to do with the scarcity of resources (the consequence is the chronic shortage of some - and surpluses of other - goods, known to many). My favorite author and thinker Murray Newton Rothbard brilliantly described this phenomenon in his book "Power and Market" (or "Man, Economy and State"), or the great economist Ludwig von Mises in his famous book "Bureaucracy". For central planners (even democratic ones), this phenomenon results in several fatal problems, which we will discuss in turn.

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: The first problem is the need for constant monitoring of possible resource shortages. A central planner would have to be aware of the potential deficiencies of hundreds and thousands of different resources; and not only with the fact that something is happening, but also with how much and how fast it is happening. In a free market economy, all these questions are automatically answered by the price system - there is no need to pay anyone for it, everyone does their small part of this work only as part of the effort to achieve the highest possible benefit.

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: The second problem is that even if the central planner gets all this information, it has to choose a solution. Even on a very general level, there are several of them: invest in making that resource easier to obtain, import from a greater distance, use a substitute, raise the price. These solutions can be combined, and each of them has countless ways of execution. Free market entrepreneurs each try what they think is best; some of them will do well and become rich, others will choose poorly and go bankrupt. Even if we completely ignore motivation (when an entrepreneur makes a mistake, he loses a lot - unlike a politician) and expertise (businessmen often - unlike politicians - understand their fields), the biggest difference is that when many entrepreneurs try many solutions, they will take the ones that people appreciate the most (and the losses for bad solutions are borne by their authors), but the central planners will simply try to solve the problem somehow, and it is not even clear how to know whether the solution is good, because there are no other realized alternatives to compare (and if the solution is bad, the costs are borne by the subjects).

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: The third problem is the wishes and demands of consumers. The price system conveys this information to entrepreneurs on the free market. The central planner must spend resources (who pays the cost, the reader will surely guess) to find out the same information, and what it finds out will always be biased; if some central planner had done a survey in 1975 on how many people wanted/needed a computer at home, they would have found that practically no one (considering that no one - not even those who invented and manufactured computers - could imagine their use back then), so there is no need to spend any precious resources in this direction.

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: The fourth problem is that even if the central planner somehow magically got information from people about what services or products they actually want, it has no way of finding out the ratio in which these goods are in demand: "Mr. Novák, would you rather have an ambulance travel time of 4 minutes, half a kilo of beef a week, a new subway line and go to the movies once every two weeks, or would you rather have an ambulance travel time of 7 minutes, a kilo of beef a week, a repaired highway and go to the theatres?' When we imagine the immense number of properties that Mr. Novák is asking for, and the countless combinations in which he can ask for them, we realize that it is simply impossible to compile such a list realistically. And now let's look at the absurd role of the central planner, who theoretically should find this out not only from Mr. Novák, but from millions of citizens! Even if he could somehow magically do it, it is only the beginning - he would have to somehow find the optimal result based on the demands of all his subjects. To do it really as well as entrepreneurs in the free market, he would have to deal with questions like: "Is Mr. Procházka's request for a tourist trail around Prague or Mrs. Vodičková's request for a swimming pool in Pilsen more beneficial for society?" To answer each such question, he would have to solve a lot of sub-questions such as: "Does Mr. Procházka's vote have the same weight as Mrs. Vodičková's? And does Mr. Procházka want the hiking trail as much as Mrs. Vodičková wants the swimming pool, or does one of them want more?" Let us realize the astronomical number of combinations of all relevant persons and wishes that must be compared; at the same time, neither one is easily solvable, because it is impossible to reliably compare the preferences of two different people other than to let them show themselves how much they are willing to sacrifice time and effort for the fulfillment of their wishes. But, as we have already shown, the best universal means of general expression of time and effort is money, and the only way of arranging things according to individual people's preferences remains to let these people freely choose and buy what they think best.

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: Unfortunately, central planning is not just what some of us had the opportunity to see during totalitarianism. Partial central planning is attempted by every state; some more, some less. It must be remembered that every regulation, every state enterprise, every "consumer protection" law and even every tax are all elements of central planning that run into the above problems.

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: If the entire market is in the hands of the state, citizens live in poverty and scarcity (take the USSR as an example). When the state frees up a part of the market for free entrepreneurs, it starts working like a magic wand in the image of consumers (for example, a part of the current market that the state regulates relatively little: IT, hospitality, tourism, retail and others). On the contrary, the part of the market that the state has kept works desperately (education, social system, healthcare, judiciary and so on).

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: Let's imagine that we have two ways to control the course of events: First we will control everything in one way, nothing will work, so we will try to do maybe half of the things in another way - and they will suddenly start working, while the other half still does not work. Who, other than a complete fool, would not try to manage everything the other way in such a situation? Nevertheless, we foolishly believe that the state simply has to do some things. Why? Because that's what they tell us in (state) school and what (state) politicians tell us. During totalitarianism, we became convinced that the state was desperately unable to handle the production and import of food (a shortage of meat, queues for bananas), the production of cars (car directories), the production and sale of drugstore goods (a shortage of pads, toilet paper) and electronics (television directories, refrigerators), which the free market can handle with ease and without problems. On the other hand, we foolishly believe that, for example, education and healthcare in the hands of the state is the right choice (although we see sad results). We assume that an institution incapable of solving problems as utterly trivial as the supply of toilet paper will somehow be successful at something as incredibly complicated as educating our children.

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: There will probably be more reasons for such an absurd belief. I consider propaganda, which is served to us since primary school, to be the most fundamental. In the second place, however, I see the fact that even today we have some "private" entities that do not work very well in some markets overregulated by the state; definitely no better than the state ones (especially private schools or hospitals). It is then easy to point to them and say, "Look, a private institution doesn't work any better than a public one."

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: The careful reader will surely understand by now why this argument is flawed. Such private institutions, which do have a private owner, but otherwise have to do practically everything the way the state wants, do not have much in common with the free market - that is, it solves the (small) problem with motivation, but it does not solve any of the (big) problems mentioned in this chapter (when the state says how private companies must work, the moment when many of them try it in various ways and those who did it right will stick). Competition issues notwithstanding; in the last chapter we explained that those who do it badly go bankrupt, which means that those who do it well take over their clients - but the state does not get money from customers paying it voluntarily, it collects it through taxes, ergo state institutions can waste scarce resources as much as they like, but they still do not go bankrupt (and when they expand throughout the market, those who do better go bankrupt instead). Finally, the state imposes high barriers to entry in similar markets, thereby artificially reducing competition and harming consumers.

title: 2. Why does central planning fail?
text: Thus, the free market is more efficient than central planning; which cannot be avoided by the state increasing the motivation of managers or reducing corruption and embezzlement, because the fundamental problem lies in something else entirely. Let's note that this applies in general - to all fields of human activity. There is no reason why some should be an exception; however, many think otherwise, so we will discuss these individual areas in the coming chapters.

section: Nemožnost ekonomické kalkulace v centrálním plánování
title: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text: The phenomenon dealt with in the second chapter is called "the impossibility of economic calculation in central planning". Since this is one of the most fundamental things on which many theses throughout the book are based, I decided to expand this chapter somewhat. A deep understanding of this topic is probably necessary to fully understand the rest of the book.

section: Nemožnost ekonomické kalkulace v centrálním plánování
title: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text: Let us imagine a centrally planned society and its government, which may be formed by an individual, or even by a group; unless this society is at a completely primitive level of technological development, it cannot be considered realistic that these rulers understand all the fields of human activity that their subjects engage in. They must therefore necessarily create a hierarchical structure of individuals, which can be imagined as a pyramid, the foundations of which are made up of, for example, workers, above whom are their superiors, and above them, in turn, their superiors; and so on up to the government, which is at the very top.

section: Nemožnost ekonomické kalkulace v centrálním plánování
title: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text: To show that the problem of central planning of society is absolutely fatal even under absolutely ideal (unattainable) conditions, let us assume for all the reasoning in this chapter that all members of a given society are unreservedly honest, put the welfare of the whole above their own welfare at all times, never steal, and have nothing at heart but the building of a better tomorrow, for which they will toil from dawn to dusk. Very often one can come across the opinion that central planning does not work precisely because people do not have the above-mentioned characteristics; however, I intend to prove that even if they had, central planning would still remain a woefully inefficient way of running society.

section: Nemožnost ekonomické kalkulace v centrálním plánování
title: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text: Of all the thousands and millions of resources that need to be coordinated and distributed, we will focus on just one: titanium. The applications for this silvery white metal are – thanks to its remarkable properties – many. Leaving aside that it is used to build the casings of space probes, satellites and stations, which we will not deal with here, there are enough other uses left, of which we will focus only on the production of ship propellers and chemical reactors; suppose there are some shipyards and a highly developed chemical industry in our centrally controlled country.

section: Nemožnost ekonomické kalkulace v centrálním plánování
title: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text: In accordance with the initial assumptions, let's assume that all relevant positions are staffed by top professionals whose goal is nothing other than the welfare of society. The chemist knows exactly and can describe the advantages and disadvantages of a titanium reactor compared to another. The boat designer, on the other hand, understands and can explain all the pros and cons of titanium boat screws. Both will communicate these conclusions to their superiors, who will understand them in everything, as they are also experts taken at their word. So they calculate how much titanium they need for their entire industry and apply for it. However, let's assume that the metal is in short supply, so a wise central planner summons everyone who requests titanium, as well as the person responsible for its production (in the real world, of course, this will work completely differently, but here for simplicity we assume ideal conditions free of cronyism, ignorance and the like).

section: Nemožnost ekonomické kalkulace v centrálním plánování
title: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text: How will such negotiations take place? We must not forget that this is a centrally planned society in which there are no market prices. So everyone gets together, the applicants explain why they need titanium; the person responsible for its production will tell you what resources are needed to make more titanium. The central planner must now make a decision; but how? What factors should it even include? If it was clear how many chemical reactors and ship propellers "are needed", he could at least investigate where it is less expensive to use a substitute. But the "need" depends on, among other things, how costly the resulting solution will be; the more complicated the construction of the ship, the more it pays to have fewer of them and use other means of transport (not to mention that the wishes of millions of consumers come into play here, who sometimes don't even know what they want until they try it). It is also possible to increase production, which of course costs other resources, but of course there are many other uses for them; one problem leads to another. And this is just the beginning, because titanium itself can still be used, for example, in the health sector, the aviation industry, some people want to make watches out of it, and so on; above all, it is necessary to make similar decisions not only for one metal, but for each of the countless sources.

section: Nemožnost ekonomické kalkulace v centrálním plánování
title: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text: One might argue that a central planner can solve the whole problem by setting the prices of individual goods. However, prices are the result of market processes; then they express the scarcity of resources and human preferences. If one establishes them arbitrarily, one does not avoid the above problem, it only shifts it elsewhere; in fact, he will face questions similar to those from the previous paragraph in the framework of price creation, since in this process he still has to compare the relative rarity of all goods (and confront this with the demand of buyers). Another major problem with arbitrary pricing is that the state of the world is ever-changing and the pricing process should be inherently dynamic and never-ending.

section: Nemožnost ekonomické kalkulace v centrálním plánování
title: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text: The market, on the other hand, can solve these problems arbitrarily, since the prices are created by the trading individuals themselves in an effort to maximize their profits; the whole process is very robust, reacts to changes over time, reflects the preferences of all participants in the market process and the scarcity of resources. All the decisions described above are not made by any central authority, but by all buyers, sellers, producers, consumers, employees and employers. If the free market is not distorted in any way (for example, by state interventions), then maximizing the profit of each individual is equivalent to maximizing his contribution to society (because on the one hand, providing the most requested services means the highest income, and on the other hand, reducing costs means saving scarce resources that can then be used by others).

section: Nemožnost ekonomické kalkulace v centrálním plánování
title: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text: It is often objected that giant corporations are also centrally planned, which should be proof that a centrally planned society could function in the same way. The difference, however, is that even a very large corporation can orient itself in the market environment with the help of prices. It can be divided internally into individual divisions and departments so that the results of their activities can be converted into money, which can serve as a key to the distribution of scarce resources. If the economy as a whole is centrally planned, then it has no such possibility, because market prices arise only and only through the unregulated interaction of free (ie not centrally controlled) individuals. The above-mentioned corporation thus orients itself with the help of prices from the outside; however, if the entire company is centrally controlled, it loses this option (or it can be guided by foreign prices, which will probably be better than nothing, but definitely grossly inefficient). However, if a private entity were to grow up in a territory of the size of a state and become a dominant player in so many areas, it would begin to face the same problems; but crucially, as long as people can refuse its services, it can go bankrupt, giving way to more efficient competitors. This will hardly happen in the case of the state, as taxpayers do not have much of a choice.

section: Nemožnost ekonomické kalkulace v centrálním plánování
title: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text: The vast majority of states are, of course, governed by some combination or compromise between the free market and central planning; however, it is important to realize that the above conclusions apply to every field of human activity, so that when the state usurps an industry, it necessarily introduces inefficiency into it. Therefore, the larger part of the market the state controls or regulates, the more centrally unsolvable problems discussed in this chapter will manifest themselves.

section: Nemožnost ekonomické kalkulace v centrálním plánování
title: Impossibility of economic calculation in central planning
text: In conclusion, I would like to point out that the search for all sorts of compromises of the free market and central planning only leads to the fact that the more deviations from the undistorted market there are, the more noticeably the efficiency of the given society as a whole decreases. And if we ask the government for help because of this, we will get lost in a vicious circle: The worse it is, the more intensively we call for state interventions, which, however, cause further deterioration of the situation.

title: The problem of economic calculation through the eyes of an individual
text: Since I definitely refer to the second chapter most often in this book, I believe that the given topic deserves one more expansion, because it is really absolutely essential. So far we have looked at the problem of economic calculation only from the point of view of the central planner; however, I would like to show how the consequences of the impossibility of economic calculation in central planning look like from the perspective of his subjects.

title: The problem of economic calculation through the eyes of an individual
text: The key is to realize that each individual has limited resources that they use to meet their needs. These needs can be completely arbitrary - material, spiritual, hedonistic, ascetic; in any case, the priority of these needs is always best known to the person concerned. No one can, in general, decide for another what will make him happy, more thoroughly than he himself. Of course, it can sometimes happen that an individual chooses the wrong means to satisfy his needs, so that the result will not correspond to what he originally intended. Just as it is possible that someone else could choose the appropriate means to achieve the same goal. Unfortunately, however, we can never say it with certainty in advance, and even retrospectively it can only be evaluated on the assumption that we know the actual (not only declared or estimated) goals of the person in question, which in principle we never know with certainty.

title: The problem of economic calculation through the eyes of an individual
text: Therefore, the absolutely essential knowledge is that no one can generally make decisions for another as well as if he were to do it himself; and while it may occasionally work out for a decision, there is no way anyone can know beforehand, and certainly not afterwards, so it's always a game of hidden cards. The principles briefly discussed in this chapter are the measure of the life's work of the great economist Ludwig von Mises; his book is called "Human Action" and belongs to the basic works of economic theory, because the ideas contained in it are necessary for a real understanding of economics as a science and not only as a field based on what is just modern and desirable for the current social and political demand.

title: The problem of economic calculation through the eyes of an individual
text: Each of us will therefore, from the resources available to him, satisfy those needs which appear to him to be the most urgent; this is always the case without exception, no model of a perfectly rational and informed individual is needed. In practice, this means that we take our resources and our time and do with them as we see fit; we'll buy what we think is best, we'll do what we think is best to achieve our goals (yes, even a junkie who goes to hit another high does what he thinks is the best means to his goals; and none of us can say for sure that it's wrong, because we don't know what the junkie's goals are, and even if we did know, it's not up to us to evaluate them in any way or consider them objectively inferior to ours).

title: The problem of economic calculation through the eyes of an individual
text: However, what happens when someone (and it's usually the state) takes part of an individual's resources and uses them as someone else sees fit? In the ideal and very unlikely case, it will hit exactly what the person wants to buy anyway, thereby not harming him, but not helping him either. In other cases, he gets something for his money that he would rather buy something else instead, if left to his choice. This is exactly how taxes work.

title: The problem of economic calculation through the eyes of an individual
text: Regulations have an effect very similar to taxes. Their purpose is supposedly to "help ordinary people" by limiting someone's choice somewhere. But the truth is that when all impacts are included, regulations will at best help some group of people at the expense of others; in a typical case, they harm the group they are supposed to favor, or you can even find one that harms practically everyone. The classic and probably the most common example of regulations that are supposed to "help the poor" are all kinds of quality control of goods, which are supposed to protect poor customers so that merchants do not sell them "scum". Even if such a regulation really fulfilled its purpose without other side effects (which is rarely possible) and simply cleared the market of low-quality products, it will certainly not reduce the price of quality goods (on the contrary, it will quite possibly increase it, because those who bought lower-quality products are now forced to buy better ones, so the demand will rise and with it the price), so the poor who were supposed to be helped, because they were only deprived of the opportunity to buy low-quality goods cheaply, so often they can't afford anything at all instead of "scum". Some may argue that this situation "forces" them to wait and buy something better later instead of buying lower quality items, but this brings us exactly to what was stated at the beginning: No one can decide for these individuals better than themselves whether it is better for them to have nothing first, so that they can then buy something of better quality, rather than having at least a lower quality item all the time (with all the resulting disadvantages).

title: The problem of economic calculation through the eyes of an individual
text: Another objection to central planning (and thus to the free market) tends to be the redistribution of wealth; that some services are supposed to be paid by the rich to the poor. This, on the one hand, does not change anything at all about the above, i.e. that it would be much better for the poor if the rich gave them this money directly and they chose what to buy with it, rather than someone else deciding it (if we even admit some immoral and disgusting compulsory redistribution); but especially the whole forced redistribution thing doesn't make much sense, since wealth is a free market measure of how much a person has done for others according to their own rankings of values. Directive redistribution (and any violent distortion of the market, i.e. not only the state, although it is by far the most common) then favors individuals less beneficial to others at the expense of those more useful.

title: The problem of economic calculation through the eyes of an individual
text: In conclusion, I would like to emphasize again that an understanding of the second chapter and its subchapters is key to understanding most of the economic arguments contained in this book. A detailed and comprehensible explanation of the phenomenon discussed here is offered in particular by the book "Bureaucracy" by Ludwig von Mises; if you don't want to read the whole book, I can recommend a different view of the matter in the very high-quality article "Neglected economic calculation" by Petr Málek, one of the founders of the Ludwig von Mises Institute (the text is freely available on the Internet). As a test of understanding of the given issue, each reader can try to refute for himself the favorite argument of statists (supporters of the state): "If the state did not pay for this or that, people would not voluntarily give money for it." Why can this sentence never be a valid argument for the preservation of the state? Although this question will be answered in one of the final chapters of this book, I sincerely hope that everyone will find it for themselves before reading the answer.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: In the previous two chapters, we have shown why the free market is generally better than state central planning in meeting human needs. Many people are willing to agree with this, but they argue that the free market economy is efficient but heartless, amoral, unethical and unfair. Is that really the case? Does a really big state mean less efficiency, but more justice? Let's break down and answer these questions.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: Every human society in history recognized some set of rules that determined what was right and what was wrong. We call such a list of rules (laws) law. There are countless different laws: common law, currently valid laws of the Czech Republic, the codex of King Hammurapi or perhaps the code of the Third Reich. However, if something is legalized by law, it does not have to be moral and right - even if one considers the laws of the Third Reich to be ethical, it is easy to see that different concepts of rights, the meaning of which contradict each other on fundamental moral issues, cannot be right at the same time.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: What should "correct law" look like? A tough question. So I will try to summarize at least some minimum, which I assume most people will not have any fundamental objections to:

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: • No one should have the right to initiate violence against others.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: • Everyone should have the right not to be robbed by others.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: • The law should apply equally to everyone.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: • The law should be clear and understandable; After all, if everyone is to live according to it, they should understand it and carry it in their heads. The absurd thing is that, although most people probably agree on this minimum, not a single one meets our right from the above points.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: The first point can be crossed by the police. For example, it has the right in some cases to forcibly seize the cars of drivers who are not involved, or – even worse – to use these innocent drivers against their will in their cars as roadblocks and human shields (relatively well-known cases took place in May 2011 in Legerova Street in Prague or in March 2013 on the D1 highway). Less obvious - but much more frequent - violations of this rule are demonstrated by the police during house searches, taking suspects into custody, and the like. Whenever an innocent person refuses any of the above, the police may use violence against him.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: The second point is violated by taxes, which are nothing more than robbery legalized by law. The state says: "Subject, give me the money, if you deal with evil, and we will take even more by force." It is basically the same as a robber saying to us, "Money or life!" The only difference is that the state will give us some counter-service for this money, the robber typically will not. On the other hand, it is difficult for a robber to take so much from us (and so often), but especially even if he buys something from us with the stolen money, it does not change the robbery and he does not stop being a robber because of it.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: The third point is most obviously not fulfilled by the politicians with their parliamentary and other immunities, with which they tell us "out of the blue" that we are not equal before the law. Furthermore, different laws apply to police officers on duty (and other public officials) than to ordinary citizens.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: The fourth point is particularly interesting in combination with the fact that ignorance of the law is no excuse. When even lawyers are routinely represented by specialized colleagues in their disputes that do not concern their specialization, there is probably no one in our country who knows all the rules perfectly. Isn't having to live by a thousand rules that virtually no one understands something that could be written about in a comedy that would be seriously hilarious if it weren't our reality?

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: The overwhelming majority of the legislators of almost all contemporary and historical states could be subjected to similar criticism. This is not a coincidence. On the one hand, the very existence of the state in principle contradicts equality before the law (different rules must apply to state representatives than to subjects), and on the other hand, the state must rob (collect taxes) in order to earn its existence.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: One of the few concepts of law that meets these (and many other) requirements, and at the same time probably the only one that respects private property and according to which some human communities have long-term framework functions in history, is called natural law. Throughout history, many philosophers have touched upon various areas of natural law in their works: in antiquity, for example, Heraclitus or Aristotle, whose works in the Middle Ages were the basis of Thomas Aquinas, and modern thinkers such as John Locke; it was most comprehensively and, in my opinion, best described by my favorite author and thinker Murray Newton Rothbard in his book "The Ethics of Liberty" and partially also in the manifesto "For a New Liberty", where he formulated natural law as the so-called principle of non-aggression, which is then written about in detail by contemporary authors such as Walter Block or Hans-Hermann Hoppe, while such Clint Eastwood summed up the principle of non-aggression very aptly in a single sentence: "Everyone leaves everyone else alone." I would describe the principle of non-aggression like this:

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: 1. Ownership is a relationship that assigns physical objects to people (a person can be the owner of an object). No one may deal with an object that has an owner without his permission, except in cases where it is necessary to correct a situation in which the owner himself has violated someone else's property or violated a contract.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: 2. Ownership can be freely transferred and exchanged if both parties to the transaction agree (without coercion); transactions can be implemented using contracts.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: 3. Each person owns himself until he transfers that ownership to someone else (some libertarians argue that self-ownership is inalienable; others—including me—are of the opinion that a person is free to do with himself as he pleases).

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: 4. Something that no one owns at the moment, someone can start to own by starting to use it (mixing it with his work, so-called homesteading, see the work of John Locke). Homesteading addresses the issue of initial appropriation; when something doesn't belong to anyone (like newly discovered land and the like), anyone can get it by being the first to start using it. The principle of non-aggression corresponds to a certain minimum of what most people consider to be right, moral, ethical and fair: It follows from it in particular that people should not rob each other, attack each other (they can defend themselves) and kill; murder is a violation of the victim's property rights to his body - and as the astute reader will surely have noticed, natural rights, formulated as the principle of non-aggression, are actually property rights.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: Although perhaps everyone agrees that the principle of non-aggression corresponds to some minimum of what is right, many will argue that it is not enough; that it would be moral if the right included more things, such as necessary medical care. No matter how noble such an idea may seem, its inclusion in the principle of non-aggression is simply impossible. Why? Well, someone has to provide and pay for such health care; but if no one could be found who would do it voluntarily, he would have to be forced to do so by force, which would be a violation of property rights (and therefore aggression).

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: When we think about it more deeply, we find that adding anything else - however noble - to this system of law contradicts its meaning, or creates inconsistencies in it (which, after all, contains most legal concepts). In addition to the right to health care, there is also the right to education, a dignified life, a pension, housing - all these rights (if they are defined positively, i.e. not for example "everyone can get an education", but "everyone must be provided with an education") contradict the simple "you shall not steal". I certainly don't mean to say that people shouldn't help each other; it's just that no one should force them to do so. In all known historical societies, whose law was based on the principle of non-aggression, there was a considerable degree of voluntary solidarity (this is logical - when you know that you have a "right" to have someone help you in a crisis, you don't have to worry too much about others; on the contrary, if you depend only on them, you will help, for example, so that you can get help next time).

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: Despite the simplicity of the principle of non-aggression, answers to complex questions can be derived from it, for example regarding freedom of speech, labor relations, disputes over "public spaces", freedom of religion, but even the rules of transport, carrying weapons, abortion, prostitution and general management of society (which states formulate into thousands of confusing laws). Although anarcho-capitalism is in full agreement with the principle of non-aggression, this does not mean that this principle must be followed in every situation without exception in an anarcho-capitalist society, as there are no universally valid collections of laws; among the favorite pastimes of statists is inventing improbable and even absurd scenarios that show strange results after the literal application of the principle of non-aggression, while completely ignoring the fact that if someone acts contrary to the principle of non-aggression, but in accordance with common sense and generally accepted ethics (which, moreover, hardly happens), people will probably accept his behavior (therefore, we will not encounter arbitrary punishment for completely understandable behavior with reasoning that "the law is the law").

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: Although it cannot be assumed that the principle of non-aggression in a real anarcho-capitalist society would be followed unconditionally by everyone (after all, even the laws of today's states are not always observed), they are related as follows: First, anarcho-capitalism as a school of thought is derived from the principle of non-aggression, and secondly, in practice in places where real (even if not formal) anarchy reigned in some historical period (for example, medieval Iceland or the USA during the time of colonization), society governed by rules that were very close to the principle of non-aggression.

title: 3. The principle of non-aggression
text: Why the concept of law described above is sometimes called natural law is a rather philosophical question. Some claim that we all have them somehow encoded in our brains (because they are property rights and owning things is natural for humans) or that it is given by God. In my opinion, however, it is more important that it is a moral, ethical, consistent and non-arbitrary law (applying equally to all). I leave the evaluation of these approaches to the reader - as well as the comparison of the principle of non-aggression with the law imposed on us by the state. It probably did not escape anyone's attention that we only dealt with the law as such, not with its enforcement, i.e. putting it into practice; we will get to both of these in chapters fourteen and fifteen of this book, while the next one will focus on state protection of the irresponsible.

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: “He who sacrifices liberty to gain more security loses both and deserves neither,” said Benjamin Franklin, eighteenth century American thinker and scientist; I begin the chapter with this quote, which will be dedicated to state interventions that aim to ensure people's safety and protect them. What can we say about such interventions?

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: It follows from the first chapter that they are not needed; on the other hand, that they are not effective; from the third, moreover, that they are not moral; and now, in the fourth chapter, we will show that, regardless of their unnecessaryness, ineffectiveness and immorality, the consequences of these interventions are negative for the very subjects for whose sake they allegedly occur.

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: First, I will list a few state interventions that promise people safety in exchange for freedom, so that everyone can imagine what I am actually talking about: unemployment support, legal arrangements for contracts "noticeably disadvantageous to one party", social benefits, consumer and employee protection and many others.

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: What is the problem? Well... except that the market will provide all this better than the state (the general principles are described in the first two chapters, we will deal with this specifically in the following chapters) and that it is immoral, because in order for the state to provide any of the above, it must first rob. Even if this were not a problem for someone - what will people do who are assured (or create the illusion of assurance) that they cannot be cheated, that they cannot starve, that they will be provided for in their old age, that their children will always be taken care of? Well, they probably won't behave in the most responsible way.

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: One of the supposed "functions" of most states is to take care of the poor and helpless; it is realized, of course, by forcing the subjects to take care of someone by force. For a smooth enforcement, of course, people still need to be made to feel that no one would do it otherwise (Vladimir Putin perfected it in 2013, for example, with his effort to outlaw Yevgeni Grekov's charity organization, which "threatened the motherland" by building a hospital). However, charitable associations existed even at a time when the state had not intervened in this area at all (we can read about the details of how such associations functioned in the Czech lands, for example, in the research of Professor Karel Engliš).

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: So what is the main difference between the charity of voluntary associations and the state? On the part of the payers, it is understandably either a matter of charity or of being robbed; but let's look at the side of the recipients. While voluntary associations choose well whom, how much, how long and in what form they will help, the state guarantees the "right" to help. Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk saw it this way in 1919: "In the Czechoslovak Republic, there will be no more place for the old charity, which was always considered a grace, which always humiliated the poor recipient and dulled his human consciousness. Today, we put social duty in the place of humiliating grace."

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: But what is the natural consequence of the fact that if a person in need does not have to ask for alms, it will not humiliate him, the poor man, but it will be his "right"? People will definitely not be so embarrassed to reach out. Those who reach out will then not try so hard to improve their situation. And most importantly, all people in the whole society will not be so worried about getting into such a situation.

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: In discussions on this topic, many object to me: "Just look around you. Look at the people on the street. Look at those demented people who take out holiday loans again and again with ridiculous interest rates, they only care about beer and TV, they choose Paroubka or Babiš for a free sausage or doughnut, they are unable to take care of themselves because they have no idea how the world works, because they just don't care, they don't care. How will these people take care of themselves without a state?' Far better, I say! They are not interested in anything simply because they have no motivation to do so. The state declares that it will take care of them; they believe him (and for the purposes of this discussion whether it is true is irrelevant), ergo they have no reason to care. Economists call this phenomenon rational ignorance (when people believe that the state cares, then the expected benefit of knowing some information about how the world works is often lower for them than the effort expended to obtain that information).

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: Another example of rational ignorance is democratic elections. In order to make a truly well-founded choice between the candidates, one would have to read election programs, politicians' statements, familiarize themselves with the opinions of each of them, follow their past and estimate from it how sincerely the person in question means his promises, and so on. Such a study costs dozens or small hundreds of hours. And what does one get for this time? Almost zero chance of his vote making a difference when everyone else is throwing in whoever gives them a free hot dog and beer anyway. Coughing it up can then be a completely rational and logical choice.

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: Let's say you have a roof over your head and something to eat too. You know that if you take out a loan that you're going to have a hard time repaying, or lose your job, it'll all "work out" anyway, and you'll probably still have a roof over your head and food to eat. What is your motivation to behave responsibly? Compare that to a situation where you know that if you do something similar, maybe once or twice a charity will help you, but then you'll lose a roof over your head, you'll be cold, you'll be hungry, you'll lose everything. What is your motivation to act responsibly now?

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: We see the consequences everywhere, including in the labor market. The modern state tries to increase the number of people with university degrees, education is set up like this, demands are reduced; Nowadays, almost anyone who wants a little can have a university. What does it lead to? On the one hand, the employment offices are overwhelmed by social anthropologists with diplomas from anywhere in Upper Lower Saxony, whose number exceeds the demand, so they cannot find work, which is why they receive benefits. On the other hand, a programmer from Matfyz puts up a CV on the Internet and is overwhelmed with job offers literally within a few hours, not to mention the fact that it is becoming more and more difficult to find an electrician or a plumber, because there are fewer of them than are needed. That magical "how many are needed" means exactly what no mortal has a chance to count; the answer is only the market (the same applies in the labor market as in any other - it is about the principles we described in the first two chapters). This situation is a typical consequence of central planning in education, but it also has another cause: If we look at the average student in the last year of high school, who chooses a university, he decides according to what he likes and what he likes, or which school is the best place to hang out, while the criterion of "applying in the field" is usually secondary and unimportant. The question is whether this would be the case even if those concerned knew that if they studied a field in which they were not interested, they would have existential problems, would not be able to start a family, and so on; the attitude of the parents of the students concerned would probably change accordingly.

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: Some will argue, "Okay, but what about people who try but are just incapable?" Something similar applies to incompetence as well as to lack of motivation. The world is a wonderful place whose great qualities include a huge degree of predictability: You reach into the fire, you get burned; you do it again, the result will be the same. This enables all thinking creatures to learn and develop; if the world worked completely randomly, nothing like this would be possible. However, this predictability is far from being limited to the laws of physics, it also works quite well within socio-economic relations and, in fact, almost everywhere. Thanks to her, we can learn from our mistakes; however, when the state mitigates the consequences of these mistakes, it makes it difficult for us to learn, thereby creating not only the irresponsible, but also the incompetent (not that they would not exist without the state, but in far smaller numbers).

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: In general, then, it can be said that the more the state supports the irresponsible and incompetent, the more there will be; and these will hardly raise responsible individuals from their children, so their number will increase with each generation and their dependence on the state will deepen. This creates an artificial argument for why the state is actually needed. Why artificial? The human instinct for self-preservation is still quite strong; at the moment when something is really at stake and people will be seriously faced with the choice of whether to start behaving responsibly or starve and freeze, it can be assumed that most of them will - for purely existential reasons - prefer thinking over freezing (although both sometimes hurt). And the more we buy into politicians' rhetoric that people can't take care of themselves, so the state has to do it for them, the more we'll see around us that it's true; but as soon as we say no, and we stop supporting irresponsibility, we will witness its decline.

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: Inextricably linked to this is a phenomenon I call the "deadly cycle of democracy": A politician promises voters protection from the consequences of their mistakes; they elect him, he fulfills his promise (at least partially), the state mitigates (obviously at someone's expense) the negative consequences of some bad decisions; it will start to pay less to be responsible (the costs will remain, but the price we already pay for irresponsibility will decrease), so there will be more irresponsible and dependent on the state (including civil servants who implement the politician's promises); these people (and in subsequent generations their descendants) will typically vote for politicians who promote a strong state. This completes the circle; democracy inherently tends towards socialism, as it creates people dependent on the state the more the more such voters there are.

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: However, I am certainly not saying that we should not care for people in need (I do so abundantly myself); and history shows that those who care are not few, they just choose who to help and who not to (typically they don't help those who get into bad situations repeatedly and don't try to get back on their feet as soon as possible). On the contrary, the state claims that everyone has a "right" to help in an emergency, which leads to a huge increase in addicts who do not even try to actively solve their problems.

title: 4. Supporting irresponsibility creates the irresponsible
text: This chapter concludes the first part of the book, which deals with the general principles of human action, economics, the market and the state. In the following chapters, we will analyze the individual areas of human activity, which are now held by force in the hands of the states. We will consider how they could function without violence based on the actions of free people; in the very next chapter we will focus on state-controlled money and banking.

title: 5. Money
text: I will preface this chapter with a well-known quote: "Give me the power to print and control the money, and I will not care who makes the laws," authored by none other than Mayer Amschel Rothschild, who, in my opinion, omitted one very important fact when formulating this sentence; any of the readers may be wondering why Mr. Rothschild could possibly not really care who makes the laws?

title: 5. Money
text: Almost all of us already perceive it as a completely natural thing, so we often forget that the state has a monopoly on money enforced by force. So what would happen if Mr. Rothschild started merrily printing and controlling the money, but the law makers abolished the legal obligation of the citizens to accept the currency? Apparently what happened virtually any time in history when the state gave the people the option or when state money failed (typically too much was printed, leading to massive inflation): Private money spontaneously arose in the free market, usually backed by a precious metal. People would rightly say, "Why should this Rothschild be allowed to print money, devalue our savings, and live comfortably off it? Away with his money! Let's start using others!"

title: 5. Money
text: In the first chapter, we described why and how money was created. People exchanged goods and services. When two people each possessed something that was more useful to the other than to themselves, they voluntarily exchanged these goods, increasing the welfare of both without producing anything new. The complication arose when one had something to exchange that the other did not want; then they had to find some chain of people through which they exchange their goods (for example, exchange bread for potatoes, which can then be exchanged for steak, because the person who has steak is not interested in bread). This is, firstly, complicated, and secondly, it is not very clear which offer is the most advantageous, if there are several such exchange methods.

title: 5. Money
text: This problem was elegantly solved by the free market: Some commodity spontaneously established itself as the universal medium of exchange. People began to accept it even when they had no direct use for it, but knew that they would be able to exchange it easily. The prices of all goods were then expressed precisely in proportion to this currency. Examples of such universal means of exchange were especially precious metals, iron, cloth scarves, leather, grain and many others. Of course, these commodities continued to fulfill their normal function (which, incidentally, made counterfeiting problematic: if, for example, the currency is grain, then "counterfeiting" means that you grow grain; this is not a harmful activity, you simply become a farmer).

title: 5. Money
text: Over time, precious metals became established as currency almost everywhere: They could be easily divided and melted together again, they did not spoil, it was possible to store a lot of value in small volumes and, above all, their total amount on the market only changed unexpectedly or in leaps and bounds (for example, when the Spanish fleet with gold cargo was sunk).

title: 5. Money
text: Many people made their trades in metalworking: goldsmiths and jewelry makers, but also coiners and makers of private money (people brought their precious metals to them, which were processed in mints into coins on which the weight was stamped, facilitating transactions where the precious metals did not have to be divided and weighed again). Over time, institutions operating in this sector began to function both as lenders and as depositories: So that people did not have to carry precious metals directly with them, they deposited them with trusted goldsmiths, from whom they received confirmation of deposit; they then began to trade these confirmations as precious metals themselves—and paper money was born.

title: 5. Money
text: Since the same institutions that issued certificates of deposits of precious metals (i.e. paper money) often also made a living by providing loans, loans were often made in such a way that the borrower did not receive the coins directly, but these certificates (paper money). This naturally tempted individuals endowed with a higher degree of enterprise and a lower degree of morality to lend more than they actually had. It was simple: The person issued a certificate of deposit of more precious metals than he owned. That usually worked until he overdid it and word got around. They then quite understandably started asking for precious metals for their confirmations; the cheater didn't have that much and the cage fell. He was dealt with according to local customs, which in the best cases meant hanging; in worse burns, flaying and similar pastimes.

title: 5. Money
text: As is often the case, when the state sees an evil, it does not take long to establish a monopoly on it. It was the same with lending money that doesn't exist. In the vast majority of cases, the historical development was something like this: The state issued paper money as a confirmation of the deposit of gold in the state bank, then started a war that there was nothing to finance, so it printed more money than it had gold as a "temporary measure". The subjects were simply told that the state money was no longer backed by gold; of course, this was not met with enthusiasm, and citizens preferred gold to worthless paper, but this did not usually pose much of a problem for the state, which had a monopoly on violence: Failure to accept the state currency was often punishable by death (somewhere "only" by prison). Although in the beginning it was always necessary to impose state (uncovered) money on the people by force, it was not such a problem during a few generations of brainwashing to convince the subjects that it doesn't really matter; and a new way of legalized robbing was born.

title: 5. Money
text: How exactly does such a robbery take place? Actually, exactly the same as counterfeiting (only when the state is counterfeiting, it is called quantitative easing). If the amount of money in the economy increases, its value falls, so prices rise (money is a commodity like any other; when there is more of it, it is less scarce, so its value falls relative to other goods, see chapter one). As a result, everyone who has savings in a given currency transfers part of their value to the counterfeiter (state, banks). The nominal value of savings will remain the same, but their owner will be able to buy fewer goods with them, so their real value will fall. So when someone prints a billion crowns, they actually steal everything they buy with that billion from all holders of that currency (they are robbed in proportion to how many crowns they have).

title: 5. Money
text: After government money was forced upon the people, the masses - with the help of heavy propaganda - got used to it over time. The majority of states then relaxed their repressive strategy: Although the law imposes the obligation to accept state currency, in theory private currencies are not prohibited in many states (however, they are disadvantaged by the fact that everyone must accept the state currency by law, and in addition, taxes are collected in it). However, when someone tries to succeed in this market in practice and starts to do well, he is somehow cleared by the state anyway.

title: 5. Money
text: In 1998, Bernard von NotHaus created the Liberty Dollar, a silver-backed private currency. Within a few years, over seven million US dollars worth of silver (in the form of Liberty Dollars) had entered circulation, and the Liberty Dollar was becoming more and more popular. The United States government was frightened by the potential competition, so it had to be nipped in the bud. In 2007, the FBI launched a crackdown on NotHaus, only to have him indicted in 2009 and sentenced to 25 years in prison in 2011 (the trial lasted just 90 minutes) for conspiracy and counterfeiting. The plot was to create competition to the US dollar, and the alleged counterfeiting of money was even more absurd: One of NotHaus's coins was said to resemble a US quarter (although the quarter has a male likeness, the Liberty Dollar has a female likeness); even if the likeness actually existed, the alleged "forgery" made of silver was worth 160x more than the quarter it was supposed to fake. Imagine expecting a quarter, but a rogue counterfeiter slips you a coin worth 160x more, or $40; wouldn't that make you angry?

title: 5. Money
text: And so Bernard von NotHaus became another victim of the regime; although he was released after several years, the government sent a clear message. The state simply took all Liberty Dollars from him - and his innocent customers - by force. And what did Bernard von NotHaus actually do? What crime did he commit? He minted silver coins and sold them. No one was forced to buy those coins. The man was merely satisfying market demand, nothing more. Who did he hurt? To no one. Unlike illegal drugs, which the government bans under the pretense of protecting ourselves, these silver coins didn't hurt their own owners (the government did when they seized the Liberty Dollars), they just gave them a choice in what to do with their money. So why are governments all over the world usurping a monopoly on money? Well, simply so that they can rob the subjects. There is really no other reason here, it cannot even be said that they would protect citizens from anything. Free entrepreneurs in the money market have operated for hundreds of years to everyone's satisfaction; but then the states saw another way of subtly robbing their subjects, and immediately seized upon it.

title: 5. Money
text: In conclusion, it should be added that states usually do not do these machinations with money themselves, so that it is not too messy. In fact, they use banks to do similar shenanigans, which create money out of nothing in a relatively sophisticated way (they get permission from the state to do this; profits are shared between governments and banks using other complicated and non-transparent mechanisms). A detailed description of these practices would probably take up many books. However, we don't have that much space, so we'll just show the two most fundamental consequences of the above actions: constant inflation and economic cycles (which are the cause of economic crises). A more demanding reader can read about the principles of how economic cycles arise, for example, in the book "What has government done to our money?" from my favorite author Murray Newton Rothbard, or "The Theory of Money and Credit" (published already in 1912!) by Ludwig von Mises, or search the Internet for "Austrian business cycle theory"; a less discerning reader will perhaps be satisfied with the reasoning that there was no such thing as economic cycles or constant inflation until states began to control money. I would really like to go into more depth on this subject, because the instruments by which governments, with the help of banks, control money are almost diabolical; however, their detailed description would take another separate book. Now let's turn to something that fills me with hope - and that is cryptocurrencies.

title: Cryptocurrency
text: In 2013, when the Money chapter was created, the fundamental importance of cryptocurrencies was not yet completely clear to me, and therefore I did not include them in it; however, I would consider it a significant omission if I did not mention them even today in the second edition. Cryptocurrencies are digital money whose existence and transfers through cryptography are ensured by decentralized networks instead of central authorities; this means that they do not need any central bank, but at the same time they provide all the advantages of online means of payment.

title: Cryptocurrency
text: The consensus among economists is that in order for an asset to be classified as money, it must fulfill three basic functions: store value, serve as a universal medium of exchange, and fulfill the role of a unit of account (that is, be a measure of the prices of goods and services in the economy); I personally believe that a unit of account cannot be anything that is not a universal medium of exchange, so the second described function is redundant, as it directly follows from the third. History shows that these functions are performed by commodities that have the following six properties: rarity (limited quantity), durability, fungibility (ideally the indistinguishability of the units of a given item), divisibility (possibility of being "exchanged" without loss of value), easy transferability, and distinguishability (verification of authenticity). Not everything that possesses these attributes automatically becomes money; good money, however, must meet all these parameters (at least to a considerable extent).

title: Cryptocurrency
text: All six characters are very well fulfilled by a number of assets that are commonly called cryptocurrencies; some of them serve as great stores of value, but none of them is yet widely used as a universal medium of exchange, and therefore not even as a unit of account. State (fiat) currencies meet most of these six criteria more poorly, but their acceptance is enforced by law (in addition, there is an obligation to pay taxes and keep accounts in them); as a result, they function as units of account as well as mediums of exchange, but fail as stores of value (since there is no guarantee of their rarity when banks keep issuing new ones). Therefore, no cryptocurrency (due to insufficient liquidity) or fiat (due to a persistent decline in real purchasing power) fulfills all the functions of good money today. For cryptocurrencies capable of long-term storage of value, I prefer the term cryptomoney, thereby distinguishing them from liquid - but constantly depreciating - sovereign currencies, as well as from the vast majority (over 99.99%) of cryptocurrencies, which are called by the established term "shitcoin" in the crypto community.

title: Cryptocurrency
text: Bitcoin is the oldest, most widespread, most liquid and, for many (so-called Bitcoin maximalists), the only cryptocurrency. This protocol for an open-source peer-to-peer payment network was defined in late 2008 by a person or group of people using the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto; On January 3, 2009, it was launched to initially serve as a toy for a few enthusiasts. A year and a half later, for the first time, someone used it to make a purchase - programmer Laszlo Hanyecz ordered two pizzas for 10,000 BTC; little did he know at the time that in honor of this transaction, crypto-anarchists would start celebrating May 22nd as "Pizza Day" a few years later. Today, for the same number of bitcoins, we could buy, for example, a large private island with a luxurious palace, a power plant, an airport, a port, a jet, a helicopter, a yacht, and perhaps even a submarine; at the same time, we wouldn't have to worry too much about the budget - there would be enough left over for operating costs for the rest of our lives. How could the price go up so much? More and more people understand that Bitcoin is a great store of value; far superior to any current fiat currency.

title: Cryptocurrency
text: From the point of view of a (crypto)anarchist, I see the absence of any central authority as the most important feature of Bitcoin; it is a decentralized network that anyone can join at any time and start participating in its operation. While records of current account balances are managed by banks (and can therefore be frozen and similar), all Bitcoin transactions (including the complete history) are simultaneously stored by tens of thousands of computers located around the world; and if by chance someone decides to block my funds, the request for their transfer will simply be handled by another. Bad language people claim that the secret services of some of the great powers may be hiding under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto, which I do not consider very likely; however, the beauty of decentralization is that it's completely irrelevant - even if it were true, the creator of Bitcoin has no actual power over it (and not even a backdoor, since it's open source software).

title: Cryptocurrency
text: On the contrary, I consider Bitcoin's greatest weakness to be that it is not fully anonymous; although it does not show who owns which funds, but their transfers can be tracked - the history of all transactions is public (although they cannot be linked to specific people without additional information, states are gradually beginning to spend more and more resources to obtain this "additional information"). Although this problem can be solved in most cases and privacy can be protected, it requires an advanced level of understanding of the functioning of the entire network as well as blockchain analysis tools; not to mention the fact that anyone can simply make mistakes, which unfortunately has led to many seasoned crypto-anarchists knowing the inside of a prison cell. In response to this, for example, the Monero project was created - it can be imagined as the "younger brother" of Bitcoin, which, however, operates in complete anonymity and no one can monitor third-party transactions in it without the permission of their author; this is also why it is commonly used on illegal darknet markets (although it has other limitations). For the sake of completeness, I state that Bitcoin has tens of thousands of different "siblings"; however, almost without exception, these are broken or outright fraudulent projects (the aforementioned "shitcoins") in which you can easily drown your savings - but their existence provides much-needed competition that separates the wheat from the chaff (and some of them I still consider more trustworthy than sovereign currencies).

title: Cryptocurrency
text: As I mentioned a few paragraphs ago, no cryptocurrencies yet fulfill all the necessary functions of (good) money; and due to the inflationary nature of absolutely all fiat currencies, I dare say that unfortunately there is no such thing as good money in the world today. The six properties that constitute a necessary (but not sufficient) prerequisite for a commodity to become such money are currently, in my opinion, best fulfilled by Bitcoin and Monero. Let's do a quick comparison of these cryptocurrencies, precious metals and sovereign currencies:

title: Cryptocurrency
text: I feel it is important to add that not all properties are equally important; for example, the poor recognizability of money may not be such a fundamental obstacle (for example, if the commodities for which it can be exchanged are also rare), while the minimal rarity or extremely short durability of the good essentially makes its monetary use impossible. In addition, it is not the case that the item that best meets the above-mentioned parameters must always become money; changing money entails high transaction costs, which is why people only give it up when they stop fulfilling the necessary functions - not just because something could fulfill them a little better. For example, Bitcoin has (and has always had) the highest market capitalization (that is, the product of the number of Bitcoins and the current unit price) of all cryptocurrencies; because it serves as a good store of value, which allows it to be quickly and cheaply transferred between individual holders at essentially any distance. Although other cryptocurrencies (such as Monero) later brought certain advantages (such as anonymity), the time-tested trustworthiness of the first and oldest open-source peer-to-peer payment network is clearly more important to most users; for this reason (at least for now) it does not seem that Bitcoin should lose its position as "number one" (at least in the foreseeable future).

title: Cryptocurrency
text: If (any) money ceases to be scarce, its value decreases, which may lead to people refusing to accept and use it as a universal medium of exchange; in the case of state currencies, this fate can to some extent be delayed (or even averted) legislatively - for example, by enacting their mandatory acceptance by merchants or by not allowing taxation (or accounting) by other means. Even these steps are understandably not a panacea; for example, during hyperinflation, debased money alternatives typically come into play. However, until the situation is unsustainable, the state successfully enforces the use of bad money by force, thereby harming its holders; inflation (of virtually all current fiat currencies) is a hidden form of taxation.

title: Cryptocurrency
text: It probably won't surprise anyone that as a (crypto)anarchist I prefer cryptocurrencies over state ones; above all, however, I am a supporter of full voluntariness, freedom of choice, and therefore a free money market - I consider this to be far more important than my personal preferences for Bitcoin (or Monero). I believe that the only way to know really good money is to let people choose the ones that suit them. Even if centrally controlled inflationary currencies should turn out to be most desirable (which I think extremely unlikely), I will humbly accept that choice, unless it is conditioned by violent coercion; although for many reasons I consider Bitcoin to be the money of the future, I don't want to impose anything on anyone - let everyone decide for themselves what they (don't) want to pay for.

title: 6. Firefighters
text: Private firefighters. Absence of state firefighters. When a person says something similar in mainstream society, the reactions tend to be different. Mostly very emotional, we are often treated to various colorful images featuring burning houses, from which paying customers are rescued, while others end up in flames, jumping out of windows like living torches. Since these emotions are exactly what the state manipulates its citizens with, let's try to put them aside for a moment and think about things more deeply.

title: 6. Firefighters
text: Since in this chapter we will talk about the method and quality of fire service provision, it should be mentioned at the outset that this quality depends a lot on their price; in general, for almost every condition, it can be said that for some extra money it is possible to achieve an increase in quality. One extreme corresponds to the fact that fire services will not be provided by anyone and in any way, so that all costs will be equal to zero. The other theoretical extreme may look approximately like that a fully equipped fire station will be located near every house. Between these extremes there are many intermediate states, which correspond to a network of varying density of the most diversely equipped stations. It is obvious that by adding money to such a system, quality improvements can be achieved - for example, by buying better equipment, reducing travel times, and so on.

title: 6. Firefighters
text: Common sense, the famous book "Human Action" by Ludwig von Mises, observation of the environment and the first two chapters of this book suggest that people have their needs, which they satisfy in order from the most urgent to the least urgent (resources are limited, so they cannot satisfy all of them). What this means in practice is that a person typically knows that they need to eat, live and go to work, which will be the things they buy first (so they will pay for food, housing and transport to work first with their money); furthermore, for example, he knows that he would still like to go to a concert and have a couple of dinners in a good restaurant (he will pay for this with the money that is left over); then, for example, he knows that he wants to go to the beach in the summer and buy a car in a year (from the money left over after food, housing, transport to work, concerts and dinners, he will put some aside for savings); and finally, he would also like to go to the cinema, but for example he may find that he has no money left for that - that is, he will not go to the cinema because his other needs are more important. Each of us thinks approximately in this way: They prioritize their needs and desires and satisfy the most urgent, the biggest ones. Some may argue that there are also people who do not plan it directly like this and act more impulsively, or are too lazy to think about it and make some reasonable calculations; in short, one can answer these objections that for these people, impulsiveness or laziness (whose manifestations are also needs in a way) is more important than satisfying some of the needs mentioned above (for whom this answer is not enough, I refer to the above-mentioned book "Human Action", in which Ludwig von Mises describes this action in great detail).

title: 6. Firefighters
text: How does this relate to firefighters? Well, fire protection is among the needs of the vast majority of people; and everyone feels this need to varying degrees. Someone is willing to pay a lot for very high-quality services, while others would prefer to pay little for inferior services. What happens when the state sets some fixed quality of service?
