Those for whom the quality is not sufficient will typically buy something better; after all, many industrial enterprises and more valuable real estate are today protected against fire by private fire companies (the owners of protected buildings, however, still have to pay for state fire protection in an absolutely immoral and senseless way). But there are also those among us for whom state fire brigades are too expensive and would be satisfied with a cheaper – but worse – option. These people are forced to pay something they don't want. The state simply takes one of their less urgent needs and forces them to satisfy it at the expense of a more urgent need, for which the person may no longer have sufficient resources.

title: 6. Firefighters
text: So this (and, of course, the fact that forcing someone to pay for a service by force is extremely immoral) are the main - and quite fundamental - reasons against the existence of state firefighters. So if we assume that the fire service will be provided by a purely free market without state interventions, what could such a thing look like? Given that market solutions to problems are the result of the interaction of vast numbers of free individuals, it is impossible to say exactly how this will work off the table, but one can guess a lot. So I'll outline one way the free market could provide fire services - it's likely that the reality would be even better, as millions of entrepreneurs around the world will surely come up with a much more efficient solution.

title: 6. Firefighters
text: Considering how private fire departments have operated historically and now, one can assume that payment for these services would be similar to insurance. Entrepreneurs will set up fire stations in various places, and people in the neighborhood will pay for their services at a flat rate: They will pay a small amount every month, regardless of whether there is actually a fire in their place or not; then when it really burns, the company in question intervenes. It is reasonable to assume that entire houses would be insured in this way (it is difficult for individuals, who are practically impossible to locate in time during a fire), thus eliminating scenarios where firefighters pull paying customers out of a burning house and let the rest burn (the insurance will probably cover the whole house and all the people inside - a fire company that would protect property but let people burn would probably not have many customers).

title: 6. Firefighters
text: Another huge advantage of this principle is that the price for fire protection would be set individually - it would be higher for buildings with a higher probability of fire and lower for those with a lower probability. Similar to the price of flood insurance today, the location of the house plays a role (it is more expensive in flood zones). For houses better secured against fires, the fire protection fee will be lower. When these services are provided by the state and their price is independent of the risk of fire, there must be clouds of fire regulations that no one has much incentive to comply with (and those who build houses have little reason to do more than the bare minimum). If the price of fire protection is market-based, compliance with (and creation of) "fire codes" will be economically beneficial to those who build buildings, as well as those who maintain and live in them. No one will have to force anyone to do anything, people will be motivated by simply saving by following certain rules.

title: 6. Firefighters
text: Let's admit that some people don't take out fire insurance. It is very likely that companies that provide firefighting services on a regular fee basis will be willing to fight a fire even for a direct payment, which will logically be much higher than the payment of that regular insurance; in any case, considering that the house is extinguished, it is practically always worthwhile for the owner to pay such a fee, since the price of the house is typically higher than the price of its extinguishment. Therefore, it cannot be argued that the poor will not be able to pay for fire protection: Whoever owns a house or an apartment also has money for firefighters; even if he chooses not to pay the regular fees, he can still call a company to extinguish the property in the event of a fire - he will be paid for practically any amount that is less than the price of what is left of the property after it is extinguished.

title: 6. Firefighters
text: Other free market options are, for example, company firefighters (the factory has its own fire brigade, which also extinguishes the surrounding area) or volunteers (this profession brings social prestige), for example in Austria these cover a significantly larger part of the market than the state ones; in Denmark, most fires are extinguished by commercial companies. Historically, too, private fire brigades have proven themselves. State-funded fire departments are a relatively recent phenomenon; they mostly didn't start appearing until the end of the nineteenth century, when they didn't cover nearly as much of the market as they do today (which only came in the twentieth century). Previously, fire services were provided and paid proportionately

title: 6. Firefighters
text: differently. In London, for example, the first professional fire brigades were established as early as the seventeenth century; they were paid by insurance companies and were very successful - in a city that was practically entirely wooden, they intervened several times a day and put out hundreds of thousands of fires (for those who are interested in the details, they can be found, for example, in the book "An Economic History of London 1800 - 1914" by Michael Ball and David Sunderland). In the territory of the Czech Republic, fire brigades were rather voluntary and financed on the basis of charity or they were factory fire brigades (their primary task was to extinguish possible fires in factories, but they typically also protected the surrounding area); the means for their operation were sufficient even without state intervention (more details can be found, for example, in the book "History of Moravia. Part 4, Free State and Occupation" by Josef Bartoš).

title: 6. Firefighters
text: Market prices will also ensure adequate salaries for firefighters (what they deserve, which is what people are willing to pay them voluntarily) and the "right" number of them. Everyone has already heard from the mouth of some politician that they will stop the slimming of fire brigades, or take care of an increase in their numbers; we keep hearing about the fact that there are too few civil servants and they are not able to do their job to the required extent. How often, on the other hand, do we hear about directive increases in the status of bakers, programmers, workers or salespeople? None of this is necessary, as the invisible hand of the market can ensure the right number of them (if there are few people practicing a profession, their wages rise, which attracts more people to learn the profession, and vice versa - these principles are described in more detail in the first two chapters of this book). It would be exactly the same with firefighters - if the state stopped regulating the industry and left room for the free market.

title: 6. Firefighters
text: Although fire protection is generally seen as a good that should be provided by the state because "otherwise it wouldn't work", on closer examination we find that it worked a long time ago and still works today in some countries; plus, there's really no reason why it shouldn't work. On the contrary, there are many arguments why private fire services are not only more moral (no one forces anyone to pay for them), but also more efficient. Unfortunately, we have no choice, the state forces us to pay for its services by force; the same can be said about the subsidization of culture, which we will pay more attention to in the next chapter.

title: 7. Art and culture
text: Culture - and art in general - enriches a person spiritually and mentally, it is beneficial to society; therefore, it should be subsidized by state subsidies, otherwise many beautiful things would disappear from our world. Some art will pay for itself, others would disappear without subsidies; after all, we must protect such from extinction. Most people say something similar when we ask them what they think about state funding of culture. But let's think more deeply about the implications before jumping to any conclusions.

title: 7. Art and culture
text: At the outset, I want to say that I am definitely not an "art opponent". People often tend to think that when someone condemns the subsidization of culture, they are against art as such. That may not be true, and in my case it certainly isn't. I consider both art and culture very important because they really enrich individuals and make them happy; me personally, for example, especially rock and classical music.

title: 7. Art and culture
text: Defenders of cultural subsidies from public budgets justify their positions mainly by the fact that without subsidies, many artists would not be able to create, theaters would disappear, "non-commercial" cinematography would not support itself, exhibitions and museums would not cover costs from admission fees alone. To begin with this objection, it is necessary to note that many great artists created without state support; for example (across various types of art): Shakespeare, G. B. Shaw, Beethoven, Mozart (who, as part of his eccentricity, refused to serve the masters and became a free artist), Queen, Pink Floyd, Deep Purple, The Rolling Stones, Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael, Vincent van Gogh, Picasso, Dalí...

title: 7. Art and culture
text: Above all, however, it is necessary to realize what it actually means when, without state subsidies, an artist cannot create, a theater ceases to exist, a film cannot be made, or a museum cannot cover operating costs. When such art does not support itself, it is because people voluntarily (without state coercion) do not want to pay enough for it, so that the cost of running such art is greater than what people are willing to pay for the result. However, we know from the first chapter that such a state means that someone is wasting precious resources (for example, an artist's time, a theater building, a canvas or paints, musical instruments); people value these resources as something more valuable than what is produced from them (if this were not the case, the art in question would be profitable). This means that the utility of such an artistic act is negative for people.

title: 7. Art and culture
text: I can imagine readers who will indignantly object at this point that art and beauty can't be calculated only in terms of money! Please, let's recall the opening few chapters of this book. What is the main function of money and prices? After all, transmitting information about the rarity of goods and their benefits. Converting something to "mere" money means converting it to the benefit and satisfaction of people at the same time. Of course, the fact that it would be necessary to spend more money to implement a project than what people are willing to pay for it is not important. What is important is what this information tells us: People do not want such a project. It is necessary to remember the cost of the sacrificed opportunity - in addition to the benefit that the above-mentioned project brings, it is also necessary to take into account the fact that other things could not have arisen due to its creation; the people involved in the project could have done something else, the material could have been used differently - even the value of the time of those people and the material used is higher than the value of the final work (although the value is numerically expressed in money, but of course it is a benefit for society).

title: 7. Art and culture
text: Most people live with the idea that the "value of art" is something that only experts or critics can determine, because many ordinary people "don't understand art". But what is the purpose of art or culture? After all, the purpose is to enrich a person in spirit, in heart and mind, to make him happier, to evoke pleasant feelings, to make him think. But what kind of person? Everyone! Not just a few insiders. He who "does not understand art" is not enriched. But he is no less a man than those who understand; his wishes, desires, feelings and dreams are no less important - and therefore it is monstrous to force him to pay for something he has no interest in. I am not suggesting that "quality art" is that which earns itself; I just don't want to force anyone to pay for it.

title: 7. Art and culture
text: One can often meet the objection that if the state did not support art, only "commercial" and "junk" things would survive, but some truly "valuable" things would not; that, for example, stupid TV series or monotonous pop music would be enjoyed, but some really deep works would have a problem with it. But what does that mean? That the monotonous pop music and stupid TV shows that make money for themselves make people happier than those works that can't support themselves without state subsidies! The objection that this is because "they are uneducated barbarians" may be true, but irrelevant - why should the happiness of a "civilized man" take precedence over that of an "uneducated barbarian"? I also don't understand how someone can prefer, for example, Michal David over Brian May, Freddie Mercury, Beethoven or Vivaldi, it seems completely crazy to me. Nevertheless, such people exist. And nothing gives me any right to force them to pay what I like at the expense of what they like. If someone is happy with the series "Rose Garden Surgery", it is immoral, unethical, monstrous and inexcusable to force them to pay for the series "Italian classics of the second half of the 20th century", which he does not watch and does not bring him anything; regardless of my opinion of his taste (I'll leave it to the reader to decide whether the greater barbarian is the one who peacefully watches his favorite soap opera or the one who forcibly forces him to patronize his favorite theater).

title: 7. Art and culture
text: In addition, the choice does not always stand as it is presented to us and as I did in the previous paragraph. People who do not pay for a theater or museum do not automatically donate this money to some "fallen waste". They often don't dedicate them to any form of art at all, but use them to buy a house, educate their children, eat, or donate them to charity. And even if experts in the field of culture were able to decide (and for others) which art is mere cinders and which, on the contrary, is of sufficient quality to "deserve" government subsidies, perhaps no one can seriously believe that there could possibly be an expert in everything who could decide for others whether theater or food is more beneficial for them, or whether an exhibition of paintings or a charity collection brings more benefit.

title: 7. Art and culture
text: If anyone is worried that art would cease to exist without government subsidies, then they can rest easy. Art has always existed; this human need is much older than any state. Throughout history, artists have created regardless of whether they had to support themselves or were supported by a patron or government. There is no reason to believe that right now culture needs the state to exist. After all, governments take money to subsidize culture from citizens' pockets; if they didn't, people would have more money to pay for, say, a more expensive theater ticket (or other art or whatever; just whatever gives them the most benefit). Not to mention that, according to the CZSO, even at present (research from 2011), the state participates in the financing of culture by less than fourteen percent; the remaining eighty-six were paid voluntarily.

title: 7. Art and culture
text: In addition to subsidizing contemporary artists and cultural institutions, governments often care about the preservation of older works of art and historical monuments. Why will this also ensure a free market to the greater satisfaction of the people? When works of art are not managed by the state, this role falls to their owners. Who will these owners be? The free market will, over time, ensure that it is those willing to pay the most for the thing in question to whom it has the most value; such owners can be assumed to also take care of the work (or historical monument) in question when they have paid dearly for it. And these owners do not have to be only rich individuals, it can also be a voluntary association of many people who have the same interest and are willing to agree to it.

title: 7. Art and culture
text: Common objections to abolishing state supervision of works of art or monuments are something like this: "What if someone bought St. Vitus' Cathedral and opened a supermarket there?" "Who's to stop someone from buying the Mona Lisa and destroying it?" The answer is easy: Why would someone pay a fortune for a painting that they then simply destroy? In the case of the supermarket in the St. Vitus Cathedral, it is similar: If someone wants to have a supermarket in the center of Prague, why would they pay huge money for the cathedral, which many people value much more for other purposes, when they can buy some other object in a similarly lucrative location for less? Even if someone already owned the temple and wanted to open a supermarket, it would be worthwhile for him to sell it as a temple and buy a cheaper object with the money taken (and make a profit on the difference). It can be argued that none of the above are 100% guarantees, but neither the state gives us these; for an example, you don't have to go far, just remember how many works of art and historical monuments were damaged or destroyed by the state in the Czech Republic between 1948 and 1989.

title: 7. Art and culture
text: Many also object that if works of art and historical monuments are owned by the rich, they will not be able to be enjoyed by the general public. On the one hand, this may not be true, because even private owners can exhibit their property (either for free or for a fee), or lend it to various exhibitions (they have always done this to varying degrees and still do today). But if the owner is not willing to do anything like that, people can always get together and put together such a sum to buy the work of art or historical monument from him. If they fail to collect such an amount voluntarily, it means that the current owner values the thing in question more than the general public, who understandably has no right to take the thing from him by force.

title: 7. Art and culture
text: When thinking about government subsidies for culture, we must never forget that no matter how wonderful the art might not (or could) pay for itself, government subsidies always mean the forced extortion of money from people who want to use it in other ways (otherwise they would fund the art voluntarily). Works that people are not willing to pay for themselves and voluntarily bring them less benefit than what it costs them money. If culture is left to the free market, only art will emerge that brings more to people than it takes from them; which no one else can decide for them but themselves.

title: 8. Education
text: Schooling and the educational system have been - at least in our territory - inextricably linked to the state for over two hundred years. Today, this means that the "rules of the game" in education are determined by the government, which decides what must be taught, how it can be taught, who can teach it, who can learn it, who must learn it, how long it must be taught, how it must be assessed, and what punishment awaits anyone who goes against any of the above regulations. And this chapter was written especially for readers who find the above reasons alone insufficient for the abolition of state education.

title: 8. Education
text: The Achilles heel of our public education is... our public education. Practically nothing works well in it (except for a few individual schools). Critical thinking is punished, individuality is suppressed, students' attitude towards authorities is distorted, they are required to memorize completely useless information, graduates of many schools lack useful knowledge, students allow themselves to be teachers more and more, some teachers tyrannize students, teacher salaries are low, many lousy teachers just hang around in schools and are overpaid for doing nothing, students are not interested in teaching.

title: 8. Education
text: Do you feel that some of the solutions to the above problems may contradict each other? That feels right to you. So isn't such criticism of state education unfair, when it can demand something and at the same time the opposite of the same thing? It is not, on the contrary - it quite correctly points out the first fundamental problem of state education, which the free market can solve: In state education, there are some uniform rules that differ in certain details, but their basic direction is determined uniformly (see "National Education Program"). There is no such thing in the free market. Each school can teach what customers want.

title: 8. Education
text: Not all parents have the same idea about raising their children. For some, education about religion (of which there are many) and, for example, sexual abstinence is important; others want to protect their children from religion and are comfortable with today's modern concept of sex education. For some, conformity, discipline, obedience and submission to authority are more important; still others emphasize individuality, own opinion, searching for the causes of rules instead of automatically following them and following only such authorities as their descendants choose for themselves. Some of us prefer friendship (anti-manipulative education) to classical education. There are countless approaches; and since we are not all the same, it cannot even objectively be said that any one of them is the universally best for everyone. And why look for compromises or golden middle ways when there can be different schools with different rules and different teaching? And this is something that the free market, by its very nature, will offer incomparably better than the state, which simply cannot provide such a thing to the required extent (due to the impossibility of economic calculation - see Mises' book "Bureaucracy" or - for short - the second chapter of this book).

title: 8. Education
text: Another intractable problem of public education is the fact that there is - and cannot be - any way to distinguish a good teacher from a bad one. Virtually anyone who gets the appropriate diploma can go into teaching. The government then supervises (poorly at that) only to see if any teacher is so extremely bad that it is obvious (for example, drunkenness at work). Apart from such marginal cases, the state simply does not know how to differentiate teachers according to quality. And considering that the quality of a teacher cannot be measured exactly, and different teachers are good or bad for different students, this task is impossible for central planners. The market will solve this problem quite automatically, just like in any other industry: The better someone is at what they do, the more people are willing to pay for their services. There is no need for any central algorithm to determine the quality of architects, programmers, graphic designers or even chefs (a good chef wins customers for his restaurant and vice versa). The same would be true for teachers in a free market.

title: 8. Education
text: The logical consequence of the impossibility of assessing the quality of a teacher is tabular salaries. And what happens if an employee receives the same amount of money for a job well and poorly done? That it motivates everyone to slack off is probably obvious at first glance. Moreover, another consequence must be realized: For capable experts, learning is a poorly paid job, because they can get more elsewhere; on the other hand, for budižknic people who are able to get a diploma at some lousy pedagogical school with great difficulty, such a job is well-paid, because they won't be able to get more elsewhere. Unfortunately, it follows that the more capable a person is in a certain field, the less motivation for learning state education gives him (and vice versa).

title: 8. Education
text: A fairly typical objection to free-market education is that allegedly some poor (or miserly, or those who do not understand the value of education) parents would not pay for their children's school, which could lead to the fact that some - perhaps talented - children would not receive an education. Well, if a child is really capable, it pays for schools to teach them for free (or very cheaply), because such students raise the level of the school (on the one hand, they "pull" less talented classmates up, and on the other hand, they improve the school's statistics of successful graduates) and make good advertising (this is not an empty theory, this is already happening in many private schools today). Another solution is offered by home or community teaching, charity, or company schools, whose graduates can then become employees (which can also be anchored in a contract).

title: 8. Education
text: Of course, these solutions require at least minimal cooperation on the part of the parents, which at first glance may appear as a disadvantage; however, upon closer reflection, it is obvious that if the parent is an ignoramus who simply does not care about his child, the state will not help him much anyway (although he usually gets the child into school, but it typically gives the student in question practically nothing; on the contrary, he often spoils the lessons and enriches his classmates with things that their parents - or teachers - don't really care about). If someone now objects that even a slight increase in the chances of a good life for a "problem child" is worth the effort, I ask him: "Are the chances for problem children so important to you that you would not mind if their classmates - and often the targets of bullying - were your own offspring?" Because it has to be someone's children. In addition, the state quite possibly does more harm than good to them as part of "giving chances to problem children", who are placed in an environment where everyone shows them their inadequacy (see the fourth chapter).

title: 8. Education
text: A common objection to leaving education to the free market goes something like this: "Even now we have private schools, just look at them, they are mostly worthless and often just sell diplomas." Here it is necessary to note that even if the school is owned by a private person, the state dictates to it what it cannot, must and must do, ergo it has practically nothing to do with the free market (regardless of the artificial competition in the form of state schools). In such an environment, it can be really profitable to simply teach poorly and hand out diplomas. However, the value of the diploma in the free market would correspond to the reputation of the given school (and if anyone can easily get it, it will become worthless - just as today the value of certificates from educational courses is determined by their quality); in addition, it can be assumed that there would be certification companies that would assess the education of students independently of the school from which the person concerned came. The motivation of such certification authorities to do their job well is clear: If they certified (perhaps for a fee) everyone, their certifications would then lose value, so there would be no interest in their services.

title: 8. Education
text: However, the main advantage of the free market, which today's private schools under the baton of the state lack, is the possibility of choosing to learn in their own way. That is the main power of the free market! Millions of people start schools, try all kinds of teaching methods; the good prosper, the bad fail. The state has no room for such a thing; on the one hand, he cannot try an inordinate number of possibilities at once, and on the other hand, he cannot afford too much experimentation.

title: 8. Education
text: Throughout the chapter I refer to the fact that the state allows schools to teach basically only one way and restricts them too much. Despite this, our laws allow schools to specialize in different fields, within which they can have significantly different hourly subsidies for individual subjects, so what's the problem? Such reasoning shows that we are already so bound by the practice of state education that we cannot imagine anything else. But with a little imagination, we can ask ourselves, for example, the following questions: Is it necessary for any subjects to be taught in school at all? Do students have to be assessed (at all)? Is age segregation into classes necessary? Do teachers have to motivate children to learn? While we may think we have the answers to these – and all other – questions, how can we know for sure until someone tries?

title: 8. Education
text: There is also a theory of education that describes a school that would function like this: Students would not be segregated by age in any way, there would be no classes, although the age range is planned to be quite large (from about four to nineteen). No subjects would be taught in the school. Students would have available tools and things (computers, playground, library, workshops, tools, notebooks, stationery, garden...) for free use. No one would even force them to learn to read and write. There would be no grades, no exams, no tests. The teachers would not give directives, they would only help if the children asked them. But the impulse must always come from the student, no one can force anyone to do anything. All important matters in the school, which cannot be individual and must be decided somehow, are decided by simple voting, where the votes of students and teachers have equal weight; so the voice of a four-year-old is the same as the voice of a nineteen-year-old, which in turn is the same as the voice of a teacher. This vote would include, for example, deciding which teachers will get a contract for the next year.

title: 8. Education
text: Would you choose a similar school for your children? I do. If there were more of us, perhaps the market would show that this education system makes sense. However, no one would have to participate in this experiment against their will. There is nothing wrong with someone having a different idea about raising their children. At the same time, countless different solutions can be implemented in the free market, as it is not bound by any central planning by the state.

title: Education and freedom
text: I ended the previous – i.e. the eighth – chapter by presenting a non-standard and very free educational model, which describes another possibility of how a school could look like. Does it seem unrealistic to you? Have you ever thought that I can't even be serious about this anymore? Is this just salon theory that has no basis in practice? Is this a concept that could never work with real children?

title: Education and freedom
text: When I first read about this educational model, these are the thoughts that went through my head. Whenever I discussed the topic with a teacher, the reactions were basically always negative. It is precisely one of those methods of teaching which no government would dare to introduce, because it contradicts everything we know about education; so of course it can never work.

title: Education and freedom
text: But Hanna and Daniel Greenberg were of a different opinion. In 1968, they decided to found just such a school. Sudbury Valley School, in which there are no classes, no subjects are taught, no one forces students to do anything, does not know them and does not evaluate them in any other way; they are just given space to do whatever they want. They don't have any classes there, they don't segregate children by age; on the contrary, they leave everyone together - from four-year-olds to nineteen-year-olds. Decision-making (including which teachers will and will not have their contract extended) is decided by voting, in which the votes of all (four-year-olds, nineteen-year-olds and teachers) have equal weight.

title: Education and freedom
text: The results? Excellent. Over the fifty years of its existence, the Sudbury Valley School has produced hundreds of successful graduates who, among other things - surprisingly - are able to enter public education: Eighty percent of them received a university degree. Over the years, there has not been a single graduate of this school who did not know how to read and write (although this is a very frequent objection of opponents of this style of teaching). Sudbury Valley is also free of bullying. Psychologists who have dealt with this phenomenon explain it in two ways: First, they believe that the absence of age segregation has a big influence on it, thanks to which weaker children (frequent victims of bullying) are not forced to compare themselves with their peers, but can spend time with younger ones (in addition, it often happens that the older ones stand up for the younger ones). And secondly, they believe that children often adopt patterns of behavior that they see around them. This is also why bullying is rampant in schools where teachers treat students authoritatively (the same can be observed on a more severe scale in the military), not in Sudbury Valley, where no one encounters such behavior. You can read more about this school, for example, in the publications of psychologist Peter Gray, or just search the Internet for "Sudbury Valley".

title: Education and freedom
text: Although Sudbury Valley is probably the most popular and well-known of the independent schools, it is not the only one or the first. The oldest known similar project in modern history was started by the anarchist Francisco Ferrer Guardia in 1901 in Barcelona; five years later, however, he was arrested for allegedly collaborating in another anarchist's attempt to kill the king, which the state did not prove, but still imprisoned him for over a year, during which his school disappeared. The first still functioning (and extremely successful) educational institution of this type was founded by Alexander Sutherland Neill in 1921 in Germany, from where it moved to Austria, and since 1923 it has been based in England.

title: Education and freedom
text: The successes of these schools inspired many other enthusiasts and entrepreneurs; dozens of similar institutions were founded in several other countries of the world. Their results are very similar to those I described above for Sudbury Valley. Despite these demonstrable and fascinating successes, the legislation of many states rejects such schools. This means that if, for example, someone were to open such an institution here in the Czech Republic, the state would not recognize it as a school, which would lead to the fact that the students' studies there would not be recognized as part of compulsory school attendance, and their parents would have problems with social welfare, like those who do not take care of their children. Makes sense, right?

title: Education and freedom
text: I consider it important to emphasize that I definitely do not claim that all education should look like this and that all schools should function according to the Sudburg model. I assume that for some children such a method of education is suitable, for others it is not (after all, the same can be said about any system, including the current one). But this does not mean that it should be banned across the board. People are different; why then suppress their individuality and try to indoctrinate them under the threat of violence and do everything possible to cram their education into some uniform pattern created by the state?

title: Education and freedom
text: But as long as the government determines the rules of the entire education system, many good ways of education will never have a chance to emerge. After all, when someone comes up with rules for a school like the one they have in Sudbury Valley, the vast majority of people (and especially educators and all kinds of education experts) say it could never work. So no one tries it and the concept remains a barren theory. Of course, it's not just a Sudburg model! There are countless different theoretical ways of education; and the only way to find out which ones work in practice is for someone to just come and try it (while of course no one will force any parents to send their children to such a school, that will be entirely up to them). However, until people are free to experiment like this, they cannot try, so many good educational models remain only on paper.

title: Education and freedom
text: Unfortunately, one of the reasons why most countries have conquered education and the educational system is precisely the effort to ensure that each individual is properly indoctrinated and thoroughly instilled in him already in childhood that it is morally justifiable and justified for some to rule over others, that he is just a citizen who needs a ruler, and he should be happy that he can at least choose one. Don't you believe? Pick up any textbook on the basics of social sciences, or some civics education (the very name of the course suggests citizenship education). Still don't believe? It is enough to read the "National Education Program", where you will read about (I quote) education for democratic citizenship, strengthening of belonging [...] to national traditions, key competences focused mainly on [...] citizen education or about introducing elements of democracy into the life of schools. I completely understand and respect that some readers may think this is right, but please don't make me expose my children to it.

title: Education and freedom
text: I have discussed the Sudbury model with many people. Often with educators. Even with two education experts who have dedicated their entire professional careers to teaching, learning how to teach, publishing textbooks and various work for the Ministry of Education. I have always started by describing the model as a theory and discussing it only hypothetically; those concerned had no idea that such schools really existed somewhere. Most often, I encountered approximately this answer (and the more experience the person had with pedagogy, the more categorically and confidently he uttered it): "It's a beautiful theory that sounds very nice, but it can never work in practice. I know what I'm talking about, students just behave differently." Sure, they behave differently! Not even when they are being educated in a completely different environment. The problem with every such pedagogue (or pedagogical expert) is that they only judge everything based on what they see in current education. But it is not reasonable to assume that if students behave in a certain way in one educational model, they will behave in the same way in a diametrically different model.

title: Education and freedom
text: In connection with this, a parallel about the functioning of society comes to mind. When discussing a stateless polity, many people very often assume that people will behave in such a society as they do now. This is, of course, a big mistake. People now don't care about some things and don't do some things simply because the state does them for them. It is a mistake to think that if the state stopped caring, they would not change their behavior. It is just as short-sighted as condemning the Sudbury model on the grounds that if students behaved in it as they do in current schools, it would not work.

title: Education and freedom
text: Give people shackles and they will be aggressive, distrustful. Pin someone to a wall, they will try to break free, be hostile, distrustful. Then unchain him from the wall, give him slightly longer chains. What do you notice? He will be even more aggressive, he will see a chance, he will try to escape even harder because now he can at least do something. What do you conclude from this? That more shackles and shorter chains are needed because a person chained to a wall is calmer than one who can at least move around the room? Because that's exactly how many think of the state: The more the state "loosens the chains", the more people allegedly start to misbehave and abuse it. But the completely obvious truth lies in the exact opposite. The solution is to release the person from the shackles and give him freedom. Because freedom is natural, then he will be satisfied.

title: Education and freedom
text: I can observe it on myself. As long as I believed in the state, obeyed its laws, lived under the influence of propaganda, I was more interested in what was written than what was right. I followed the laws on principle - even when I had the opportunity to help myself by breaking them; it seemed to me that a good person respects the law. When I freed myself from this view, two things happened. For one thing, my mind is free. It's a wonderful feeling, believe me. And on the one hand, I understood that morals and ethics are superior to laws; I follow them either in cases where I voluntarily decide to do so, or when I would be punished for violating them; otherwise they mean nothing to me but shackles that I never consented to and that were forcibly imposed on me by a government I have no interest in and no longer chose. So I feel no obligation to respect her bonds and have no qualms about leaving them at any time. But that doesn't mean I've become a badass. On the contrary. I also got into situations in which I could have helped myself by simply appealing to the law, but I preferred to behave correctly rather than in accordance with the law. I no longer look at what is written, but at what is good and what is bad. And I dare say that this transformation has made me a better person than I was before.

title: Education and freedom
text: I am certainly not saying that if the state did not exist, all people would start behaving honestly and correctly. It's clear to me that they haven't started. However, I am convinced that a non-negligible group of people would become more responsible because they would have to take care of themselves. And I believe that responsibility is a virtue that leads to other virtues...

title: Education and propaganda
text: Sudbury Valley School is based on one of a huge number of different educational models; however, there are also those that completely reject any school (no matter how independent it may be) (so-called unschooling) and often include the complete voluntariness of the educated individual as a necessary condition for them to function at all, which of course excludes their legal application in any country with legislatively anchored compulsory schooling or compulsory education (ie de facto everywhere). Although I do not claim that every educational model is suitable for everyone, I see no reason why some (or indeed most of them) should be outlawed.

title: Education and propaganda
text: For example, in the Czech Republic, almost the only legal model of education is the so-called "Prussian cadet" (and its modifications), i.e. schools with teachers, lessons, classes, grades, discipline, age segregation, obedience and compulsory attendance; why is he sometimes called "prussian cadet"? Well, once upon a time the Prussian generals complained that the schools prepared bad soldiers for their needs, who thought too much and carried out orders too thoughtlessly; therefore, there was a reform, the aim of which was to change education so that it produced ideal obedient killing machines - and it is in this model (after some minor modifications) that our children are still educated today. In relation to this, it seems laughable when teachers talk about developing students' critical thinking, independence and the like, while trying to achieve all this within a system that was designed to do the exact opposite; it's like wanting absolute silence, going to a music festival in search of it, and being surprised that by adjusting the parameters of the earplugs we don't get the desired result.

title: Education and propaganda
text: An integral part of today's education is represented by teachers, who are typically not chosen by the students, but still have to listen to them and often even show them a kind of respect (one example for all may be standing up when the teacher comes to class); in this way, even young children are made to feel that it is desirable and right to submit to an external authority that they have not chosen for themselves. First of all, he is a teacher, who is replaced over time by the government, a politician, a policeman, an official, simply any oppressor that the state invents. One might argue that similar training is appropriate for future employment, since most people have a boss at work; but a person chooses such a place and is there voluntarily (not that he necessarily likes it there, but no one forces him to be there).

title: Education and propaganda
text: To be clear, I have no objection whatsoever to the natural authority that man chooses of his own free will and recognizes to the extent he sees fit; I consider it healthy and natural to respect someone, value them and learn from them. The key, however, is that everyone chooses for himself who is worth following for him; the imposition of authority, on the other hand, leads to a loss of self-confidence and unnecessary conformity simply because it is expected and learned completely automatically. It is precisely the forced imposition of authority and its voluntary acceptance that forms the boundary between "throwing away self-respect and learning to hunch our backs before anyone who is meant for us" and "accepting another person, respecting him, valuing him even with his mistakes and wanting to learn from him." I want my children to have the healthy self-esteem and perspective to be free to decide for themselves who deserves their respect, but I resolutely refuse to be forced to show it to whomever is assigned to them. What about you? Do you want your offspring to be primarily obedient citizens or good people? Do you want them to do what someone tells them or what they think is right?

title: Education and propaganda
text: The effort to enforce conformity by force where there is a lack of natural authority is not the only, and unfortunately not even the biggest, problem of state education; I consider the indoctrination of the youngest by state propaganda to be at least as insidious. How would you like it if, for example, a private company introduced the promotion of its products into compulsory education, which would not be labeled as advertising, but presented as objective truth? Do you find this completely unacceptable? If so, do you mind if the state does exactly the same thing? Without any discussion, he presents himself as the only solution where there is supposed to be "market failure"; sure, not everyone will agree on whether the market is failing or not, but even then, it's an open question, not a given, how these alleged "market failures" are presented. As a result, the atrocities of the state (the curtailment of our liberties and the use of offensive violence) are excused as a matter of necessity; and sometimes the means of such behavior include completely obvious lies.

title: Education and propaganda
text: Do you think I'm exaggerating? I can demonstrate my claim, for example, on the example of freedom of speech; we learn in schools that before 1989 we didn't have it, while now we do. But try publicly promoting Nazism or racism, or approving certain criminal acts; if you're consistent, they'll eventually pick you up and lock you up. So no, we definitely don't have freedom of speech, it's just that things that we're not allowed to say in public have changed; the truth is that we are now less constrained, but it is still not freedom. And it's not at all about whether we agree with such laws or not - I'm just pointing out that the declared freedom of speech is nothing but a lie; even if the laws prohibiting certain expressions were fine, that would not make it true that they are not prohibited, which is contrary to the declared freedom. Non-freedom of speech simply cannot be turned into freedom by stopping silencing educated and wise people, but instead silencing, for example, racists and neo-Nazis; freedom is when everyone can speak - including those whose opinions we find perverted, nonsensical, disgusting or stupid.

title: Education and propaganda
text: I consider the deification of the state and its symbols to be the most disgusting practices of the current educational system; why are our children taught, for example, to respect the flag, anthem and other national symbols as part of compulsory education? After all, it is nothing but idolatry! If a free man chooses, based on his life experience, to honor a flag or a song, that is of course his business, and I am the last person who would want to prevent him from doing so; however, this is diametrically different from forcing a small child to sit somewhere where they are being manipulated into doing something like that. How are people who have already gone through this educational system supposed to look at the state dispassionately and critically, if they have to worship it as an idol from an early age? Incidentally, this also applies to democracy, which is uncritically presented as a good in a similar way; note how often the word "undemocratic" is used as a synonym for "bad" (even in entirely democratic processes).

title: Education and propaganda
text: It is impossible that such powerful propaganda at the most sensitive age should not leave consequences on the people; everyone then "knows" that society cannot function without the state, without ever really thinking about it. When you first introduce the idea of a stateless society to someone, in the vast majority of cases, a negative reaction occurs within seconds. I can't help but wonder how anyone can take a stand on such a complex issue that takes tens or hundreds of hours to really think through in an instant; unfortunately the answer is that there is only one way - the person must have "known" it beforehand without any real submission to critical thinking and dealing with the arguments. Unfortunately, in moments when we "know" something without having arrived at that "knowing" by some reasonable path, we simply do not accept logical arguments; we hear them, but automatically consider them to be false and do not even admit that they could possibly be true.

title: Education and propaganda
text: Unfortunately, this does not only apply to discussions about the state, but also to many other topics; and none of us are spared from it. The only way to combat this is through a lifelong pursuit of awareness, where we accept all sorts of dogmas everywhere without critical evaluation. When I discovered several such cases myself, I was first pleased that I had "finally got rid of" them; however, years later, I realized that this pursuit probably has no end, and I will constantly discover new and new ones. How to do it? The first step is being honest with yourself; when I'm debating with someone, do I even consider as a real alternative that I could be wrong and the person in question could be right? Not in some hypothetical "we are all fallible" kind of way, but am I admitting that in the discussion? Another fairly clear sign of dogmatism is that we are more convinced of the conclusion than of the reasons leading to it; how often do we come across that someone defends his thesis with a certain argument, but after refuting it, there is no reflection and possible reconsideration, but an immediate frantic search for anything else to support that thesis?

title: Education and propaganda
text: On similar principles, compulsory schooling ensures a very effective blanket indoctrination by statism; children must by law be exposed to state propaganda for a long time and repeatedly. The state will send welfare to parents who defy it; and if they insist, their children can be taken away (and eventually indoctrinated anyway). If any other entity acted in this way, we would quite rightly find it absolutely unacceptable, however, precisely because of the indoctrination we have undergone, we even accept the state telling us how to educate our children and - if we don't - threatening to kidnap them; yes, by kidnapping - that's exactly what it's actually about (although of course the laws - the laws written by the kidnapper - say they're not).

title: Education and propaganda
text: I consider state education to be the most powerful tool for creating and consolidating the power of the state; while the military enforces it, the educational system plants in all of our minds all sorts of exceptions to the general moral rules we otherwise follow. Taking someone's resources under threat of violence is wrong; however, when the state does it, we somehow excuse it, because we have been told that there is no other way. Forcing someone to instill certain values in their children under the threat of abducting them is not only wrong, we find it highly reprehensible; but it is enough for the state to do exactly the same thing - and then we not only understand it, but even typically approve of it. Come on, when we've all been told since childhood that it's for our own good and it wouldn't be possible otherwise; what else can one think who does not want to think about this topic for long hours? Unfortunately, similar - perhaps even more popular - myths are also spread about the state welfare system; we will deal with their analysis and demolition in the next chapter.

title: 9. Social system
text: Pensions, unemployment support, all kinds of social benefits and care for the poor in general are domains in which modern states are involved so significantly that many people already consider them to be one of the key roles of the state, and one can even often come across the opinion that if none of the above was addressed by the government and if solidarity were not forced by force, it would practically disappear. Because these views are already deeply rooted in society, people often forget the fact that governments controlling the welfare system are a relative novelty; however, previously these things also took place normally - only on a voluntary basis.

title: 9. Social system
text: I definitely categorically reject variations on the theme that "it wouldn't work"; mainly because it has worked for hundreds of years, but also because if solidarity really is so important to people that they are willing to argue in favor of the government restricting their own freedom, I see no reason why it would need states and their laws to implement it.

title: 9. Social system
text: The social system existed long before the state took on this task. It is even clear from the available sources that the voluntary social system at the time was probably relatively more effective than the current state system. Information on this topic is widely scattered in a number of historical sources, but an excellent compilation work dealing with charity, especially in the territory of the Czech Republic and Great Britain (also with references to corresponding historical writings), was written by Hynek Řihák, founder of the Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk Institute; those who are interested in the details can search on the Internet for example his texts "Education for the poor or let's not forget about charity", "Not so wild 'wild' capitalism", "Private education in Great Britain, child labor and the state in the 19th century", "Voluntary hospitals, medical care and the state in Victorian Great Britain", "Self-help societies", or "An outline of charity in Victorian Great Britain - old women for the poor".

title: 9. Social system
text: Although the forms of the voluntary social system were numerous, they were mostly various charitable associations, of which two types were the most important. The first type were classic charitable organizations in which the wealthy joined together to support various groups of the poor. The other ones were like that

title: 9. Social system
text: local "social insurance companies", which functioned in such a way that a large number of people joined them, regularly paid (relatively low) fees, and then when one of them had a problem, the association helped him. In the vast majority of cases, such associations did not generate any profit and were owned directly by their members. In addition to these mechanisms, there were many others (we can read about them in the files mentioned above).

title: 9. Social system
text: In the past, people were in solidarity voluntarily, today they are forced to do so. How is it different? First of all, it is necessary to mention the most important thing: The state welfare system is implemented in such a way that it is first necessary to rob and beggar someone, only then can you help. After all, no one but the state has the audacity to first take most of the fruits of their labor from the people, and finally to say presumptuously to their faces: "You see, you don't have enough to feed your children or to buy bread in your old age. Be thankful that you will at least see a pittance from what the government stole from you."

title: 9. Social system
text: The vast majority of the money that the government collects as part of the welfare system is paid out on old-age pensions. In connection with this, it is first of all necessary to realize that the state does not evaluate the selected funds in any way; on the contrary, it takes a significant part of them (even if we ignore corruption and waste, at least it has to pay for the army of officials who implement it all) and only redistributes the rest. It follows logically that if people saved the same money they pay for state pensions for themselves, they would be much better off. The most common counter-arguments are two. The first is that if someone saves in a bank, the bank can go bankrupt and deprive them of their deposit - sure, it can happen, but it can be prevented; for example, we can divide the money and deposit it in several banks, buy real estate, invest in shares, or maybe buy gold and hide it in a secret stash under the floor (none of this brings 100% certainty, but neither does the state; after all, we can observe how the retirement age keeps increasing). The second counterargument is that people are irresponsible and many would simply not save for retirement; and practically the entire fourth chapter of this book deals with its refutation.

title: 9. Social system
text: Another essential difference between voluntary charity and a coercive state welfare system is that the government must essentially create a uniform system that applies to the whole country and all citizens, while the voluntary solidarity of free people works in a much more direct way. The advantage of a decentralized charity is that it can look different in each place according to what is needed where, and it is not bound by any universal rules that cannot in principle be good for everyone. As an example, the above-mentioned charitable associations can serve as substitutes for social insurance: Associations of those who performed riskier professions - for example, miners - typically collected more money, for example, to provide for families in the event of the death of a breadwinner, or to pay for health care, and so on; the central planning of a welfare system can never be so effective.

title: 9. Social system
text: The addressability of charities and charitable associations also prevents the abuse of the welfare system much better. In the case of a local charity, abuse was overseen directly by those who contributed their own money to it; their motivation is therefore incomparably higher than the motivation of officials who are supposed to watch over parasitism on money that is not even theirs.

title: 9. Social system
text: State officials, and generally those who implement and implement the social system, may not really care how long the recipients of support will be dependent on the state. On the contrary, it is in the enormous interest of charitable associations that the recipients of support stand on their own two feet as soon as possible! The functioning of the entire charity and the way of providing that support are mostly subordinated to this. Charitable associations, which actually functioned as insurance companies for their own members in case of job loss, typically actively monitored whether the recipient of any support found work, and often reimbursed him for related expenses (for example, travel expenses, retraining costs, and so on). Voluntary welfare systems - unlike state ones - are often guided by the fact that it is better to give a poor person a rod and teach him to fish than to just give him a fish.

title: 9. Social system
text: An equally important problem with the state welfare system is that there is a "right" for someone to receive funds from it. It is not so difficult to imagine the difference in the approach to one's life situation between a person who realizes that he lives on handouts (and is therefore duly grateful for them) and a person who is convinced that he has a so-called "right" to the state money from which he lives (and instead of gratitude, there is often dissatisfaction with the fact that he does not receive more - after all, he has the "right" for others to provide him with a "dignified life"). In connection with this, it seems strange to me when I hear the opinions of some - especially right-wing - people who are already able to curse at "socks and nemakachenka who only live on support" and in the same breath add that "some kind of social system must be provided by the state", which also implies that there must be someone's "right" to support; how can someone claim to receive welfare benefits as a right and yet criticize the people who use this "right"?

title: 9. Social system
text: A frequent argument in favor of maintaining the state welfare system is, among other things, that we are civilized people and as such we cannot let the poor die of hunger. Even if we leave aside that charity based on voluntariness can do the same thing (in addition, the help is better targeted), I would like to point out that in our geographical regions, realistically, no one is in such a financial situation that would force them to suffer from hunger. Even people on the street, the homeless, who sometimes don't even receive any support from the state (I personally know several of them and there are certainly not a few of them in general), do not starve, because it takes at most a few hours (and with a bit of luck, only a few minutes) to beg for food for the whole day in a busy place.

title: 9. Social system
text: A very interesting question is why this is so. Some hundred years ago, the poor were starving (and often with the support of the state), five hundred years ago, the middle class was also often starving; but today in the "western world" even the homeless and beggars are not hungry. Of course, this is due to the fact that the entire company gets richer over time. What everyone else has today was only yesterday a matter for the rich. After all, for example, of people who live below the so-called "poverty line" in the United States, 76% have air conditioning, 66% more than two livable rooms per person, 97% at least one color TV, 62% satellite or cable TV, 75% a car, 30% two or more cars, 73% a microwave, 50% hi-fi equipment, 33% a dishwasher, 99% a refrigerator and 46% of them live in their own house. A hundred years ago, such conditions would have been considered absolutely luxurious. When we think about why the things we consider common today were once seen as luxuries, the answer is easy: Greedy and selfish businessmen in their pursuit of profit made all these goods available to the common people so that they could sell them and get rich; and for this they are so often condemned. Certainly this growth, which especially helped the poor so much, was not caused by robbing the rich; on the contrary, it effectively hinders it (one can only guess how many bankrupt companies could survive and make all the above achievements even more accessible to the poor, if they were not eliminated by the tax burden or state regulation).

title: 9. Social system
text: And the indisputable fact is that the more the state takes care of the poor and declares it to be its role, the less the citizens care (why should they, if the state is already taking care of them; after all, for their money), which Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk understood as early as 1919: "Today we put social obligation in the place of humiliating grace." I ask the readers, when assessing the necessity of a state welfare system, to think not only about what is visible at first glance, but also about what does not work and does not exist because of it, and especially about what inevitable and unwanted consequences it brings with it, if you grant someone a "right" to other people's money just on the basis of being poor himself. It is not dissimilar to the "right" to medical treatment, which we will discuss in detail in the next chapter.

title: 10. Healthcare
text: Health care is one of many areas that are so heavily regulated that they are de facto state-run and subject to central planning. The government accredits hospitals and individual doctors, thereby determining how many and which hospitals there will be where; at the same time, it also legislates practically everything that happens in those hospitals, thus - even if they do not directly own them - they actually manage them more than their potential owners. And as is the case with similar things, today almost no one can even imagine them without the state.

title: 10. Healthcare
text: The most common argument against free market health care is that health services are so expensive that only the richest of the richest could afford them, and without the state it would not be possible to provide health care on the current scale. I honestly don't understand how anyone can come to such absurd conclusions. After all, the state doesn't do anything other than forcefully take the funds from the people, from which they then pay for their health care. It does not have any mysterious charms with which it somehow mysteriously evaluates the selected funds and pays from them something that people would otherwise not be able to afford. On the contrary, it has certain - considerably less magical - tricks to devalue a fairly significant part of the collected money. So the state definitely does not provide any greater scope of health care that people cannot pay for themselves (they pay for it themselves through the state, after all). On the contrary, unregulated waste, ubiquitous corruption, the impossibility of economic calculation (explained in detail in the second chapter) and the need to pay the army of officials who carry out the entire redistribution significantly reduce the scope and quality of available health care.

title: 10. Healthcare
text: So how could the average person afford health care when surgeries cost tens to hundreds of thousands and there are even procedures and treatments costing millions? Should everyone have this money saved in a straw for Uncle Příhoda? Of course not. The insurance model (even health insurance) has been successfully operating here for hundreds of years even without the state. The principle is that if someone occasionally needs expensive treatment, it is not necessary for him to save the funds for it himself. It is richly sufficient for many people to pay a relatively small amount regularly, and then if something happens to one of them, the treatment is covered from the common fund. But the state is not needed for this at all.

title: 10. Healthcare
text: And what about those who simply do not pay for insurance and do not have direct payment? Do we leave them to die in the streets? Well, charity is the last chance for such. In the past, such a charity typically assessed to what extent the disabled person was responsible for his situation, how much he could influence it, what his current options were and how expensive treatment the person in question needed. Help was therefore understandably provided mainly to children or the disabled; on the contrary, not idlers and irresponsible ignoramuses (but sometimes even such people got help, especially if it was not very expensive). More on the functioning of charity without the state can be found in the previous chapter. So the answer to the question is that we probably won't let the sick die on the streets if they are those who could not influence their situation much (children, the elderly, the infirm, the crippled), but maybe we won't be so lenient with irresponsible peccadilloes. Why this approach is desirable is explained in the fourth chapter of this book.

title: 10. Healthcare
text: There is a certain humane idea that says something along the lines of: "Equal health care for all." I'm afraid that most of its supporters defend it only because they haven't seen it through. This is because "equal health care" can mean anything from a top-notch clinic full of the best experts to getting a vein in a dirty basement; the sentence does not say anything about a specific quality, but only that it must be the same for everyone. The misconception most people have is that in practice this means some average quality medical care for everyone; so their intuitive understanding of the idea is that the average person will have about as much medical care as they could pay for themselves, with the rich paying more to the poor to average it out.

title: 10. Healthcare
text: However, almost nothing is further from the truth! The state spends part of the collected money on the salaries of officials who keep the whole juggernaut running, and also on corruption (which is an integral part of the state and bureaucracy; not something that can be "eradicated"). The rest, which is not stolen and paid out in official salaries, is then invested desperately inefficiently due to the impossibility of economic calculation (details can be found in the second chapter of this book). So the result is nothing like "average medical care for all", but very substandard to desperate care in proportion to the amount of money people are forced to pay; so even the "ordinary person" that politicians flaunt so much is beaten. If someone argues that this is the right thing to do, and that we should reduce ourselves so that everyone can be treated, even if they don't care about anything (and the "ordinary person" is not the case that should not be treated, as we explained above), then I ask them: "Do you really think it is morally right for your children to receive worse health care just so that a handful of irresponsible people can get the same treatment?"

title: 10. Healthcare
text: Another - slightly less extreme - idea can be formulated as follows: "Okay, not everyone has to have the same health care, but some basic treatment should be provided to everyone." Something similar can be achieved through voluntary charity (a more detailed explanation can be found in the previous chapter). However, when the state does it, it is certainly not just about shifting resources from everyone to the poorest; an enormous amount is lost along the way and the rest is invested incorrectly (see above). So again, the state has no other option to achieve this goal than by worsening medical care for everyone else.

title: 10. Healthcare
text: Another emotional argument that often comes after rebutting the above is that many ordinary people are already struggling to make ends meet, so there would be no way to pay for private health insurance. In addition to being refuted by the previous paragraphs, I would like to explicitly point out that these people have so little money precisely because they are so extremely taxed; the total tax burden of our state is so great that if we did not pay taxes, we would usually have several times more resources available than we have now.

title: 10. Healthcare
text: The huge problem in health care is not just the payment system through the state; there are also a lot of laws and regulations that make it impossible for entrepreneurs to find effective ways to treat patients. A typical example is that any new drug must first go through a series of lengthy and expensive laboratory tests, and possibly even animal tests, before the government allows it to be tested on humans; and unfortunately even the consent of those people does not change anything, first it is necessary to ensure at least some security. Such regulation is correct, isn't it? We don't want evil pharmaceutical corporations testing on humans to increase their profits, do we? About 99% of people nod at this. And who is against it? Just a few crazy extremist libertarians advocating individual liberty at all costs, no one else... So everything is fine? Oh, I almost forgot, there is one more group: People who are currently being killed by a disease for which someone is developing a cure, but it still has to pass some tests, so they are out of luck. Are we really letting them die just so that some pharmaceutical company doesn't make money by testing drugs on people, even if they agree, it can help them and the person wants to live? And I am not talking about all those who are dying today from a disease that could have been successfully treated for many years if the state had not hindered the development of medicines. Let me add that I am categorically opposed to testing drugs on people who do not agree. Similar legislative obstacles can be encountered, for example, in connection with the ban on the sale of organs: It is said that it is not humane for someone to sell a kidney, so it is probably better if one dies rich of kidney failure and the other ends up on the street.

title: 10. Healthcare
text: The existence of regulations is defended by saying that if there were none, every butcher could be a doctor and every lice-infested cellar a hospital. Sure, it can in principle. The question is who would go to such a doctor and which insurance company would conclude a contract with him. If there were no regulation, exactly those doctors and hospitals that people are interested in would make a living, unsuccessful ones would go bankrupt. A frequent question is how would it be possible to find out if the person standing in front of me has a medical degree at all, or if he derives his education from regularly watching Dr. House. Well, apart from the fact that something similar would probably already be provided by the insurance company (which wants to keep clients, so it is not in its interest to conclude contracts with doctors and hospitals about which it knows nothing at all), it will certainly not be difficult to open the website of the school (or some certification authority; it is described in more detail in chapter eight) at which the doctor allegedly studied, and perhaps find his benefit there. Today, such a service does not exist mainly because doctors and hospitals are accredited by the state; but if they didn't, a demand would be created and, of course, an offer.

title: 10. Healthcare
text: Sometimes you can come across the objection that in some countries healthcare is "more market-based" after all, but the results are not very good; however, the catch lies in the misunderstanding of the greatest advantages of the free market, which include not only free competition, but above all the ability of people to try whatever they see fit, to fail if they fail, and to prosper if they succeed. The so-called "more market" does not mean only more private and less state entities, but above all freedom of business; even the number of regulations is not decisive, it depends on what and how it is regulated: Even health care, where all entities would be private, but the state would determine who and under what conditions is allowed to practice, can (depending on those conditions) fail more fatally than health care, which at first glance is much more regulated.

title: 10. Healthcare
text: Many people think of key sectors - such as health care - that the state may mismanage them, but if we had more moral politicians, wiser advisers, more capable civil servants and more efficient government, it would be a good thing. If we leave aside that democracy does not lead to anything like that (which can be observed all around), then even if by some miracle it succeeds, something will improve, but in principle it will never be as effective as a market solution (see the second chapter). The same applies to the management of public spaces, which is covered in the next chapter.

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: All around us there are spaces that do not have a private owner, because the administrator of such territory is the state; it can be squares, parks, forests, meadows, fields, rivers and various buildings, but also roads and paths. In this chapter we will consider whether such lands could be better managed by free people. The only thing we will not focus on yet is transport and all transit functions of public spaces (especially roads and paths); the whole next chapter is devoted to this great subject.

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: I consider the most serious reason why the state (and by the state, I mean its municipalities) should not own any land, the same as for all other domains in which the state intervenes: Managing public space costs money; no government of any state is, and has never been productive in history, so that the means it spends must and always has had to rob its subjects. I see robbery as a strongly amoral act; and behind every state square, forest, building and road, of which we can see many around us, there is looted money. For this reason, I cannot agree to the state managing public spaces.

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: And as is often the case in a free market, morality goes hand in hand with efficiency, so there are also practical arguments. One of them was presented by the well-known scientist, Dr. Garrett James Hardin, in his famous essay "The Tragedy of the Common Pasture", where he compares the private person's access to his own pasture with the people's access to the state's pasture. The owner of the land grazes on his meadow only enough cattle so that he does not destroy it and that it can feed him. On the contrary, in sixteenth-century England there were pastures where anyone could drive his cattle; the result, of course, was that people allowed cattle to graze there too much, rendering the land no longer usable for that purpose.

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: Many other thinkers based their works on this idea. For example, my favorite author, Murray Newton Rothbard, in his book "The Ethics of Liberty" describes the tragedy of the commons like this: "If the state owns the land and allows individuals to use it freely, this naturally leads to overuse of the resource and waste."
