In practice, this problem can be encountered, for example, in the state administration of unique natural monuments (there is no motivation to properly guard them), some protected animal species (if private individuals could make a profit from them, it would be in their own interest to protect them from poachers) or pollution of rivers or air (more on this in the thirteenth chapter).

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: However, I see a bigger problem (than overuse) in deciding how to use a space. If the state owns an empty lot, how does it decide whether it will be a park, shopping center, playground or parking lot? A group of officials will determine this somehow. Their motivations can be different - from someone bribing them, to the fact that they themselves live nearby and their children have nowhere to play, to the crystal clear belief that the park is exactly the best for the citizens of the neighborhood. In principle, the fairness of the motivations of such an official does not matter; he cannot know what is best for people, even if he happened to care. Even the results of a possible referendum will tell only about how many people voted for which option, but they cannot take into account the degree of how much someone wants this or that. Moreover, such a vote can show different results depending on how wide the neighborhood is included (commuters may be satisfied with a parking lot, or at home with a park, for example). When the work is finished, the state administers it from public money, and without an economic calculation (see the second chapter) there is no measure to determine whether it is beneficial or harmful.

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: However, when these lands are owned by entrepreneurs, what will be their goal? Generate profit, of course. And the biggest profit will come from building what people are willing to pay the most for, which is the very thing they want most. So entrepreneurs have an incentive to build exactly what people want (albeit for purely selfish reasons). Similar to officials, even entrepreneurs cannot know in advance which of the possibilities of using the given land is the best; so everyone will try something, many different projects will be created. The better they meet the wishes of consumers, the more they earn; bad projects are unprofitable, which leads quite naturally to being replaced by ones that people want.

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: A common objection is that if we leave the management of all land to private individuals, they will build shopping malls, parking lots and office buildings everywhere, but no parks and playgrounds. Similarly, after the Velvet Revolution, many people (including politicians and economists) argued that it was necessary to centrally plan grocery stores, because otherwise they would become scarce as entrepreneurs would run only boutiques instead. The reality, however, is that there is always an adequate supply for the demand; this goes for grocery stores as well as parks. If there is sufficient demand for parks, then they will certainly be created. If people aren't willing to pay for them, that means these parks shouldn't exist, because people are actually more demanding of something else (whatever they're willing to pay for). This idea (explained in more detail in the second chapter) is very important because it applies quite generally. It's good to remember that "demand for parks" doesn't just mean that people are willing to pay entrepreneurs to enter the park; it can also manifest itself in the way that enough people in the neighborhood get together, buy land and set up their own park there (unlike the state, however, it does not force anyone to do such an activity).

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: Private ownership of what are now called public spaces solves another significant problem. I imagine that many readers, after reading the title of the chapter, asked themselves what public spaces have to do with freedom of speech. Well, let's first examine the problems of trying to come up with some reasonable definition of freedom of speech. Virtually all states suppress freedom of speech: They typically prohibit either speech against the current regime, or promotion of other regimes, or both; often something more. The Czech Republic is no exception; for example, the promotion of fascism or racism is prohibited (I am definitely not a racist and as a libertarian I consider fascism to be pure evil; nevertheless, I will always defend freedom of speech even for those with whom I fundamentally disagree). Even so, they lie to us in schools that we have freedom of speech after the Velvet Revolution; this is simply not true - although the current regime persecutes fewer people, even today we can face brutal violence for some public statements and then sit down (the legitimacy of such actions can be debated, but freedom of speech is definitely not).

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: So should everyone be able to say what they want, otherwise it's oppression? At first glance, it might seem that way, but it is not. It also depends on where he will do so. It is obvious that if Jehovah's Witnesses ring your doorbell and you don't immediately let them into the living room and let them preach about the faith there, you are certainly not restricting their freedom of speech. However, if the law comes into force that prohibits Jehovah's Witnesses from evangelizing, it will be a clear violation of their freedoms. A fairly well-known example is the man who, for the sake of amusement, shouts "on fire" in a crowded theater and thereby causes panic; many philosophers and thinkers have dealt with this, but also the American judge Oliver Wendell Holmes, who came to the conclusion that the right to freedom of speech cannot be absolute and must be weakened and tempered with regard to "public policy". The weakness of this approach is that depending on changes in "public policy", freedom of speech can be completely suppressed (see totalitarian regimes).

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: So what is the moral and practical solution to this problem? Let everyone decide on their property what they can and cannot say there; there will be no state spaces. And just as everyone decides what they can and cannot say in their living room, they also decide what they can and cannot say in their park. This solution is completely natural and in accordance with property rights.

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: There is a feeling that if free speech was left purely to landowners, it could lead to a lot of pointless regulations and unnecessary restrictions on speech. However, this is extremely unlikely; if an entrepreneur provides his land (parking lot, cinema, park, swimming pool...) to people for the purpose of profit, it is not in his interest to issue senseless restrictions to discourage customers. Another concern may be that some views would remain prohibited - similar to now. However, this is completely unrealistic; while in a state it is sufficient for a ban to be approved by the government, in a free society all landowners would have to enforce it at the same time. And even if that happens by chance, the supporters of the suppressed opinion can buy their own land on which their rules will apply.

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: The argument from the opposite side, on the other hand, is that if only the owner decided what could and could not be said on a plot of land, there would be many places where people could say what they wanted. This is very likely. What could be wrong with it? Some might promote various ideas leading to violence, often lies. Sure, that would happen sometimes; on the other hand, their opponents have the opportunity to refute such delusions. Of course, this is no guarantee that a skilled manipulator will not win the crowds over; but - as history shows - not even the states, where there is also a danger that such a manipulator will appear directly in the government, from where he then has much more options to suppress his opponents with the help of legislation.

title: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text: On further reflection, we find that with the same elegance with which freedom of speech can be defined in terms of property rights, we can do the same with freedom of religion, freedom of assembly, freedom to use one's own language, and so on. The rules in a space are always determined by the owner of the place. It is quite simple, clear, there is no need to define limits or generally applicable laws; above all, it is moral (everyone makes their own decisions) and consistent ("basic human rights" are thus defined using property rights, so they can never be in dispute). Although in this chapter we dealt with the effectiveness of the management of public spaces and the issue of freedom of speech, religion and assembly, the issue of freedom of free movement still remains open; however, the following chapter is devoted to just that and, of course, to the statist's favorite question: "If there was no state, who would build roads?"

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: Perhaps the most frequent question of statists, which is heard after an anarcho-capitalist mentions a stateless society, is curiously not directed at the courts, the police or the army, but rather: "And who would build roads without the state?" Although this question is the basis of many a libertarian joke, which might indicate a very obvious answer, I personally do not find this topic particularly easy to explain; yet I will try to show why the correct answer is: "A free people, ruled by no one, will build roads; moreover, far more efficiently than the state."

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: First, let's focus on the problem of state highways and intercity roads, the construction and maintenance of which are extremely expensive today. The attentive reader can already guess that the causes of these problems are twofold: lack of motivation and the impossibility of economic calculation.

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: A manifestation of the lack of motivation is the omnipresent corruption, which practically eliminates all market prices and which makes it possible that the expenditure on highways - ranging in the order of hundreds of billions - sometimes varies from highway to highway by several times (and sometimes it is possible to build more cheaply in mountainous Austria than in the relatively flat Czech Republic, where, moreover, salaries are generally lower). The true market price of the highway is scarcely imaginable; but it could be significantly lower than now (just for comparison, a square meter of a Czech highway is more expensive than a square meter of an ordinary family house; building some space with family houses - without gardens, stuck on top of each other - is cheaper than running a highway there).

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: A manifestation of the impossibility of economic calculation is the fact that no one really knows from where to where it is worth building a highway for the given money; just as it is unclear how often it is beneficial to repair roads given their need and cost of repair. Not to mention that there is no way for the state to know whether we have too few (and which ones are missing) or too many (and which ones are over) roads overall. Any surveys of real road use cannot provide meaningful answers, because as long as the maintenance costs of each particular road are completely separated from its use, prices cannot express the scarcity of resources, so no one knows whether a driver currently using a road would do the same if he had to pay the market price for it (further explanation of this phenomenon can be found in the second chapter).

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: Private road ownership solves both of the above problems very elegantly. Corruption is minimized because entrepreneurs guard their money better than officials and politicians guard state money (and if they don't, then such entrepreneurs will soon have nothing to do business with). The problem of the impossibility of economic calculation completely disappears, since the profitable road is clearly beneficial; on the other hand, the road it passes through is not beneficial in its given form (people get less benefit from it than they would from the resources it consumes). In addition, from the above data it is possible to estimate how frequent and expensive repairs it makes sense to carry out on that road.

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: The most common objection to private highways is that when their owners (or owners of individual parts) raise the prices ad absurdum, people will have no choice but to accept and pay such prices. This could be partially true if there was no other transportation option. However, this condition is difficult to fulfill, because in reality there is an alternative to every road; both in the form of other roads (even if it is a detour) and other modes of transport (e.g. the railway competes with the overpriced highway). If someone sets their prices extremely high, they will lose customers. And even if by chance the owners of all transport routes between two points agree to raise prices, a new route can be created (cartels are generally unviable in the free market, details about this can be found, for example, in the chapter "Waste Producers" of the fantastic book "Defending the Indefensible" by the well-known libertarian thinker Walter Block).

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: The only "advantage" that the state has in the construction of highways over a free society lies in the possibility of expropriating the land through which the road was planned. I put the word advantage in quotation marks because it is a very confidential advantage; especially because the very act of expropriation is extremely immoral, since it is a robbery of land, the price of which is obviously higher for the owner than that offered by the state (if not, it would not be necessary to force him to sell it). So it might seem that buying up land for highways would be very expensive under anarcho-capitalism. However, the price without state intervention would be market, i.e. completely natural, and lower with state intervention; but at the expense of the owners of expropriated land! And if we remember the second chapter of this book, we find that if the cost of the freeway due to land acquisition would be so high that it would not be worth building (or would have to include detours), that means that the utility of the land that the freeway should run through is greater if the freeway is not there. If we think this statement through, we will find that the post-fidential advantage at the beginning of the paragraph actually represents a disadvantage.

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: Sometimes I come across the opinion that private highways could probably work, but they shouldn't be owned by too many different owners (and since the construction of a highway is not a cheap matter, it can be expected that more investors and entrepreneurs would join forces to finance it) so that it is not necessary to stop at a toll gate every few kilometers. The same argument is then usually used against the private ownership of city streets, because if tolls were collected at every corner, it would bring with it discomfort for drivers and traffic would not be very smooth. Of course, toll gates are not the only solution. Street owners can sell permanent tickets (something like highway signs) or GPS beacons, or – if someone wants a device in the car that will always record their location – chips that can be read by readers only on the relevant streets, or the cars could be equipped with something like a "taxameter" that would activate and deactivate external signals. All of these solutions (and the free market would surely come up with many more) can be used in parallel, and most importantly, multiple owners of streets and roads can use a common system; thereby reducing their transaction costs and providing greater convenience to customers (so no toll gates on motorways every few kilometres).

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: Although it can be assumed that highways and intercity roads would be mostly built by businessmen for profit, in the case of city streets and roads, on the contrary, it is possible to assume that many of them would be owned by the owners of adjacent houses (such a road can be created at the same time as those houses and there is no reason for it to be sold and residents have to pay for the passage). Relatedly, there is concern that cities could become congested because some owners would not allow foreign cars on their streets. Well, maybe some would. In any case, the bigger the problem, the more the prices would naturally rise, which always leads to an increase in supply (that is, for those for whom it was not worth it to let other people's cars drive through their street for a few bucks, it can already be worth reasonable money). Associations of street owners could also be formed with agreements on mutual access.

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: To the possible objection that the prices for using city roads owned by homeowners would be too high (which, of course, no one can say with certainty; but the opposite is also not the case), all that can be said is that they would cause precisely the kind of traffic situation that would ultimately bring the greatest benefit to society. It is hypothetically possible (although there is no evidence for this; but also for the opposite) that this would reduce traffic in the city - but only if the real benefit of city residents from quiet streets would exceed the benefit of drivers from traffic (this is a principle described in the second chapter).

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: It can also be assumed that the prices for using the roads would vary depending on the time of day; they would probably be higher at peak times (which would prevent road owners from overfilling them), and lower at off-peak times (thus attracting more customers). This would naturally incentivize drivers to plan their journeys (if they can) for non-congested times. Likewise, people's motivation to travel in groups (more people per car) would also increase - especially during peak hours, when prices are the highest. Many of the things that various transport experts are trying to do in vain, that we now pay for with taxes, would be solved by the free market quite naturally and spontaneously; moreover, these market goals are really set by the wishes of the public, as they are shaped by every driver and road owner every time they enter into a business transaction (as opposed to state management, where the ideas of various experts or officials about what people want can differ greatly from reality).

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: What about the rules of the road? This would always be determined by the owner of each road. In connection with this, one can encounter a very common objection that these rules would differ from road to road. Yes, it could be a little different, which - if it's about small things - is not a bad thing, because then the rules can be tailored to each specific road. However, the basic things (which side to drive on, where to give priority...) would be the same practically everywhere, because every road owner is interested in the fact that there are as few accidents as possible, traffic is smooth and his customers feel good (nonsensical - or too different - rules thus deprive him of profit). Examples of where the same principles already work today can be seen, for example, in the form of credit cards or barcodes. Despite the absence of state standards and regulations that would regulate the form of the barcode or the shape of credit cards at the time of their creation, credit cards from different companies are compatible with each other with readers, and millions of entities around the world use a few barcode standards. No one makes up any crazy or different rules because that would hurt themselves. There is no reason to believe that it would be any different with the rules of the road.

title: 12. Road and traffic rules
text: In conclusion, I would ask the esteemed reader to notice how many problems that various governments around the world have been unsuccessfully struggling with for many years could be solved by the free market without the need for some crazy social engineering, promotion of alternative means of transportation, traffic calming and other regulations at the taxpayers' expense. Something similar can be said about the environment, the management of which we will look at in the next chapter.

title: 13. Environment
text: Environmental protection is one of the areas that is commonly cited as an example of a field where the so-called free market has failed, so that it is supposed to be regulated by the state. Unlike most state-regulated industries, around which much debate and emotion revolve, environmental protection is not so often shaken up in discussions of anarcho-capitalism; just as usual almost everyone "knows" that the state has to do it because otherwise "it wouldn't work". So let's think a little deeper about this topic.

title: 13. Environment
text: Sometimes I ask myself how the state actually plays the role of environmental protector from a practical point of view; and unlike other industries, strangely, I can't answer at first glance around me that it does wrong. In the case of environmental protection, it is not very clear what it means that it is done well. It can be completely untouched nature and people living in trees, or "sustainable development" or whatever. So the only acceptable standard is probably that nature should look the way it suits people best; and the best way to achieve such a state is the free market. So here we could end with a reference to the eleventh chapter and a statement that the state should not exist, that is, should not own anything, and let the owner decide on the protection of nature on each plot; however, let's break it down in detail.

title: 13. Environment
text: Environmental protection shows - perhaps better than anything else - the futility of the various methods of collecting data for central planning based on the government asking people something, letting them vote on it and so on. There are not a few people in our population who, on the one hand, claim that nature is suffering, evil industry is destroying it, people are tormenting animals, big cities are swallowing up forests, and when they are done, they go to their warm city apartment, where they enjoy genetically modified chickens, drink them artificial industrial soda, wash themselves in warm water and go to sleep in a wooden bed. It is precisely these people who often devalue the results of the vote by proudly advocating for the strictest possible protection of nature, without understanding that by doing so they are not only restricting some "bad businessmen", but especially their customers, i.e. themselves. For this reason, democratic decision-making on nature protection can go against the voters.

title: 13. Environment
text: But why should private land owners care about nature? Wouldn't they prefer financial gain? Well, these two things very often go hand in hand. If someone owns a piece of nature that people appreciate, it is possible to make money from it; and the more they appreciate it, the higher the possible earnings. Many may also buy unspoilt places with no financial gain in mind, just for the nature itself; interested parties can also participate in such purchases within various associations and associations. Furthermore, the more "threatened" nature becomes and the rarer untouched places become, the higher their price will be and the lower the motivation to dispose of them (see the first chapter).

title: 13. Environment
text: Sometimes one can come across the argument that if the various nature reserves had their own owners, no one could prevent them from building, for example, a production line in the middle of their pristine and beautiful forest. They could theoretically do that, but it is not very likely. Those who want a production hall are mostly looking for profit; and that is exactly why there is no reason to build it in the forest, for which some are willing to pay just to keep it untouched (which can be individuals, but also an association of people who agree to it, or an entrepreneur who wants to make some money from the nature reserve). Therefore, it is generally more advantageous for a manufacturer to buy land whose market price will be lower (or the location is better).

title: 13. Environment
text: The same applies to the protection of endangered animals. Since the state typically does not allow such animals to be profited from (for example, ivory), the motivation to protect them is not very high, and poachers kill them no matter what (see the tragedy of the communal pasture in chapter eleven). One example for all: There were several million bison in America, on which the culture and society of the Indians, which the American government wanted to get rid of, were very dependent; therefore, in 1871, Congress passed a law that authorized the total extermination of bison (any hunter could shoot any bison regardless of who owned it), which almost led to their complete extermination (in 1889, there were a total of 542 left). When that law was repealed, the "Bison Rescue Society" and many private bison farms were formed. Today, bison are no longer an endangered species; their number is estimated at three hundred thousand pieces.

title: 13. Environment
text: Pollution is a big problem for the environment. Who will prevent waste from chemical and industrial production from being discharged directly into rivers? The owners of those rivers, of course; in such a case, they can sue whoever pollutes their river (the possible course of such lawsuits in a stateless society is described in the next two chapters). Even if the polluter were to buy the piece of river into which he discharges his waste, it still doesn't solve anything, because he still damages all the downstream owners of that river who might sue him or try to assert their rights in some other way; in light of this, the construction of a treatment plant and the non-discharge of pollutants appear to be a reasonable investment. A similar principle can be applied to air pollution.

title: 13. Environment
text: But what about waste? Without the existence of states, wouldn't we make the planet one big dump? In such considerations it is necessary to realize that without states there would be no "public lands"; each plot of land would have an owner who would be damaged by the dump. Waste disposal would therefore be operated by entrepreneurs who would be paid for this service by those who want to get rid of waste.

title: 13. Environment
text: Many argue in relation to waste that the state supports and subsidizes recycling, so it is necessary. What is such recycling actually good for? On the one hand, it reduces the amount of waste and, on the other hand, saves new natural resources. On the other hand, the recycling process itself consumes some resources (both natural, but also human labor and the like). So how do you find the right measure of what to recycle and what not? Astute readers probably already guess that the answer to this question can be found in the first chapter of this book. When it is cheaper to make new products from waste than to process the waste on the one hand and extract other raw materials on the other, it means that recycling actually saves resources. If it is the other way around, it means that the resources consumed by the recycling process are more scarce than the resources needed to dispose of waste and extract new raw materials. In other words, recycling saves resources if and only if it is – without any subsidies – profitable. So government subsidies for recycling are harmful and lead to waste.

title: 13. Environment
text: Another popular topic is sustainable development. This doctrine preaches that we should not consume so-called non-renewable resources (or only under the condition of complete recyclability). There is an assumption that a stateless society would not follow this thesis; after all, they don't do it even the current states, although it can be argued that some governments try to do so to a certain extent, at least occasionally. But what is the biggest flaw in this doctrine? It completely ignores development. It is not entirely dissimilar to the medieval theory of the maximum possible size of the city, which was based on the fact that such a city would be supplied by horses carrying grain from the surrounding fields, while due to the given minimum amount of land necessary for the sustenance of man and horses, the distance from a certain number of inhabitants would grow to such an extent that the horses overcoming these distances would consume all the grain that had to be transported for their own sustenance. The doctrine of sustainable development is equally short-sighted and naive when it assumes that humanity will continue to obtain energy in the same ways. For example, such oil: It is running out, thirty years ago it was supposed to run out in thirty years, today it is supposed to run out in thirty years, and in thirty years it will probably also run out in thirty years. All these forecasts take into account the current amount of known oil, but do not consider that the shortage increases the price, which motivates entrepreneurs to search for additional resources. And they don't take into account the possibility that over time oil may not be the basis of our fuels at all (coal used to be). In the words of Professor Julian Lincoln Simon: "Nor did the Stone Age end because we ran out of stone."

title: 13. Environment
text: A similar problem is the cutting down of rainforests. This is not yet a threat to life on Earth; if it starts to happen, people will understandably be willing to devote their resources to finding a solution (planting new trees, buying up relevant land from opponents of felling, or whatever). Just because we can see a hypothetical crisis in the future doesn't mean the government has to regulate and tax us today; the closer we are to a threat, the more willing people are to donate funds voluntarily (which is already starting to happen - for example, billionaire Johan Eliasch bought a piece of the Amazon forest to prevent mining). Not to mention that the states "protect" us even from problems they don't even know how to solve yet; let's take global warming as an example, because of which we were forced to spend a huge amount of resources even on inefficient or even counterproductive solutions (for example fertilizing the oceans with iron, quotas for biofuels leading to deforestation, planting monocultures or electric cars in countries where energy comes from coal), just to "make something happen" - without sufficiently analyzing the impacts and consequences beforehand.

title: 13. Environment
text: History shows that attempts to solve "global problems" tend to be either ineffective, or they solve something that isn't even a real problem, or both. Despite how many times someone has sounded the alarm in the name of "saving the planet" and how many times people have been forced to finance "solutions to the problem", only rarely has such an effort led to at least a somewhat meaningful result; however, it turned out more than once that we were just wasting resources unnecessarily. The free market, on the other hand, has already demonstrated its ability to solve problems (for example, by mechanizing agriculture or replacing coal - as a fuel for means of transport - with oil).

title: 13. Environment
text: In conclusion, I would like to point out that even in the case of environmental care, we have - similarly to other fields of human activity - two options: Let free people decide for themselves what they actually want and express their preferences on the free market; or decisions about scarce resources can be placed in the hands of governments and their experts motivated to view problems only one-sidedly to meet (perhaps only an implicit) political agenda (see the "Climategate" affair). I will leave it to each reader to decide which is better. And already in the next chapter, we will finally get to one of the basic differences between anarcho-capitalism and minarchism (the theory supporting a minimal state), namely private and state justice.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: Judiciary, security forces, defense against an external enemy. Finally we come to the most interesting and at the same time the most controversial topics of this book; in addition to the fact that most people do not even allow the hypothetical possibility of the existence of the above without states and their governments, they also make these areas stand out due to differences of opinion between anarcho-capitalists and minarchists (advocates of a minimal state). In this chapter we will focus on courts and the judicial system; however, we will leave aside for now the question of how to judge someone who refuses to cooperate, or how to subsequently force them to respect the court's decision - this is dealt with in chapter fifteen.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: Why replace state courts with private ones? There are two basic reasons: the judiciary in the hands of the state is both immoral and inefficient. The immorality lies, as always, in governments funding the courts from taxes they have collected under threat of violence; everyone has to pay whether they want to or not, which is unethical and unacceptable. The inefficiency can be seen in the functioning of the courts themselves: Judges sometimes make completely absurd decisions, they often put the letter of the law above its spirit and practically always above the wishes of the litigating parties, no one is held responsible for court errors (unless it is demonstrably bad intent), and it is not an exception that court proceedings last for years (and almost nothing can be decided in less than a number of months).

title: 14. Judiciary
text: At the very beginning of the defense of a free judiciary, I consider it important to mention that the ideas presented in this chapter certainly do not describe some unproven theory. There are many examples of well-functioning non-state courts. Leaving aside anarchist societies such as medieval Iceland or Ireland, where there were no state courts at all, one can also find many examples of private justice functioning in parallel with state courts. For example, mercantile law, which arose in England due to the inability of the state courts to resolve merchants' disputes, was not supported by state power in any way, and the decisions of the merchant courts were not enforced by force; yet – or perhaps because of that – it was so successful that it eventually became an internationally recognized law. Maritime law also underwent an almost identical development. In recent history, there has been a great boom in arbitration companies in the US, which have decided millions of disputes; although their decisions were not legally binding until 1920, their services were widely sought and used.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: These examples clearly disprove the fairly widespread myth that the judicial system is useless without a repressive component enforcing its decisions by force; this is demonstrably not the case. Why? There are many reasons. First, there are other "punishments" than violent aggression (for example, merchant law was enforced by ostracization: With a merchant who disobeyed the court's decision, others stopped making contracts, thereby practically destroying his business; nowadays information spreads very efficiently, which makes ostracization probably much more effective than before, when the ostracized could solve his situation by moving far enough away). Second, violent dispute resolution is generally expensive; it may often be more beneficial for both parties to go to an arbitrator voluntarily – and respect his decision – than to enter into an open conflict (especially if the arbitrator finds a reasonable compromise). Thirdly, there may be disputes in which even the participants are not quite sure who is actually in the right and really care about finding the truth; there then a wise judge can help without using violence very easily. And fourth, the arbitrator can discover a solution to the problem that suits both parties, but for various reasons they did not come to it on their own. I am certainly not advocating the thesis that perhaps all conflicts could be resolved only by courts without force components enforcing their decisions; I am only pointing to the fact that even courts whose decisions are not enforced by force can solve problems on a mass scale to the satisfaction of their participants.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: Who would appoint a judge in a stateless society? The answer is simple: Arbitrators would be "appointed" by the people themselves simply by requesting their services. The judge could be anyone agreed upon by both sides of the dispute, whether it be a totem pole-carving grandpa from Canada who decides a neighborhood dispute in a village, or a renowned corporation with many years of judicial experience who conducts a complicated arbitration between other huge corporations. The demand for such services would give rise to companies in the free market that would make a living precisely by deciding disputes.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: So anyone can be a judge. But how do the disputing parties in a dispute agree on which arbitrator will resolve their dispute? Well, first of all, there is a huge group of cases in which this problem is likely to disappear completely. These are disagreements over some existing contract; in a free society without a centralized judiciary, it can be assumed that every contract will contain a clause about which arbitrator will resolve any disagreements related to the given contract - this way, problems can be avoided with minimal effort. The arbitration company can take care of more complicated contracts comprehensively, i.e. from their proposal to the resolution of possible issues. When there is no contract and the dispute arose spontaneously, two possibilities remain: Either both parties are interested in reaching an agreement (because fighting would be expensive and risky), so they agree on an arbitrator that is acceptable to both parties; or at least one of the parties is not interested in a peaceful solution, which we will deal with in the fifteenth chapter.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: The most common—albeit very short-sighted—objection to such a system goes something like this: "And what's to stop private arbitrators from deciding the dispute in favor of whoever pays more?" The answer is very simple: The main thing private arbitrators live by is their reputation. Once they lose them and prove to be venal, people will stop seeking their services. The opinion of the disinterested environment determines the credibility of the court, which is critical for its survival. On the other hand, the tendency to bribery is much higher in the state sphere, where a corrupt judge can make one dubious decision after another, but until someone catches him practically with a bribe in his hand, he remains a judge and people simply have to entrust him with their cases. The fact that private arbitrators are much more difficult to bribe than state ones is best shown by the fact that for hundreds and thousands of years people have turned to them with confidence and paid for their services, even though they usually have the opportunity to use the so-called "free" services of the state.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: The good reputation of a private court is, of course, not only based on impartiality and incorruptibility, but also on its efficiency, reliability, quick decision-making and customer friendliness. Unlike state courts, which have their income from taxes certain and cannot lose it, so they don't really care how their services are perceived by customers, private arbitrators have to work hard to keep their clients and attract others. There is no reason why there should not be a competitive struggle to lower the price and increase the quality of service precisely in the delivery of justice in the free market.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: Despite all these indisputable advantages of independent arbitrators over state judges, one crucial question remains. Under what laws will private arbitrators adjudicate in the absence of uniform state legislation? Well, according to those that suit people the most; that's how it is in the free market. Each of the millions of entrepreneurs who decide to make a living as freelance judges will have their own vision of what the law should look like "correctly". Some of them declare in advance the laws according to which they intend to decide, others rely on common law, others choose a system of precedents combined with enlightened arbitrators, or anyone can come up with a combination of the above or with something completely new. Those whose ways will please the people will earn; others go bankrupt.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: But won't there be total chaos in the judiciary if each arbitrator decides according to different laws? Here again, it should be remembered that the solutions that are successful in the free market are precisely those that suit people the most. In a society where legal confusion prevails, there will probably be a demand for unification, which will also give rise to a supply: Groups of judges will unify their laws and decision-making methods in an attempt to gain a competitive advantage over others and attract more clients, no longer wanting to study different rules or laws for every dispute (or contract they enter into). It can be assumed that in the end there will be a few less proven methods that will be changed only at least when needed by customers; after all, history shows that the problem of too many different ways of resolving legal disputes does not arise in a free market judiciary.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: This way of making laws has one fascinating consequence: The rules are made just as the people they affect want them to be. There is no need to pay any (potentially corruptible) legislators to forcefully impose their idea of law on society; there is no need for a comedy called "democratic elections" in which we try to guess which of the political parties will fulfill at least a fraction of their promises. People can make decisions about laws simply by making them and supporting those whose laws suit them, directly by paying them to settle disputes.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: One can often meet with the objection that the entire stateless judiciary will end up in such a way that the laws will be set only in favor of the rich and powerful, while the "ordinary person" will not have a chance to get the right. Little could be further from the truth. To enforce a harmful law in anarcho-capitalism requires a large number of independent judges to start enforcing it, and people would have to agree with it at least to the extent that it is not worth it for them to start using the arbitration services of other arbitrators en masse; however, when the rules of justice are determined by the state, the consent of a few (often paid) individuals is sufficient to enact such a malevolent law.

title: 14. Judiciary
text: Although the idea of private provision of court services is not as absurd and crazy as it may seem at first glance, we have so far avoided analyzing cases in which at least one of the parties does not cooperate and is not inclined to settle the dispute amicably. What then? The answer to this interesting question can be found in the fifteenth chapter.

title: Free judiciary and the principle of non-aggression
text: The third chapter of this book discusses the principle of non-aggression (a system of law based only on property rights), which I assume to be "valid" in anarcho-capitalism (by validity here I do not mean its unconditional observance by everyone, always and under all circumstances, but only so much that most conflicts will be resolved approximately in accordance with it). Despite this, in Chapter Fourteen, where we dealt with courts and dispute resolution, the principle of non-aggression was not mentioned at all. For those who find it strange, this sub-chapter is intended, in which I will try to clarify the connection between property rights and a free judiciary; however, it is not a completely relaxing read, so whoever does not want to deal with this topic (which I am writing about only to maintain completeness and correct argumentation), should feel free to skip it.

title: Free judiciary and the principle of non-aggression
text: From the previous chapter, private arbitrators in the free market decide disputes in the way that is most convenient for the people. At the same time, throughout the book, I am based on property rights. Aren't these thought constructs incorrect? Not if it turns out that free market arbitrators will typically rule in accordance with the non-aggression principle. That they do so judge is "coincidentally" shown by the whole history of private justice; almost all known human societies in which free stateless courts functioned (examples of which can be found in the previous chapter) were governed by natural (property) law roughly in the sense of the principle of non-aggression, or something very similar to it. This fact suggests to some extent that property rights may indeed be somehow "encoded" in our brains, as mentioned in chapter three (although there is probably no way to conclusively prove such a thing, this observation can be taken as some indication). Historical experience also gives rise to the assumption that since private judges have so often ruled approximately in accordance with the principle of non-aggression, they could continue to do so; yet it does not by itself explain why this is so, which I will attempt to do in this subsection.

title: Free judiciary and the principle of non-aggression
text: Probably, each of us has already encountered the sentence: "The freedom of one ends where the freedom of another begins." Personally, I don't really like this vague phrase, because it's actually a tautology that applies under all conditions. After all, the freedom of the camp guards ended where the freedom of their prisoners began. In order for the claim to make sense, moreover, the unspoken assumption must hold that the limit of freedom lies "in the middle" between those affected. In that case, it is a very noble idea. Let's look at it now from two different points of view.

title: Free judiciary and the principle of non-aggression
text: First, let's compare it with the principle of non-aggression. This is clearly not contradicted by the fact that a property-only system of law is completely non-arbitrary and does not grant anyone a priori more authority than anyone else, so that the limit of freedom between arbitrary individuals is always precisely "in the middle" in accordance with this principle. Of course, one can imagine other concepts of law that do not contradict the thesis that the freedom of one ends where the freedom of another begins (extended with the premise that the border must be "in the middle"), but such concepts are highly unsystematic and, moreover, contrary to property rights.

title: Free judiciary and the principle of non-aggression
text: Second, let us compare this thesis with the decision-making of free judges. As stated in the previous chapter, the impartiality and impartiality of these courts form the cornerstone of their very existence. If a private arbitrator is not impartial, people will stop asking for his services. But what else is impartial decision-making other than trying to draw the line of freedom between the parties to the dispute as close as possible to the "mean"? That is exactly what private arbitrators will attempt.

title: Free judiciary and the principle of non-aggression
text: These two perspectives on the same thing partly explain why free judges usually try to rule in accordance with property rights. Why is the explanation only partial? Because, as already stated above, there are still other concepts of law that do not contradict the search for the limit of freedom "in the middle" between conflicting individuals, but they contradict the principle of non-aggression. An example would be the imaginary legal system, which does contain the principle of non-aggression, but also its "extension", which imposes on everyone the duty to take care of their parents when they are old; such an idea may be noble, but contrary to property rights and requiring offensive violence - that is, aggression against those who reject this "law". However, opinions on similar modifications of the law based on the principle of non-aggression differ widely; each would prefer to apply others. If an arbitrator admits something like this, his decision-making process begins to differ from the others, putting him at a disadvantage against them and he may lose customers (see the previous chapter). The more he moves away from property rights, the more different his decisions will be compared to other judges, because the principle of non-aggression is a kind of smallest subset of rules that can be said to apply equally to everyone (and the judge therefore decides impartially according to them).

title: Free judiciary and the principle of non-aggression
text: An objection to such considerations, which can sometimes be encountered, can be put something like this: "And where is the guarantee that the courts will actually recognize the principle of non-aggression? What if there is a market demand for mass trampling of property rights?" Of course, there is no such guarantee. Although history shows that this does not happen in free societies, it cannot be guaranteed that it will not be different in the future. But what guarantees does the state give us that it will not become a totalitarian state? Also none. However, there is one difference; all of history is full of examples of this actually happening. And the absence of such a guarantee in anarcho-capitalism also brings with it one more advantage: The principle of non-aggression is not an absolute given that people must follow no matter what (this is how states try to present their laws); a judge can - if he finds the strict application of property rights inappropriate in a specific case - simply decide otherwise (and if people think this decision is wise, the judge will gain customers, otherwise he will lose them; in this way, he bears - unlike state judges - full responsibility for his decisions).

title: Free judiciary and the principle of non-aggression
text: I hope that after including all the above aspects, it is no longer a mystery to the reader why courts in free societies have mostly followed the principle of non-aggression, or some very similar concept. For the same reasons, property rights can be expected to be recognized in any civilized society that is not corrupted by the state. Today, however, it ensures the enforcement of court decisions in cases where at least one of the parties to the dispute refuses a peaceful solution; therefore, in the next chapter, we will focus on how this area could also function without state intervention.

title: 15. Law enforcement
text: The preceding chapter deals with a free judiciary; shows why private arbitrators resolve disputes more morally and efficiently than state judges, but deals only with dispute resolution as such - completely ignores the enforceability of court decisions; this is especially crucial in cases where someone commits a crime and knows very well that any court would find him guilty, so he is not interested in any arbitration. The aim of this chapter is to explain how an anarcho-capitalist society could deal with such evils.

title: 15. Law enforcement
text: Most states use the police for these purposes. What's wrong with that? Apart from the two usual arguments, namely that it is not moral (the police are paid from forcibly collected money) and efficient (the free market can allocate resources for police protection better than the state - see the second chapter), there is one more fundamental reason why police power - the monopoly on violence - should not be entrusted to the state: History shows that whenever things go wrong and a despotic tyrant comes to power, this power is always used against its own citizens. Even so, most people argue against power components in private hands by saying that they could be misused against the population, although we know anarchist societies (medieval Iceland or Ireland) in which nothing similar happened on a mass scale not once in the many hundreds of years of their existence; on the other hand, history is full of cases of massive abuse of state forces, and it is actually impossible to find a populated area in the hands of the state where this has not happened repeatedly over such a long time horizon.

title: 15. Law enforcement
text: It can be assumed that not everyone will want to rely on their own abilities in the event of becoming a victim of crime; even the assumption that there will not be a majority of such people is not very bold. Demand for protection against criminals creates supply; entrepreneurs will be able to make money by offering people the services of their security agencies to help them in case they become victims of an aggressor. Payment for such services can be either one-time or flat-rate. These security agencies would likely employ both detectives to investigate crimes and mercenaries trained in the use of weapons to openly fight criminals.

title: 15. Law enforcement
text: So what will happen if, for example, someone robs a customer of such a security agency? The first problem is to find the perpetrator. The detectives begin to search and find evidence. If no one is found, the victim may – depending on the wording of the contract – receive compensation from the security agency because it failed to perform the task for which it is paid (this service is not unlike theft insurance). If the culprit is caught, it depends on how he reacts to the whole thing. When he capitulates and settles with the victim for compensation, everything is settled. However, if he protests (for example, he may plead not guilty, or plead guilty, but call the victim's demands for compensation absurdly high), the security agency will refer the matter to a private arbitrator (see Chapter Fourteen), who will decide on it; if the person submits to his verdict, all is well. If he does not comply, the security agency will force him to do so (in this case, however, it is not offensive violence, as it is committed against the person who first himself did not respect the victim's property rights).

title: 15. Law enforcement
text: I imagine most readers might have thought something along the lines of, "Why would an agency go to an arbitrator when it can force the alleged perpetrator to cooperate anyway and save court costs?" Well, such a reasoning supposes that the use of violence is cheaper than a settlement by arbitrators, which cannot be considered too probable; even if the salary of a private judge in the free market exceeded the salary of a mercenary, there are still a number of other factors that make violence more expensive: Even a trained mercenary can hypothetically be overpowered and killed by his target (especially if an attack is expected), someone else could be harmed as part of a violent solution (a potential or even a current client of a security agency), anyone can try to take revenge on the person in question (which potentially causes further losses) and last but not least, by extrajudicial killings, the security agency will make many enemies and will not enjoy a good name, which is important for such a company not only because people ask for its services, but also because it will often make its job easier if disinterested people cooperate with it in the search for criminals (if in the eyes of the public such a security agency is really a fair organization that pursues criminals, it can certainly be imagined that it will receive much more support for such an activity than if people perceived as a bloodthirsty mafia). Furthermore, security agency clients typically do not demand the death of the person who harmed them; much more often they want to be compensated, which murdering the criminal does not solve in itself.

title: 15. Law enforcement
text: It should also be noted that while all of the above arguments apply to those who are not clients of any security agency, there is an even stronger argument for everyone else (which may be the majority): If a given security agency were to try to eliminate a customer of another agency, an armed conflict could easily ensue, costing both sides money; war is expensive (especially for someone who pays for it out of their own money, not out of taxes) and waging it just to avoid a court service fee is absurd.

title: 15. Law enforcement
text: Thus, each security agency will likely have contracts with arbitrators. In the event of a conflict between two clients of the same agency - or a conflict between its client and someone who is not protected by any agency - one of the judges with whom the agency has a contract will decide. If there is a dispute between clients of two different security agencies, the decision will be made by one of the arbitrators with whom the two companies involved have a contract (if there is none, they can agree on something, which is still cheaper than war).

title: 15. Law enforcement
text: People often ask for assurances that the biggest security agencies won't band together and take over the entire company. Of course, this cannot be guaranteed. But what is the guarantee that any state will not become a dictatorship? Also none; and how many times has this happened! However, there are many arguments against a stateless society being controlled by its own security agencies. In addition to the fact that a corporation so large as to have the potential to enslave some larger territory is usually not decided by one person, but by many shareholders, it is not just about controlling "ordinary people", as there are many economically powerful entities in such a territory (of which there are - in all fields combined - probably more than security agencies); and they can defend themselves effectively - even if combat is not their primary focus, they can hire mercenaries. Not to mention that in an anarcho-capitalist society "ordinary people" will also be armed much more often, making it much more difficult to control them by force. In addition, even the remaining security agencies that do not join the "bad" ones will face the aggressors in the first place, because what is better advertising for a company doing business in the given field than to eliminate such a danger? And what if everything still failed and the company was taken over by a few powerful corporations? Well, then our fates would not be decided by a few deputies as now, but by a few shareholders; the most catastrophic result is the creation of a monopoly on violence, i.e. the state.

title: 15. Law enforcement
text: So far we have dealt with cases where the crime has already occurred; but how would it be possible to prevent the ones that are happening right now? Suppose that a robber has robbed an innocent person in the street, and there is a mercenary patrolman of a security agency standing nearby, who does not know whether the person in question is a customer of his employer; what now The victim can call that law enforcement officer for help, making a verbal contract with the security agency. But what if the attack is already in an advanced stage and the victim is unconscious? Will that private policeman intervene even without being asked? Most likely, his employer will give him such instructions. First, he cannot know whether his client is in danger; if that was really the case, the ranger would not have intervened and the case would have become known, people would probably have lost interest in the services of such a security agency. Secondly, with such help, the security agency can win a new customer, because the one whose property and maybe even his life were saved will be more amenable to concluding a contract. Third, it is possible that even if this robber's attack was not directed against a client of the given security agency and the mercenary let him escape, the next victim could be another customer of his employer, costing him additional resources. And fourth, there is a rational assumption that security agencies will enter into agreements to provide mutual aid to their clients in an emergency, since it is cheaper to prevent crime on the spot than to investigate it retrospectively.

title: 15. Law enforcement
text: It is often argued that if private security services are provided, the poor will not be able to afford them, so everyone will rob and kill them with impunity. This problem was solved with remarkable elegance by the free market of medieval anarchist Iceland: The aggrieved poor man – as the victim of a crime – was entitled to compensation from the perpetrator (in the case of murder, the heirs were compensated); he donated part of the claim in advance to someone rich who had the means to extort it. Such a gift was beneficial for the rich (he could demand compensation from the criminal without anything happening to him) and also for the poor (no one could harm him with impunity). It can be assumed that the poor could just as well enter into contracts with security agencies, which would take part of the compensation instead of a fee (the victim would receive less, but would gain a defense against the aggressor that they could not otherwise afford).

title: 15. Law enforcement
text: Much more could certainly be written about private security components, but the goal of this book is to provide the reader with a comprehensive idea of the possible forms of a free market society, which, in my opinion, could be harmed by too much detailed analysis. However, who would like to deal with this issue in more detail, I warmly recommend my favorite author, Murray Newton Rothbard, who has devoted himself to stateless provision of security to a large extent in many of his works; or also the first comprehensive texts on this topic, written in the nineteenth century by the French free-market economist Gustave de Molinari. So much for protection against internal danger; in the sixteenth – the last regular – chapter we will deal with the defense against the external enemy.

title: Crime and Punishment
text: Although the fifteenth chapter on the free market enforcement of law by security agencies mentioned the compensation that the criminal would have to pay to his victim after being caught, so far in the entire book we have not had the opportunity to read anything about punishing those who in some way violate someone else's property rights. I would like to remedy this in this chapter, in which I will offer several alternatives for how the free market in anarcho-capitalism could deal with the given problem.

title: Crime and Punishment
text: Why several? Well, as we already learned in the very introduction, no one can predict with certainty a free market solution to any problem; if it were possible, there would be no need for a free market at all, as it would be enough to set everything exactly that way through central planning. However, the second chapter explains that such a thing is not possible, so we have to settle for uncertain assumptions, which can be variously accurate depending on the detail of the problem they relate to. Therefore, although most anarcho-capitalist thinkers agree on, for example, how free market education, healthcare, the judiciary or protective services could work, there are considerable disagreements in the area of punishing criminals, within which many theories arise, of which I am going to present three and add my fourth. I leave it to the reader to judge what seems most reasonable to him, or I shall be glad if he himself suggests another alternative and sends it to me; I'm certainly not averse to discussion, and I still haven't found a solution to the issue of punishing criminals that I find completely satisfactory, although I'm sure the free market would come up with one.

title: Crime and Punishment
text: Before I start listing those theories, I would like to clarify the term "repair the damage", as I will use it in describing them. Damages repair means two things. First, an attempt to restore things to their original state: If it is theft, it is about returning the property to the owner; if damage occurs to non-unique tangible property (this can be a fence, for example), this means the purchase of a new such thing (or its repair, if the result is identical or if the owner agrees); if a unique material property (for example, the Mona Lisa) or someone's health is damaged, the solution is to pay all the expenses associated with trying to restore the thing to its original state (restoration of the painting, treatment of a fracture, etc.) and to pay compensation, the amount of which is determined by the judge based on an estimate of how much of the original value was lost (for the victim), or what the victim had to suffer (pain or permanent consequences). The distinction between unique and non-unique property in disputed cases is up to the judge. Second, reparation includes paying the costs of prosecuting the criminal and any courts, plus compensation for the time the owner was unable to use his property (for example, if someone breaks a programmer's arm and he can't program because of it, he - or his employer - should be reimbursed for lost profits).

title: Crime and Punishment
text: The strictest of the theories says that if someone infringes someone else's property rights with proven intent, the victim is the only person who can judge how painful the aggressor caused him, so the punishment for him is determined by the victim to a completely arbitrary extent. In the event of an unintentional violation of property rights, the person who violated them must repair the damage. Personally, I find this theory the least acceptable, as it allows draconian punishments to be imposed for ridiculous misdemeanors.

title: Crime and Punishment
text: According to another theory, the attacker, who disrespected the victim's property rights to a certain extent, must on the one hand repair the damage, and the victim also has the right to disrespect his property to the exact same extent that the person in question did it to the victim before. Therefore, if someone steals a million crowns, they must return the million (and pay all the expenses associated with obtaining it and any losses that the robbed person suffered because he could not dispose of the money) plus - as a punishment - pay the victim another million. If someone breaks another's arm, he must both repair the damage, and he can also break his arm (or agree with him not to do so if he pays him additional compensation beyond what he has already paid - as punishment).

title: Crime and Punishment
text: The mildest theory, on the other hand, says that the aggressor should in any case only repair the damage and nothing more. His punishment should be additional expenses, as he would have to pay court costs, the costs of his prosecution, compensation for the time during which the victim could not dispose of his property, possible pain and so on. This solution seems to me the most natural of all; however, some may argue that perhaps it makes life too easy for criminals.

title: Crime and Punishment
text: The above approaches can be combined in various ways; for example: In the event that someone intentionally violates another's property rights, the victim should be able to choose whether he wishes to have the damages remedied or whether he would prefer to violate the aggressor's property rights to the same extent. For damage caused to property, the differences will be minimal (someone took a million, so the robbed person either demands the million back from him or wants to take another of his millions; it probably differs only in that, as part of repairing the damage, the aggressor still has to pay court costs, other compensation, and so on). A more interesting situation occurs when someone damages another person's health. In such a case, he can either ask for standard compensation, or he can want to harm the aggressor out of a desire for revenge, but there is another possibility: The victim can choose to violate the aggressor's rights to the same extent that he did it to her, but the goal is not to maim him, but to ask him for money for not doing so, which can be more than what the victim would get in the standard way (or the attacker does not comply, he prefers to let himself be injured and the victim gets nothing). In case of unintentional infringement of property rights, the infringer would then have to repair the damage.

title: Crime and Punishment
text: Implicit in all the above examples is the assumption that the victim of the violation of his property rights survived. But what if not? Well, in that case, her claim against the assailant passes to the heirs (which, of course, doesn't have to mean just family members; especially not if the murderer is among them), who sue the aggressor instead of the victim. For this reason too, I find the theory that the attacker should only try to repair the damage insufficient - if someone kills your child, the most they can do is pay you a lot of money. According to my theory, you can choose whether you want compensation or punishment (either you can kill the offender outright or come up with practically any other punishment for him, as he is very likely to accept it rather than death).

title: Crime and Punishment
text: Are you wondering why the word "prison" has never been mentioned in this chapter yet? Well, that's because, although most states are so fond of using them as a universal means of punishing criminals, I consider this method to be probably one of the stupidest that can be invented. The victim of the criminal's stay in prison does not bring any financial benefit, at most a feeling of satisfaction from revenge, which can be achieved much easier (and cheaper; especially for taxpayers who have nothing to do with the crime in question). It is true that the criminal usually suffers in prison, which may deter him from further criminality, but this can also be achieved through other sufferings; incarcerating the person with other criminals and forcing him to live in this chosen society will give him enough space to adopt its moral values as his own, despite the fact that he can learn many new and interesting tricks from seasoned and experienced criminals that will allow him to improve in his "profession". And finally, there are "everyone else", who have absolutely nothing to do with the crime, but are nevertheless forced by the state to pay its punishment, which neither they nor the victim chose. It is easy to imagine that for a huge number of crimes, the victim would choose high financial compensation rather than revenge, the offender would also prefer payment to imprisonment, and citizens would welcome not having to pay for the criminal's stay behind bars; but why choose a solution that would suit all parties involved, when we have other, much worse, politicians and bureaucrats recognized as "proven"?

title: Crime and Punishment
text: Regardless of the fact that even in a stateless society, the imprisonment of criminals as such is not completely excluded. For example, if someone inflicts an injury on you with serious permanent consequences, under most of the above theories you have the option of inflicting the same injury on them in return. But if you give him the choice of letting you lock him up for a few years instead in a prison you build for him on your property, pay him a guard and feed him there and provide him with the basic necessities of life, he will probably agree. An interesting question arises, how many people would probably voluntarily choose this solution (instead of, for example, getting compensation paid, or - if they wanted revenge - doing something to the perpetrator in return), which would mean only expenses and no profit for them except for a zoo with a prisoner in the yard. Something tells me that there probably wouldn't be many of them if it was their money, their land, their worry, their lost profit. But when "society" pays the bills, it's easier to squander it in the interest of the "higher good".

title: Crime and Punishment
text: Although there are countless alternatives to how the free market in an anarcho-capitalist society could solve the problem of punishing criminals (and I hope to learn about some new possibility from one of the readers), I consider it almost certain that the result would not be as senseless as the state we can see around us. Indeed, if prisons were to function somehow in a stateless society, the prisoners would probably be forced to work in them and the fruits of their labor would be divided between the victims and the prison company; but something like that is just very hard to predict, because millions of entrepreneurs in a free market will practically always come up with a better solution.

title: 16. Army
text: In this chapter we will deal with what is probably the most difficult subject - namely, the defense of a stateless territory against an external aggressor, which can almost certainly be assumed to be a state, for as the world stands, free people, ruled by no one, have never attempted to occupy a large territory and subjugate its population; From time immemorial, wars have been the affairs of governments and rulers, not of their subjects, who, however, always bear the consequences and suffer for the decisions of their rulers, who are able to convince them from time to time - for their money - with mass propaganda that they actually want war. As an answer to the question why an area should be managed by free individuals and not by the state, I have always presented two reasons throughout the book - morality and efficiency. Nothing changes on the side of morality; the levying of funds by a State for national defense from its subjects by threatening them with violence if they do not pay, cannot be called moral by any stretch of the imagination. But what's worse, this "national defense" very often degenerates into a "national attack" in the hands of politicians, even if it's not called that (probably every country has a ministry of defense and probably none has a ministry of attack; despite what such ministries of many countries do in practice). The number of victims of all wars in the last century amounts to roughly three hundred million; all these lives were ruined by states (the ones we have here so that people don't kill each other in anarchy) and their armies.

title: 16. Army
text: But what about efficiency? Although even in the running of the military the typically great anarcho-capitalist thinkers credit the free market with its usual efficiency, I cannot agree with them on this point. Indeed, if we think again about why free market solutions are so much more efficient than state ones, we will come to the fact that the reason is mainly a huge number of entrepreneurs, each of whom will try to satisfy customers in the way he considers best, with those who do it well making money while others lose (see the first and second chapters); a huge advantage of the market over the state is its self-cleansing ability, meaning that the authors of bad solutions lose their capital and go bankrupt. Although none of these laws lose their validity even in the field of running the army, a failed defense against an external enemy, who must necessarily be someone who does not respect the principle of non-aggression (otherwise he would not be an aggressor), logically means the end of the free market in the given territory; it is therefore not possible to try different solutions "with impunity" and distinguish good from bad using profits and losses, which is the alpha and omega of market efficiency. Of course, it does not follow that the state solution would be more effective; only in my opinion it cannot be said that it would automatically be inefficient compared to the market, which is typically assumed by the great anarcho-capitalist thinkers - even the brilliant Murray Newton Rothbard, who deals with national defense in some detail in his works, argued for the effectiveness of the market compared to the state in this area without first dealing with this objection in any way.

title: 16. Army
text: I see the greatest weakness of an anarcho-capitalist society in the very limited ability to prevent the movement of enemy troops on its territory. States usually have a large amount of heavy weapons and technology developed directly for the purpose of warfare and destruction. It may be supposed that free men, who are not compelled to acquire such instruments, will (assuming the same amount of wealth in society) have fewer of them; and even the limited amount they will have cannot be moved anywhere without the consent of the owners of the given lands (and if someone tries to do so by force, they risk resistance, which costs at least time to suppress). It is possible to expect considerable motivation to cooperate against a common enemy, but it will never be as easy as in a state that owns land communications and whose citizens are governed by government orders rather than the principle of non-aggression.

title: 16. Army
text: As for the total volume of funds that a country with a given number of inhabitants will be able to invest in possible armaments, I do not find an advantage on either side. An anarcho-capitalist society will certainly be far more economically efficient than a state (which is the central theme of the entire book), but people are unlikely to be willing en masse to voluntarily sacrifice everything they have, including their lives, to warfare; although - except in exceptional situations - they will not do this even for their government, however, it has the means to force them to do so if necessary.

title: 16. Army
text: The indisputable advantage of an anarcho-capitalist society, on the other hand, lies in the fact that, although it is probably not so difficult to penetrate the territory where it is located, its effective control appears to be an extremely difficult task. If the army of one state occupies the territory of another state, the defeated government capitulates and the existing power structures in the given territory begin to enforce the will of the conqueror, who suddenly gains effective power over the population, because it was already registered, controlled, paid taxes and generally obeyed the government's orders; so there will only be a change in who gives the orders - the already existing means of violently subjugating those who disagree will simply be used by someone else. There is no such thing in an anarcho-capitalist society. The conqueror faces not masses, but individuals, for whom no one can speak and negotiate, and who, moreover, often speak a language that the invader's soldiers typically do not speak.
