Not to mention that free people - without state regulations and prohibitions - will probably be much better armed. In order for an aggressor to take control of such a territory in a conventional way, he would have to build all the power structures on it from scratch, which includes registering the entire population and forcing them to submit to laws that contradict everything these people have ever known and are accustomed to; all this must be done despite the language barrier and the weapons in the hands of free individuals who - unlike citizens of states - are used to solving their problems on their own. An invading army may, of course, begin to use brutal methods of coercion, razing cities and killing the inhabitants of the conquered territory on the spot; however, when this becomes known and the attacked understands that they have nothing to lose by meeting a foreign soldier, they will be in the given territory practically like a shooting range (it must be remembered that for every soldier of the aggressor there will probably be several armed inhabitants of the attacked country; and they will most likely shoot at each other).

title: 16. Army
text: Great Britain has been convinced at least twice in history that the difficulty of controlling a stateless society is not just a theory. It took her several centuries to conquer the much smaller and weaker Ireland, as the Irish had no state and power structures that would transmit orders to the common population. The English could not understand that, without any form of state, the Irish warriors who made treaties with them could only speak for themselves; they could never bind any other group of the Irish population. The British encountered a similar problem when conquering Africa, when they tried to subjugate the territory of the Ibo tribe (with an area of between seventy and eighty thousand square kilometers, i.e. about the size of the Czech Republic); its inhabitants lived in real anarchy (and in accordance with some libertarian principles), so they had no chiefs or leaders to follow. Controlling (that is, not just conquering by army) such a small piece of land was more difficult for the British than subduing the whole of India, where they could rule for centuries without much trouble, because they only transferred their orders to the ruling Indian princes, who then enforced them on their subjects.

title: 16. Army
text: "Oh well," many readers may be saying to themselves now: "but in the end the British conquered the Ibo territory anyway and Ireland as well, so that anarchy won't be very viable after all." Well, although most of the historical anarchist societies really disappeared by being conquered by some state, it must be remembered that the same end awaited most states. Some bigger and stronger empire just appeared and crushed and occupied the smaller and weaker one. All of the above analyzes of the advantages and disadvantages of states and stateless societies in war are based on the assumption that it is a conflict between two comparable rivals. However, if we consider a fundamentally unequal conflict, it is probably irrelevant to its outcome what kind of social arrangements we can find on the individual sides. For example, if we assume a conflict between the USA and the Czech Republic, the USA will most likely win, regardless of whether anarcho-capitalism or the state will be on one side or the other.

title: 16. Army
text: But what is the actual reason why no one is attacking the Czech Republic at the moment? None of the governments of larger and stronger states is apparently interested in our territory. If such an interest were strong enough, a reason would always be found (and international agreements will not change that, as they have been violated to the world's cost). Would the establishment of anarcho-capitalism be such a reason? In my opinion, no one can answer this question in a sound manner. Either a stronger and larger country would mercilessly take such territory, or not. Anyway, even if the invasion were to happen and be successful, the anarcho-capitalist society will end up as a state again, nothing worse can happen. The absurdity of the argument that we need a state because anarcho-capitalism could end up having a state in the worst case scenario probably doesn't need to be discussed too much.

title: 16. Army
text: However, even if the indefensibility of an anarcho-capitalist society on some small territory were to prove practical, it is not necessary to discard this entire concept as unusable. It would only mean that it probably can't withstand overwhelming odds, which a state generally can't either. The inability of a small territorial unit to resist says nothing about the defense possibilities of a huge anarcho-capitalist country.

title: 16. Army
text: And finally, it is also possible that if anarcho-capitalism proved to be functional in some territory for a certain time, it would be a compelling reason for the citizens of all states to try to establish the same system; in the case of mass success of such efforts, our world could reach a state in which defense against an external enemy would not be necessary. A world without states also means a world without wars. To be sure, there would continue to be local conflicts in various places, but as long as these were paid for out of the pockets of those who lead them, they would probably not have the potential to grow to such gigantic proportions as state wars.

title: Myth busting
text: In this bonus chapter, we will discuss some widespread misconceptions that are very often encountered in discussions of a stateless society, and which are typically characterized by the fact that they contain some kind of implicit assumption that is usually very well hidden in them and, moreover, appears to be true at first glance. The task of this chapter is to point out such assumptions and subsequently refute them.

title: Myth busting
text: I cannot begin otherwise than by mentioning a brilliant French thinker and economist who undertook this task absolutely brilliantly in the first half of the nineteenth century. He is none other than Claude Frédéric Bastiat. He dedicated his work "What is and what is not seen" precisely to the refutation of widespread errors; reading it, one can hardly help but be amazed at how many things that burned people two hundred years ago are still relevant today, as well as how many mistakes - disproved for two centuries - politicians are able to keep repeating and their voters believe. I strongly recommend everyone to read "What is and what is not seen" - it is a short reflection that is freely downloadable on the Internet; an hour or two will be enough to read it, during which you will gain more - and better - knowledge than by taking some economic - not to mention political science - course. However, within this chapter I will not deal with the fallacies that have been refuted for two centuries; anyway, the aforementioned French thinker did it much better than I could ever do.

title: Myth busting
text: A huge mistake, which in my opinion deserves a more detailed analysis, consists in the relatively widespread confusion of price and costs in fields that are practically completely controlled by the state. Just as the fact that Carl Menger - one of the founders of the Austrian school of economics - already in 1870 refuted Ricardo's cost theory of value (according to which the value of a good corresponds to the effort expended to create it) and replaced it with a subjective theory of value (the value of a good is equal to the highest price someone is willing to pay for it), did not prevent communists from following Marx's teachings in droves based on this disproved error, nor does it prevent today the general acceptance of the subjective theory of value (at least on an intuitive level) means that people often slip into the cost theory when judging the actions of the state. Then, for example, when the state pays price X to build a road, its value is assumed to be X (if there has been no embezzlement); however, this is obviously not true, because the value of the road is still equal to the amount that people would voluntarily be willing to pay for it, which could easily be less than X. In that case, the road should not have been built at all (or should have been built - perhaps worse - more cheaply). The same considerations can be encountered, for example, in the healthcare sector (people assume that the price of an intervention is fixed and equal to the current costs; they do not consider that it can be lower and the intervention should be performed cheaper - even if of a lower quality): Many people live in the idea that capitalist healthcare would look practically the same as the state one, only it would be financed differently; however, this idea (and all like it) contradicts the subjective theory of value and replaces it with the long-overdue cost theory.

title: Myth busting
text: Another mistake, which comes from the same roots, is often expressed by the objection: "If the state didn't pay for this or that, people wouldn't voluntarily give money for it." Even if we leave aside that such claims are typically based on the transfer of the current state to the anarcho-capitalist world (for example, the thesis that the state must provide people with pensions because they would not be able to do it themselves, since almost no one voluntarily saves for retirement now; however, the fact that people do not voluntarily save for pensions mainly because the state already does it for them is neglected), there remain some goods for which it is really true that if the state did not pay, people would not be willing to voluntarily finance them on the current scale. But what does that mean? Only so much that people prefer other things to these goods. Why? Because they'd rather buy something else with their money. So when the government forces people to pay something they would not voluntarily pay, they are worse off than they would have been without the coercion.

title: Myth busting
text: Very often, one can come across the following argument from the opponents of anarcho-capitalism: "What is the guarantee that one of the security agencies - or other powerful corporations - will not control the entire society and enslave everyone?" Well, of course there is no such guarantee. But not even in any state. Moreover - even if this were to happen - such a corporation would have a monopoly on violence and would effectively become a state. So this "brutal failure" of anarcho-capitalism means that it will turn into a state. "Sure," many argue, "but a state isn't like a state; a corporation that takes over an anarcho-capitalist society can be incredibly cruel and evil." It can, but why do so many people assume that the shareholders of large corporations will always do the worst, while politicians in government (however arbitrary) will not? Just look at the moral profiles of our current politicians! What is the probability that the shareholders of a corporation will be worse off?

title: Myth busting
text: Another popular argumentative nonsense is to compare anarcho-capitalism with a non-existent and unrealizable mythical ideal society that has no flaws, instead of comparing it with some concrete model (albeit a theoretical one). I have been a participant or witness countless times in discussions of anarcho-capitalism in which the proponent has been pushed by his opponents into a position where he has to defend a stateless society in completely absurd scenarios (the most extreme one I witnessed even involved a home-made black hole-creating device), while acknowledging that the result would be some kind of injustice, possibly someone's death, anarcho-capitalism is immediately ridiculed and considered bad. As if states did not cause anything like this, as if there were no wars in the modern world in which people die by the millions, as if there were no gulags and concentration camps, as if there were no evil. It must always be borne in mind that probably no anarcho-capitalist regards a stateless society as ideal and flawless; only for the best realistically possible. We do not claim that removing violent governments will solve all the world's problems; only that they will decrease.

title: Myth busting
text: When there is a general problem in a state-controlled society, people tend to call on the government to fix it. Is something wrong? Well, it will simply be banned, there is no easier solution. However, few people think about the side effects such a ban will have. And when someone rarely thinks about the direct consequences of a ban as such, they rarely include in their considerations the cost of enforcing it. If we are going to spend resources to enforce the ban, these must logically be missing elsewhere. Calling for state intervention should always be the last option (preferably so last that it doesn't happen at all).

title: Myth busting
text: Moreover, in our society we can see quite a few cases where the problem itself is caused by some law or regulation. A typical example is when states first force their citizens to accept unbacked currency and give banks the option to issue this currency, only to then have to create additional "regulations" to restrict banks in this activity, even though it would be sufficient to repeal the laws that cause this situation. By the way, who guessed why the word regulation is in quotes? Well, if something is regulated by one law, while a second law weakens the first, it makes sense to consider the second as deregulation, not regulation. From this, among other things, it follows that the so-called "deregulation" of banking, which is so often cited as the cause of the economic crisis, was in fact regulation (laws imposing the obligation to accept the national currency and enabling banks to issue it are regulatory; laws that weaken them are then deregulatory; ergo the weakening of these weakening laws constitutes regulation).

title: Myth busting
text: Considering that hundreds of such myths are planted in the minds of the general public, I could go on for a long time; and since new ones keep popping up, I've created a section on my website where I deal with refuting widespread falsehoods. You can view it at ankap.urza.cz; you can count on the fact that I will gradually expand it (at least I have done so so far).

title: Myth busting
text: However, I cannot close this chapter in any other way than with the words of the famous chef Zdenek Pohlreich, whose views are sometimes socialist, but he beautifully captured the principle why people are so prone to rejecting arbitrary changes (which of course also includes the transition from the state to anarcho-capitalism): "You know what most people consider the worst thing about every change? That then it's different." And indeed; how many arguments against anarcho-capitalism are de facto merely that something would be different?

title: Conclusion; and what next?
text: With this conclusion I would like to close the main part of this book on anarcho-capitalism; my primary goal in writing it was to present this school of thought in a nutshell, to inspire the reader to think and to familiarize them not only with what anarcho-capitalism is, but also to explain what it definitely is not. I don't consider it very important whether you all agree with me; however, I try to ensure that your agreement or disagreement flows from deeper reflection and is not just the result of a first impression. And if, in addition, the world view of at least some of you is at least a little more liberal after reading this book, then the time spent writing has brought me double fruit; and you certainly don't need to immediately identify yourself as an anarcho-capitalist. I can very well imagine that many consider the state necessary in some industries and not in others, which is perfectly understandable; even if I haven't convinced you about the necessity of state courts, police and army, for example, there's no need to immediately reject, for example, the idea of free-market schools or money. And if you're not satisfied with anything I've written, please try to at least take this book as inspiration to come up with something better.

title: Conclusion; and what next?
text: From time to time I am asked how I actually imagine the "introduction" or "establishment" of anarcho-capitalism in practice, but the answer to this question does not belong to the description of a stateless society, so you will not find it in any of the previous chapters; however, I will use this space for her. The only way to turn our society into an anarcho-capitalist one is to convince enough people of the beauty of freedom and the inviolability of property rights as the way to it. The more we are made to believe in this idea, the more will be its spreaders; at the same time, in democratic elections, people will give their votes to more liberal political parties, which can cancel both the laws that limit us the most, but also those due to which the state effectively spreads its propaganda, especially within the educational system.

title: Conclusion; and what next?
text: Make no mistake, I am certainly not in favor of "change from above" (from politicians); very fundamentally I believe that the initial impulse must come "from below", however, for change, more forces coming from both "from below" and "from above" are needed. We need theorists, debaters, thinkers and think tanks, but also populists, charismatic faces, entertainers and catchy slogans, in addition to the desperate, the underground, civil disobedience and the gray economy, but also lobbyists, diplomats and unfortunately also politicians with their political parties; I don't claim that politics will save us, because I myself consider it to be dirt, but even the contents of a stinking cesspool must be manipulated from time to time, even if one gets dirty. I personally am very happy that others do it for me, because I don't want to sell my own soul; however, I will not condemn these people, although it seems likely that any successful political party will eventually be corrupted by its own power - but until then it can serve the ideas of freedom.

title: Conclusion; and what next?
text: And when the state, as a result of this ants' work, is small enough to allow private entities to compete fully - without regulation - in all the areas in which it somehow interferes today, people will be able to convince themselves that it is not really needed; and if there is a sufficient number of such individuals with a non-negligible strength, the possibility of adequate defense against an aggressive state will arise for them. However, this one will by then be weak and - compared to the current one - relatively peaceful, so the opponents will probably not even try to take over by force, but will allow them to co-exist in parallel with it without interfering with their property rights, which I personally would consider an absolute victory; I don't need to destroy the state, I just want it to let me (and all those who wish the same) live in peace (even if such a "state" based on voluntariness will basically be a business).

title: Conclusion; and what next?
text: I have just indicated how, in my opinion, anarcho-capitalism could be put into practice. However, I would like to explicitly write a few words about how this should definitely not be the case, or how it cannot even be done in any case. In principle, the path to anarcho-capitalism cannot be a revolution or a coup; if a revolutionary seizes power, he can establish almost any regime, but not one that in principle excludes the very fact that someone holds power. Anarcho-capitalism certainly cannot be enforced by force, for it is impossible to force people to value their freedom if they do not do so out of their own convictions; they can be forced to build a better tomorrow in communism, to occupy more space for a superior race in Nazism, to follow the results of elections in a democracy, to listen to the word of the ruler in a monarchy, but it is not possible to push them to freedom by force, because such means are in direct conflict with the goal. Even if someone took over the government by force, then abolished it and relinquished power, another government would soon be established, if the people did not wish to have no government; if the revolutionary in question forbade them, he would become the ruler and the state himself. Offensive violence is not only an inappropriate and morally unacceptable means, but also does not lead to the goal, as it is in sharp contrast to it. Revolution is certainly not the way (and especially not a bloody revolution a hundred times).

title: Conclusion; and what next?
text: Although this conclusion is a full stop to the regular chapters in which we have always dealt with the free-market form of some whole industry now in the hands of the state, there are still other areas of state influence which I think deserve our attention; the following several - additional - chapters will be devoted to them, with which I will try to cover a few controversial topics that are often discussed in discussions about a stateless society.

title: Conclusion; and what next?
text: Although I have a weakness for similes, I have tried to avoid them throughout the book, as they are often misleading and inaccurate; here, after all, I won't forgive myself one thing at the end under the line.

title: Conclusion; and what next?
text: Let's imagine a country where people live unrestricted; they freely exchange their goods with each other, and no one interferes with their business. Then comes a group of "smart heads" who build a huge tunnel in the middle of the area. They will gather consumers on one side of this tunnel and producers on the other. "Smart heads" listen to the wishes of consumers, adjust them at their discretion, collect money from them and transport them through the tunnel to producers who produce on the basis of orders that also come to them from the tunnel. All exchange of certain types of goods outside the tunnel is prohibited. Producers and consumers thus become indifferent masses, individuality is lost. Consumer wishes are interpreted through an intermediary; the goods that come out of the tunnel are distributed among consumers regardless of payment, the key is the will of the "smart heads" and also how much someone shouts that they need. On the other side of the tunnel, producers do not try to provide their services tailored to consumers (they don't even know their preferences anyway), but only according to the wishes of the tunnel administrators.

title: Conclusion; and what next?
text: It is sheer madness to look for the primary cause of people's dissatisfaction - as opposed to the situation where they can trade directly - in the fact that, for example, "smart heads" keep something for themselves here and there (embezzlement), that some money is sometimes lost in the tunnel (high bureaucracy costs), that sometimes one of the producers or consumers bribes the tunnel manager to gain an advantage for himself (corruption), or that the tunnel managers are incompetent and unwilling (normal state of civil service). These problems certainly exist; however, they are secondary. Even if they could be solved or removed, the resulting situation would not improve much. The primary problem is, of course, the very existence of that tunnel, in which individuals with individual preferences become gray masses, a lot of information is lost there, and in general it only brings ruin and destruction.

title: Conclusion; and what next?
text: Above all, however – and I consider this much more important – it is not ethical for someone to dictate to another with whom and under what conditions they may and may not do business, or take their resources under the threat of violence; if he does so, he commits aggression towards him, which means only evil. The state is evil.

title: Drugs
text: It is not uncommon for people to believe that state regulation of narcotics—based on outlawing the sale and possession of many of them—protects society from drug addicts and related crime; I will now try to show why this reasoning is so incredibly misguided that even its opposite can be called a true statement.

title: Drugs
text: Personally, I consider the main reason why the state should not interfere in who and how much destroys their body with what drugs, the simple fact that this body does not belong to the state, but to the individual in question; and therefore he, not the state, should have the right to decide on it. If the government and the police prevent him from doing so, it grossly violates his rights. Although I myself consider this argument so fundamental that I no longer need any more, I fully understand that many readers think more pragmatically and are primarily interested in the overall impact on society; this is exactly what I would like to address in this chapter.

title: Drugs
text: When assessing the effects of prohibited narcotics on their users, one must first of all realize that addictive substances are not automatically bad for everyone, because only the person concerned can decide what benefits them and how much; if we try to impose our own assessment of life happiness on others, it will not work. There are people who will not even touch alcohol or even coffee (and if we were to adopt their standards, we should ban these drugs as well); then most have nothing against alcohol and coffee, but they do against many other drugs; some consider marijuana or LSD to be acceptable; and there are those who do cocaine from time to time but wouldn't touch heroin for anything in the world. There is no universally correct measure that we can prescribe for everyone. What gives us the right to judge which of the above approaches is the only correct one? Yes, some are riskier, but by that logic we might as well ban climbers from scaling mountains because many have miscalculated and paid with their lives.

title: Drugs
text: Within the framework of the war on drugs, various anti-drug school events often do not differentiate between individual illegal narcotics, essentially describing the effects of heroin, whose properties are implicitly attributed to all prohibited substances; the dangers of legal drugs are typically glossed over in such lectures (we often hear the strange phrase "alcohol and drugs" - as if alcohol is not a drug at all). I am certainly not suggesting that taking drugs is safe, as the use of any addictive substance is always associated with risks; on the other hand, I don't think it's wise to lie to children about the effects of narcotics, because if they reveal this lie in the case of less risky drugs, they will probably lose respect even for the hellishly dangerous ones.

title: Drugs
text: Although there are a number of ways to assess the danger of individual narcotics (for example, the degree of damage to the organism, the speed of addiction, the strength and type of addiction, withdrawal problems, withdrawal symptoms), for all decent people who would "never touch drugs, but like beer", I have bad news: Alcohol is one of the more dangerous narcotics (although there are even worse ones) and, for example, compared to LSD (which, by the way, is a non-toxic drug, so you can't overdose). it comes out disastrously wrong by almost every conceivable criterion. In fact, the differences between individual drugs are vast (I'm not talking about the hard and soft division now), and just as many people drink and smoke without getting drunk to death or dying of lung cancer (although it does happen), it's possible to use most narcotics for decades without serious consequences. Some can be habit-forming incredibly quickly (heroin), others are difficult to get used to (ecstasy), some cause physical addiction (nicotine), others psychological (cocaine), some damage health very fundamentally (barbiturates), others negligibly (LSD), and existing addictions to some drugs can be gotten rid of relatively easily (marijuana), with others it is extremely difficult (alcohol). Although many addictive substances can be considered a relatively reliable tool of slow suicide (crocodile), most drugs (LSD, alcohol, cocaine, caffeine, marijuana, ecstasy, tobacco and many others) can be used for a lifetime (of course with very different frequency depending on the user and the drug) and live a happy long life. Theoretical.

title: Drugs
text: Why in theory? Because in practice, many drugs are absurdly overpriced, as the price is several orders of magnitude higher than the production costs due to their illegality. As a result, on the one hand, producers and sellers of narcotics, whose livelihood is anyway illegal and they are persecuted for it, regardless of the quality of the goods they supply, mix drugs with some kind of plaster, which makes them even more dangerous, but above all, drug addicts get into financial problems, before which they run back to the drug, so that their life is reduced to just looking for the next dose and addiction develops even faster; many then commit crimes in this state, thereby endangering others - but if it were not for the war on drugs, which increases the prices of narcotics by an order of magnitude, drug addicts would in most cases only destroy themselves, similar to what we can observe, for example, with homeless people drinking boxed wine. Please do not read this text as a defense of those who rob for the next paycheck; I don't excuse them, I just state that state repression worsens the whole situation (if the dose costs a unit of crowns, there is no need to rob or even kill for it - even for a drug addict there are easier ways to get change; however, if a drug addict needs to satisfy his needs - thanks to the state - many hundreds of crowns a day, he is much more likely to resort to violence).

title: Drugs
text: I admit that in addition to the direct threat posed by predatory drug addicts, there is another problem - drug addicts are, on average, much sicker than other people (both because of the narcotics themselves, and also because of their illegality, which raises drug prices and thus brings their users misery, need, crazy living conditions, dirty needles, and the like). Others then pay for their health care; however, this is not an argument for drug prohibition (which makes the situation of drug addicts – and secondarily everyone else – even worse), but for free market health care, which solves this problem (see chapter ten).

title: Drugs
text: A non-negligible objection of the supporters of drug prohibition is often the health of our children. If narcotics become legal, they can be sold around schools! Sure, but they are even now; if a schoolboy wants drugs, he will get them, let's not be under any illusions. We can take comfort in the fact that it is a "system failure" and "better policing" would solve everything, however, this is not true, but above all, it does not matter at the moment; the important thing is that it just happens. In the case of drug legalization, it would probably be a little easier, but the allure of forbidden fruit would disappear. Above all, the responsibility for children would be transferred back to them and their parents, who should protect and educate them, not rely on the state's illusion of safety (and recover from their mistakes by blaming the state). Do we want children not to fet just because no drug has accidentally gotten to them yet, or to understand why they should refuse?

title: Drugs
text: Sometimes we can face the fear that if drugs were legal, the whole society would destroy itself and everyone would eat themselves to death; however, this can also be done with the use of legal narcotics. It is absurd to assume that the legalization of addictive substances would cause a drug apocalypse, since most people simply have no interest in destroying their lives (if they did, they still can today); moreover, increasing the amount of money spent on the war on drugs has not been proven to reduce the number of addicts in society, clearly showing that repression simply does not work. In Portugal, for example, drugs became a serious problem in the 1990s; huge numbers of people were dying of overdoses and the number of people infected with HIV continued to rise. In 2001, the local government legalized the use and possession of small amounts of all drugs (including heroin); the results? Within fifteen years, the number of overdoses dropped twenty-seven times (!) and the number of HIV-positive people stopped increasing.

title: Drugs
text: The fact that Portuguese politicians - when they came under public pressure - decriminalized drugs shows that they were well aware of what the war on drugs was causing, they were just fine with it until they started losing political points (if they were serious about the effectiveness of repression, they would only tighten up then); it is no different in other countries, the politicians and officials who are already dealing with the issue know the data (not only from Portugal), but they are not interested in a real solution, because their career is based on drug problems. Which is also related to how the war on drugs actually started (I don't mean its main wave from 1971, but the very beginning in the 19th century in the USA); it was not about any protection of the population at all, but about lobbying (hemp competed with nylon in the production of fabrics and wood in the paper industry) and racism (Asians typically took opiates, South Americans and Africans took drugs from coca; by banning these substances it was possible to bully their users), which is not even a secret, because at that time it was not yet politically incorrect to announce it publicly (and politicians did so).

title: Drugs
text: The war on drugs was not, is not, and never will be for the protection of society (it has been proven that it leads to the opposite), but only for reasons of power. Such a thing will never be admitted by those whose current careers depend on the fight against drugs, but the Global Commission on Drug Policy, a body composed of former powerful people who dedicated their lives to the war on drugs, but are no longer alive today (for example, ex-presidents of South American countries, ex-Secretary of State of the United States, former head of the United Nations, ex-Secretary of NATO, former high representative of the EU), openly declares: "The global war on drugs has failed with with devastating consequences for individuals and societies around the world.”

title: Drugs
text: Drug prohibition is exactly the same nonsense as alcohol prohibition in the twenties in the USA; the only difference is that it does not affect so many people, so its disastrous consequences are not seen at every turn. In a stateless society, however, one can imagine the sale of drugs in the same way as the sale of any other goods, which will undoubtedly have an impact not only on the purity of those substances; something like this would mean, among other things, the complete end of drug mafias, which are clearly created only and only by the war on drugs, because what is the point of smuggling or secretly storing and producing something that is normally available in stores?

title: Arms
text: It can be expected that in a stateless society everyone would arm themselves according to their discretion and financial possibilities; owners of private land could set arbitrary rules on their own land, i.e. restrict the carrying of weapons, but these would only be restrictions of a local nature. The idea that practically everyone can carry a firearm anywhere else is not doubly pleasant for many of us, because we are used to regulations whose creator - the state - instills in us from a young age the belief that without it and its laws, it would not be possible and we would all shoot each other here.

title: Arms
text: Empirical data from the past and the present clearly show that this is just a god-fearing scaremongering. So on one side are the strong emotions fueled by state propaganda that everyone "knows" that total gun deregulation would cause the apocalypse without ever really thinking about it, while on the other we have the facts; it's up to each of us what we lean towards. In the past, firearms were a common part of people's lives and their regulation was typically minimal or non-existent - for example, in the United States before 1934 anyone (regardless of age or any state permit) could buy any weapon (including heavy ones), and even in our territory restrictions were negligible until 1918; nevertheless, there were no disasters - not even massacres in schools, which were not "gun free" at the time - and people did not shoot each other (even children were used to guns, they were learning how to handle them, so accidents rarely happened).

title: Arms
text: Many will argue that without gun regulation we would have a "Wild West" here; we know it from westerns as a very bloody period and place. But there is a catch in the sources used - few people look up historical data when they think they know what it was like back then. However, the reality in this case is far from romantic ideas; the roughest of rough towns can serve as an example (to this day they are the inspiration for many westerns): Abilene, Ellsworth, Wichita, Dodge City or Caldwell, where between 1870 and 1885 there were 19 murders per hundred thousand inhabitants annually - which is less than in contemporary Washington - not to mention that the statistics of the number of inhabitants at that time do not include various passing individuals (with their inclusion, the annual number of murders per hundred thousand inhabitants decreases from 19 to just over 1). Or let's look at the most famous gunfight of the Wild West, the shootout at the O.K. Corral (also a great subject for westerns), in which a total of nine (!) people participated, six of whom survived; and compare this famous battle with the gang wars of today.

title: Arms
text: When I talk about the Wild West, someone often comes up with the idea that there was a genocide of the Indians at that time; yes, that is indeed true. But who did it? They were not farmers and free people, already - although well armed - making (more or less non-violent and mutually respectful) agreements with the natives, but the state army, whose officers started the biggest and most terrible massacres to prove their indispensability in the territory. If you want to know more about this period, I recommend the book "The Not So Wild, Wild West" by Terry Lee Anderson and Peter Jensen Hill.

title: Arms
text: But back to the present. Proponents of regulation like to argue with statistics that the more affordable firearms are, the more people end up being shot; and they're right, this is indeed true, but... it's not relevant. Where rifles and pistols are hard to come by, people don't actually shoot themselves much, but stab, strangle, beat and hang themselves all the more (the anti-guns typically include suicides in those statistics). But why should we be interested only in the number of people shot? After all, what matters is how many people lose their lives (in any way), which firearms no longer have a demonstrably negative effect on; and as for the total number of murders, there their influence is even positive. If we look at all the countries of the world from which data can be obtained (as a source I can recommend the "Small Arms Survey"), we will find that statistically, there are fewer murders where the population is rather more armed (although you can also find such pairs of countries whose comparison indicates the opposite, there are many more that confirm this conclusion); the availability of firearms does not reduce the number of suicides, but it does not increase either (it only affects the way they are carried out).

title: Arms
text: One very important (and not very surprising) conclusion emerges from this observation: People typically don't start figuring out who to kill based on obtaining a firearm; rather, they first decide to kill and only then choose an effective means. If they have a firearm at their disposal, they will reach for it because it is effective, however, in the absence of one, they will not disdain a knife, an ax or a car. This brings us to the main reason why it makes no sense to regulate guns; we can kill a person with a stick or a stone (not to mention a hammer or a screwdriver), which are tools that no state can realistically enforce a blanket ban on, so whoever wants to murder will find a way.

title: Arms
text: On the contrary, regulation actually helps the killers. For weapons represent a means of equalizing the natural imbalance of power; some of us are physically weaker by nature (especially women and children), others are stronger. With the help of weapons (and especially fire ones, because with cold ones the strength of their user still depends significantly) even those who are not endowed with great physical strength can effectively defend themselves; thus, their bans will significantly disadvantage the weak versus the strong. And not only that! If I have the element of surprise on my side and the possibility of an ambush, the effectiveness of the weapon does not matter nearly as much to me as when there is a fight and I need to defend myself (in an unexpected attack from behind, it is not a problem to succeed even with a knife, while defending with it is very difficult); therefore, banning firearms hurts the defender more than the attackers.

title: Arms
text: And unfortunately that's still not all; gun regulations restrict law abiding citizens much more than criminals. Sure, banning firearms will make life a little more difficult for them, but given their disrespect for the law, it's far from disarming them all; however, it disarms all law-abiding citizens in one - precisely because of their respect for valid legislation. As a result, there will be another imbalance of power in favor of "the bad guys". When criminals know their victims have no defense, they can do whatever they want (because law enforcement simply can't be everywhere even if they tried), which is not the case where almost everyone carries a thunder stick; an armed society is a decent society.

title: Arms
text: Many people feel an aversion to firearms, usually only caused by the state demonizing these tools; however, this propaganda is nothing more than another (unfortunately quite successful) attempt to consolidate state power and instill in subjects that they cannot defend themselves and need to stand up for it. Not to mention that a disarmed populace has no way to resist government oppression (and it's no coincidence that dictators—Stalin, Adolf Hitler, Mao Zedong, Pol Pot, the rulers of the DPRK from the Kim dynasty, and others—have always confiscated people's guns); the founding fathers, for example, were well aware of this, as a result of which the US Constitution has the Second Amendment (which seeks to preserve the "anarchist freedom" of arms even for citizens subject to state power).

title: Arms
text: In the hands of an individual, the weapon has another fundamental meaning: thanks to it, the person in question has to take on more responsibility; the use - but also the non-use - of a weapon in a crisis situation is an act whose consequences often cannot be undone, one can only learn to live with it. Although this looks like a disadvantage at first glance, the one who voluntarily remains unarmed also makes that decision - in advance, without knowing the situation in which he might find himself; yes, most likely it will be easier for him to defend himself against his own conscience that "he couldn't do anything anyway", but in reality he could, only if he had thought about it earlier. In any case, the carrying of arms has the exact opposite effect of the suppression of responsibility, the consequences of which are addressed in the fourth chapter of this book.

title: Arms
text: Related to this is the fear of firearms in the hands of juveniles or various lunatics; sometimes even today they do enormous damage with them. However, this currently occurs precisely because there are unarmed people around the attacker who cannot effectively defend themselves, making them tempting targets. A man with a gun is the greatest threat where no one else has one; otherwise, a person who attempts a massacre with a knife or an ax will hardly do more harm than today - he kills one or two victims, then others stop him (in an armed society, shooters can be neutralized just as quickly, which puts murderous madmen at a disadvantage compared to today).

title: Arms
text: "But what about heavy weapons?" the reader may argue, "Why not regulate them?" Mainly because in order to do so, the state has to have even heavier weapons, which - considering the way it is financed - is immoral; not to mention the direct restriction of property rights. Moreover, such regulation does not make sense even from the point of view of "protecting society", because those who have enough funds to buy heavy weapons and want to do harm can already invest these resources much more effectively today; compared to the price of, for example, a modern tank, an attack using poisons or explosives (which can be produced from legally available raw materials) is a cheap matter. In addition, for example, in the USA, the sale of all weapons was completely free until 1934, and thanks to the second amendment, the weapons purchased at that time could not be taken from their owners, so even today some people there have (legally inherited) artillery - although it is outdated, but it is still possible to attack densely populated cities with it now; however, no one uses it to commit crime. And nuclear weapons? For those, state regulations lose their meaning completely, because whoever is rich and powerful enough to buy them, circumventing the law is no problem at all (and has a huge range of ways to do harm in other ways as well).

title: Arms
text: So even though governments try to tell us how much we need their regulation—it's in their best interest to trust them and not resist—let's never stop trying to see things as they really are. Let's not close our eyes to the facts (the statistics speak very clearly in the area of weapons), even though emotions can greatly distort our vision due to the omnipresent state propaganda. Consider, for example, the relationship between the number of guns and the number of people shot that I mentioned above; even if it is true information, it is far from enough to reveal the whole truth, on the contrary, it serves to distort it.

title: Science
text: Who would finance research without the state? Companies often make a direct profit from the applied one, they would certainly invest in it, but what about basic research, the results of which we typically only see after a long time? Who would invest their resources in something so uncertain? Well, inquisitive free people - that's my answer. But Jeff Vail once said, "The free market will ignore solutions that are not capable of generating profit." Wasn't he right?

title: Science
text: Yes and no. It follows from the context of his work that by profit he meant only financial profit; and in such a case he is definitely not right, because the end customer (customer) in the free market typically pursues non-financial benefit. He who mines quartz sand is apparently doing so for monetary gain; the same reasons will surely be given to the factory worker who makes rods of pure silicon from that sand; the one who squeezes microchips out of those bars also wants to make money; and it will be no different in the case of whoever uses those chips to make a mobile phone... However, many buyers of this device do not get any financial benefit from it, they simply want to be in contact with their loved ones; this solution (buying a phone) is not profitable for them in terms of money (on the contrary, loss-making), but they still choose it because it will bring them a great non-financial benefit.

title: Science
text: So, if we include in the term "profit" absolutely everything, i.e. not only money, but everything that a person acquires (even on the non-financial side), then Jeff Vail was absolutely right, but the above statement ceases to be a criticism of the market; on the contrary, it becomes his ultimate defense, because ignoring solutions that benefit no one is precisely what reduces waste in a world of limited resources. But how does this relate to science? Well, research doesn't have to be just a means of making money; it can also be a goal, an obsession, a passion. Humans have been very curious since time immemorial, and many scientific discoveries (even in the field of basic research) were made simply because someone wanted to know the answers to their questions; and this does not have to be only the scientists themselves, but also the rich sponsors of their research.

title: Science
text: Many will argue that in today's society, although there are a lot of entities funding applied research, not so many are flocking to the basic one, so it "must" be done by the state; however, the catch lies in the fact that when the state first takes most of what they produce from people and then finances research, their motivation to do so on their own decreases rapidly, because on the one hand they have far fewer resources at their disposal, but above all they have no reason to finance from their own something that will anyway be paid for with "public" money.

title: Science
text: After all, the Czech state subsidizes research and development at a stable rate of about two percent of the budget, which is probably nothing that people would not be willing to pay voluntarily, if they are not so massively robbed by the state; the poorer among us would probably contribute even less or nothing at all, on the other hand, many of the rich would undoubtedly contribute not only a larger amount, but also a higher percentage. Not to mention that everyone could contribute where they see fit, and there would be no need to fund all the twisted projects just because someone can skillfully apply for subsidies. In connection with this, there is understandably a concern that the importance of some research will not be appreciated by the general public, which is a very good reason to spread education, but certainly not to force coercion; if some research is really important, then it is certainly possible to explain why it is so - and if it is no longer possible to popularize it and get hundreds of crowns from the masses, a few rich people can be convinced to make larger contributions. Failing either, the question then arises as to whether (and for whom) the research in question is really that important when no one is willing to voluntarily bear the cost.

title: Science
text: Of course, it can be argued that some discoveries will only be important in the distant future and people don't think that far ahead. The simple (and from my point of view, not very convincing) answer is that even the state is run only by people, and there is no reason why they should be more "enlightened" than others (especially when we look at them and see what they are). In my opinion, however, there is another problem with this argument; because it assumes that "thinking far ahead is good" and by extension that the more, the better. But what if I said I wanted to plan ten thousand years ahead? And that I need your money for that... Most people would probably disagree with that. But why?

title: Science
text: Although it may seem that my example with the ten thousand years is an argument ad absurdum, I am going somewhat elsewhere. How far in advance does it make sense to plan development? Ten years? Certainly. Fifty years? Probably yes. A hundred years? Um, maybe, but that's enough. A thousand years? Definitely not anymore. But what answers would people living in the Middle Ages at a much lower technological level give to this question? Their time horizons would most likely be shorter. What about early humans who were just learning how to use tools? It made sense to them to plan maybe another day; and who knows if. However, I would not be surprised if, in a few hundred years, technology had advanced so much that development planning would begin to make sense even for the millennia. A superficial conclusion might be that early humans got it wrong and the further into the future we plan, the better off we are; but it is rather the opposite – the richer and more technologically advanced we are, the more we can afford to plan ahead. How would a primitive man have fared, who, instead of worrying about what he will eat now (or tomorrow), was interested in planning the future for his distant descendants? He would probably go hungry.

title: Science
text: In general, the richer and more technologically advanced a society is, the further into the future it can afford to plan; also because it has more knowledge and information on the basis of which it can make reasonable predictions. But who is to decide what is the "right" level of planning for the future? Politicians? No. This is not objective, everyone has their priorities and needs, some are comfortable living from day to day, others building a family tradition; one cannot objectively say that the latter is "better", as time preferences are a purely individual matter. So let's let people fund whatever research they think is meaningful. Although development can be artificially accelerated, it is always at someone's expense - an extreme example is wars, which are generally claimed to accelerate research, which is often true, but at what cost? And if states also accelerate development through the violent plundering of resources, it is the same principle - only applied to a lesser extent.

title: Science
text: Various educational institutions (much like universities today) would have another incentive to engage in basic research in the free market; why would they do that? Well, what better way to gain name and fame - as an entity focused on professional education - than by employing scientific capacities, publishing articles in the given field and bringing the latest discoveries? Of course, it is possible that only prestigious and top institutions could afford this "advertisement" on the free market, however, this is enough in the case of science and research, because it is here - more than anywhere else - that quality matters more than quantity.

title: Science
text: It would probably be interesting to gradually analyze the individual scientific fields and estimate how they could probably be financed on the free market, but we do not have enough space for such a thing. I consider it more important to know that what is important to people, they will pay for it voluntarily; on the contrary, they obviously don't consider anything that they don't pay for to be that important (respectively they prioritize other things over it) - if they don't like it, they can try to change their opinion, but they shouldn't force them to do anything.

title: Work
text: In a free market without regulations and the state, there can of course be no labor code; therefore, everyone should enter into any contract that they agree with the other party. In such a society, without legislative restrictions, employers could refuse to employ anyone and would not be held accountable to anyone; even the termination of employment relationships would be limited only by who contracts with whom for the given work. Such an idea quite understandably creates uncertainty and perhaps even fear in some people; in most of them, state propaganda created the feeling that workers would be lost in a free market without regulations. This myth - along with several others - I will try to debunk in this chapter.

title: Work
text: At the outset, I would like to state that the labor market is a market like any other! Some offer their time and skills on it, others buy them. Here, shoppers are in a similar position to sellers as customers are to stores; they too can simply not buy what they don't like or don't like. And there is nothing wrong with that at all. On the other hand, I find it completely reprehensible if someone should be threatened with violence to buy something they don't want, or at a price they don't agree with. After all, everyone understands that even desperation does not justify a bankrupt innkeeper to force anyone to become his guest, or to pay him more than he is willing; so why should the desperation of the unemployed be a reason to use force against a potential employer in order to negotiate better terms?

title: Work
text: To be more concrete, I will give some examples: minimum wage, mandatory breaks, maximum number of hours worked, minimum number of vacation days and many others; the Labor Code is full of such regulations. And what exactly does this legislation mean in practice? Aggressive violence can be used against employers who already offer their employees different conditions (regardless of whether they agree or not), and in extreme cases the state will liquidate their business. I consider something like this to be highly unethical and fully comparable to the above-mentioned pub man forcing someone to go and have a beer with him instead of with a competitor.

title: Work
text: Here too – perhaps more than anywhere else – morality goes hand in hand with efficiency. However, it is not obvious at first glance, because the most common objection against a free (unregulated by the state) labor market sounds something like this: "The labor market may be in theory a market like any other, but in practice the employers are in a much better position than the poor employees, who often have to accept terrible jobs just because they have no better option." I agree with this comment; however, it is necessary to look for the cause of that condition. As incredible as it may seem, state regulation is also to blame here; they put enormous obstacles in the way of anyone interested in becoming a tradesman or entrepreneur, which increases the number of those applying for work and, conversely, causes a decrease in the number of those offering work. We often forget that employees and employers are not fixed groups of people; one person can be an employee, a self-employed person or an employer - the decision is made based on, among other things, what conditions he has for what.

title: Work
text: Without legislative obstacles, there would be nothing to prevent a newly fired saleswoman from getting up the next day, buying some ingredients, cooking some of them and selling them along with beer at the stand, whereas in today's over-regulated world she would have to set up a business, obtain a license to work with food, meet formal hygiene standards, keep accounts, electronically record her sales, deal with authorities and pay absurdly high taxes; if she were to succeed and want to hire someone to help, she would run into all the legislative obstacles that are meant to protect employees. Most people don't want to do something like that, so they go looking for a job; and because there are many of them (and employers for the same reason few), they do not have good bargaining conditions. In the end, therefore, any protection of the employee against the employer has one fundamental effect: It motivates people to be employees rather than employers, thereby, due to the market law of supply and demand, improving the position of employers and worsening the position of employees in the labor market; An interesting paradox, isn't it?

title: Work
text: But that's not all. In order for an employer to make sense to hire someone, the person should be able to earn for themselves (that is, bring value to the employer that they value more than the money they pay them). But "employee protection" increases the costs associated with employing him or reduces the value he brings to his employer; as a result, this will have a negative impact on his salary, or on the willingness of potential employers to hire him. An example can be the reluctance to employ women, for whom employers must hold a place during maternity leave.

title: Work
text: Another way the state tries to help workers is through the minimum wage; however, its consequences are also not as positive as it might seem. Those whose salary is high enough will not be affected at all (it won't hurt them, but it won't help them either); however, it will fatally harm those whose labor is worth less than the minimum wage on the market, as virtually no one will have the incentive to employ them. If the employee brings value to the employer through his work, which is worth ten thousand crowns to him, then the minimum wage of eleven thousand means only one thing - employing the person in question will be for the employer the same as flushing one thousand crowns down the toilet every month; but the person in question probably doesn't want to do that... And how will they solve it?

title: Work
text: Having already bitten the cost of the employee's work, I can't help but mention taxes; because they massively increase the costs of his employment. If an employee is able to produce monthly values worth, for example, fifty thousand crowns, this limit is the maximum that the employer can pay him in order not to be at a loss. But how much money does an employee who costs his employer fifty thousand get? Currently in the Czech Republic a little over half, specifically about twenty-seven thousand; the rest is swallowed up by the uneaten state in various taxes (including those called "insurance", but in reality they are taxes), not to mention the fact that when spending this money, the state also takes VAT (thus robbing the person in question of much more than half of what he earned). And we have also dealt with a situation in which the employer does not earn a single crown.

title: Work
text: Some laws, in turn, force companies to provide employees with certain workplace conditions; again, this may seem noble, but there is a catch. In principle, there are two possibilities: Either the employer would provide such conditions of his own free will, then the given legislation has no impact; or he would not provide them because the costs involved are simply not worth it and the state will force him to do so. However, these costs have to be borne by someone, so they are very likely to be reflected in the salaries of employees or in the final prices for customers; therefore, the state does not provide this improvement at its own expense - it does so out of the pockets of all of us, including those it is supposedly trying to protect.

title: Work
text: The so-called protection of jobs - be it from cheap labor from poorer countries or machines that "take people's jobs" - indeed protects some employees, but harms the whole society and hinders its development. Work is a means on the way to well-being, not a goal; and if we can do it more cheaply (whether thanks to machines or cheaper workers), we will help each other, as it will be possible to invest the saved resources elsewhere. And what will the people who lose their jobs as a result do? They will go do something that is currently in demand. Although this may seem like mere theorizing, it is a time-tested practice: In the Middle Ages, almost everyone worked in agriculture; today, thanks to technological advances, it is enough for a small fraction of us to hold this job. Is it wrong? After all, practically the entire population "lost their jobs" during this process; and what happened These people went on to do other things, and society as a whole is much richer - despite the catastrophic predictions that began to spread as early as the Industrial Revolution and, with minor modifications, are still spread today.

title: Work
text: In any case, we must also not forget that when someone accepts a job, even if it is extremely difficult and poorly paid, he demonstrates the following (if he is not forced to do anything by force): According to his own standards, his original situation (when he did not have the job) has improved after accepting this job offer; the person who made him that offer obviously helped him (and of course himself as well). If this were not the case, the employee in question would refuse the job; by accepting it, he shows that this is the best option he has in his situation. When someone then in connection with this curses evil corporations exploiting workers, then (provided that these workers were not forced to do the work by force) they are actually cursing the entity that has done at least something for them - as opposed to the one cursing.

title: Work
text: We can see a similar animosity in our society among people who set themselves against corporations using cheap labor from poorer countries; at the same time, they forget that even the little they pay the workers there is obviously more for them than they can earn elsewhere (if it weren't for that, they don't work for a multinational corporation, but go do something else - people always choose the one they consider the best from the available options). It can be argued that these companies are taking advantage of the misery of others, but what would happen if they stopped doing this? The situation of the poor would get even worse! How do I know? Well, if they had a better alternative than working for that corporation, they would have taken it by now; since they didn't, it means it was the best option available to them, ergo its disappearance will force them to choose the second best option, which means deterioration.

title: Work
text: An unregulated free labor market is nothing to fear; despite the fact that such a notion may fill some of us with an oppressive uncertainty, it is the best possible solution. On the one hand, it is more effective than state intervention and brings more benefits to people - customers, entrepreneurs, employees, tradesmen and employers - than violent regulation, but above all it does not require the use of offensive violence against those who want to run their businesses contrary to what politicians dictate to them. Giving people the freedom to make decisions about their lives is not only efficient, but also moral.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát (úřad pro hospodářskou soutěž) nebude chránit, podnikatelé budou likvidovat konkurenci skrze dumpingové ceny; až bude konkurence vyřazena, ceny zvýší a zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state (competition authority) does not protect us, entrepreneurs will eliminate competition through dumping prices; when competition is eliminated, prices will increase and the customer will suffer.
text: The answer

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát (úřad pro hospodářskou soutěž) nebude chránit, podnikatelé budou likvidovat konkurenci skrze dumpingové ceny; až bude konkurence vyřazena, ceny zvýší a zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state (competition authority) does not protect us, entrepreneurs will eliminate competition through dumping prices; when competition is eliminated, prices will increase and the customer will suffer.
text: The liquidation of the competition with the help of dumping prices may occur, but it must be remembered that the one who sells at dumping prices loses by doing so (and the customer can, on the other hand, buy at low prices); when (or rather if) subsequently the competition actually fails and the profit-seeking entrepreneur raises prices again, his profits will attract new competition into the industry and he can start over.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát (úřad pro hospodářskou soutěž) nebude chránit, podnikatelé budou likvidovat konkurenci skrze dumpingové ceny; až bude konkurence vyřazena, ceny zvýší a zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state (competition authority) does not protect us, entrepreneurs will eliminate competition through dumping prices; when competition is eliminated, prices will increase and the customer will suffer.
text: Not to mention the fact that, if the liquidated competition has at least some capital, it has the possibility to directly buy cheap competitive goods at dumped prices, which it can - after the prices return to the original level or above - later sell at a profit; it is necessary to realize that practically anyone rich has the opportunity to apply this strategy, not only competitors from the given field.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát (úřad pro hospodářskou soutěž) nebude chránit, podnikatelé budou likvidovat konkurenci skrze dumpingové ceny; až bude konkurence vyřazena, ceny zvýší a zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state (competition authority) does not protect us, entrepreneurs will eliminate competition through dumping prices; when competition is eliminated, prices will increase and the customer will suffer.
text: Despite all this, it is understandably possible that even in a free market, the strategy of dumping prices can be used to eliminate competition - under very specific conditions; however, it is a very risky strategy that may not lead to a goal, and the one who uses it does so at his own risk. However, the customer does not suffer in any case, because he buys at dumped prices for some time at most.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát (úřad pro hospodářskou soutěž) nebude chránit, podnikatelé budou likvidovat konkurenci skrze dumpingové ceny; až bude konkurence vyřazena, ceny zvýší a zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state (competition authority) does not protect us, entrepreneurs will eliminate competition through dumping prices; when competition is eliminated, prices will increase and the customer will suffer.
text: A well-known example of an entrepreneur who destroyed competition in this way was John Davison Rockefeller, owner of the Standard Oil company; however, the customer certainly did not suffer from these practices, on the contrary: During the period of operation of the Standard Oil company, the price of kerosene dropped significantly. There were also competitors who rebuilt their businesses over and over and made money by selling their infrastructure at a profit to Standard Oil.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát nebude chránit, podnikatelé mohou uzavírat kartelové dohody; těmi budou určovat ceny, zatímco zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state will not protect us, businessmen can enter into cartel agreements; they will set prices while the customer suffers.
text: The reason for the emergence of cartel agreements is, of course, primarily the desire for profit, which, however, is also what usually leads to the (sometimes secret) violation of these agreements; of course, each of the cartel members will still try to get as many customers as possible for themselves, which will very likely lead to the demise of the cartel.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát nebude chránit, podnikatelé mohou uzavírat kartelové dohody; těmi budou určovat ceny, zatímco zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state will not protect us, businessmen can enter into cartel agreements; they will set prices while the customer suffers.
text: Even if this were not the case, the possible large profits of the cartel members will begin to attract other entrepreneurs to the industry, for which it is most advantageous to set the price slightly lower than that set by the cartel agreement, whereby the new entrepreneur will begin to take over the cartel's customers; the only way the cartel can prevent something like this is by lowering prices, which then renders the whole agreement meaningless.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát nebude chránit, podnikatelé mohou uzavírat kartelové dohody; těmi budou určovat ceny, zatímco zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state will not protect us, businessmen can enter into cartel agreements; they will set prices while the customer suffers.
text: The only way a cartel can truly exist, function, and generate astronomical profits by ripping off customers is when the state prevents new entrepreneurs from entering the industry (usually through laws prohibiting business in the area without a state license). For the above reasons, free market cartels do not really arise, or they disappear very quickly.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát nebude chránit, podnikatelé mohou uzavírat kartelové dohody; těmi budou určovat ceny, zatímco zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state will not protect us, businessmen can enter into cartel agreements; they will set prices while the customer suffers.
text: The most commonly cited example of cartels is the South American drug mafias, which actually form cartels. However, this is because the drugs are officially illegal in that jurisdiction, which prevents new entrants from entering the industry (as discussed in the previous paragraph). Big and powerful mafias will defend their position against the state, but new (weak) competition will not.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát (antimonopolní úřad) nebude chránit, na trhu vzniknou monopoly; ty budou určovat ceny, zatímco zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state (antimonopoly authority) does not protect us, monopolies will arise in the market; they will set the prices while the customer suffers.
text: A true monopoly - one that can dictate its own prices - only arises when other entities are prevented from entering the industry, which is, of course, the result of state activities (specifically, laws that prohibit business in a given area without a license granted by the state), not the free market. If entry into the industry is not prevented, a monopoly - in the true sense of the word - cannot arise.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát (antimonopolní úřad) nebude chránit, na trhu vzniknou monopoly; ty budou určovat ceny, zatímco zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state (antimonopoly authority) does not protect us, monopolies will arise in the market; they will set the prices while the customer suffers.
text: Even in a free market, a firm can win the majority of customers in an industry (what some call a monopoly), but only by providing better service than its competitors; if this "big player" tries to raise prices and make dizzying profits, those very profits will attract competition into the industry, which will take away its customers (unless it is a state that prohibits competition by law).

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát (antimonopolní úřad) nebude chránit, na trhu vzniknou monopoly; ty budou určovat ceny, zatímco zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state (antimonopoly authority) does not protect us, monopolies will arise in the market; they will set the prices while the customer suffers.
text: Perhaps the most famous example of a free-market "monopoly" was the petroleum company Standard Oil, which was outlawed by the United States government in 1911, although during its forty years of operation the price of kerosene fell almost constantly (and no competition could keep up with Standard Oil); prices began to rise only after the state—in the interest of “protecting consumers”—abolished Standard Oil.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Když nás stát (antimonopolní úřad) nebude chránit, na trhu vzniknou monopoly; ty budou určovat ceny, zatímco zákazník bude trpět.
title: When the state (antimonopoly authority) does not protect us, monopolies will arise in the market; they will set the prices while the customer suffers.
text: An occasional objection is that these theories would cease to apply if one obtained a unique source of some natural raw material for which there is no substitute; everyone would then have to obtain the given raw material only from its sole owner. This objection is correct, but such a situation has never occurred before, and I cannot imagine any realistic situation in which it could occur.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Jak by mohlo fungovat volnotržní školství či zdravotnictví? Jen pohleďte na soukromé školy či nemocnice, nejsou o nic lepší než ty státní!
title: How could free-market education or healthcare work? Just look at private schools or hospitals, they are no better than public ones!
text: This very frequent objection certainly does not only apply to education and health care, it is often also directed at other areas that are controlled by the state, but under certain conditions allow private institutions to operate in the given area as well. The rules and regulations that bind such institutions are typically very strict, as the entire industry is firmly in the hands of the state.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Jak by mohlo fungovat volnotržní školství či zdravotnictví? Jen pohleďte na soukromé školy či nemocnice, nejsou o nic lepší než ty státní!
title: How could free-market education or healthcare work? Just look at private schools or hospitals, they are no better than public ones!
text: To deal with this objection, it is first of all to realize that a "private institution" is not a charm of success; although the power of the free market also partly lies in the fact that companies are owned by private individuals, but above all it lies in the fact that millions of entrepreneurs around the world try their solutions, while those who do it well prosper and others fail (this is how the market "filters" the right solutions).

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Jak by mohlo fungovat volnotržní školství či zdravotnictví? Jen pohleďte na soukromé školy či nemocnice, nejsou o nic lepší než ty státní!
title: How could free-market education or healthcare work? Just look at private schools or hospitals, they are no better than public ones!
text: However, if these private institutions are heavily regulated by the state, the main advantage of the market is lost, as the owners of these institutions have almost no room to create non-standard solutions to problems, since these often contradict various regulations; the difference between a state institution and a private institution, which the state binds with strict rules and regulations, is therefore relatively small or negligible.

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
section: Jak by mohlo fungovat volnotržní školství či zdravotnictví? Jen pohleďte na soukromé školy či nemocnice, nejsou o nic lepší než ty státní!
title: How could free-market education or healthcare work? Just look at private schools or hospitals, they are no better than public ones!
text: There are also many other (in my opinion, not so important) reasons why private institutions usually do not show very good results for customers in an environment overregulated by the state: Barriers to entering the industry prevent natural competition, artificial state competition providing its services "for free" does not allow to compete with a lower price, and so on (the list is far from complete).

chapter: AMEN: analýza mnohých etatistických námitek › Ekonomie
