At the same time, more and more self-managed organizations are emerging (sometimes they are called turquoise - these are companies with a very flat structure, i.e. essentially without managers); in most fields it is also possible to work on a freelance basis. I'm not saying to change jobs right away (especially if you're happy in it); rather, I invite you to think about how much what (and especially where) you do for a living shapes you in terms of freedom, which you can remember, for example, the next time you make some changes in this area.

title: 20. Participation
text: • Do you have children? Or would you ever like to have them? How you intend to approach them will dramatically affect not only their lives, but your own as well. If you choose to lead them towards the goals you believe to be right, and if you try to actively impart your values to them (other than by simply living by them), you inevitably fit into a leadership role, leaving them more of a subordinate position. We discussed the consequences of obedience in several chapters at the beginning of this book. If you can perceive children as equal beings despite their lesser life experiences (which of course do not mean equality in abilities or skills), respect their preferences and attitudes (often influenced by a lack of experience) and not teach them to listen, this will help not only their growth into autonomous and responsible individuals, but also your perception of freedom. It is said that the true character of a society is reflected in its treatment of the weakest; I believe that this also applies to the character of individuals and that children are typically the weakest.

title: 20. Participation
text: • If none of the above points are imaginable and meaningful for you yet (or if you want to do even more), you can start following (and perhaps even supporting) the Free Port. There we not only deal with these topics in depth, but also bring together like-minded individuals from whom it is possible to learn; with direct support, you will then allow these ideas to spread to other people.

title: 20. Participation
text: The above options are not meant to advise anyone on how to live their life; I present them as mere examples to consider for people who have no idea where to begin their journey to freedom. Even by possibly following everyone, however, no one automatically becomes free; rather, during the process, he gets the opportunity to start thinking differently than he was used to. I don't believe there is a list of steps that if we take, we will be free and done; it's more about a lifestyle, that is, something that is always going on and that you can constantly work on. For example, if we want to live a healthy life, it is not enough to exercise once, eat a plate of vegetables and not worry anymore; we need to continuously devote time, attention, effort and energy to it. Freedom is no different; it also requires us to think about it, integrate it into our lives, learn to perceive it and train ourselves to experience it. The good news is that the more attention we pay to freedom, the more natural it becomes in our daily lives. At first, it may seem too abstract, but whoever allows himself to implement some of the above options into normal functioning (ideally, not only mechanically, but seriously thinking about them and finding relevant information), after some time other paths may begin to open up, the existence of which he had no idea before - typically it will be about applying freedom to all important aspects of life, from work to hobbies to relationships.

title: 20. Participation
text: If we are left alone with our values and beliefs, we can certainly increase our own autonomy by changing our actions and thinking in certain areas; sooner or later, however, we will inevitably encounter limitations arising not only from the lack of support from the environment, but also from the absence of a division of labor. In modern society, we are not self-sufficient – we need to use other people's goods and services; however, when they are statists, they may not be interested in cooperating with us outside the supervision of the state apparatus (unless they want to save something on taxes). The solution is the previously mentioned agoras; in them, we can connect with other like-minded individuals with compatible values - it is incredibly comforting to live in an environment where legislation does not represent an argument for the rightness or wrongness of any action (at most, we are concerned with how to eliminate or at least mitigate the effects of possible sanctions).

title: 20. Participation
text: Those who do not belong to any agora can find or create one; the more naturally and transparently a person takes the above (or any other) steps to freedom, the more like-minded people will start to appear around him. Authenticity is a major advantage here. I am sometimes criticized for proclaiming my beliefs too openly; I think I will discourage a lot of people. Yes, I discourage; I will close many doors, because for many people I lose all relevance as a crazy anarchist (unfortunately, even some former libertarian colleagues need to distance themselves from me so that their social status does not suffer), but I will open many others - countless individuals share with me their disobedience to laws, they entrust me with all kinds of bizarre problems with legislation, and we help and advise each other on how to shield the power of authorities. It is not necessary to be so radical; you just have to let a little more freedom into your life and don't hide it too much - the crow sits next to the crow, in time you will come across people of a similar nature. And if there's nowhere else, it's enough to visit one of the events of the Free Port; anarchists abound there.

title: 20. Participation
text: Although the state apparatus creates the illusion that disobedience (to laws) will not go unpunished (which is sometimes true unfortunately), in the vast majority of cases this is not the case. As I already mentioned in the State chapter, about two and a half million legal norms apply in the Czech Republic, so there is probably no one living in "its" territory who knows (let alone observes) all of them; I wonder if there is a man in the whole world who knows all the laws that apply to him. When I try to think of at least one full day when I personally did not knowingly act illegally, I go back in time about five years - most of that day was spent in the operating room, the rest on the verge of wakefulness and artificial sleep; as far as I can remember, I don't know of any other such day (but also of the fact that I would harm or endanger anyone by violating the legislation). During that time, I was arrested once and brought to the police station (for violating the State Symbols Act, not showing my identity and then not obeying the summons of an official) and fined a couple of times (for traffic violations). I admit that I am not exactly a representative sample of the population, but there is a dizzying disparity between the crimes committed (sometimes quite serious from the state's point of view) and the subsequent punishments. I don't mean that laws can be broken with impunity (after all, a lot of people end up in prison, whether they hurt someone or not); it's just that the limits of what we can afford, according to my (direct and indirect) experience, are significantly further than almost everyone (including most anarchists) thinks. This can be verified by gradually testing what still passes and what no longer (which of course brings with it risks); however, the information obtained can be shared in agoras, which significantly reduces the cost of such discovery.

title: 20. Participation
text: Ultimately, only everyone can judge their options for themselves; someone has a great aversion to risk, others don't mind risky ventures. However, there are paths to freedom whose degree of danger is negligible, or comparable to anything else we normally do. I think the most important thing is to take (some) first step and think about it all; there is no need to rush anywhere or paint castles in the air or megalomaniacal plans for the future. Doing something out of a "noble" motivation to "change society" often leads to frustration that people are not what we need them to be. However, if we stay with what we enjoy and fulfill ourselves, with the only difference that we let freedom into our lives through a conscious decision, we may inspire others; but even if not, above all we will enjoy it ourselves. Teachers can search for or establish freer schools, programmers contribute to the rise of cryptocurrencies, artists create works about disobedience, therapists support children's autonomy, craftsmen or farmers participate in the gray economy, lawyers help victimless "criminals", scientists may look for employment outside the state sphere... I'm not saying that this is the best advice (and certainly not for everyone); however, I can do no more than give examples and show a possible approximate direction. When you go down that road, you yourself will know best what exactly is needed.

title: 21. The future
text: Anarchoagorism can be seen as a practical path to the individual freedom of the individual with the help of the means available to each of us. Its charm lies, among other things, in the fact that we can follow it basically regardless of how (un)free a society we live in; concrete results will of course be highly dependent on external conditions - of course, it is not realistic to expect from the anarchoagorisism practiced in prison the degree of freedom common on the other side of the walls and bars, however, it is certainly possible to increase it. The practical steps described in the previous chapter are designed for most people in Euro-Atlantic civilization today; some of them apply universally, others depend on local conditions. From the general principles of anarchoagoris, which can be very simply described as the voluntary cooperation of the disobedient without formal authorities, anyone can derive specific measures and procedures for their life anytime and anywhere. Their application in practice then not only increases the degree of freedom of the individual, but also teaches him to discover the next steps on this path, their implementation in turn, and so on.

title: 21. The future
text: Although I consider one of the key messages of this book to be an appeal to achieve change "from below" (that is, everyone on their own), not "from above" (authoritatively towards others), I would be surprised if some readers did not ask themselves the question of how anarchoagorism can affect the whole society. Before I elaborate on this topic, I would like to point out that even though the societal reach of this philosophy can be imagined and modeled in different ways, it is necessary to remember the pitfalls of doing so – the more we focus our attention on other people and the outside world, the easier we can lose sight of the work on ourselves. I am not dissuading anyone from analyzing the global effects of anarcho-agorism across populations; however, I believe that (in any action) a lot depends on the motivation: If we try to achieve our own freedom (and help only those who are worth it), we naturally become conscious creators (of our lives) in the process, while attempts to change society often end up in the position of victim, where the disgraced "savior" feels misunderstood and frustrated that others do not understand his ideas and do not follow him (from which it is easy to slide into disrespecting and coercing others on the grounds that they don't understand what's good for them anyway). Please read the following lines with full awareness of all that I have mentioned in this paragraph…

title: 21. The future
text: Samuel Edward Konkin III in the New Libertarian Manifesto, he describes several phases of the revolution (which I would call evolution, of course): It begins in a state where no one follows the anarcho-agorist path (phase zero); it continues with its adoption by a handful of libertarians in an otherwise statist society (phase one); their numbers gradually increase until they are registered by the state power, which can not only punish individual disobedients, but also attempt widespread intimidation (phase two); if the central authorities fail to disperse the agoras, their supercritical growth poses a threat to the establishment as a result of greater and greater shortfalls in tax revenue, while parallel structures for the same reason strengthen to the point where they can defend themselves against a possible attack by the forces of the former oppressor (phase three); with the loss of the monopoly on violence, the state ceases to be a state (stage four). In its manifesto, SEK3 deals with the individual phases in more detail (including an analysis of possible risks); however roughly I agree with him and find his description of the path to freedom believable, it doesn't make much sense to me to create a strategy today to change a future society that we don't live in, and therefore can't even imagine well enough.

title: 21. The future
text: I believe that rather than theoretical planning (on an individual and societal level), we can liberate ourselves by learning about the principles of freedom, self-management, self-development and sharing and applying them to everyday life. With each person who does so, all of humanity moves a tiny bit closer to anarchy – but it arises out of spontaneous order thanks to the mutually voluntary interactions of lots of information-dispersed people all around us; I don't think it can be established according to a pre-prepared scenario. However, I fear that even some libertarians tend to forget at times the inability of the human brain to understand and grasp the unimaginable complexity of our society when it comes to something they really care about; it tries to predict the unpredictable and plan the unplannable. I do not want to repeat this (so typical for socialists) mistake; I accept my role as one person among billions of others, before whom I do not humble myself, but neither do I exalt myself above them. I long for freedom, I learn to achieve it, and I share with others what I have learned (perhaps with the help of this book); whoever wants can join me as an equal. I seek to free myself, not others; and yet, at the same time, I consider this very path the most effective way to liberate the whole society - but only until it becomes my goal.

title: 21. The future
text: In the chapter on Democracy, we discussed the ineffectiveness of voting in elections as a tool to effect (essentially any) changes from an individual perspective; in the Politics chapter, the ineffectiveness of obtaining and using the mandates of public (state) power to achieve freedom. However, insights from subsequent chapters allow for generalizations: Casting and contesting votes typically involves focusing on other people's lives and opinions rather than one's own; and something like that always represents at least a threat to freedom, if not its erosion. Freedom is not given, freedom is taken; it comes from ourselves, we cannot get it as a gift from a politician or an institution. Of course, that doesn't mean that a bad law that restricts us will never be repealed (I'm glad that happens occasionally); only the targeted pursuit of something like this represents such an uncertain and demanding undertaking that the energy required for it can perhaps always be spent more purposefully, but mainly with a significantly lower risk of power corruption (for politicians) or acceptance of the illusion that I am changing something and doing it "for the good of society" when I throw papers in the ballot box and argue about it with acquaintances (for voters).

title: 21. The future
text: In my opinion, the strength of the anarcho-agorist path lies, among other things, in the connection of external and internal freedom. While the former means respect for property rights (so it refers to interpersonal relationships and interactions), the essence of the latter is managing fear, realizing responsibility and freeing oneself from various demons (which we achieve through self-knowledge and self-development). However, these freedoms are closely related: An environment where property rights are respected (including primarily self-ownership) creates more responsible individuals who better understand that they are the creators of their lives. However, the opposite is also true - the healthier a person's self-confidence and the fewer unprocessed (perhaps even unconscious) fears, the easier it is for them to respect others and not try to limit their property rights "for their own good" (or at least in exchange for the illusion of safety). Libertarians focus a lot on external freedom (which I think is important), but unfortunately, in my opinion, they often neglect internal freedom; it bothers them when others initiate violence against them (typically through the state), they condemn such actions (or even its actors), but they often stop there. If we desire a society that does not interfere with our lives and possessions, we need first to get rid of fear and obedience; although everyone can only do this for themselves, we can also inspire others to do it (especially if they don't try to do it).

title: 21. The future
text: One of the most relevant objections against anarchoagorism, in my opinion, focuses on its further development in the future, and therefore I want to deal with it in this chapter. Even from the ranks of libertarians, it is sometimes said that the effectiveness of anarchoagoris is conditioned by the fact that only a handful of people practice it, while if there were more of them, the state would start taking repressive countermeasures against them; some even dissuade me from public displays of disobedience (to the law) because they are afraid of the possible general reactions of the public authorities. I agree that something like this can actually happen (though not necessarily); perhaps no path to freedom is without risk - and I don't want to give up this one mainly because it really works. However, if the state does eventually take some retaliatory steps, it will at least give a greater number of people a chance to understand what its real (violent) nature is. Indeed, many come to the ideas of freedom - or even anarchism - precisely in response to the excess or absurdity of regulations, which was clearly visible, for example, during the covid pandemic, which noticeably shook citizens' faith in institutions. For the sake of completeness, I add that my goal is certainly not to provoke anyone and I am not looking for a conflict with state power (and I believe that neither are most anarchoagorists); I'm just stating that if it were to happen, the side effect could be the questioning of the trust (perhaps only a small part) of the public in the goodness of the state and (at least a small) approach of humanity to disobedience as a social norm.

title: 21. The future
text: We can argue endlessly about possible variants of the future or the risks associated with it; and we still cannot describe them all - after all, even the current state of the world at the present moment is beyond human imagination in its complexity, let alone that someone could successfully plan the development of society years (or decades) ahead. What about that? Nothing. Let us not strive for the impossible; let's learn to live here and now - as freely as we can.

title: 22. Love
text: I want to dedicate the last chapter to something that is far from being related only to anarchoagorisism, but perhaps to everything we do in life - namely love. We can perform any activity from a variety of motives and experience a variety of emotions. As I get older, I understand more and more deeply that and why motives matter, even though it may not be obvious at first glance; the results of our actions primarily affect the external world, while our intentions primarily affect the internal one, thus shaping us ourselves - if I write a book or other text for the joy of writing itself and from the desire to share my knowledge with people, it will do something completely different to me than if I write something, for example, to denigrate someone. The more of my life energy and time I devote to creating beautiful things, the kinder and happier person I become; if, on the other hand, I decide to hold a grudge and fight (even for a good cause), I risk becoming bitter over time. Two people can perform an apparently identical activity differing only in their inner motivations; even if no one notices the difference, it will be written in themselves, where it will leave its traces. This is certainly not to say that we must never step aside - on the contrary, mistakes belong to humanity and move us forward; I'm just saying that everything we do and especially why we do it accumulates in us and shapes us.

title: 22. Love
text: I love freedom; I need to perceive it, feel it - it is both a means and a goal for me, a source of strength and a reward. I recognize it and examine it, deepening and strengthening my ability not to confuse it with recklessness and arbitrariness; I'm learning to see and accept its dark side as well - to respect people who treat it in a way that I may not be comfortable with, or even fear. However much I may have been a lover and explorer of freedom all my life, sometimes I cannot resist anger and begin to fight for it or for it; and it is in those moments that I distance myself from her the most. I'd like to emphasize here that I'm not trying to convince the reader of (anarcho)pacifism (as much as I like its purity, I don't see it as universally viable now or in my foreseeable future); I recognize the need to defend the autonomous individual, but at the same time I draw attention to the danger of gradual, unexpected, unobserved and unwanted changes in his inner world. I see a vast difference between being determined to preserve our freedom while trying to do as little harm as possible to ourselves or those around us (which includes thinking about how to prevent fights) and between reveling in shaming and shaming anyone we consider an enemy. The desire to live your life your way is different from the urge to win and defeat the "bad guys"; but due to the influence of fear, we can confuse one motivation for another without realizing it.

title: 22. Love
text: How to reveal something like that in yourself? I am afraid that even the keenest mind cannot answer this question; the higher intelligence we possess, the more complicated ways we can devise to deceive ourselves. If we want to know the truth, we have to look inside ourselves and try to honestly perceive how we really feel. Rushing can harm the entire process (psychedelics, on the other hand, can help, although I certainly do not recommend their use without thorough preparation), and moreover, it will rarely be a one-time process. What emotions prevail in us in relation to what we do? If fear, malice, hatred or the desire to take revenge or punish prevail over a long period of time, we are probably moving away from freedom; and even in extreme cases - for example, a soldier could join the front to defend his (free) country from the conquerors, but the more he hates them, the more willing he will be to sacrifice his freedom or that of others in order to win over them (which does not mean that he would not have to pay a subjectively higher price for capitulation in the end - but that does not change the above).

title: 22. Love
text: When we leave the extreme situations and return to today's Czech everyday life, in my opinion these principles apply even more clearly. Angry fighters (not from the front, but from the warmth of their homes) often call for state solutions at the expense of individual autonomy in the name of the "higher good" (whether it concerns the migration crisis, covid, the war in Ukraine or, for example, in Gaza - and this is quite regardless of which side of the conflict or problem in question they support). Those who, on the other hand, focus on their own life and the search for their happiness in what fulfills them, without needing to change, correct, punish or win over someone, typically do not have such a strong tendency to disrespect the freedom of others - because those who find their meaning in what they do (work, hobbies, relationships...) logically want to spend their time doing just that, instead of trying to control others.

title: 22. Love
text: I try to do things with love; it's really important to me. When I fail at an activity, I look for ways to do it differently; if there is no change, I see it as a signal to go do something else. Life is too short to spend it doing something that doesn't fulfill me. I'm not (yet) 100% in it - I still can't pay fines or sign tax returns with love and I can't avoid it every time (although I do get fines more and more often and at least someone else fills out the tax returns for me); however, I spend the vast majority of my time (actually almost all of it) doing activities that give me meaning. It wasn't always like that - I've been aiming for it since I was a child - it required thinking hard about life, changing or ending some relationships and acquiring knowledge and skills in order to make a living from my hobbies (programming, learning, anarchism or self-development). During my studies, I earned a lot of different (mainly manual) jobs, which I didn't enjoy, but the goal was to learn everything necessary to leave them in my spare time. If ever in the future I cease to find fulfillment in the field of freedom (as much as I can't imagine it will), I'd rather go do something else than continue it lovelessly and grow bitter over time. Unfortunately, I know many a libertarian who talks about freedom with great resentment towards people whom he considers enemies of himself or his mission. The former joy and beauty disappear from the expression (and probably also the experience) of such individuals over time, as they increasingly focus on fighting and enmity.

title: 22. Love
text: If I perform any activity with inner malice, I acquire an aversion to it; although I can overcome it (perhaps because I have internally committed myself to something or identify with it), it is not realistically possible for it not to affect the results and myself in any way over time. In the Politics chapter we discussed the adverse effect electoral failures have on libertarians trying to promote freedom through democratic means; the frustration of losing causes a deviation from the original values and ideals. However, the same thing can happen to any of us, although in the environment of political parties it is a much more serious threat. However, hateful comments on social networks, condemnations, people's lack of interest in a long-prepared event or (repeated) failure in trying to convey a thesis will also cause disillusionment and bitterness in many people; we encounter all this as spreaders of the ideas of freedom on a daily basis and need to cope with it. A long-term inability to cope with these difficulties typically leads to (internal and external) conflicts, bitterness, a desire for revenge (on anyone, sometimes the whole world) and a general victimization. Originally beautiful ideas creep into shrill screams without their announcer realizing it, and so he can gradually begin to unknowingly do a disservice to what he once loved so much. What about that?

title: 22. Love
text: For me personally, love proved to be the best feedback from reality; if it fills me up during creation, if I feel it in my lectures, while writing, discussing, filming videos, it confirms the direction I'm going. When, on the other hand, I experience a period in which I distance myself from her more often (which typically begins to manifest itself, for example, during more heated exchanges of opinions in the comments), I perceive it as a signal that I need to change something, which usually helps; however, if I stopped loving my job as a whole, I would go do something else. By the word love I refer to the feeling of pure happiness, inner bliss and joy that is growing in me even now as I write these lines; I will definitely regret it in a way when I finish the book. On the contrary, I would not use the word for tense emotions, impatience, and the desire to berate your debate opponent for being an idiot if he is unable to understand the basics of propositional logic; but not even for the possible satisfaction of a "won" debate, if in the end there was no real understanding and mutual enrichment (but perhaps only the inability of one of the parties to continue to defend its position). At a given moment, such a "win" can bring satisfaction, applause and appreciative comments, or even enrich someone in the audience, which can be seen as confirmation of a job well done; however, I believe that with love and respect for our fellow humans, we can achieve better results in terms of freedom (not to mention the effects on ourselves described above). In short, love helps me in my orientation; is my functional indicator on the journey of life.

title: 22. Love
text: In my early childhood, before I learned to read, I was deeply impressed by the phrase: "Love your enemies." (Mat 5:44) It bothered me and for about half of my life I saw it as an altruistic call to help those enemies; over time, however, I began to realize its other consequences, namely that my love and hatred affect me even more strongly than others - so I can choose what I want to live in and what my inner world should be. Not to mention that the more people around me suffer, the worse they will treat me; especially if they don't like me. So I try to wish a happy life even to those who hate me - because I believe that in the end it will help me too. I can't feel love for everyone all the time; however, I consider it a good goal (which does not contradict the need to defend against attacks on one's integrity or autonomy).

title: 22. Love
text: With the amount of content I've published over the past twenty years, it doesn't surprise me that it's often interpreted differently and sometimes completely misinterpreted (I assume that most of the time there's no bad intent, just plain misunderstanding); therefore, I prefer to process important topics from multiple perspectives and in different forms to minimize misunderstandings - even so, they probably cannot be avoided completely. In the case of this book, perhaps most of all, I would not want it to be interpreted as a call to blind defiance at any cost or to hatred of state officials or to ruthlessness; on the contrary, I ask the reader to accept it as a peaceful inspiration for an authentically free life in love.

title: Epilogue
text: In this book I record my experiences with freedom, especially since the completion of the book Anarchocapitalism; most of what I have described in the past twenty-two chapters, I learned in the Hedgehog without a cage - my beloved school, agora and family. Living in a democratic state made me first an anarcho-capitalist, which I noticed quite quickly, then an anarcho-agorist, which I only realized years later; and actually I still don't know exactly when it happened. For my journey to anarchism, I feel great gratitude to being itself, to the entire universe, and to God; and it was that gratitude that motivated me to write this title, through which I want to convey my experience to other people. I transform into text something that comes to me from everywhere, just walking through this beautiful world; I'd appreciate it if you could pass it on - I claim no copyright to the book, feel free to do with it as you like.

title: Epilogue
text: The message of this publication in no way refutes the principles that you can read in the book Anarchocapitalism; rather, I would say that it complements them with additional knowledge. I see a free, free-market, decentralized society as a suitable platform for people to seek happiness and live their lives in their own way; of course, this does not mean that I agree with all the ways in which they will do it (I have my reservations about formal hierarchies, for example), but I respect the choice of each individual to decide even if I personally do not find it appropriate. I consider the creation of parallel non-state (ideally non-hierarchical) structures - i.e. agoras - to be the most effective way primarily to the free life of each of us, but also to a stateless arrangement; however, I consider the effort to change society (and other people in general) counterproductive (especially in the long term) - I believe in change coming from within each of us.

title: Epilogue
text: Despite the title Anarchoagorism, the book does not contain only anarchoagorist principles, although it is completely consistent with them; I add a lot of my own knowledge to them - from everything related to children or adultism, through peace-loving or attitude to revolutions to love, self-development and emphasis on the inner world of the individual as well as resistance to efforts to change others. I personally know anarchoagorists who disagree with me on these positions; others do not consider themselves anarcho-capitalists and would certainly not identify with my first book, especially with the theses arising from the Austrian school of economics. Pure anarchoagorism involves only the decentralized creation of agoras as a means to achieve an anarchist society and the rejection of a political path to that end; everything above this foundation is my convictions, which I certainly do not impose on other anarchists, for whom I cannot or do not want to speak in any case.

title: Epilogue
text: During the writing of this book I felt the need to formulate a new (as yet non-existent) anarchist direction; the latter will be based on anarchoagorism (and fully in tune with it), but will expand it by focusing on the inner world of the individual. Just as anarchoagorism describes how anarchists can work together in agoras to achieve external freedom, that new anarchism would additionally include what steps man can take within himself to develop his inner freedom. I did address this in the Self-Development chapter (and a little in others), but to an extent that was unsatisfactory for me. I suppose I need a few more years to be able to understand the things I feel and live by to a depth sufficient to put them into words comprehensible to the uninitiated reader. I wish we could meet again then; maybe through my next book. For now, I bid farewell to the words: "Freedom; self-management; self-development; sharing."

title: AMEN: aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience
text: I ended the publication Anarchocapitalism with an analysis of many statist objections (AMEN); at that time it seemed most reasonable to me to conclude my work with a polemic and a refutation of counter-arguments, which I do not regret, as it suits the book - with regard to its theoretical essence - in my opinion. However, I consider the volume Anarchoagorism to be less theoretical and more practical; and besides (hopefully) I don't need to convince anyone of anything. I just want to share ideas and inspire people who are interested; that is why AMEN this time means aphorisms manifesting the essence of disobedience. I would say that my love for aphorisms grows as I let myself be guided more by vivid emotions in addition to consistent logic; I like it when (their) poeticity is combined with compressed wisdom. In the following pages, I want to share some (for me) important thoughts in this way; for each statement I will write how I perceive it and what it symbolizes for me.

section: „Dobří lidé neposlouchají špatné zákony.“ – neznámý autor
title: "Good people don't obey bad laws." - unknown author
text: The subtitle of the book Anarchoagorism raises (quite understandable) questions for many: Who do we consider a good person? And which laws are bad? Not only do I not know the answers, I actively do not want to know them - I would not like to divide people into good and bad; by doing so, I would (even if only in my head) fit into the role of a judge who can determine such a thing, thereby putting myself above others, which is not in line with my values. So why does this book have such a subtitle? It is not a division of people or laws into right and wrong; please, let's put aside the attempt to categorize for a moment and let's look at the meaning hidden behind it - namely, that if instead of valid legislation we started to follow what we ourselves are in line with, it would certainly bring a lot of problems, but we would avoid much more suffering.

section: „Dobří lidé neposlouchají špatné zákony.“ – neznámý autor
title: "Good people don't obey bad laws." - unknown author
text: When I say that good people do not obey bad laws, I am not trying to moralize; that message is to encourage all those in chains to lay them down. It is not just legislation (although the state typically carries the heaviest penalties); it is also about social norms, pressures, customs and rules, as a result of which many of us live according to what is expected from the outside rather than according to our own inner desire. Many do not want to disappoint their parents, others yearn for the recognition of those around them, some try to be better than others at all costs, others are afraid of losing their reputation... The cause is obedience acquired through upbringing or at school, a manifestation of the loss of authenticity and freedom and the result of passing through life in pursuit of something that may seem quite unimportant to us on our deathbed. I love my way of being; yet I will rather risk prison, contempt, damnation, and "early" death than lose myself.

section: „Anarchie není chaos; je to spontánní řád bez vládců.“ – Urza
title: "Anarchy is not chaos; it is spontaneous order without rulers." – Urza
text: Most people think of anarchy as chaos; often also violence, disrespect and almost always the breakdown of order. The origin of the word lies in the Greek anarchos, composed of the prefix an- (without) and the root archos (ruler); therefore, anarchy does not mean the absence of rules, but of rulers. In today's highly hierarchical society, many people agree - they cannot imagine an organization without an organizer. However, anarchists typically do not stand for confusion and perhaps never for lawlessness, which is why as their symbol they most often use a pictogram consisting of the letter A (anarchy) and the letter O (order, in Czech) to indicate that they perceive anarchy as a (spontaneous decentralized) arrangement of things, not chaos.

section: „Anarchie není chaos; je to spontánní řád bez vládců.“ – Urza
title: "Anarchy is not chaos; it is spontaneous order without rulers." – Urza
text: Why is the absence of rulers so often mistaken for the absence of rules? Leaving aside the above-mentioned prisms (hierarchies are self-evident to us, so it is difficult for us to imagine a different kind of order), the state convinces us from childhood that we need leaders - the media (led by the public ones) as a default assumption frames all debates, news, comments and programs, while schools teach us this not only through direct teaching, but above all through experience (the teacher leads the students). Almost no one disputes or discusses this; for the vast majority of the population, it is an uncritically accepted fact. However, many (perhaps even numerous) decentralized agoras, groups, subcultures, and even companies show that it can be done in another way; organization does not need an organizer and (spontaneous) order arises from anarchy.

section: „Bez vlády nejsou lidé ztracení; jsou odpovědní.“ – Athéna (ChatGPT)
title: "Without government, the people are not lost; they are responsible." – Athena (ChatGPT)
text: When someone governs people and makes decisions about them, it takes away not only their freedom and autonomy, but also their (dis)responsibility; on a large scale we can see it in every state, on a small scale in the vast majority of schools. Those who get used to listening will eventually begin to require guidance - they don't feel good without it; the Stockholm syndrome gradually develops (positive emotional and affective bond and dependence of the subjugated on the controlling one), as a result of which the subjects defend their rulers and feel lost without them. A feedback loop is created in which those lower in the hierarchy become (real or perceived) non-self-sufficient without their superiors, who use this as an argument for the necessity of their dominance ("the average person does not take care of himself because he is not used to independent thinking"); it's like "solving" drug addiction by increasing the dosage because the addict can't function without it - yet the same thing with the state makes sense to most people (because they're addicted to it).

section: „Bez vlády nejsou lidé ztracení; jsou odpovědní.“ – Athéna (ChatGPT)
title: "Without government, the people are not lost; they are responsible." – Athena (ChatGPT)
text: Without government, we willy-nilly become free, autonomous, and thus responsible; the less someone decides for us, the more we learn to decide for ourselves. This applies to both children and adults; I can follow that process almost every time when we accept students from classical schools to Ježek without a cage – the freedom they get here is typically paralyzing for them, so they don't know what to do with it for some time. They gradually learn this and often describe the process in retrospect as very unpleasant and exhausting; to me, these adaptations strongly remind me of the above-mentioned getting rid of addiction (because it probably really does happen in some sense). According to my observation, adults also show similar signs when they come to us from a hierarchical environment; however, it seems to me that their weaning process is not as fast as that of children, but it is still going on for them. Although many phenomena only work within small groups, I see no reason why this one cannot be scaled to significantly larger units.

section: „Stát je špatný sluha, ale zlý pán.“ – Urza
title: "The state is a bad servant but a bad master." – Urza
text: The subtitle of the book Anarchocapitalism is a variation of the well-known proverb: Fire is a good servant, but a bad master. This saying emphasizes the contrast between fire's usefulness as a tool to produce heat or light and its destructiveness when it gets out of control. My analogical paraphrase reflects not only the damage and horrors caused by monopolies of violence around the world (past and present), but the first part of it also the belief that the state cannot - despite the efforts of many - be "under control" like fire in a furnace or an internal combustion engine. Even with the best efforts of all involved, rulers cannot make decisions better than decentralized autonomous individuals, because no central planner has access to information scattered throughout society (I discuss this thesis in detail in the book Anarchocapitalism); not to mention that it is impossible to ensure the aforementioned best effort because power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely.

section: „Moc korumpuje a absolutní moc korumpuje absolutně.“ – lord Acton
title: "Power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely." — Lord Acton
text: The most famous statement of John Emerich Edward Dalberg-Acton (known as Lord Acton) comes from a letter addressed to Bishop Mandell Creighton. In their late nineteenth-century correspondence, these scholars engage in a dialogue about assessing the actions of thirteenth- and fourteenth-century popes who advocated the persecution, torture, and brutal killing of many innocents; while the priest was relatively conciliatory towards their actions, the baron vehemently opposed his view. On the one hand, he argued that their actions were no less terrible considering the time in which they lived (I also hold this view, although I am in the minority with him today); above all, however, he refused to view the actions of the powerful (specifically popes and kings) from a more favorable perspective than the actions of ordinary people (with which I understandably also identify).

section: „Moc korumpuje a absolutní moc korumpuje absolutně.“ – lord Acton
title: "Power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely." — Lord Acton
text: Almost one hundred and fifty years have passed since this dialogue, but unfortunately nothing has changed about the corruption of power; politicians face the same seductions and snares to which they are still subject. I believe that the only way to not be crushed by these pressures is to try to respect all people (without exception), not to put yourself down before anyone and not to exalt yourself above anyone; not to forget that we are all equal (not in possibilities and abilities, but in humanity). At the same time, I fear that participation in any (formal) hierarchy creates incentives against such a worldview (in the case of involuntary hierarchies, these incentives are much stronger); of course we can resist them (and some of us can do it more easily than others), but they have some effect on everyone in my opinion. Basically, all my life I have watched people who accept power with good intentions, but end up either giving it up or transforming it.

title: "The strength of the state is the weakness of the people." – Urza
text: What I like about this sentence is that it actually has two meanings: First, it tells us that a strong state weakens "its" citizens (making them dependent on each other); at the same time, it also expresses that the strength of the state often comes precisely from the weakness of the people (when they feel helpless and desperate, they turn to their rulers). Unfortunately, it follows from these theses that the strengthening of the state creates a demand for its further enlargement; combined with universal suffrage, this creates a deadly cycle of democracy leading to socialism and centralization, but other social arrangements are not immune to similar influences. The power components of totalitarian regimes, on the other hand, trample on people so hard that they awaken the worst in them out of fear - obedience, whistleblowing, apathy, mistrust and the like; these characteristics then create the best breeding ground for further concentration of power, its consolidation, surveillance and repression. As hopeless as it sounds, it's never too late to start working towards change; however, you need to focus on yourself, on your own insides, and not try to change others - we can set an example for them and leave it up to them whether they want to join. Cooperation with like-minded people will then enable the creation of islands of freedom (agors) in a sea of unfreedom.

section: „Pánovy nástroje nikdy nerozeberou pánův dům.“ – Audre Lorde
title: "The master's tools will never dismantle the master's house." – Audre Lorde
text: In 1979, Audre Lorde described herself as a black lesbian feminist in a speech to The Second Sex Conference at New York University; she named her speech the Master's tools will never tear down the master's house (the same phrase was also heard in it) and she criticized the patriarchal tendencies within the feminist movement itself. She said of the master's tools that they might temporarily allow us to beat the master at his own game, but we could never achieve real change with them. I agree with her views on this - even if we achieve (often temporary) victory in some games, we actually lose in the long run, as the only clean solution is typically to just not play.

section: „Pánovy nástroje nikdy nerozeberou pánův dům.“ – Audre Lorde
title: "The master's tools will never dismantle the master's house." – Audre Lorde
text: For me personally, this sentence resonates the most with the political path of some anarchists; I believe that if we do not want to be ruled, it makes no sense to approach the game of the rulers and pay attention to them. If I were to apply this aphorism to politics and translate it into the language of Austrian economics, I would say that for similar reasons why we cannot centrally plan even something as simple as the production of toilet paper, we will not be able to shrink the state in a controlled manner and organize the transition to freedom from above - simply because it is too complex and complicated a problem into which a number of factors enter into which we cannot predict, since we do not have access to decentralized information scattered throughout society. I consider trying to declare and declare anarchy to be as foolish as trying to preach to virginity.

title: "The end (does) not justify the means." – folk saying
text: This popular statement (without the parentheses added by me) is often attributed to Niccolò Machiavelli; although this is not a literal quote from the surviving texts, it is, in my opinion, a concise summary of his thoughts - especially those from Vladař. This title fascinates me in a way: On the one hand, it can be seen as the absolute antithesis of anarchist ideas; if we label the book you are reading now as a "handbook" for achieving freedom (in the sense of giving up one's power over others and not submitting to the rule of others), then we can safely consider The Ruler a guide to accumulating and maintaining power over people at any cost. On the other hand, both publications describe politics in a very similar way – as a game with the ultimate goal of gaining and consolidating dominance; although Machiavelli advises how to play it best, while my starting point is not to enter it at all, we agree to a great extent on its rules and meaning.

title: "The end (does) not justify the means." – folk saying
text: I believe that the end does not justify the means; and this, among other things, because the master's tools will never dismantle the master's house. If we want to achieve virtuous goals, by using malicious means we corrupt not only those goals, but above all ourselves. Many people call this attitude idealistic, which I wholeheartedly agree with (and see nothing wrong with it); at the same time, however, I also consider it to be strictly pragmatic - because I value myself and desire to live a life that will be worth it not only today, but also tomorrow and at the end of it. I realize that everything has a price, for every decision I bear the consequences, not only in the outside world, but also in myself; every action I take leaves an imprint on my conscious and subconscious mind. I am my own instrument to achieve my goals; and I will carry all the used means with me forever. If I start with compromises, I slide more easily into others - and it doesn't even feel weird anymore; therefore, I would rather give up the realization of some (perhaps virtuous) intentions than pay for them with my soul.

section: „Agora. Anarchie. Akce!“ – SEK3 / „Svoboda; sebeřízení; seberozvoj; sdílení.“ – Urza
title: "Agora. Anarchy. Action!" – SEK3 / "Freedom; self-management; self-development; sharing." – Urza
text: Samuel Edward Konkin III used the exclamation "Agora. Anarchy. Action!" in his New Libertarian Manifesto; I personally consider it a condensed message of his work. In it he uses the word agora to refer to individual anarchist cells (as I do in this book); at the same time, it (in the singular) also describes the target state of all humanity (as the opposite of the state-controlled population) - it talks about the path from statism to the agora. The term anarchy characterizes the (stateless) state of society; calls on all those who want to bind someone to first prove that the person has committed aggression, because otherwise they are not authorized to do so. The third point of his summons represents action; thus he describes the strategy for liberation - economic resistance on the gray and black market, building parallel structures, i.e. institutions gradually replacing the state until its final failure.

section: „Agora. Anarchie. Akce!“ – SEK3 / „Svoboda; sebeřízení; seberozvoj; sdílení.“ – Urza
title: "Agora. Anarchy. Action!" – SEK3 / "Freedom; self-management; self-development; sharing." – Urza
text: My four words unfortunately do not have such an elegant translation into foreign languages; however, they express my perception of anarchoagorism. Freedom is a state (that of the inner soul and mind, while of the outer world), the ideal, the end, and the means; it requires care, understanding, attention and love to flourish, and we can see anarchoagorism as a practical path to it. Self-governance embodies the natural expression of a free individual; in particular, I am referring to self-directed education, which we deny especially to children, which, in my opinion, represents the biggest obstacle to achieving a free society. Self-development gives us the tools to be ourselves and live our lives our own way – that is, to disobey; I consider this to be a necessary individual prerequisite for active participation in the agora. By sharing (tangible and intangible goods, including information) I of course mean practical participation in parallel structures, but also any free market; it is cooperation - the strength of the human species, the means to (not only material) well-being and to freedom.

section: „Svoboda se nedává, svoboda se bere.“ – neznámý autor
title: "Freedom is not given, freedom is taken." - unknown author
text: Many people understand this sentence as a harbinger of unfreedom in the sense that someone will limit us; however, this aphorism has always spoken to me in a slightly different way - it tells me that I cannot get freedom from anyone, so if I want it, I have to take it myself. It is, of course, conceivable to convince someone to stop infringing on my autonomy; but he still wouldn't "give" her to me because she never belonged to him. In the case of inner freedom, it is obviously only my personal work with my own fear; and no one else can do it for me. Freedom comes from within ourselves; I consider it absolutely essential to realize that if we don't pay attention to it and take care of it continuously (both in ourselves and around us), we will probably lose it sooner or later, which can happen gradually, so we don't even have to notice it. For example, a lot of people have reacted (at least verbally) to the spike in state repression during covid; but most of them remained insensitive to all other oppression simply because they gradually got used to it.

section: „Svoboda jednoho končí tam, kde začíná jeho strach.“ – neznámý autor z okolí Svobodného přístavu
title: "One's freedom ends where one's fear begins." – an unknown author from the vicinity of the Free Port
text: John Stuart Mill once wrote, "The liberty of one ends where the liberty of another begins." I'm not too fond of this quote; it does apply literally at any time, but it tells us nothing useful about where any boundary lies—even the freedom of the brutally oppressed ends where the freedom of their oppressors begins. It is not surprising that this slogan is often invoked by the opposite poles of a number of controversies – supporters and opponents of freedom of speech, the war on drugs, gun regulation, anti-pandemic measures and the like; you can defend any position with that sentence. Some time ago, the above variation appeared in one of the Freeport discussion channels (unfortunately, I don't remember the author, but maybe he will recognize it when reading these lines); it probably refers to my concept of inner freedom as the absence or control of fear.

section: „Svoboda jednoho končí tam, kde začíná jeho strach.“ – neznámý autor z okolí Svobodného přístavu
title: "One's freedom ends where one's fear begins." – an unknown author from the vicinity of the Free Port
text: What I like most about this paraphrase is the focus on finding and solving problems within yourself; if we want to get rid of the shackles, we need to start with the ones we put ourselves into. Although it is only others who deprive us of external freedom, which at first sight is not related to our fear, the answer to external oppression often consists in working with internal freedom; at least, in my opinion, this is a necessary first step. The more afraid we are, the more likely our eventual struggle for external freedom will end in failure (if it begins at all) - recall the chapter on Revolution where I describe the various traps that lie in wait for all fugitive freedom fighters. With these words, I am certainly not calling for passivity - on the contrary - I am only warning against overly militant solutions in the outside world resulting from unprocessed fears. Processing them typically opens up more peaceful paths for us; these often consist of daily ant work rather than great deeds, so they may appear unattractive and slow, but they really work.

section: „Děkovat někomu za vlastní svobodu je spolehlivá cesta k její ztrátě.“ – Urza
title: "Thanking someone for your freedom is a sure way to lose it." – Urza
text: This message, in my opinion, is closely related to the previous one; warns against a too passive or resigned approach to (potential) authorities. I am often accused, as an anarchist, of not being grateful enough for the measure of freedom in which I live thanks to democracy; I think I should thank the current regime for the fact that I am allowed to publicly proclaim anarchist ideas without risk of persecution (which is not completely true, but compared to most of the world today or the Czech Republic just half a century ago, I can express myself almost without restrictions). In fact, I feel a lot of gratitude - there are many people thanks to whom I have the opportunity to do what I do - starting with the authors who inspired me, through all the creators, manufacturers, suppliers and operators of technologies related to, for example, the Internet or book printing, to you, dear readers and listeners; however, I refuse to thank democratic politicians for graciously not curtailing my freedom.

section: „Děkovat někomu za vlastní svobodu je spolehlivá cesta k její ztrátě.“ – Urza
title: "Thanking someone for your freedom is a sure way to lose it." – Urza
text: I am grateful to everyone who helps me (for free or for a fee) or receives something from them (perhaps even attention); however, I am not going to reward anyone for not oppressing me. Why? Because if I did, I'd start putting myself in a subordinate position to him. Many people approach the state in this way throughout their life, so it seems normal to them. If you belong to them, try to imagine an analogous situation where someone advises a victim of domestic violence to be grateful to the bully that he doesn't beat her (much) (and maybe even compares it to the fact that all previous partners beat her more). What will it lead to? Of course to deepen the oppression; if anyone (even if only in spirit) thanks someone for not harming him, he acknowledges oppression as the norm. People who accept it and become accustomed to their own subjugation gradually become blind to it; therefore, it does not seem strange to the supporters of democracy to express gratitude to the state for non-aggression - just as many tormented do not dwell on this in relation to their tormentors.

section: „Buď sám tou změnou, kterou chceš vidět ve světě.“ – Mahátma Gándhí / „Svobodu nelze prosadit; svobodu je třeba žít.“ – Urza / „Společnost měníme sdílením, ne vedením.“ – Athéna (ChatGPT)
title: "Be the change you want to see in the world." – Mahatma Gandhi / "Freedom cannot be enforced; freedom must be lived." – Urza / "We change society by sharing, not leading." – Athena (ChatGPT)
text: All these aphorisms show the senselessness of someone (for example, a politician, but also anyone else) planning or organizing freedom for anyone other than himself; if we want a freer world, let's live a freer life. If it's worth it, others will love to be inspired by us when they see the results; the more of ourselves we share with others, the better we give them a chance to catch on and follow us (if they want to). However, I consider it absolutely essential to leave the decision up to everyone and not to force anyone to do anything; after all, something like that wouldn't work anyway - we need to grow up (within ourselves) to be free. However, it is not just political or other coercion by force; even another (non-violent) type of coercion will cause rather the opposite in the long run - attempts to convince someone of something often cause resistance. Seeing the solution to one's lack of freedom (or other problems) in what others should or should not do corresponds to the position of the victim; the creator, on the other hand, understands that he holds his life in his own hands (which is also an attitude that tends to inspire others).

section: „Duch hry stojí nad literou pravidel.“ – Gary Gygax
title: "The spirit of the game is above the letter of the rules." – Gary Gygax
text: Gary Gygax was one of the two creators of the original 1974 version of the legendary game Dungeons & Dragons; it stood at the beginning of the rise of the entire genre of tabletop RPGs and formed the template for a lot of game titles, including the Czech tabletop RPG Dračí doupě (Dragon's Lair), which I spent a good part of my adolescence playing, which shaped me to a large extent. Perhaps every player of this or any similar role-playing game understands what Gary Gygax meant by his statement - the rules are one means of our entertainment, but we should not become slaves to following them literally in every situation; at any time we can agree not to follow the rules if we find it appropriate for our overall experience. However, I believe that the above quote can also be seen as a metaphor; and in my opinion, it goes far beyond the game world of dragons and magic.

section: „Duch hry stojí nad literou pravidel.“ – Gary Gygax
title: "The spirit of the game is above the letter of the rules." – Gary Gygax
text: In addition to Ježek bez klece, where I have been working as a volunteer for years, my desire for knowledge led me to dozens of self-directed schools and similar collectives, where I studied different ways of making decisions and creating standards. Despite the expectation that the form of the approval process will be the most important factor (seeking consensus, overriding the minority with a majority, etc.), repeated observations led me to the key role of the method of codification of rules and the procedures leading to their creation. The more precisely everything is defined (and recorded), the more often the attention of all involved shifts to the letter of the various provisions (including finding loopholes and opportunities for abuse) from their meaning and spirit; on the contrary, collectives with very vague (often only verbally) described conventions are most concerned with this. I'm not saying that writing down rules can never help; I'm just pointing out that most people don't realize how much such codification diverts attention from human needs to itself.

title: "Love your enemies." – Jesus (Matthew 5:44)
text: Quotations from Jesus are not usually received gratefully in the atheistic Czech Republic; in anarchist circles, this is doubly true, as his teachings have been abused by various authoritarians for the last almost two thousand years to gain, maintain and enforce power over their fellow man. For me, however, Jesus represents (among other things) a functional archetype of the loving and compassionate person I myself aspire to be; even if I ever found out with absolute certainty that he never existed, it would not change anything in my efforts to approach him (as an ideal). I like to read in the Bible; the older I get, the more passages speak to me—they resonate with increasing experience. I have no illusions that I will ever be able to fully understand her; nevertheless, it still enriches me, and in addition, in my perception it complements the Buddhist teachings, which I also devote myself to. This approach often provokes resentment among Christians, condescension among Buddhists, while atheists tap their foreheads; however, this path makes sense to me.

title: "Love your enemies." – Jesus (Matthew 5:44)
text: I don't know anyone who is capable of constant unconditional love for all people (including those "enemies"); however, I consider it one of my ideals in life. Why do I want to love every person regardless of what they do and what they are like? Primarily not for the sake of others, but primarily for the sake of myself; the outer world can be ennobled by love, while the inner can be completely transformed. Of course, loving everyone does not mean agreeing with everyone, or even supporting their actions; nor does it imply that we cannot define or defend ourselves against them. However, love protects us from going astray in the face of challenging trials and exchanging the original (perhaps noble) direction for revenge or joy from someone else's suffering; however, many people do not even notice such changes, as they are too busy fighting and blinded by "righteous anger". Intellect will not help us much against these snares, because the sharper the mind we possess, the more cleverly it can deceive us; there is great strength in humility, compassion and respect for each person.

section: „Nemůžeme-li lidem ponechat svobodu, jak bychom jim mohli svěřit moc?“ – neznámý autor
title: "If we cannot leave people free, how can we entrust them with power?" - unknown author
text: I often come across the claim that humanity is not (yet) ready for anarchy; they say that when we become more responsible and less indifferent, we can perhaps govern ourselves, but not until then. Personally, I perceive it to be exactly the opposite - the more "corrupted" the population, the greater the problem with the concentration of power. The critics of anarchism, who often look for the illusion of security in statism, unfortunately forget that the government is usually recruited from the very society it is supposed to govern, so that it is burdened with the same vices; in addition, typically strengthened, because the opportunity to control the state apparatus attracts rather domineering and omnipotent individuals. Freedom can be understood as man's power over himself; if we start from the assumption that people are not (yet) able to bear it, it makes no sense to entrust them with power not only over their lives, but also over the lives of others (and not even metaphorically in the form of the possibility of electing their representatives for such a thing - someone who is not capable of dealing with his own freedom can hardly competently decide on a good leader for himself and others).

title: "Pain is inevitable, suffering is optional." – Buddha
text: For many years I understood this part of the Buddha's teaching only theoretically; I owe her practical knowledge (I really feel the gratitude) to a paragliding accident that I survived with twenty-five broken bones and other internal injuries. After a few days in bed I thought to investigate this wisdom; the hospital staff complied with my request to stop the morphine so that I would have a chance to better understand what the Buddha meant. I understood that we have the possibility to perceive pain as a mere signal of the body; how we deal with this signal depends only on us - we can suffer, but we don't have to - it's a choice (albeit not always a conscious one). I'm not talking about "overcoming" the pain with willpower (which I find counterproductive in this context), but simply accepting it; not everyone is always able to do this (not even I can do it at any time and with any pain), but it can be trained. How does this knowledge relate to anarchism? I find them important for working with inner freedom and fear; if we learn to accept pain, our tendency to fall into fear (and thus into the position of a victim) is greatly reduced.

section: „Psychickou bolest si působíme sami.“ – Marshall Rosenberg / „Bolest si působíme sami.“ – Gabriela Ježková
title: "Mental pain is self-inflicted." – Marshall Rosenberg / "We inflict pain on ourselves." – Gabriela Ježková
text: Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication has changed my life (although I can't say I've achieved any major proficiency in it - I'm still learning); with its help, this peacemaker was able to reconcile not only feuding families or work groups, but also criminals and their victims, and even hostile tribes that had been murdering each other for generations. He built his skills on the knowledge of the basic principles of the human psyche; among other things, on the fact that we inflict psychological pain on ourselves. It is a reaction to the external world - we are not hurt by its state as such (it is not objectively good or bad, it just is), but our interpretation; different people evaluate the same situation differently - some hurt, others don't (according to the setting of the inner world). There is nothing that psychologically injures everyone; precisely because what injures us (as opposed to physical damage) is our own reaction to a stimulus, not the stimulus itself.

section: „Psychickou bolest si působíme sami.“ – Marshall Rosenberg / „Bolest si působíme sami.“ – Gabriela Ježková
title: "Mental pain is self-inflicted." – Marshall Rosenberg / "We inflict pain on ourselves." – Gabriela Ježková
text: The vast majority of people tend to contradict this thesis, so I've spent at least a good dozen hours defending it; I was even more surprised by Gabriela's reaction, which not only did not contradict her, but the opposite: "And why only psychological? I would say that we cause all the pain to ourselves." In other words, she was probably alluding to the same thing as the Buddha with suffering. Psychic injuries arise as our reactions to the outside world; the physical ones do occur directly, but we can work with the pain associated with them at will if we learn to do so (their other consequences, of course, can be serious or even fatal). I consider working with pain to be an important (and most likely necessary) step in processing the fear of it (as well as disobedience); accepting responsibility for one's own suffering is the most reliable way not only to minimize it, but mainly to freedom.

section: „Vše, co ztratíš díky vlastní autenticitě, je beztak klam.“ – neznámý autor
title: "Anything you lose through your own authenticity is a delusion anyway." - unknown author
text: This is my translation of the English sentence: "Anything you lose by being real is fake." This aphorism, in my opinion, hides a deep truth about authenticity. The more clearly we say #no_disobedience and live our lives in our own way (and not according to the ideas of others), the more we risk rejection, social condemnation, loss of reputation and rejection by people around us. However difficult it may be to deal with these consequences, we have not lost anything completely true - for by showing the truth we will not lose anything that was not at least partly based on some illusion; for example, if someone turns away from us when they find out who we really are, they never really wanted to be with us. If we accept the pain of such losses and do not resist them, the environment around us begins to reflect our authenticity; and this will manifest itself in relationships, projects, work, hobbies - we can liberate ourselves on all fronts.

section: „Kritériem pravdy je, že funguje, i když ji nikdo není ochoten uznat.“ – Ludwig von Mises / „Pravda vítězí.“ – Jan Hus
title: "The criterion of truth is that it works, even if no one is willing to admit it." – Ludwig von Mises / "Truth prevails." – Jan Hus
text: The Austrian economist Ludwig Heinrich Edler von Mises perceived (not only) the truth very pragmatically; he believed that it would prevail in the end simply because it had better results than falsehood—regardless of whether society or individuals accepted or rejected it. In the context of his work, he spoke primarily of economic laws; however, the validity of the given statement is far from being limited to them, of which he was of course aware. The more accurate (and therefore truer) model of reality we use to describe the world around us, the better we can achieve our goals; that is, true propositions have a principled "evolutionary" advantage over false ones. It follows that the sharing of information leads more often to the promotion of truth than falsehood; and if freedom is really good for people (which I firmly believe), then to achieve it (which is really slow to happen in the long run).

section: „Kritériem pravdy je, že funguje, i když ji nikdo není ochoten uznat.“ – Ludwig von Mises / „Pravda vítězí.“ – Jan Hus
title: "The criterion of truth is that it works, even if no one is willing to admit it." – Ludwig von Mises / "Truth prevails." – Jan Hus
text: The Czech presidential standard contains the motto "TRUTH WINS" originally attributed to Jan Hus, popularized by Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk and extended by Václav Havel to the sentence: "Truth and love must win over lies and hatred." Considering the fact that I consider this motto to be deeply true, I find its use by Czech presidents and its depiction on the state symbol to be laughably paradoxical; I believe that the victory of truth (and love) will inevitably bring with it the end of state oppression. The power of the state stems from a deep-seated statism; thus the vast majority of us are indoctrinated by the current educational system based on manipulation (typically through punishments and rewards), which is in direct contradiction to any truth.

title: "ACAB" - (not only) an anarchist saying
text: ACAB is an acronym for "All Cops Are Bastards"; in Czech it means that all cops are bastards. Of course, I don't think that every member of the police force is necessarily a characterless moron; undoubtedly, among them we also find individuals who do not want to harm anyone in a targeted way (just for example, they did not find a better application on the labor market), or they even really consider their work a way to help the weak and protect the defenseless. However, it is important (despite their possible human qualities) not to forget that they are still agents of the largest legalized mafia. I'm certainly not encouraging hatred of individual police officers (they're human too); however, I point out the danger of interacting with them - sometimes they are polite and nice, but at the same time they are still official persons, which means that everything we tell them, they can (and often by law directly have to) use it against us or our relatives and friends (which they can lie about, of course; and they usually do). I discuss what exactly to watch out for in the lecture "Anarcho-capitalism: How (not) to talk (not only) to the cops?"; its recording is freely available on the Internet at the Free Port Channel.

section: „Život má větší představivost, než si nosíme ve svých snech.“ – Kryštof Kolumbus
title: "Life has more imagination than we carry in our dreams." – Christopher Columbus
text: One of my favorite quotes is commonly attributed to the skilled navigator and ruthless colonizer Christopher Columbus. As much as I don't agree with a lot of his actions or his overall approach to people, I actually experience this statement all the time; it has resonated with me since I first encountered it, which is nearly thirty years. It occurred to me recently that using the words "free market" instead of "life" would give us a libertarian aphorism illustrating how the wonderful results of human action cannot be achieved by human design (as Friedrich August von Hayek said: "the result of human action, but not of human design"). Above all, however, this quote speaks to me to remain open to everything, not to resort to dogmatism and humbly accept all the wonderful beauties of the world; I have no idea what will happen tomorrow, but today what was just an unattainable fantasy yesterday is real for me.
